r209.a: React is a JavaScript library for building user interfaces out of reusable components. You describe what the UI should look like for a given state, and React updates the DOM efficiently when that state changes.

JSX syntax for describing markup in JavaScript
Efficient updates via the virtual DOM and reconciliation
One-way data flow; runs on web (ReactDOM), native (React Native) and the server

r210.a: JSX is a syntax extension that lets you write HTML-like markup inside JavaScript. It isn't valid JavaScript on its own: a compiler such as Babel, SWC or TypeScript turns each tag into a function call (`jsx()` or `React.createElement()`) that returns a plain object describing the element.
p: Compiles to `React.createElement(type, props, ...children)` or the new `jsx()` runtime
Curly braces `{}` embed any JavaScript expression
Escapes values by default, which helps prevent XSS
Must return a single root (or a Fragment)

r219.a: `&&` returns the left operand when it's falsy, and React renders the number `0` as text (it only skips `false`, `null`, `undefined` and `true`). So when `count` is 0, `count && <Badge />` evaluates to `0` and a stray "0" appears on screen.

Same trap with `NaN` and empty strings in some cases
r219.f: Which values does React skip rendering entirely?

r257.a: `<StrictMode>` is a development-only wrapper that turns on extra checks. It double-invokes component bodies, initializers and effects (mount, unmount, mount) to expose impure rendering and missing cleanup, and it warns about deprecated APIs. It has no effect in production builds.
p: Double-renders to surface side effects during render
Runs effects twice to catch missing cleanup
Warns about legacy APIs like string refs and findDOMNode
Can wrap the whole app or just part of it

r29.a: Parent to child: pass props. Child to parent: pass a callback prop the child calls. Between siblings: lift the shared state up to their closest common parent. For data many distant components need, use Context or a state library (Redux, Zustand), and for server data, a cache like React Query.

r364.a: React was created at Facebook by Jordan Walke (inspired by XHP) and first used in the News Feed in 2011 and Instagram in 2012, then open-sourced in 2013. Major milestones were React Native (2015), the Fiber rewrite in React 16 (2017), Hooks in 16.8 (2019), concurrent rendering in React 18 (2022) and Actions, the `use` hook and stable Server Components in React 19 (2024).

React 19: Actions, use(), Server Components, React Compiler work
r364.f: What problem did the Fiber rewrite solve?

r365.a: React's main features are JSX, a component model, a virtual DOM with efficient reconciliation, one-way data flow and hooks for state and side effects. It also supports server rendering, concurrent rendering and a large ecosystem.
p: Virtual DOM diffing for efficient updates
r365.f: How does one-way data flow make an app easier to debug?

r366.a: An element is a plain, immutable object describing what to render (type, props, children), created by JSX or `createElement`. A component is a function (or class) that takes props and returns elements. Components are the blueprint; elements are what they return for a given render.
p: Element = description object, cheap to create
Elements are immutable; new ones are made each render
`<Button />` creates an element whose type is the Button component
React calls components; you don't call them directly
r366.f: Why shouldn't you call a component as a plain function, like Button()?
r366.c:
const element = <Button label="Save" />; // { type: Button, props: { label: 'Save' } }
function Button({ label }) { return <button>{label}</button>; } // component

r367.a: Today you create components as functions that take props and return JSX; class components extending `React.Component` with a `render()` method still work but are legacy. Name them with a capital letter so JSX treats them as components.
p: Use hooks for state and effects
Class components: extend React.Component and implement render()
r367.f: What are the remaining cases where you still need a class component?

r371.a: Inline conditional expressions are ways to choose what to render inside JSX: the ternary `cond ? <A/> : <B/>`, the logical `cond && <A/>`, and sometimes `??` for fallbacks. For anything more complex, compute the value in a variable or early return before the JSX.
p: Move complex logic into variables or helper functions

r380.a: Inside JSX, comments go in curly braces as JavaScript block comments: `{/* comment */}`. Outside JSX, use normal `//` or `/* */` comments.
p: Inside a tag's attribute list you can use `/* */` between props
HTML `<!-- -->` comments don't work in JSX
r380.f: Why doesn't the HTML comment syntax work in JSX?

r387.a: ReactDOMServer (`react-dom/server`) renders components to HTML on the server. Its APIs include `renderToString`, `renderToPipeableStream` (Node streaming with Suspense support) and `renderToReadableStream` (web streams); the browser then hydrates that HTML with `hydrateRoot`.
p: Used for server-side rendering and static generation
Output is hydrated on the client with `hydrateRoot`
Frameworks like Next.js use it under the hood
r387.f: Why is streaming SSR better than renderToString for slow data?

r388.a: Use the `dangerouslySetInnerHTML` prop with an object `{ __html: string }`. The awkward name is deliberate: inserting raw HTML can cause XSS, so only use it with trusted or sanitized content (for example via DOMPurify).
p: The element can't also have children
Prefer rendering data as JSX when you can
r388.f: How would you safely render user-written Markdown?

r39.a: Conditional rendering means showing different UI depending on state or props, using normal JavaScript: `if` statements with early returns, ternaries, `&&`, or picking a component from a map. React just renders whatever the expression evaluates to, and `null` renders nothing.
p: Return null to hide a component
r39.f: Does hiding a component with null keep its state?

r396.a: Build with `NODE_ENV=production`, which bundlers (Vite, webpack, Next.js) set automatically for production builds (`vite build`, `npm run build`). That loads React's minified production build, strips development warnings and checks, and is much faster.
p: Use the production build command of your tool
Development build is slower due to extra checks
React DevTools icon shows whether a site uses the production build
r396.f: What extra work does React do in development mode?

r400.a: JSX uses capitalization to decide what a tag means: lowercase tags like `<div>` become strings (built-in DOM elements), while capitalized tags like `<Button>` refer to a variable in scope (your component). A lowercase component name would be treated as an unknown HTML element.
p: Lowercase → string type, a DOM element
Assign to a capitalized variable for dynamic components
Applies to JSX, not plain createElement calls
r400.f: How do you render a component chosen at runtime?

r402.a: JSX can't contain `for` statements, so you map an array to elements with `array.map()` and give each item a stable `key`. You can also build an array in a loop before the `return` and render it.
p: Each item needs a unique, stable `key`
Build arrays outside JSX for complex loops
Don't use the index as key if the list can change order
r402.f: Why does React need keys on list items?

r404.a: `PropTypes.arrayOf(PropTypes.shape({...}))` validates that a prop is an array of objects with a given structure. PropTypes run only in development and were removed from React 19's built-in checks, so TypeScript is the modern alternative.
p: `shape` for object structure (`exact` disallows extra keys)
TypeScript interfaces replace this in modern code
r404.f: What does TypeScript give you that PropTypes doesn't?

r405.a: Build the `className` string with a template literal or ternary, or use a helper like `clsx`/`classnames` that takes an object of class-to-boolean pairs. Avoid string concatenation that can leave stray spaces or "undefined".
p: `className` is a plain string in the DOM
r405.f: How would you implement a tiny classnames helper yourself?

r406.a: React was split into `react` (components, hooks, elements) and `react-dom` (rendering to the browser DOM) because the core is platform-agnostic. The same `react` package is used with other renderers: React Native, react-three-fiber, Ink for terminals, and server renderers.
p: Enables React Native and custom renderers
r406.f: What is a custom renderer and when would you write one?

r407.a: Use the standard `<label>` element but write `htmlFor` instead of `for`, matching the input's `id`, or wrap the input inside the label. `useId()` generates unique ids so components can be reused on the same page.
p: Or nest the input inside the label
`useId()` for unique ids in reusable components
Labels improve accessibility and click target size
r407.f: Why shouldn't you generate ids with Math.random() in components?

const id = useId();
return <><label htmlFor={id}>Email</label><input id={id} type="email" /></>;

r409.a: Use `JSON.stringify(data, null, 2)` to indent the JSON and render it inside a `<pre>` element so whitespace and line breaks are preserved.

r409.f: What happens if the object has circular references?

r412.a: Read `React.version` (for example `import { version } from 'react'`) in code, or check the React DevTools extension, which shows the version of the page's React.

Check package.json/lockfile for the installed version

r415.a: Use ES modules: `export default` for a file's main component and named exports for others, then import them with `import Button from './Button'` or `import { Card } from './Card'`.

Named exports are easier to refactor and tree-shake
Re-export from an index file for cleaner imports
r415.f: When would you prefer named exports over default exports?

r416.a: Components must start with a capital letter, with one exception: member expressions. `<forms.input>` or `<ui.button>` work even if the property is lowercase, because JSX treats a dotted name as a reference rather than a DOM tag. For a dynamic component, assign it to a capitalized variable first.
p: Capitalized names are required for plain identifiers
Assign to a capitalized variable for dynamic tags
Hyphenated lowercase tags are treated as custom elements
r416.f: How does React treat a tag like <my-widget>?

r417.a: Not directly in the component body: a component must return JSX synchronously, and an effect callback can't be async. You can define and call an async function inside `useEffect`, use event handlers that are async, or in React 19 pass a promise to `use()` inside a Suspense boundary (and async Server Components can await directly).
p: Component functions must be synchronous (client side)
Call an inner async function in useEffect
Async Server Components can use await
r417.f: Why can't the effect callback itself be async?

r418.a: Two common approaches: grouping by type (components/, hooks/, utils/, pages/) for small apps, and grouping by feature or route (features/cart/, features/auth/ each with its components, hooks and tests) for larger ones. React has no required structure; consistency matters most.
p: By type: simple, fine for small projects
By feature: scales better, keeps related code together
Co-locate tests, styles and stories with components
Shared UI in a separate folder
Frameworks like Next.js impose routing folders

r421.a: ESLint is the standard, with `eslint-plugin-react-hooks` (enforces the rules of hooks and effect dependencies), `eslint-plugin-react` (JSX and component rules) and `eslint-plugin-jsx-a11y` (accessibility). Many teams add the React Compiler lint rules and Prettier for formatting.

r421.f: Why shouldn't you disable the exhaustive-deps rule casually?

r466.a: React Developer Tools is a browser extension (and standalone app) that adds Components and Profiler tabs. You can inspect the component tree, view and edit props, state, hooks and context, find which component rendered an element, and profile render timings.
p: Components tab: tree, props, state, hooks
Edit values live to test behaviour
Profiler: record renders, flame graph, why it rendered
Works for React Native through the standalone app

Better: run a local server (Vite, http-server)
Also check you're on a development build

r468.a: Polymer elements are web components, so you can import the element definition and use its custom tag in JSX like any other element. Pass simple values as attributes, and set complex properties or listen for custom events through a ref (React 19 has better built-in support for custom element properties and events).

Complex data via properties set on a ref
Custom events via addEventListener on the ref
React 19 maps props to properties for custom elements

r469.a: React's main advantages over Vue are its larger ecosystem and job market, the flexibility of "just JavaScript" with JSX, React Native for mobile, and strong backing from Meta and frameworks like Next.js. Vue offers a gentler learning curve, built-in reactivity and official router and state libraries, so the "better" choice depends on the team.

Vue: templates, built-in reactivity, official tooling
Choice depends on team skills and project needs

One-way data flow vs two-way binding options
Angular uses TypeScript and DI by default
React re-renders and diffs; Angular uses change detection (now signals)

Enable file URL access for local files
Check the right frame is selected

r480.a: Render hijacking is when a higher-order component controls what the wrapped component renders: it can render it conditionally, wrap its output, change its props or replace it entirely (for example rendering a spinner while loading). It was a common HOC pattern before hooks.

Can wrap, modify or skip the wrapped output
Used for loading states, permissions, logging
Hooks and composition are preferred today

Can serve stale content until all tabs close

Fragments group without wrapper or keys
Portals and Suspense can also be returned

Function names usually make it unnecessary
Works on function and class components

`key` is the only prop Fragment accepts

r50.a: `React.Fragment` (or `<>...</>`) groups several elements without adding an extra DOM node. It keeps markup valid (for example inside tables or lists) and avoids wrapper divs that break flexbox or grid layouts.
p: Return multiple elements from a component
Keeps CSS layouts and HTML semantics intact
r50.f: When must you use the long form <Fragment>?

r500.a: React supports all standard HTML attributes, using camelCase names for most (`tabIndex`, `onClick`) and `className`/`htmlFor` for reserved words. Custom `data-*` and `aria-*` attributes pass through as-is, and since React 16 unknown attributes are forwarded to the DOM.

r500.f: Why does style take an object instead of a string?

r506.a: Elements are immutable, so you don't change them; you update state (or props), and React re-renders the component, compares the new elements with the old ones and applies only the DOM changes needed.
p: Call a state setter to trigger a re-render
React diffs and patches the DOM
Never mutate the DOM React manages directly

r513.a: Yes. Custom elements can be rendered like normal tags, and React 19 fully supports them, setting properties instead of attributes when they exist and supporting custom events with `on` props. In older versions, complex props and events needed refs.

React 19: properties and custom events supported
Older versions: attributes only, use refs
Mind `class` vs `className` (both work on custom elements)
Web components can also host React apps

Splits bundles to load code on demand

In an interview, explain why each choice fits the project.

Testing at unit and end-to-end levels

r53.a: JSX is an HTML-like syntax in JavaScript. A compiler (Babel, SWC, esbuild, TypeScript) transforms each element into a function call: with the classic runtime `React.createElement(type, props, children)`, with the automatic runtime `jsx(type, props)` imported from `react/jsx-runtime`, so you no longer need to import React in every file.

r53.f: What does the resulting element object contain?

Wrap in a React component to hide imperative details

p: Function that takes props and returns JSX
r54.f: What does it mean for a component to be pure?

r542.f: Can you use React without any build step?

r546.a: Yes, the basics. React code relies heavily on modern JavaScript: arrow functions, destructuring, spread, modules, classes, template literals, array methods like map/filter, and promises/async-await. Knowing them makes React much easier to learn.
r546.f: Which ES6 feature do you use most in React code and why?

r550.a: Imperative code describes how to change the UI step by step (find this node, add a class, append a child). Declarative code describes what the UI should look like for the current state, and React figures out the DOM changes. React is declarative, which makes UI easier to predict and reason about.
p: Refs are an escape hatch for imperative needs
r550.f: When do you still need imperative code in React?

r559.a: In development, Strict Mode intentionally calls component functions, state initializers and reducers twice (and mounts, unmounts and remounts effects) to reveal impure render logic and missing effect cleanup. Production renders once.
p: Checks that effects clean up properly
Console logs from the second render are dimmed
Not a reason to remove Strict Mode
r559.f: How should you write an effect so double-running it causes no problems?

r560.a: JSX must return a single root element (use a Fragment), every tag must be closed (including ``), attributes are camelCase (`className`, `onClick`), and JavaScript goes inside curly braces. Comments use `{/* */}`.
p: Close all tags, self-close empty ones
r560.f: Why can't you use an if statement inside JSX?

r561.a: A JSX expression compiles to a single function call that returns one object, and a function can't return two values at once. So sibling tags must be wrapped in a parent element or a Fragment, which is effectively an array of children.
p: Each JSX expression = one createElement call
r561.f: What's the downside of always wrapping in a div?

r564.a: When state changes, React re-renders the affected components (the render phase), compares the new element tree with the previous one (reconciliation), then applies the minimal DOM changes in the commit phase and runs effects. Updates are batched and, in React 18+, can be interrupted and prioritized.
p: Trigger: setState, props or context change
Render: call components to get new elements
Reconcile: diff old and new trees
Commit: update the DOM, run layout effects, then effects
r564.f: What's the difference between the render phase and the commit phase?

r572.a: Defining a component inside another creates a brand-new component type on every render of the parent, so React unmounts and remounts it each time: its state is lost, its DOM is recreated and inputs lose focus. Define components at the top level and pass data via props.
p: New function identity each render = new type
Move it outside or render a helper function instead
r572.f: How is calling a helper function that returns JSX different from rendering it as a component?

r58.a: Fragments let a component return several elements without adding a wrapper DOM node. Write them as `<>...</>` or `<React.Fragment>`; the long form accepts a `key` for lists.
p: Avoids wrapper divs that break layouts
r58.f: Why would an extra div break a CSS grid layout?

r59.a: `react` contains the core: components, elements, hooks and context. `react-dom` connects React to the browser DOM (createRoot, hydrateRoot, portals, flushSync) and has a server package for SSR. Splitting them lets the same core power other renderers like React Native.
p: Same core used by React Native
r59.f: Where does createPortal come from and why?

r84.a: Function components and class components. Function components are plain functions that use hooks for state and lifecycle; class components extend `React.Component` and use `this.state` and lifecycle methods. Function components are the modern default.
p: Old terms: stateful vs stateless components
r84.f: What's the one thing you still need a class component for?

r86.a: Write a function with a capitalized name that takes a props object and returns JSX. Add hooks inside for state or effects.
p: Hooks at the top level only
r86.f: How do you give a prop a default value in a function component?

r89.a: JSX looks like HTML but is JavaScript underneath. Differences: `className` and `htmlFor` instead of `class`/`for`, camelCase attributes and events, `style` as an object, all tags must close, expressions in `{}`, and a single root per expression. Values are escaped automatically.
r89.f: How does JSX help prevent XSS?

r94.a: Use plain JavaScript: early returns, the ternary operator, `&&` for optional content, or a variable set by `if`/`switch` before the return. Return `null` to render nothing.
r94.f: Does conditionally rendering a component reset its state?

r95.a: `cond && <Element />` renders the element only when `cond` is truthy, because `&&` returns its right side when the left is truthy and the left side otherwise. It's a short way to show something or nothing; be careful with numeric conditions like 0.
p: Renders right side if left is truthy
Returns the falsy left value otherwise
r95.f: What exactly gets rendered when the left side is an empty string?

r96.a: Use `condition ? <A /> : <B />` inside JSX when you need to pick between two outputs. Keep it simple; nested ternaries get hard to read, so move complex choices into variables or early returns.
p: Works anywhere an expression is allowed
Use null for "nothing" on one side
r96.f: How would you refactor a three-level nested ternary?

n22.a: Split the context so frequently changing values don't share a provider with stable ones, memoize the provider value with `useMemo` so it only changes when its contents do, and put the provider as low in the tree as possible. Components that only need setters can read a separate dispatch context, and expensive subtrees can be wrapped in `memo`.
p: Separate contexts for state and setters/dispatch
Pass children through so the provider's own re-render doesn't re-render them
Use a store with selectors (Zustand, useSyncExternalStore) for fine-grained updates
n22.f: Why does passing `children` help avoid re-renders in a provider component?

r13.a: Prop drilling is passing props through several intermediate components that don't use them, just so a deeply nested component can access them. It makes code noisy and refactoring harder.
p: Middle components become coupled to data they don't need
State libraries for complex shared state
r13.f: How can component composition reduce prop drilling without using context?

r153.a: `useContext(MyContext)` reads the current value from the nearest matching `Provider` above the component and re-renders it when that value changes. Use it for data many components need, like theme, locale or the current user, rather than passing it through every level.
p: Not a replacement for all state management
In React 19 you can also read context with `use()`
r153.f: What happens to consumers when the provider value is a new object every render?
r153.c:
const ThemeContext = createContext('light');
function Button() { const theme = useContext(ThemeContext); return <button className={theme}>OK</button>; }

r160.a: State management is how an app stores and updates the data that drives its UI. Local state lives in one component (useState/useReducer) and is only relevant there; global state is shared across many components (context, Redux, Zustand), like the logged-in user or a cart.
p: Local: form inputs, toggles, UI-only data
Global: auth, theme, cart, cross-page data
Keep state as local as possible
Server data belongs in a cache (React Query/SWR)
r160.f: How do you decide where a piece of state should live?

r162.a: Client state is owned by the browser and changes synchronously (UI toggles, form inputs, selected tab). Server state lives on a backend: it can be changed by others, is fetched asynchronously, can become stale and needs caching, refetching and deduplication, which is why tools like TanStack Query exist.
p: Server state: remote, async, shared, can go stale
Server state needs caching and invalidation
Don't copy server data into global stores by default
Use React Query, SWR or RTK Query for server state
r162.f: What problems appear when you keep server data in Redux by hand?

r164.a: Persist state outside memory: localStorage/sessionStorage for small client data, IndexedDB for larger data, cookies or the server for auth, and the URL for shareable state. Libraries like `redux-persist` or Zustand's persist middleware automate it; read the stored value in a lazy initializer and handle missing or invalid data.
p: Sync with an effect on change
Handle JSON parse errors and versioning
Sensitive data (tokens) shouldn't go in localStorage
r164.f: What issue appears when reading localStorage during server-side rendering?
r164.c:
const [theme, setTheme] = useState(() => localStorage.getItem('theme') ?? 'light');
useEffect(() => { localStorage.setItem('theme', theme); }, [theme]);

r223.a: When two components need the same data, move the state to their closest common parent and pass it down as props, along with callbacks to change it. This keeps a single source of truth so the components stay in sync.
p: Too much lifting → consider context or a store
r223.f: What are the downsides of lifting state very high in the tree?

r323.a: Start with local state; lift it up when siblings need it. Use context for low-frequency, widely needed values (theme, auth, locale). Reach for an external store (Zustand, Redux Toolkit, Jotai) when many components update shared state often, you need selectors to avoid re-renders, or you want devtools and middleware. Server data goes in a fetching cache.
p: External store for frequent, complex shared updates
r323.f: Why is context a poor fit for rapidly changing values?

r332.a: Server state is a cached copy of data that lives elsewhere: it's async, shared with other users, can be stale and needs refetching and invalidation. Local UI state (open menus, input text) is owned by the component, synchronous and always up to date.
p: Server state: async, remote, can go stale
Different tools: query cache vs useState
Avoid duplicating server data into UI state
r332.f: How does React Query decide when to refetch?

r338.a: Every consumer re-renders when the context value changes, so putting frequently changing or unrelated values in one context causes wide re-renders. Other pitfalls: creating a new value object each render, overusing context instead of props, missing providers (silently using the default), and harder-to-follow data flow.
p: All consumers re-render on any change
New object each render breaks memoization
Split contexts by concern and update frequency
Default value used when no provider
Not a full state manager (no selectors)
r338.f: How would you let consumers subscribe to only part of a context?

r378.a: Lifting state up means moving state from a child into a common parent so multiple components can share and stay in sync with it. The parent passes the value down as props and passes functions to update it.
p: Shared state lives in the common parent
r378.f: When does lifting state up lead to prop drilling?

r45.a: The Context API lets a parent provide a value that any descendant can read with `useContext`, without passing props through every level. Use it for values many components at different depths need (theme, auth, locale, feature flags); keep using props when only a few levels are involved.
p: Props stay clearer for a few levels
r45.f: What are the performance implications of context?

r518.a: The default value passed to `createContext(default)` is what `useContext` returns when there's no matching Provider above the component. It's useful for tests, stories and as a safe fallback, but it isn't updated by anything.
p: Good for testing components in isolation
Often set to null and checked in a custom hook
Providers can't override it via undefined value
r518.f: Why do many custom hooks throw an error when the context is null?

r552.a: Context state is in memory and resets on refresh, so persist the session: keep auth in an httpOnly cookie set by the server (preferred) and on load call an endpoint like `/me` to restore the user, or store a token and rehydrate from it. Show a loading state until the check finishes.
p: Fetch the current user on app start
Render a loading state during the check
Avoid storing tokens in localStorage if possible (XSS risk)
r552.f: Why are httpOnly cookies safer than localStorage for tokens?

r577.a: `useContext` reads a context value. Steps: create the context with `createContext(default)`, wrap part of the tree in `<MyContext.Provider value={...}>` (or `<MyContext value>` in React 19), then call `useContext(MyContext)` in any descendant.
p: Provide a value high in the tree
Optionally wrap in a custom hook
r577.f: What does React 19 change about providers?

r592.a: Yes. Call `useContext` once for each context you need; each subscription is independent, and the component re-renders when any of them changes.
r592.f: How would you avoid a "provider pyramid" in the app root?
r592.c:
const theme = useContext(ThemeContext);
const user = useContext(UserContext);

r593.a: Passing an inline object like `value={{ user, setUser }}` creates a new object every render of the provider, so every consumer re-renders even when nothing changed. Memoize the value with `useMemo` (and stable callbacks with `useCallback`) or split it into separate contexts.
p: Fix with useMemo on the value
r593.f: Why is the setter function itself stable?
r593.c:
const value = useMemo(() => ({ user, setUser }), [user]);
return <UserContext.Provider value={value}>{children}</UserContext.Provider>;

r594.a: If there's no matching Provider above the component, `useContext` returns the default value given to `createContext`. If no default was passed, it's `undefined`.
p: Often a sign of a missing provider
Custom hooks can throw to catch the mistake
r594.f: Can a component read a context provided by a sibling?

r635.a: Create the context and a provider component that owns the state, then export a custom hook that reads it and throws a helpful error if used outside the provider. This keeps context details private and gives consumers a clean API.
p: Provider component owns state and memoizes value
Export only the provider and the hook
Easy to test by wrapping in the provider
r635.f: How would you make a generic createContext helper with this pattern?

n17.a: In development, Strict Mode mounts, unmounts and remounts each component to check that effects clean up properly, so the fetch effect runs twice. Production runs it once. Write the effect so a second run is harmless: ignore or abort the stale request in the cleanup, or use a data-fetching library that dedupes requests.
p: Development-only double mount from Strict Mode
Not a bug to "fix" by removing Strict Mode
Use an ignore flag or AbortController in cleanup
Libraries (TanStack Query, SWR) dedupe and cache
n17.f: Why is a ref-based "has run" flag the wrong fix?

n18.a: The effect doesn't clean up: when the room changes, the old socket subscription is still active, so its messages keep arriving. Return a cleanup that unsubscribes (or disconnects), and include `roomId` in the dependency array so React tears down the old subscription before creating the new one.
p: Missing cleanup leaks the old subscription
Cleanup runs before the next effect and on unmount
Also ignore late messages tagged with the old room
n18.f: What would happen if roomId were left out of the dependency array?

r12.a: Side effects are anything that reaches outside rendering: data fetching, subscriptions, timers, manually changing the DOM, logging, or storing to localStorage. React distinguishes effects that need cleanup (subscriptions, timers, listeners) from those that don't (a one-off log or analytics call); both go in `useEffect` (or `useLayoutEffect` when they must run before paint).
p: Effects without cleanup: logging, one-off requests
Effects with cleanup: subscriptions, timers, listeners
Run after render, not during it
Event-driven work belongs in event handlers
r12.f: Why should data you can compute from props not be set in an effect?

r128.a: With no dependency array at all, the effect runs after every render. With an empty array `[]`, it runs only after the first mount. If you omit values the effect actually uses, it captures stale values from an earlier render and won't re-run when they change, causing bugs.
p: No array → runs after every render
[] → once on mount (twice in Strict Mode dev)
Use functional updates to reduce dependencies
r128.f: How can you remove a dependency without lying to React?

r146.a: CORS is a browser rule: a page can only read responses from another origin if that server sends headers like `Access-Control-Allow-Origin`. Axios can't bypass it; fix it on the server (allow your origin, methods and headers, handle OPTIONS preflight) or use a dev-server proxy so requests appear same-origin during development.
p: Enforced by the browser, not Axios
`withCredentials: true` needs Allow-Credentials and a specific origin
Use a Vite/webpack proxy in development
r146.f: What makes a request trigger a preflight?

r148.a: Axios is a promise-based HTTP client. Compared with fetch it parses JSON automatically, rejects on HTTP error statuses, supports interceptors, timeouts and request cancellation. In React you call it from an effect or (better) through a data library, and cancel it in cleanup.
p: Interceptors for auth headers and errors
Often wrapped in a shared instance
r148.f: How does error handling differ between fetch and Axios?

r17.a: `useEffect` runs code after React commits a render, so you can synchronize a component with something outside React: fetching data, subscribing to events, timers or updating the document title. It can return a cleanup function, and its dependency array controls when it re-runs.
p: Cleanup runs before re-run and on unmount
Not for transforming data for rendering
r17.f: When would you use useLayoutEffect instead?

r262.a: If a value can be computed from existing props or state, compute it during render (with `useMemo` if it's expensive). Storing it in state and syncing with an effect causes an extra render, a frame of stale UI and more bugs. Effects are only for syncing with external systems.
p: Effects cause an extra render and stale frames
Reset state with a key, not an effect
r262.f: How would you reset all state when a prop changes?

r263.a: React runs the previous effect's cleanup (unsubscribe from the old source) and then sets up the effect again with the new dependency value. So the component is always subscribed to exactly the current source.
p: Cleanup of the old effect runs first
Same pattern for timers and sockets
r263.f: In what order do cleanup and setup run during a re-render?

r265.a: The interval callback was created during the first render and closes over that render's state, so it keeps seeing the initial value (a stale closure). Fix it with a functional update `setCount(c => c + 1)`, by including the state in the dependencies, or by reading the latest value from a ref.
p: Closures capture values from the render they came from
Empty deps means the callback is never recreated
Functional updates avoid needing the value
r265.f: How would you implement a useInterval hook that always calls the latest callback?

r273.a: Common approaches: fetch in `useEffect` with loading/error state and cleanup; use a data library (TanStack Query, SWR, RTK Query) that adds caching, deduplication and retries; or use framework loaders, Server Components, or `use()` with Suspense so loading is handled by boundaries.
p: Prefer a caching library for real apps
Fetch early (route loaders) to avoid waterfalls
r273.f: What causes request waterfalls and how do you avoid them?

r274.a: Typical pitfalls: race conditions where an older response overwrites a newer one, missing cleanup, no loading or error states, refetching on every render because of unstable dependencies, waterfalls from nested components each fetching in turn, and duplicate requests without caching.
p: Race conditions → ignore flag or AbortController
Waterfalls → fetch in parallel or at the route
r274.f: How does an AbortController fix a race condition?

r534.a: `useEffect` runs side effects after render. To fetch data, start the request inside the effect, store the result in state, and handle cleanup so a stale response doesn't overwrite newer data. For production apps, a library like TanStack Query is usually simpler.
p: Store data, loading and error in state
r534.f: What happens if the component unmounts before the fetch finishes?

r595.a: React compares each dependency with its previous value using `Object.is`. If any changed, it runs the cleanup and then the effect again after the commit; if none changed, the effect is skipped. Objects and functions created during render are new every time, so they make the effect run on every render.
p: New objects/functions each render break skipping
Move objects inside the effect or memoize them
r595.f: How can you make a function dependency stable?

r596.a: Setup runs after the component mounts (after paint). Before each re-run caused by changed dependencies, React runs the previous cleanup and then setup again with new values. Cleanup also runs once on unmount. In development with Strict Mode there's an extra setup + cleanup cycle on mount.
p: Cleanup then setup when deps change
Strict Mode adds one extra cycle in dev
Empty deps: once (plus the dev cycle)
r596.f: Does cleanup see the old or the new props?

r597.a: Effects must return nothing or a cleanup function. An async function returns a promise, which React can't use as a cleanup, and React warns about it. Define an async function inside the effect and call it instead.
p: Effect return value must be a function or undefined
r597.f: How would you clean up an async request in that pattern?

r598.a: Yes. You can use several `useEffect` calls in one component, and it's encouraged to split unrelated logic into separate effects, each with its own dependencies. They run in the order they're declared.
p: Each has its own dependencies and cleanup
Easier to read and extract into custom hooks
r598.f: How would you decide when to extract an effect into a custom hook?

r599.a: Infinite loops happen when an effect sets state that is also a dependency, or depends on a value recreated every render. Fix by removing derived state, using functional updates, moving objects inside the effect, memoizing dependencies, or reconsidering whether an effect is needed at all.
p: Effect updates its own dependency → loop
Missing dependency array runs every render

r621.a: Return a function from the effect; React calls it before the effect re-runs and when the component unmounts. Use it to remove event listeners, clear timers, close connections, abort fetches and unsubscribe from stores.
p: Runs before re-run and on unmount
Mirror every setup with a teardown
Prevents leaks and setState on unmounted components
Strict Mode tests it in development
r621.f: Why does Strict Mode run cleanup immediately after the first mount?

r622.a: `useEffectEvent` (formerly the experimental `useEvent`, stable in React 19.2) creates a function that always sees the latest props and state but isn't reactive, so it doesn't need to be in an effect's dependency array. `useEffect` re-runs when dependencies change; an effect event lets the effect read fresh values without re-subscribing.
p: useEffect is reactive to its dependencies
useEffectEvent reads latest values without being a dependency
Only call effect events from inside effects
r622.f: Why shouldn't you pass an effect event to child components?

r14.a: Error boundaries are class components that catch JavaScript errors during rendering, in lifecycle methods and constructors of their children, show a fallback UI instead of a blank screen, and can log the error. They implement `static getDerivedStateFromError` and/or `componentDidCatch`.
p: Catch render-time errors in the subtree
Must be class components (or use react-error-boundary)
Don't catch event handler or async errors
r14.f: How do you handle errors thrown inside event handlers?

r492.a: `componentDidCatch(error, info)` runs in the commit phase after a descendant throws. `error` is the thrown value and `info.componentStack` shows which components were rendering. It's used for side effects like logging; the fallback UI is usually set via `getDerivedStateFromError`.
r492.f: Why is getDerivedStateFromError preferred for rendering the fallback?

r493.a: Error boundaries don't catch errors in event handlers, asynchronous code (setTimeout, promises), server-side rendering, or errors thrown in the boundary itself. Use try/catch in handlers, catch promise rejections, or rethrow into render (for example via state) to reach a boundary.
p: Can surface async errors by setting state that throws during render
r493.f: How can you make an async error show the nearest error boundary?

r494.a: Since React 16, an error that isn't caught by any error boundary unmounts the whole React tree, leaving a blank page. The reasoning is that showing corrupted UI is worse than showing nothing, which is why you should add error boundaries.
p: Uncaught render errors unmount the entire root
Add boundaries at app and feature level
Errors are logged to the console with the component stack
r494.f: Where would you place error boundaries in a large app?

r495.a: Place them at a few strategic levels: one at the top to avoid a blank screen, then around independent features or routes (sidebar, chart widget, page content) so one failure doesn't break the rest. Granularity is a trade-off between isolation and a fragmented UX.
r495.f: How would you let users retry after an error boundary shows?

r496.a: The component stack (from `info.componentStack` in development and production) shows the chain of components that were rendering when the error happened, so you can locate the failing component quickly, even when the JavaScript stack is minified.
p: Shows component hierarchy at the error
r496.f: How do source maps help with production error stacks?

n23.a: Keep form values and "touched" flags in state (one object or a form library like React Hook Form), derive errors and validity from the values during render instead of storing them, and disable submit until valid. Show errors after a field is touched or on submit, link messages with `aria-describedby`, set `aria-invalid`, and move focus to the first error on submit.
p: State: values and touched; derive errors and isValid
Show errors on blur or submit, not on every keystroke for untouched fields
Focus the first invalid field on submit
n23.f: Is disabling the submit button good for accessibility, and what's an alternative?

r175.a: Keep one state object for all fields and use a single change handler that reads `event.target.name` to update the right key. For bigger forms, use a library like React Hook Form.
p: One state object keyed by field name
Single handler with computed property names
Libraries reduce re-renders for large forms
r175.f: Why might a large controlled form feel slow, and how would you fix it?

r232.a: The warning appears when an input's `value` starts as `undefined` or `null` (uncontrolled) and later becomes a string (controlled). Initialize state with an empty string (or `false` for checkboxes) so the input is controlled from the first render, or use `defaultValue` if you want it uncontrolled.
r232.f: Why can't an input switch between controlled and uncontrolled?
r232.c:
const [name, setName] = useState('');
<input value={name ?? ''} onChange={e => setName(e.target.value)} />

r261.a: Give the form component a `key` tied to the record id (`<EditForm key={user.id} user={user} />`). When the id changes, React treats it as a different component, unmounts the old one and mounts a fresh one with clean state.
p: Cleaner than syncing state in an effect
r261.f: When is resetting state with a key not appropriate?

r300.a: Use real `<label>` elements, mark invalid fields with `aria-invalid`, connect error text with `aria-describedby`, and announce errors (a live region or an error summary with `role="alert"`). On submit, move focus to the first invalid field or the summary, don't rely on color alone, and keep native validation semantics like `required`.
p: Error summary with links on submit
Move focus to the first error
Don't rely on color; use text and icons
r300.f: Why is validating on every keystroke annoying for screen-reader users?

r343.a: Accept both `value`/`onChange` and `defaultValue`. If `value` is provided, treat the component as controlled and use the prop; otherwise keep internal state initialized from `defaultValue`. Call `onChange` in both modes. This is often wrapped in a `useControllableState` hook.
p: Don't switch modes during the component's life
Warn in development if it switches
r343.f: How do native inputs handle switching between modes?

r384.a: Historically with the `prop-types` package (development-only runtime checks); today mostly with TypeScript, which checks props at compile time. For runtime validation of external data (API responses, URL params), use a schema library like Zod.
p: defaultProps removed for function components in React 19
r384.f: Why isn't TypeScript enough to validate API responses?
r384.c:
type ButtonProps = { label: string; variant?: 'primary' | 'ghost' };
function Button({ label, variant = 'primary' }: ButtonProps) { return <button className={variant}>{label}</button>; }

r510.a: React Hook Form is the most popular choice today: it uses uncontrolled inputs with refs, so it re-renders very little, and it integrates with schema validators like Zod or Yup. Formik was the earlier favourite; React 19's form Actions with `useActionState` also cover simple forms without a library.
p: React Hook Form: minimal re-renders, small bundle
React 19 form actions for simple cases
r510.f: Why does React Hook Form re-render less than Formik?

r527.a: Use the `defaultValue` prop (or `defaultChecked` for checkboxes and radios). It sets the initial value once; after that the DOM owns the value, and you read it through a ref or the form's submit event.
p: Changing defaultValue later has no effect
Read with a ref or FormData on submit
r527.f: How would you reset an uncontrolled form to new defaults?

r540.a: Formik is a form library that manages values, errors, touched state and submission for you, with helpers like `<Formik>`, `<Field>` and `useFormik`, and it pairs well with Yup for validation. It uses controlled inputs, so large forms can re-render a lot; it is less actively developed than React Hook Form today.
p: React Hook Form is the common modern alternative
r540.f: How does validation timing work in Formik (onChange vs onBlur)?

r553.a: The new JSX transform (React 17+) compiles JSX to `jsx()` calls imported automatically from `react/jsx-runtime`. You no longer need `import React` in every file, bundles get slightly smaller, and it enables future optimizations.
p: No need to import React for JSX
Enabled by default in modern toolchains
r553.f: Do you still need to import React to use hooks?

r554.a: The old transform turned JSX into `React.createElement(type, props, ...children)`, so `React` had to be in scope. The new one imports `jsx`/`jsxs` from `react/jsx-runtime`, passes children inside props and handles `key` separately, so no React import is required.
p: Old: React.createElement, React must be in scope
key passed as a separate argument
r554.f: Why is key handled separately in the new transform?
r554.c:
// old:  React.createElement('p', { className: 'x' }, 'Hi')
// new:  _jsx('p', { className: 'x', children: 'Hi' })

r70.a: In plain HTML the DOM keeps the input values and the browser submits the form by navigating. In React you usually control inputs with state (`value` + `onChange`), handle `onSubmit` yourself with `preventDefault()`, and send data with fetch. Uncontrolled inputs and React 19 form actions are also options.
p: Controlled inputs keep values in React state
onSubmit + preventDefault instead of page navigation
Uncontrolled inputs with refs/FormData also work
r70.f: When would you prefer uncontrolled inputs?

r71.a: Call `event.preventDefault()` in the form's `onSubmit` handler. That stops the browser from navigating and reloading the page, so you can handle submission in JavaScript.
p: Use onSubmit on the form, not onClick on the button
React 19 form actions do this automatically
r71.f: Why is handling onSubmit better than a click handler on the button?

r9.a: A controlled component gets its value from React state and reports changes through `onChange`, so React is the single source of truth. An uncontrolled component keeps its own value in the DOM; you set an initial `defaultValue` and read the value with a ref or on submit.
p: Controlled: value + onChange, easy validation and formatting
r9.f: Which one would you use for a search box with instant filtering, and why?
r9.c:
<input value={name} onChange={e => setName(e.target.value)} />  // controlled
<input defaultValue="Ana" ref={inputRef} />                        // uncontrolled

n911.a: Calling the setter doesn't change the current variable; it queues an update and schedules a re-render. On the next render, React applies queued updates in order (functional updaters receive the latest value), compares the result with `Object.is`, and if it changed, re-renders the component and its children. Multiple updates in the same event are batched into one render.
p: The current render's value stays the same
Functional updates use the latest queued value
Same value (Object.is) → React may bail out
n911.f: Why does calling setCount(count + 1) three times only add one?
n911.c:
setCount(count + 1);
console.log(count); // still the old value

r123.a: Hooks let function components have state, effects and context, which removed the need for classes. They make stateful logic reusable through custom hooks (instead of HOCs and render props), keep related logic together instead of splitting it across lifecycle methods, and avoid `this` confusion.
p: Reuse stateful logic via custom hooks
Group related code instead of spreading it across lifecycles
Easier for compilers and tooling to optimize
r123.f: What were "wrapper hell" problems with HOCs?

r129.a: `useState` takes only one argument, the initial state. The question usually means the second element it returns: the setter function used to update the state and trigger a re-render.
p: One argument: initial value (or initializer function)
Setter accepts a value or an updater function
Setter identity is stable across renders
r129.f: Why is the setter function's identity stable?

r130.a: If you pass a function to `useState`, React calls it only on the first render to compute the initial value. Use it when the initial value is expensive to calculate (parsing localStorage, building a large structure), so the work isn't repeated on every render.
p: Good for localStorage reads and heavy setup
Pass the function, don't call it
Works the same in useReducer's third argument
r130.f: How does useReducer support lazy initialization?

r16.a: Only call hooks at the top level of a component or custom hook, never inside conditions, loops or nested functions, and only call them from React function components or custom hooks, not regular functions. React relies on hooks being called in the same order on every render.
p: Top level only, same order every render
Only in components and custom hooks
`use()` in React 19 is the exception that can be conditional
r16.f: Why does React depend on call order to match hooks with their state?

r231.a: The argument to `useState` is only used on the first render. Later prop changes don't update the state, because state is meant to be independent after initialization. Either use the prop directly, derive values during render, or reset the component with a `key` when the prop should start a fresh state.
p: Copying props into state causes stale data
Use the prop directly if you don't need edits
Reset with key={id} for an edit form
Name it initialName to make the intent clear
r231.f: When is copying a prop into state the right choice?

r233.a: Hooks make logic reusable (custom hooks), keep related code together, remove class boilerplate and `this` binding, reduce component nesting compared with HOCs and render props, and are easier to test and type. They also work well with concurrent features and the React Compiler.
r233.f: Can you give an example of logic you extracted into a custom hook?

r24.a: Yes. Hooks are plain functions, so they work well with TypeScript and Flow; types are inferred from initial values, and you can pass generics when they can't be (for example `useState<User | null>(null)` or `useRef<HTMLInputElement>(null)`).
p: Generics for nullable or union state
Custom hooks have typed parameters and returns
r24.f: How do you type a custom hook that returns a tuple?
r24.c:
const [user, setUser] = useState<User | null>(null);
const inputRef = useRef<HTMLInputElement>(null);

r33.a: A simple example is a counter: `useState` holds the count and the button updates it with the setter. A second example adds `useEffect` to sync the count to the document title.
r33.f: Why use the updater form `c => c + 1` here?

r34.a: Classes keep state in `this.state`, update it with `setState` and split logic across lifecycle methods. Hooks keep state in function components with `useState`, group side effects by concern in `useEffect`, and share logic through custom hooks. Hooks need less code and avoid `this`; classes are still needed for error boundaries.
p: Lifecycles vs useEffect grouped by concern
Logic reuse: HOCs/render props vs custom hooks
r34.f: How would you translate componentDidUpdate into hooks?

r36.a: Almost all. Hooks cover state, side effects, context, refs and memoization, but there are no hook equivalents yet for `getSnapshotBeforeUpdate`, `getDerivedStateFromError` and `componentDidCatch`, so error boundaries still need a class.
p: Libraries like react-error-boundary wrap the class for you
r36.f: How would you use react-error-boundary in a function-component codebase?

r397.a: Mostly. Custom hooks replace most uses of render props and HOCs for sharing stateful logic, with less nesting and clearer data flow. Render props still make sense when the caller needs to control rendering (for example virtualized lists or headless components), and HOCs remain useful for cross-cutting wrappers in some libraries.
p: Custom hooks share logic without wrappers
Render props still useful for render control
HOCs for wrapping many components (e.g. connect, withRouter)
r397.f: When would a render prop be better than a hook?

r4.a: `useState` adds state to a function component. It takes the initial value and returns an array with the current value and a setter; calling the setter schedules a re-render with the new value.
p: Setter accepts a value or updater function
Each component instance has its own state
r4.f: What's the difference between passing a value and a function to the setter?

r489.a: Use `eslint-plugin-react-hooks` with its `rules-of-hooks` and `exhaustive-deps` rules (included in most templates), keep warnings as errors in CI, and name custom hooks with the `use` prefix so the linter can check them. The React Compiler also flags rule violations.
p: Code review for disabled lint lines

r537.a: `useState` returns an array `[value, setter]`, and array destructuring lets you name the two items whatever you like (`[count, setCount]`, `[name, setName]`). If it returned an object, you'd have to rename properties for each state variable.

r538.a: Hooks drew on earlier ideas such as React's own mixins, HOCs and render props, Sebastian Markbåge's early proposals, the "algebraic effects" concept from functional programming, and libraries like Recompose. The goal was to share stateful logic without classes or wrappers.

Aimed at logic reuse without classes

r580.a: An updater function is a function passed to a state setter, like `setCount(c => c + 1)`, that receives the latest pending state and returns the next one. Use it when the new state depends on the previous state, especially with several updates in one event or inside async callbacks. For values that don't depend on the old state, a plain value is fine.
p: Needed for multiple updates in a row
Avoids stale closures in timers and async code
Not required when setting an unrelated value
r580.f: What happens if an updater function has side effects in Strict Mode?

r581.a: Yes. If you pass a function, React calls it once during the first render and uses its return value as the initial state (lazy initialization). Note the difference between `useState(fn)` and `useState(fn())`.
p: Function is called only on mount
Pass the function reference, not its result
To store a function as state, wrap it: useState(() => fn)
r581.f: How would you store a function itself in state?

r582.a: Any JavaScript value: numbers, strings, booleans, null, arrays, objects, Maps, functions (wrapped in a lazy initializer), even class instances. React compares with `Object.is`, so treat objects and arrays as immutable and replace them instead of mutating.
p: Functions need `() => fn` to be stored
Prefer several simple states or one object depending on usage
r582.f: When would you split one state object into several useState calls?

r583.a: Hooks must run in the same order every render. If `useState` is inside a condition and the condition changes, React's list of hooks shifts, values get mixed up, and React throws an error like "Rendered more hooks than during the previous render".
p: Leads to runtime errors or wrong state
Put the condition inside the hook's logic instead
r583.f: How would you conditionally run an effect correctly?

r584.a: The setter is synchronous to call but the state update is applied asynchronously: React queues it and re-renders later, often batching several updates. So the variable in the current render doesn't change immediately. Use the updater form or effects when you need the new value.
p: Updates are queued, not applied immediately
Batched within events (and everywhere in React 18)
Current render keeps the old value
Use updater functions for dependent updates

r585.a: Each component instance (fiber) keeps a linked list of hook objects. On each render React walks that list in call order: `useState` reads its hook's stored value and applies any queued updates; the setter pushes an update onto that hook's queue and schedules a render for the fiber. That's why hooks must be called in the same order.
p: Hooks stored on the fiber as a linked list
Position in the list identifies the hook
Setter enqueues an update and schedules work
Updates processed during the next render
Bails out if the new state is identical
r585.f: How does React know which component to re-render when a setter is called?

r613.a: A custom hook is a function whose name starts with `use` and that calls other hooks to package reusable stateful logic, such as fetching data, tracking window size or syncing with localStorage. Each component that calls it gets its own independent state.
p: Follow the rules of hooks inside
r613.f: How would you make this hook safe for server-side rendering?

r62.a: Hooks are functions like `useState` and `useEffect` that let function components use state, side effects, context and other React features. They were introduced in 16.8 to make stateful logic reusable without HOCs or render props, to keep related logic together instead of across lifecycle methods, and to avoid the complexity of classes.
p: State and lifecycle in function components
r62.f: What are the most common built-in hooks?

r623.a: Follow the rules of hooks, keep effects for syncing with external systems only, include all dependencies, clean up subscriptions, derive values during render instead of storing them, use functional updates for dependent state, extract repeated logic into custom hooks, and memoize only where it measurably helps.
r623.f: What's a common sign that you don't need an effect?

r63.a: `useState(initial)` creates a piece of state tied to that component instance and returns `[value, setter]`. Calling the setter queues an update; React re-renders the component, and on that render `useState` returns the updated value. Updates are batched, and identical values may skip the re-render.
p: Setter queues an update and schedules a render
New value is visible on the next render
Functional updates use the latest value
r63.f: Why doesn't the value change right after calling the setter?

r633.a: HOCs wrap a component in another component to inject props or behaviour, adding layers to the tree and risking prop name collisions. Hooks share logic inside the component itself, return values directly and keep the tree flat. Hooks are the preferred tool today; HOCs remain for some cross-cutting wrappers.
p: Hook: function called inside a component
r633.f: How would you convert a withWindowSize HOC into a hook?

r98.a: The core built-in hooks are `useState`, `useEffect` and `useContext`. Others include `useReducer`, `useRef`, `useMemo`, `useCallback`, `useLayoutEffect`, `useId`, `useImperativeHandle`, `useTransition`, `useDeferredValue`, `useSyncExternalStore`, and in React 19 `use`, `useActionState`, `useOptimistic` and `useFormStatus` (from react-dom).
p: Refs and memo: useRef, useMemo, useCallback
r98.f: Which of these would you reach for to subscribe to an external store?

n21.a: `useCallback` helps only when the function's identity matters: when it's passed to a child wrapped in `React.memo`, used as a dependency of an effect or another memo, or passed to a hook that compares it. Wrapping handlers used only on plain DOM elements, or passed to non-memoized children, is wasted work and adds noise.
p: Helps when the function is an effect dependency
Useless for plain DOM event handlers
React Compiler can do this automatically
n21.f: Why doesn't useCallback make the function itself faster?

r126.a: `useLayoutEffect` runs synchronously after React updates the DOM but before the browser paints. Use it when you must measure layout (sizes, positions) or adjust the DOM before the user sees it, such as positioning a tooltip, to avoid a visible flicker.
p: Runs after DOM mutations, before paint
Blocks painting, so keep it fast
For measurements and synchronous DOM fixes
Warns during SSR (doesn't run on the server)
r126.f: Why does a measured tooltip flicker with useEffect?

r127.a: Yes. Custom hooks are regular functions, so they can take any parameters and return anything. When parameters change, the hook re-runs with new values; include them in the dependency arrays of effects inside the hook.
p: Treat parameters like props: they change between renders
Add them to inner effect dependencies
Options objects should be stable or destructured
r127.f: What's the problem with passing an inline options object to a custom hook?

r154.a: `useReducer(reducer, initialState)` manages state with a reducer function `(state, action) => newState` and returns `[state, dispatch]`. Prefer it over useState when state has several related fields, the next state depends on complex logic, many event handlers update the same state, or you want update logic you can test separately.
p: Centralizes update logic in a pure reducer
Good for complex or related state
dispatch is stable, easy to pass down
Easy to test the reducer alone
useState is simpler for independent values
r154.f: How would you combine useReducer with context for app-wide state?

r155.a: `useMemo(fn, deps)` caches the result of calling a function; `useCallback(fn, deps)` caches the function itself. `useCallback(fn, deps)` is the same as `useMemo(() => fn, deps)`. Use useMemo for expensive calculations or stable objects, useCallback for stable function references passed to memoized children or effects.
p: Only worth it for real performance needs
React Compiler can apply them automatically
r155.f: Is useMemo a guarantee that the value will never be recomputed?
r155.c:
const sorted = useMemo(() => sortItems(items), [items]);
const onSelect = useCallback(id => setSelected(id), []);

r236.a: `useId()` generates a unique, stable id that is the same on the server and the client, so it's safe for SSR hydration. Use it to connect labels and inputs or `aria-describedby` links in reusable components. Don't use it for list keys.
p: Add suffixes for multiple related ids
r236.f: Why is Math.random() unsafe for ids in SSR apps?
r236.c:
const id = useId(); return <>

We never share it.
