function Card({ title, children }) { return

{title}

{children}
; }

r147.a: A higher-order component is a function that takes a component and returns a new component with extra behaviour or props, like `withAuth(Profile)` or Redux's `connect`. It's a pattern for reusing logic; today custom hooks usually do this more simply.
p: Forward refs and copy statics if needed
r147.f: Why shouldn't you create HOCs inside a render function?

r237.a: Composition means building components by combining others and passing UI through props, especially `children`, rather than inheriting behaviour. Containers like `Modal`, `Card` or `Layout` render whatever they're given; specialized components wrap generic ones with preset props.
p: Named slot props for multiple areas
r237.f: How would you build a "WelcomeDialog" from a generic Dialog?

r258.a: Common anti-patterns: mutating state, storing derived values in state, syncing props into state with effects, using effects for things that belong in event handlers, index keys for dynamic lists, defining components inside components, huge components doing everything, overusing context for fast-changing data, prop drilling through many layers, and premature memoization everywhere.
p: Effects instead of event handlers or render calculations
r258.f: Pick one and show how you would refactor it.

r259.a: Presentational components only describe how things look: they take data and callbacks via props and have little or no state. Container components handle how things work: fetching data, managing state and passing it to presentational children. Hooks reduced the need for separate container components, but separating logic from UI is still useful.
r259.f: How would a custom hook change this pattern?

r342.a: A component defined inside another is recreated on every render, so it has a different identity each time. React sees a new component type at the same position, unmounts the old one and mounts a fresh one, losing its state and DOM (inputs lose focus). Define components at module level and pass data as props.
p: Type change at a position → remount
r342.f: Why doesn't the same problem happen with a helper function called as {renderRow()}?

r379.a: `children` is a special prop containing whatever is placed between a component's opening and closing tags: elements, text, arrays or even a function. It lets components act as generic wrappers.
p: Can be any React node or a function

r383.a: Fragments group elements without adding DOM nodes, so the HTML stays valid (rows inside `<tr>`, items inside `<ul>`), CSS layouts like flex and grid aren't broken by extra wrappers, and the DOM is slightly smaller.
r383.f: Can a Fragment have a className?

r512.a: React favours composition: you build behaviour by combining components and passing props or children, and share logic with hooks. Inheritance between components creates tight coupling and fragile hierarchies, and the React team has found no use cases where component inheritance is better.
r512.f: How would you share behaviour that you'd normally put in a base class?

r522.a: No. "Render prop" describes the technique, not the name. Any prop that's a function returning elements works, and passing a function as `children` is very common.

r556.a: A wrapper component wraps other components to add layout, behaviour or context without changing them, such as a `Card` that adds styling, a `Provider` that supplies context, or an `ErrorBoundary` that catches errors. It usually renders its `children`.
r556.f: How do providers differ from layout wrappers?

n19.a: Record an interaction in the Profiler with "record why each component rendered" enabled, change one filter and look at which widgets rendered and why (props changed, context changed, parent rendered). Typical causes are filter state held too high, a context value object that changes every time, or new object/function props each render. Fix by moving state down, splitting context, memoizing values and callbacks, wrapping widgets in `memo`, or using a store with selectors.
p: Move state closer to where it's used
Memoize values and wrap widgets in memo
Selectors so widgets subscribe only to their data
n19.f: How would a selector-based store help here?

r120.a: Reduce wasted renders (keep state local, `React.memo`, `useMemo`/`useCallback` where it matters, split contexts), reduce work per render (memoize expensive calculations, virtualize long lists), load less code (lazy loading, code splitting), keep the UI responsive with transitions, and optimize assets. Always measure with the Profiler first.
r120.f: Which of these would you try first and why?

r121.a: Memoization means caching the result of a computation so it's reused when inputs haven't changed. In React this means `React.memo` (skip re-rendering a component when props are equal), `useMemo` (cache a value) and `useCallback` (cache a function), and now the React Compiler doing it automatically.
p: Has costs; use where it helps
r121.f: What's the cost of memoizing everything?

r168.a: `React.memo(Component)` returns a component that skips re-rendering when its props are shallowly equal to the previous props, even if the parent re-renders. It helps when a component renders often with the same props and its render is expensive.
p: Skips render when props are unchanged
Pair with stable callbacks and objects
Still re-renders on its own state or context changes
r168.f: Why does passing an inline arrow function break React.memo?
r168.c:
const Row = memo(function Row({ item }) { return
  • {item.name}
    • ; });

r169.a: Code splitting breaks your bundle into smaller chunks so the browser downloads only what's needed. Lazy loading loads those chunks on demand; in React you use dynamic `import()` with `React.lazy` and `<Suspense>`, typically per route or for heavy components like charts and editors.
r169.f: What are the downsides of splitting too aggressively?

r170.a: `React.Component` re-renders whenever `setState` is called or the parent re-renders. `React.PureComponent` implements `shouldComponentUpdate` with a shallow comparison of props and state, so it skips renders when nothing changed. The function-component equivalent is `React.memo`.
p: PureComponent: shallow compare of props and state
Mutated objects make PureComponent miss updates
r170.f: Why can mutating an array break PureComponent?

r181.a: First measure: use the React Profiler, browser Performance panel and Web Vitals to find whether the problem is load time, rendering or network. Then fix the actual cause: code splitting and smaller bundles for load time; avoiding unnecessary renders, memoizing heavy work and virtualizing lists for rendering; caching and parallel requests for data; transitions or Web Workers for heavy computations; and optimizing images and fonts.
p: Fix wasted renders and expensive renders
Data fetching: caching, parallelism, no waterfalls
r181.f: How would you know the fix actually worked?

r182.a: `useMemo` caches expensive calculations so they don't run on every render, and both `useMemo` and `useCallback` keep object and function references stable, which lets `React.memo` children and effects skip work when nothing meaningful changed. They only help when there's real cost or a memoized consumer.
p: Useless without a consumer that compares
r182.f: Can you give a case where useCallback made no difference?

r183.a: Virtualize long lists (react-window, TanStack Virtual) so only visible rows render, use stable keys, memoize row components and pass stable props, paginate or use infinite loading, avoid heavy work inside rows, and keep list filtering responsive with `useDeferredValue`.
r183.f: What accessibility issues can virtualization cause?

r21.a: Track the window size in state and update it from a `resize` listener added in `useEffect` (with cleanup). Usually wrap it in a `useWindowSize` hook and throttle updates; for CSS-only changes, prefer media queries, and for element size, use `ResizeObserver`.
r21.f: How would you make this hook work with SSR?

r225.a: Re-rendering means React calls a component function again to compute its new output, because its state, props, context or parent changed. It doesn't necessarily change the DOM: React compares the new output with the old and only commits differences.
p: Triggered by state, parent render, context
Not the same as DOM updates
Children re-render by default when the parent does
Usually cheap; optimize only when slow
r225.f: Does a component re-render if its props are unchanged but its parent re-renders?

r26.a: Keep state as close as possible to where it's used, avoid creating new objects/functions as props when they're consumed by memoized children, wrap pure expensive components in `React.memo`, memoize values with `useMemo` and callbacks with `useCallback`, split contexts, pass components as `children` so they're created by a parent that doesn't re-render, and use selectors with external stores.
r26.f: Why does lifting content into children prevent re-renders?

r272.a: Lazy loading delays loading code or resources until they're needed. In React, `React.lazy(() => import('./X'))` loads a component's chunk the first time it renders, with `<Suspense>` showing a fallback; images can use `loading="lazy"` and data can load when sections scroll into view.
p: Preload on hover to hide latency
r272.f: How would you lazy load a component only when it scrolls into view?

r282.a: Debouncing waits until typing pauses for a fixed time before doing work, which is ideal for network requests because it reduces calls. Deferred rendering (`useDeferredValue`) starts rendering right away at low priority and is interrupted by new keystrokes, so it has no fixed delay and adapts to device speed, but doesn't reduce network requests.
p: Use deferred rendering for expensive client-side filtering
r282.f: How would you combine both in a search UI?

r309.a: Split large contexts into smaller ones by concern and update frequency, memoize the provider value, separate state from dispatch/setters, keep providers low in the tree, and use `memo` on consumers' expensive children. For high-frequency data, use an external store with selectors (Zustand, Redux, `useSyncExternalStore`) so components subscribe to slices.
r309.f: Why doesn't React.memo stop context consumers from re-rendering?

r312.a: Keep heavy work off the urgent path: memoize expensive calculations, mark updates as transitions or use `useDeferredValue`, break work into chunks with `setTimeout`/`requestIdleCallback` or the scheduler, move CPU-heavy tasks to a Web Worker (e.g. with Comlink), and do expensive processing on the server when possible.
r312.f: What data can you pass to a Web Worker and what can't you?

r317.a: Reproduce the slowness, then measure: Chrome Performance panel for long tasks and layout work, React Profiler for slow or excessive renders, the network tab for slow or waterfall requests, Lighthouse/Web Vitals for load metrics, and bundle analysis for oversized JavaScript. Identify the biggest bottleneck, fix it, and measure again.
p: Fix the largest cost first, then re-measure
r317.f: What does INP measure and how do you improve it?

r318.a: Virtualize when a list has hundreds or thousands of rows and rendering them all causes slow loads, scroll jank or high memory. It can break browser find-in-page, accessibility (screen readers see only rendered rows), anchor links and scroll restoration, and complicates variable-height rows and sticky elements.
p: Use for large lists with visible jank
Only visible rows exist in the DOM
Breaks Ctrl+F and some screen reader navigation
r318.f: How would you keep keyboard navigation working in a virtualized list?

r320.a: `React.memo` only skips renders caused by the parent when props are shallowly equal. A memoized component still re-renders when its own state changes, a context it reads changes, or its props are new references each time (inline objects, arrays or callbacks), or when a custom comparison returns false.
p: children prop is a new element every render
r320.f: Why does passing JSX as children defeat memo?

r333.a: Track each pending edit with an id or version, apply optimistic updates in order on top of the last confirmed server state, and when a response returns, replace the confirmed base and re-apply any still-pending edits. Use server versioning (ETags or a version number) to detect conflicts, and on failure roll back only that edit and tell the user.
p: Optimistic state = server state + pending edits
Roll back individually with a clear message
r333.f: How does TanStack Query support this with onMutate and rollback?

r335.a: A waterfall happens when a child only starts fetching after its parent's data loads. Fix it by starting all independent requests together at the route level (loaders, `Promise.all`), prefetching in parallel, hoisting data needs into one query, using Server Components that fetch on the server close to the data, or passing promises down and reading them with `use()`.
p: Combine into one API call when possible
Pass promises down instead of awaiting early
r335.f: How would you spot a waterfall in the network tab?

r35.a: Performance is generally similar. Hooks avoid the overhead of class instances and binding, but create closures on every render. The bigger wins come from simpler code and better optimization opportunities (memoization, the React Compiler). Use the Profiler rather than assuming either is faster.
p: Closures created each render are cheap
r35.f: Do inline functions in hooks hurt performance?

r381.a: No. `React.lazy` expects a module with a default export. For a named export, re-map it in the import: `lazy(() => import('./Charts').then(m => ({ default: m.LineChart })))`, or create an intermediate module that re-exports it as default.
p: Or add a small re-export file
r381.f: Why does lazy need a default export?
r381.c: const LineChart = lazy(() => import('./Charts').then(m => ({ default: m.LineChart })));

r394.a: Wrap a function component with `React.memo` so it skips re-rendering when props are shallowly equal; for classes use `PureComponent` or `shouldComponentUpdate`. Make sure props are stable (memoized objects and callbacks) or memo won't help.
p: Use for expensive, frequently re-rendered components
r394.f: When would you write a custom areEqual function?

r44.a: The main techniques are: keep state local and avoid unnecessary re-renders; `React.memo`, `useMemo`, `useCallback` where they matter (or the React Compiler); split contexts; virtualize long lists; code-split with `lazy`/Suspense; use transitions and deferred values for heavy updates; avoid fetch waterfalls and cache server data; and optimize images and bundle size. Always profile first.
r44.f: What metrics would you track to prove the improvement?

r46.a: `React.memo` is a higher-order component that memoizes a whole component, skipping re-renders when props are equal. `useMemo` caches a computed value inside a component, and `useCallback` caches a function reference. They're often used together: memo on the child, useMemo/useCallback for the props passed to it.
r46.f: Why is useMemo alone not enough to skip a child's render?

r484.a: `React.memo` wraps a function component and returns a memoized version that re-renders only when its props change (shallow comparison by default, or a custom compare function). It's the function-component counterpart of `PureComponent`.
r484.f: What does the second argument to React.memo do?

r485.a: `React.lazy(load)` takes a function that returns a dynamic `import()` promise and returns a component that loads its code the first time it renders. It must be rendered inside `<Suspense>`, which shows a fallback while the module loads.
p: Declare at module level, not inside components
r485.f: Why must lazy components be declared outside of other components?

r514.a: Dynamic import is the `import()` expression that loads a module at runtime and returns a promise. Bundlers create a separate chunk for it, so it's the basis of code splitting and lazy loading.
r514.f: How do magic comments like webpackChunkName help?

r523.a: Render props usually pass a new inline function on every render, so a `PureComponent` or `React.memo` child always sees a changed prop and never skips rendering. Fix it by defining the function once (instance method or `useCallback`) when the render prop doesn't need render-time values.
p: Inline function = new prop each render
Usually only matters for expensive children
r523.f: Is this a reason to avoid render props entirely?

r524.a: Windowing (virtualization) renders only the rows or items currently visible in a scroll container, plus a small buffer, instead of all of them. As you scroll, items are swapped in and out, keeping the DOM small and scrolling smooth. Libraries include react-window, react-virtualized and TanStack Virtual.
r524.f: How do libraries handle rows with unknown heights?

r611.a: Not by itself. `useMemo` only caches a value; children still re-render when the parent does. It helps prevent child re-renders only if the memoized value is passed to a child wrapped in `React.memo`, or if you memoize the JSX element itself.
p: Children re-render with the parent by default
Memoizing a JSX element also works
r611.f: What does memoizing a JSX element with useMemo achieve?

r634.a: No. A component that calls `useContext` re-renders whenever the context value changes, even if it's wrapped in `React.memo`. Memo only skips renders caused by the parent with equal props.
p: Use selector-based stores for fine-grained updates
r634.f: How would you let a component read only one field of a large context value?

r640.a: Normalized state stores each entity once in a lookup by id (like a database table) and references it elsewhere by id. Updates touch one place, so fewer objects change identity, selectors and memoized components skip unrelated items, and you avoid deep cloning nested trees or keeping duplicate copies in sync.
p: Entities stored once, keyed by id
No duplicated data getting out of sync
r640.f: How would you denormalize data for display efficiently?
r640.c: const state = { users: { byId: { u1: { id: 'u1', name: 'Asha' } }, allIds: ['u1'] }, posts: { byId: { p1: { id: 'p1', authorId: 'u1' } } } };

n367.a: `useUpdateEffect` runs an effect only on updates, skipping the initial mount. Track whether it's the first render with a ref, and run the callback only after that.
p: Be careful with Strict Mode double-mount
n367.f: How does Strict Mode's double mount affect this hook?

n368.a: `useClickOutside(ref, handler)` calls the handler when a pointer event happens outside the element. Add a document listener in an effect, check `ref.current.contains(event.target)`, and remove the listener in cleanup. Keep the latest handler in a ref to avoid re-subscribing.
n368.f: How would you handle clicks inside a portal rendered outside the ref?

n369.a: `useIsMounted` returns a function that tells whether the component is still mounted, useful to avoid state updates after async work finishes. Set a ref to true in an effect and false in its cleanup.
p: Ref set in effect, cleared in cleanup
Check before setState after async calls
AbortController is often a better fix
n369.f: Why is cancelling the request usually better than checking isMounted?

n370.a: Valtio-style proxy state wraps an object in a JavaScript `Proxy` so writes are tracked: mutations notify subscribers, and a hook like `useSnapshot` takes an immutable snapshot and re-renders when the parts the component read change. Build it with a Proxy that calls listeners on `set`, a `snapshot` function that copies current values, and `useSyncExternalStore` to subscribe.
p: Snapshot creates an immutable copy for render
Track accessed keys for fine-grained updates
n370.f: How would you support nested objects?

n371.a: `useArray(initial)` keeps an array in state and returns it with helpers like `push`, `removeByIndex`, `update`, `filter` and `clear`, each implemented with immutable updates.
n371.f: Why use updater functions inside each helper?

n372.a: `useFocus` tracks whether an element is focused. Attach `focus` and `blur` listeners to the element via a ref (or return onFocus/onBlur handlers) and keep a boolean in state.
p: Option: return handlers instead of a ref
n372.f: How would you also detect focus within child elements?

n373.a: Keep the raw digits in state, format them on every change for display (for example "(123) 456-7890"), and strip non-digits from input. Handle deletion and caret position carefully, limit length, and use `inputMode="tel"` and `type="tel"` for mobile keyboards.
n373.f: How would you keep the cursor in place when editing the middle of the number?

n374.a: `useEffectOnce(effect)` runs an effect only on mount (and its cleanup on unmount). It's simply `useEffect(effect, [])`; note Strict Mode still runs it twice in development.
p: Prefer correct cleanup over "run once" hacks
n374.f: Why is forcing truly-once behaviour with a ref discouraged?

n375.a: `useDebounce(value, delay)` returns the value only after it has stopped changing for `delay` ms. Store the debounced value in state and update it in a timeout that's cleared whenever the value changes.
p: Use for search inputs and API calls
n375.f: How would you write a useDebouncedCallback instead?

n376.a: `useToggle(initial)` returns a boolean and a function to flip it (optionally to set a specific value). Use a functional update so rapid toggles stay correct.
n376.f: What bug appears if you pass the toggle directly to onClick and accept a value parameter?

n377.a: `useHover` tracks whether the pointer is over an element. Attach `mouseenter`/`mouseleave` (or pointer events) via a ref and keep a boolean in state.

n378.a: `usePrevious(value)` returns the value from the previous render. Store the value in a ref inside an effect; during the next render the ref still holds the old value.
p: Update it in an effect after render
Returns undefined on the first render
n378.f: Why is reading refs during render discouraged by React docs, and is there an alternative?

n379.a: A basic `useSWR(key, fetcher)` returns `{ data, error, isLoading }`. It shows cached data immediately (stale), revalidates by calling the fetcher, and updates the cache. A shared module-level cache lets components with the same key reuse data.
p: Real SWR adds dedupe, focus revalidation, retries
n379.f: How would you deduplicate concurrent requests for the same key?

n380.a: `useIsFirstRender()` returns true on the first render and false afterwards. Use a ref initialized to true and flip it after the first render.
n380.f: Why might this return false on a visible first render in Strict Mode?

n381.a: `useTimeout(callback, delay)` runs a callback once after a delay and clears it on unmount or when the delay changes. Keep the latest callback in a ref so changing it doesn't restart the timer.
n381.f: How would you add a reset function?

n382.a: A counter app keeps the count in `useState` and renders buttons that update it with functional updates. Good answers mention accessible buttons, an optional step value and preventing invalid states.
n382.f: How would you persist the count across reloads?

n575.a: `useQuery(fetcher, deps)` runs an async function and returns `{ status, data, error }`, re-running when dependencies change and ignoring results from outdated runs.
n575.f: How would you add a refetch function?

n578.a: `useBoolean(initial)` returns a boolean and stable helpers `setTrue`, `setFalse` and `toggle`.
n578.f: Why should these helpers be stable?

n579.a: `useDefault(initial, defaultValue)` works like useState, but returns `defaultValue` whenever the state is `null` or `undefined`.
n579.f: Should 0 or an empty string fall back to the default?

n585.a: `useCounter(initial)` returns the count and helpers `increment`, `decrement`, `reset` and `setCount`, all stable.
n585.f: How would you add min and max limits?

n586.a: A richer counter adds options like `min`, `max` and `step`, clamping every update and keeping helpers stable.
n586.f: What should happen if min is greater than max?

n588.a: `useCycle(...values)` returns the current value and a function that moves to the next value, wrapping back to the start.
p: Store the index, not the value
Works with any number of values
n588.f: Why store the index rather than the value itself?

n592.a: `useStateWithReset(initial)` works like useState but also returns a `reset` function that restores the initial value.
p: reset sets the initial value back
n592.f: How would you support a lazy initializer function?

n598.a: `useMap(initial)` keeps a `Map` in state and returns it with helpers `set`, `delete` and `clear` that always create a new Map so React sees the change.
p: Mutating the Map in place won't re-render
n598.f: Why doesn't map.set() on the existing Map trigger a re-render?

n609.a: `useCountdown` counts down from a start value at a fixed interval, with start, stop and reset controls, stopping at zero.
p: setInterval in an effect while running
n609.f: Why can setInterval drift, and how would you make it accurate?

n646.a: A second version of `useBoolean` typically returns the value plus helpers that accept an explicit value, e.g. `setValue(true)`, and guarantees stable references so the helpers can be passed to memoized children.
n646.f: Why does useMemo with an empty array work here?

n647.a: `useClickAnywhere(handler)` calls the handler on any click in the document. Add a click listener on `window` or `document` in an effect, keep the latest handler in a ref, and remove the listener on cleanup.
p: Variation of click-outside without a target check
n647.f: How would you build useClickOutside from this?

n661.a: `useBreakpoint` returns the current breakpoint name (sm, md, lg…) based on the window width. Use `matchMedia` listeners for each breakpoint (or a resize listener) and update state when it changes.
p: Update only when the breakpoint changes
n661.f: Why is matchMedia more efficient than listening to every resize?

n662.a: `useEventListener(type, handler, target = window)` attaches an event listener with cleanup, storing the latest handler in a ref so it doesn't re-subscribe on every render.
n662.f: Why shouldn't options be an inline object in the dependency list?

n663.a: `useInterval(callback, delay)` sets up `setInterval` that always calls the latest callback (via a ref), restarts when the delay changes, and pauses when the delay is null.
p: setInterval in an effect keyed on delay
n663.f: Why does a naive interval effect with count in deps restart every tick?

n664.a: `useKeyPress(targetKey)` returns true while a key is held. Listen for `keydown` and `keyup` on the window and compare `event.key` with the target.
p: keydown sets true, keyup sets false
n664.f: What happens if the window loses focus while the key is held?

n665.a: `useObject(initial)` keeps an object in state and returns a `set` that merges partial updates (like class setState), plus a `reset`.
p: Accept a function for computed updates
n665.f: Why doesn't this merge nested objects deeply, and should it?

n666.a: `useSet(initial)` keeps a `Set` in state with helpers `add`, `remove`, `toggle`, `has` and `clear`, always creating a new Set on change.
n666.f: When is a Set better than an array for selection state?

n667.a: `useStep(maxStep)` manages a step index for wizards: it returns the current step plus `next`, `prev`, `reset`, `setStep` and flags `canGoNext` and `canGoPrev`, clamping the step between 1 and the maximum.
n667.f: How would you prevent moving forward until the current step is valid?

n668.a: `useThrottle(value, interval)` returns a value that updates at most once per interval. Track the last update time in a ref; update immediately if enough time has passed, otherwise schedule a trailing update for the remaining time.
p: Immediate update when the interval has passed
Trailing timeout for the latest value
Different from debounce: updates during continuous changes
n668.f: When would you pick throttle over debounce in a UI?

n669.a: `useWindowSize` returns the window's width and height and updates on resize, cleaning up the listener on unmount. For SSR, start with undefined or a default and read the real size in an effect.
p: Throttle if many components use it
n669.f: How could useSyncExternalStore improve this hook?

n693.a: `useIdle(ms)` returns true when the user hasn't interacted for a given time. Listen for activity events (mousemove, keydown, pointerdown, scroll, visibilitychange), reset a timer on each, and set idle when the timer fires.
n693.f: How would you use this to log users out after inactivity across tabs?

n694.a: `useInputControl(initial)` manages a controlled input: it returns the value, an `onChange` handler to spread onto the input, plus `dirty`/`touched` flags and `reset`.
n694.f: How would you add validation to this hook?

n695.a: `useMediaQuery(query)` returns whether a CSS media query matches. Use `window.matchMedia(query)`, read `.matches`, and subscribe to its `change` event (ideally with useSyncExternalStore).
n695.f: Why pass a server snapshot here?

n696.a: `useMediatedState(mediator, initial)` is like useState, but every new value passes through a mediator function first, for example to trim, clamp or format input before it's stored.
p: Keep the mediator in a ref if it changes
n696.f: Give an example mediator for a numeric input.

n383.a: This BFE quiz tests that updating `ref.current` doesn't trigger a re-render and that refs keep their value across renders. Logs that read the ref during render show the value from the last render, while changes made in effects or handlers only appear after something else causes a render.
p: Reading a ref during render can show stale values
Effects run after render, so ref changes appear next render
Use state for anything that should update the UI
n383.f: When is it safe to read a ref during render?

n384.a: This quiz is about what error boundaries catch and in what order things log. Boundaries catch errors thrown during rendering of descendants (including in lifecycle/effects in the commit phase) and render the fallback; they don't catch errors in event handlers or async code, or errors thrown by the boundary itself, which go to the next boundary up. In development React may re-run the render and log the error more than once.
p: Catches render and commit-phase errors of children
Not event handlers or async callbacks
A boundary can't catch its own errors
Dev mode logs extra and may re-render
n384.f: Where does an error thrown inside a boundary's fallback go?

n385.a: The useEffect timing quizzes test ordering: during a render pass, all components render (parent before children), then layout effects run, then (after paint) effects run child-first, then parent. On updates, all cleanups of changed effects run before any new effects, and state set in an effect triggers another render pass.
p: setState in an effect schedules a new render
n385.f: Why do child effects run before parent effects?

n386.a: Another effect-ordering puzzle. Key rules: render functions run top-down, `useLayoutEffect` callbacks run synchronously after the DOM update (child first), `useEffect` callbacks run after paint (child first), and on re-render React runs all relevant cleanups before running the new effects. Updates scheduled inside effects are batched into the next render.
p: All cleanups before setups on update
Effects with unchanged deps are skipped
n386.f: How does Strict Mode change the log in development?

n387.a: This quiz combines effects with state updates. When an effect calls setState, React finishes the current commit, runs remaining effects, then re-renders; the effect runs again only if its dependencies changed. Logs therefore show render → effect → render → (effect only if deps changed).
p: setState inside an effect → another render
Effects run after each commit with changed deps
Infinite loops when the effect updates its own dependency
n387.f: What does React do if setState is called with the same value?

n388.a: "All kinds of effects" covers `useInsertionEffect`, `useLayoutEffect` and `useEffect` together. Order per commit: insertion effects (before DOM mutations), then DOM updates, then layout effects (child to parent), the browser paints, then passive effects (child to parent). Cleanups for each type run before that type's new effects.
p: Children before parents within each type
n388.f: Which effect type would you use to measure a DOM node?

n389.a: The Suspense quizzes test what happens when a child suspends: React stops rendering that subtree, shows the nearest Suspense fallback, discards the partial render (sibling renders may be logged and thrown away), and re-renders the subtree from scratch when the promise resolves. State of components that never committed is not kept.
p: Suspending throws a promise to the nearest boundary
n389.f: Why might a component's render log appear twice around a suspension?

n390.a: This quiz is about `useState` semantics: the setter doesn't change the value in the current render, multiple calls in one event are batched, plain values use the stale closure value while updater functions chain, and setting the same value may skip re-rendering children (React may still re-render the component once to confirm).
p: State is a snapshot per render
Logs after setState show the old value
n390.f: Why might React render once more even when you set the same value?

n391.a: This quiz checks basic error boundary behaviour: an error thrown during a child's render is caught by the closest class boundary implementing getDerivedStateFromError, which renders a fallback; siblings outside the boundary keep working. Event-handler errors are not caught.
p: Closest boundary above the throwing component
Errors in event handlers aren't caught
Without a boundary the whole root unmounts
n391.f: How would you reset the boundary when the user navigates?

n392.a: Lazy initial state: `useState(fn)` calls `fn` only on the first render, while `useState(fn())` calls it every render (its result is just ignored after the first). Logs inside the initializer therefore appear once (twice in Strict Mode dev).
p: Strict Mode calls it twice in dev
n392.f: How does useReducer's third argument relate to this?
n392.c:
const [a] = useState(expensive());   // runs every render
const [b] = useState(() => expensive()); // runs once

n393.a: `flushSync` forces React to apply the updates inside it and commit them to the DOM synchronously before returning. Logs show the re-render (and layout effects) happening immediately inside the handler, rather than after it finishes like batched updates.
p: DOM updated before the next line runs
n393.f: What's a legitimate use case for flushSync?

n394.a: The event callback quiz tests stale closures: a handler sees the state from the render it was created in, so reading state after calling the setter, or in a timeout started by the handler, shows the old value. The next render creates new handlers with the new value.
p: Setter doesn't mutate the current variable
Use updater functions or refs for latest values
n394.f: How would you log the latest count inside the timeout?

n395.a: The memo quizzes test when `React.memo` skips rendering: only when every prop is `Object.is` equal to the previous one. Inline objects, arrays, functions or JSX children are new each render, so the memoized child still renders; state or context changes inside the child also re-render it.
p: children JSX is a new object
n395.f: How would you fix a memoized child that receives an inline style object?

n396.a: With an async event handler, updates before the first `await` are batched with the event, and updates after `await` run later as separate batches (still batched together in React 18 with automatic batching). Logs of state after `await` still show the value captured by that render's closure.
p: Code after await runs in a later task
React 18 batches updates in async code too
Each await boundary can cause a separate render
n396.f: How many renders happen if you call two setters after an await in React 18?

n397.a: This quiz is about basic `useEffect` timing: effects run after the component renders and the browser paints, not during render. So "render" logs appear before "effect" logs, an effect with no dependency array runs after every render, and one with `[]` runs once after mount (twice in Strict Mode dev).
p: Effects run after render and paint
Cleanup runs before the next effect
n397.f: Where would a log in the cleanup function appear?

n398.a: The callback props quiz tests that passing a new function on every render changes the prop, so memoized children re-render and effects depending on that prop re-run. `useCallback` keeps the reference stable when its dependencies don't change.
p: Inline functions are new each render
n398.f: When does a changing callback prop cause an infinite effect loop?

n399.a: This quiz tests `useLayoutEffect` timing: it runs synchronously after DOM mutations and before the browser paints, before any `useEffect`. A state update inside a layout effect re-renders synchronously, so the user never sees the intermediate state.
p: Children's layout effects run before parents'
n399.f: Why does setting state in useLayoutEffect avoid flicker?

n400.a: Context re-render quizzes test that every component calling `useContext` re-renders when the provider's value changes (by reference), even through `React.memo` parents, while components between provider and consumer that don't read the context can skip rendering if they're memoized or passed as children.
p: New value object each render re-renders all consumers
Intermediate components can skip if memoized
n400.f: Why does a provider that re-renders with a new object cause all consumers to update?

n401.a: This Suspense quiz looks at what is shown and logged when a lazily loaded or data-reading component suspends inside a boundary while siblings don't: the boundary shows its fallback for the whole subtree, siblings inside the same boundary are hidden too, and everything renders again when the promise resolves.
p: Siblings in the same boundary also wait
n401.f: How would you let one slow widget not block its siblings?

n402.a: The basic Suspense quiz: when a component throws a promise (suspends), React renders the nearest `<Suspense>` fallback, and when the promise resolves it retries rendering the component. Logs inside the suspending component appear on each attempt.
n402.f: Why must suspending data come from a cache?

n403.a: This context quiz asks which components re-render when a context value changes. Only consumers (and their children, unless memoized) re-render; a parent that renders the provider with `children` passed from above doesn't re-render those children, because their elements were created by a component that didn't re-render.
p: Children passed as props aren't recreated
n403.f: Why doesn't changing provider state re-render {children}?

n404.a: Automatic batching (React 18+) groups multiple state updates into a single render, not only inside React event handlers but also in timeouts, promises and native listeners. So calling several setters in a `setTimeout` logs one render, not one per setter (React 17 rendered each separately outside events).
p: React 17 only batched in event handlers
n404.f: How did legacy ReactDOM.render behave here?
n404.c: setTimeout(() => { setA(1); setB(2); }, 0); // React 18: one render

n405.a: Re-render quizzes test the default rule: when a component renders, all of its children render too, regardless of whether their props changed, unless a child is memoized with equal props or is an element passed in from above. State changes in a child don't re-render its parent.
p: Parent render → children render by default
Elements passed as props aren't recreated
Child state doesn't affect the parent
n405.f: How would you prove which components rendered?

n406.a: This re-render quiz highlights that elements created higher up and passed down (e.g. as `children`) don't re-render when an intermediate component's state changes, because React sees the same element object and bails out.
p: Same element reference → React skips it
n406.f: How would you use this to optimize a scroll-tracking wrapper?

n407.a: The first re-render quiz checks the basic rule: setting state re-renders that component and every component it renders, top-down; parents and siblings outside are untouched. Setting state to the same value may bail out early.
n407.f: Is a re-render the same as a DOM update?

n891.a: Flux is an architecture pattern from Facebook with one-way data flow: views send actions to a dispatcher, the dispatcher sends them to stores, stores update their data and emit changes, and views re-render. Its benefits are predictable data flow and centralized, traceable updates; Redux simplified it into a single store with reducers.
n891.f: What did Redux change compared with Flux?

r104.a: No. Keep state in Redux when it's shared across distant parts of the app, needs to persist, or benefits from devtools and middleware. Local UI state like form inputs, toggles and hover states belongs in components, and server data is often better in RTK Query or TanStack Query.
r104.f: Give an example of state that looks global but should stay local.

r105.a: Redux relies on immutability so it can detect changes cheaply by reference (`===`), which powers `connect`/`useSelector` re-render decisions, time-travel debugging and predictable reducers. Mutating state directly makes components miss updates and breaks history. Redux Toolkit uses Immer so you can write "mutating" code that produces immutable updates.
r105.f: How does Immer produce immutable updates from mutating code?

r106.a: Redux Toolkit (RTK) is the official, recommended way to write Redux. It provides `configureStore` (good defaults, devtools, thunk), `createSlice` (reducers and action creators together, with Immer), `createAsyncThunk`, `createEntityAdapter` and RTK Query for data fetching, removing most boilerplate.
r106.f: How does RTK Query compare with TanStack Query?

r107.a: A component dispatches an action (often from an event). Middleware can intercept it (for logging or async work), then the store runs the root reducer with the current state and action to produce new state. Subscribed components (via `useSelector` or `connect`) re-run their selectors and re-render if the selected data changed.
p: Components re-render with new selected state
r107.f: Where does an API call fit into this flow?

r108.a: `mapStateToProps(state, ownProps)` is a function you pass to `connect` that selects the parts of the Redux state a component needs and returns them as props. It runs on every store update, and the component re-renders only if the returned props shallowly change. `useSelector` is the hooks equivalent.
p: useSelector replaces it in hooks code
r108.f: Why does returning a new array here cause extra renders?
r108.c:
const mapStateToProps = state => ({ todos: state.todos.filter(t => !t.done) });
export default connect(mapStateToProps)(TodoList);

r109.a: `mapDispatchToProps` tells `connect` which action-dispatching functions to inject as props. It can be a function that receives `dispatch` (and ownProps) and returns callbacks, or simply an object of action creators that connect binds automatically. With hooks you use `useDispatch` instead.
r109.f: When would you use the function form instead of the object shorthand?
r109.c:
const mapDispatchToProps = { addTodo, toggleTodo };
export default connect(null, mapDispatchToProps)(TodoForm);

r110.a: Redux middleware sits between dispatching an action and the reducer. Each middleware can inspect, transform, delay, cancel or dispatch other actions, which is how async logic (thunks, sagas), logging, analytics and error reporting are added.
p: Can call next(action), dispatch more, or stop
Used for async work and side effects

r111.a: Synchronous middleware processes an action immediately and passes it on (for example logging or validation). Asynchronous middleware handles actions that involve async work: it lets you dispatch functions or effects (thunks, sagas, observables) that wait for promises and dispatch plain actions later.
p: Sync: inspect/transform and call next immediately
Thunk, saga, observable are async middlewares
r111.f: Why can't reducers do async work themselves?

r112.a: redux-thunk lets you dispatch a function instead of a plain action object. The middleware calls it with `dispatch` and `getState`, so you can run async code (like API calls) and dispatch real actions when results arrive. It's included by default in Redux Toolkit.
r112.f: How would you handle errors in this thunk?

r113.a: Single source of truth means the whole application state lives in one store object tree. This makes state easier to inspect and debug, enables features like time travel, server rendering hydration and persistence, and avoids different copies of the same data drifting apart.
p: Simple serialization for SSR and persistence
r113.f: Does single source of truth mean you can't have local component state?

r157.a: Redux is a predictable state container. Its parts are the store (holds the state tree), actions (plain objects describing what happened), reducers (pure functions computing new state), dispatch (sends actions), selectors (read state) and middleware (side effects). React Redux connects it to components with `Provider`, `useSelector` and `useDispatch`.

r158.a: React Redux is the official binding: it subscribes components to only the state they select, avoids unnecessary re-renders with optimized selectors, handles store subscription correctly in concurrent React, and provides hooks and `connect` so components don't touch the store directly.
p: Re-renders only when selected data changes
Clean separation of UI and state logic
r158.f: How does useSelector decide whether to re-render?

r159.a: Use `combineReducers` (or pass an object to `configureStore`'s `reducer`) so each reducer manages its own slice of state, and the root state has one key per slice.
p: Each reducer gets only its slice
Root state shape mirrors the keys
Slice reducers can respond to the same action
r159.f: How would one slice react to another slice's action?
r159.c:
const rootReducer = combineReducers({ todos: todosReducer, filters: filtersReducer });
// or: configureStore({ reducer: { todos: todosReducer, filters: filtersReducer } })

r184.a: Action chaining means dispatching follow-up actions after one completes, for example fetching a user and then fetching their posts. It's done in thunks (awaiting one dispatch before the next), in sagas, or in listener middleware that reacts to specific actions.
p: Sagas and listener middleware react to actions
Keep reducers free of side effects
r184.f: What's the downside of hidden chains in listener middleware?

r185.a: Redux-Saga is middleware that handles side effects with generator functions. Sagas listen for actions and use declarative effects like `call`, `put`, `take` and `race` to run async flows, which makes complex sequences (cancellation, retries, debouncing, background tasks) easier to express and test.
p: Effects are plain objects describing work
Easy to test step by step
r185.f: When is saga worth its complexity over thunks?

r186.a: `call(fn, ...args)` tells the saga middleware to call a function (often returning a promise) and wait for its result. `put(action)` tells it to dispatch an action to the store. Both return plain effect objects, which makes sagas easy to test.
r186.f: How do you test a saga that uses call?

r188.a: Because Redux state changes only through actions and reducers are pure, Redux DevTools can record every action and resulting state, then let you jump back and forward, replay or skip actions to see how the UI looked at each point, which makes debugging much easier.
p: Requires pure reducers and serializable state

r189.a: Reselect creates memoized selectors. A selector built with `createSelector` only recomputes when its input selectors return new values, and returns the same reference otherwise, which avoids expensive recalculations and unnecessary re-renders.
r189.f: Why does a cache size of 1 matter when selectors take arguments?
r189.c: const selectVisibleTodos = createSelector([s => s.todos, s => s.filter], (todos, filter) => todos.filter(t => filter === 'all' || t.status === filter));

r190.a: No. Reducers must be pure and synchronous; dispatching inside one throws an error in Redux. Put follow-up logic in middleware (thunks, sagas, listener middleware), or handle the same action in several reducers.
p: Reducers must not cause side effects
Redux throws on dispatch during reducing
Multiple reducers can respond to one action
r190.f: How would two slices both respond to a "logout" action?

r191.a: Export the store from its module and call `store.getState()`, `store.dispatch()` or `store.subscribe()` from non-component code (API clients, utilities). Be careful with SSR (one store per request) and circular imports; injecting the store or using middleware is often cleaner.
p: Avoid in SSR where stores are per request
Middleware or thunks are often better places
r191.f: Why is a singleton store a problem for server rendering?

r192.a: Redux (with Toolkit) offers one predictable store, explicit actions, strong devtools and middleware, but more structure. MobX uses observable state with automatic tracking and mutable updates, so less boilerplate but more magic. Recoil/Jotai use atoms for fine-grained, bottom-up state. Zustand is a tiny hook-based store with selectors and minimal boilerplate. The right choice depends on app size, team and debugging needs.
p: Choose by complexity and team preference
r192.f: Why might a team migrate from Redux to Zustand?

r193.a: On the server you create a new store for each request, dispatch or fetch the data needed for the page, render the HTML, and embed the serialized state in the page. On the client you create the store with that preloaded state so it hydrates without refetching. Frameworks like Next.js need a per-request store pattern.
p: Serialize state into the HTML (escape it)
Avoid shared module-level stores on the server
r193.f: Why must the serialized state be escaped?

r194.a: Keep auth status (user, roles, loading, error) in an auth slice; perform login/logout with thunks or RTK Query that call the API; store tokens in httpOnly cookies rather than Redux or localStorage; restore the session on app start; handle 401s with middleware or a base query that refreshes the token or logs out; and reset state on logout.
p: Auth slice with user and status
r194.f: How would you reset every slice on logout?

r196.a: Open the realtime connection (WebSocket, SSE) in middleware or a listener, translate incoming messages into actions, and let reducers merge them into normalized state. Batch or throttle high-frequency updates, handle reconnects, and use RTK Query's streaming updates (`onCacheEntryAdded`) for server data.
r196.f: How would you avoid duplicate socket connections?

r197.a: `createAsyncThunk(type, payloadCreator)` creates a thunk that runs an async function and automatically dispatches `pending`, `fulfilled` and `rejected` actions. You handle them in `extraReducers`, so loading and error state are consistent without hand-written action types.
r197.f: When would RTK Query be a better choice than createAsyncThunk?
r197.c:
export const fetchTodos = createAsyncThunk('todos/fetch', async () => (await fetch('/api/todos')).json());
extraReducers: b => b
  .addCase(fetchTodos.pending, s => { s.status = 'loading'; })
  .addCase(fetchTodos.fulfilled, (s, a) => { s.status = 'idle'; s.items = a.payload; })

r334.a: `useSelector` re-runs on every dispatched action and re-renders when the result changes by reference. A selector that builds a new array or object each time (`state.todos.filter(...)`, `{ a, b }`) returns a new reference even when nothing relevant changed, so the component re-renders after unrelated actions. Use memoized selectors (`createSelector`), select primitives, or pass `shallowEqual`.
r334.f: How would you select several fields without extra renders?

r38.a: Not entirely. `useReducer` plus `useContext` can replace Redux for small to medium apps, but Redux (Toolkit) still offers selector-based subscriptions to avoid re-renders, middleware, devtools with time travel, RTK Query and conventions for large teams. Hooks are a tool, not a full state management solution.
p: useReducer + context covers simple shared state
Many apps also use Zustand or query libraries
r38.f: At what point would you introduce Redux into a hooks-only app?

r43.a: Context is built-in and good for low-frequency, app-wide values, but every consumer re-renders on change. Redux Toolkit gives a single store, selectors, middleware and devtools, good for large apps. Modern alternatives: Zustand (tiny store with selectors), Jotai/Recoil (atoms), MobX (observables), and server-state libraries like TanStack Query, which remove most "global state" needs.
p: Server state belongs in a query cache
r43.f: How would you decide for a mid-sized dashboard app?

r431.a: Compared with Flux, Redux has a single store (less flexible separation), requires immutability and pure reducers (more discipline), can involve boilerplate (much reduced by Toolkit), and needs middleware for async logic instead of doing it in stores.
r431.f: Which of these downsides does Redux Toolkit solve?

r432.a: `mapStateToProps` reads data from the store and maps it to props; `mapDispatchToProps` maps action dispatchers to props so the component can update the store. One gives the component data, the other gives it callbacks.

r433.a: MVW (Model-View-Whatever, like MVC/MVVM with two-way binding) can produce tangled data flow: models and views update each other in both directions, cascading updates are hard to trace, and as apps grow it becomes difficult to know what changed state and why. Flux/Redux addressed this with one-way data flow.
p: Many models and views coupled together

r434.a: Both deal with streams of events over time and functional transformations. Redux reduces a stream of actions into state (like RxJS's `scan`), and redux-observable lets you handle actions as RxJS observables. But Redux is a state container with a simple synchronous model, while RxJS is a general reactive programming library.

r435.a: Handle a reset action in the root reducer by returning `undefined` (or the initial state) for the whole tree, so every slice reducer falls back to its initial state. In Redux Toolkit, slices can also respond to a shared `logout` action in `extraReducers`.
p: Root reducer checks for reset action
Pass undefined state to slice reducers
r435.f: How does redux-persist need to be handled on reset?
r435.c: const rootReducer = (state, action) => appReducer(action.type === 'auth/logout' ? undefined : state, action);

r436.a: React context is a dependency-injection mechanism for passing values down the tree; consumers re-render whenever the value changes. React Redux uses context only to pass the store, then lets components subscribe to specific slices with selectors, adding middleware, devtools and predictable update patterns.
p: Context passes values; not a state manager
Context is fine for simple global values
r436.f: Why doesn't React Redux put the state itself in context?

r437.a: They're called reducers because they have the same shape as the callback to `Array.prototype.reduce`: `(accumulator, value) => newAccumulator`. A Redux reducer takes the previous state and an action and reduces them to the next state; over time, the action history reduces to the current state.
r437.f: What does this imply about replaying actions?

r438.a: Make the request in async middleware: a thunk (or `createAsyncThunk`) that dispatches loading, success and failure actions, a saga, or RTK Query, which generates hooks that fetch and cache data automatically. Reducers stay pure and just store results.
p: RTK Query for data fetching and caching
r438.f: What does RTK Query give you beyond createAsyncThunk?

r441.a: Components (presentational) render UI from props and don't know about Redux. Containers are connected to the store (via `connect` or hooks) and supply data and callbacks to presentational components. With hooks, the separation is less strict, but keeping Redux access near the top of feature trees still helps reuse and testing.
r441.f: How do you test a presentational component vs a container?

r442.a: Action type constants (`const ADD_TODO = 'ADD_TODO'`) give one place to define action strings, so typos become errors, editors can autocomplete and find usages, and reducers and action creators stay in sync. Redux Toolkit's `createSlice` generates them for you.
p: Single definition shared by reducers and creators
r442.f: Why are action types strings rather than symbols?

r443.a: You can pass `mapDispatchToProps` as a function `(dispatch, ownProps) => ({ onAdd: text => dispatch(addTodo(text)) })`, as an object shorthand `{ addTodo }` that connect auto-binds, or use `bindActionCreators` inside the function form. Omitting it injects `dispatch` itself as a prop.
r443.f: Which form is recommended and why?

r444.a: `ownProps` is the props passed to the connected component by its parent. `mapStateToProps(state, ownProps)` uses it to select data for that instance (e.g. a todo by `ownProps.id`), and `mapDispatchToProps(dispatch, ownProps)` can create callbacks bound to that instance.
p: Adding ownProps changes when functions re-run
Hooks: just use props in useSelector
r444.f: How does declaring ownProps affect performance?

r445.a: The recommended structure is "feature folders" with the "ducks" pattern: one folder per feature containing its slice (reducer + actions), selectors, thunks and components, plus an `app/store.js`. Older layouts split by type (`actions/`, `reducers/`, `constants/`), which scatters related code.
p: Type-based folders are the older style
r445.f: How would you avoid circular imports between slices?

r446.a: A saga is like a separate background thread in your app that's solely responsible for side effects. It watches for actions, runs async work step by step using generator `yield`, and dispatches new actions, all controlled by the saga middleware.
p: Can be started, paused and cancelled
r446.f: How do takeEvery and takeLatest differ?

r448.a: Thunks are simple functions that receive dispatch and getState; they're easy to learn and handle most async needs. Sagas use generators and declarative effects, which handle complex flows (cancellation, debouncing, races, long-running listeners) more cleanly and are easier to unit test step by step, but add a learning curve and boilerplate.
p: Saga easier to test without mocks
r448.f: How would you cancel an in-flight request in each?

r450.a: Redux DevTools shows every dispatched action with its payload and the resulting state, a diff of what changed, time-travel (jump, skip, replay actions), state import/export, action tracing to see where an action was dispatched, and the ability to dispatch actions manually.
r450.f: How would you disable DevTools in production?

r451.a: Selectors are functions that take the Redux state and return a piece of it or derived data (`state => state.todos.items`). They hide the state shape from components, can be memoized to avoid recomputation and extra re-renders, and are easy to reuse and test.
r451.f: Why should components avoid reading deep state paths directly?

r452.a: Redux Form is a library that stores form state (values, touched, errors, submitting) in the Redux store and connects inputs through HOCs and Field components. r482.f: How do you move a piece of local state into Redux later if needed?

Redux Form put all form state in Redux, which was heavier and slower for large forms.
p: Local form state, no global dispatches
Both now often replaced by React Hook Form

r541.a: Typical choices: redux-thunk (default in RTK; simple async functions), `createAsyncThunk`, RTK Query (data fetching and caching), the RTK listener middleware (reacting to actions), redux-saga (generator-based complex flows) and redux-observable (RxJS streams).

r544.f: How does MobX know which components to update?

r545.a: Redux uses a single immutable store updated by pure reducers through explicit actions, which is predictable and debuggable but more structured. r574.a: Reducers should be pure: compute new state only from the previous state and the action, never mutate state (return new objects or use Immer), never perform side effects (API calls, random values, dates), return the existing state for unknown actions, and keep state serializable.
p: Return current state for unknown actions
r574.f: Why is Math.random() inside a reducer a problem?

r636.a: Redux Toolkit is the officially recommended way to write Redux because it removes boilerplate (slices generate actions and reducers), sets good defaults (devtools, thunk, immutability and serializability checks), uses Immer for simple immutable updates, and includes RTK Query for data fetching, preventing common mistakes.
r636.f: What checks does configureStore add in development?

r637.a: Select the smallest data each component needs, return primitives or stable references, memoize derived data with `createSelector`, use `shallowEqual` when selecting several fields, avoid creating objects in selectors, normalize state, and split components so each subscribes only to what it renders.
r637.f: Why are multiple small useSelector calls better than one big one?

r638.a: `createSelector` (from Reselect, re-exported by Redux Toolkit) creates a memoized selector from input selectors and a result function. The result function only runs when the inputs change; otherwise the cached result (same reference) is returned.
r638.f: How would you write a selector that takes an id argument?
r638.c: const selectDoneCount = createSelector([s => s.todos.items], items => items.filter(t => t.done).length);

r639.a: Normalized Redux state stores each type of entity in a lookup table keyed by id (`{ ids: [], entities: {} }`) with references between entities by id, instead of nested copies. It avoids duplication, makes updates simple and fast, and keeps re-renders targeted. `createEntityAdapter` provides helpers.
r639.f: How would you normalize an API response with nested comments?

r641.a: Middleware has the curried signature `store => next => action => { ... }`. `store` gives `getState` and `dispatch`, `next` passes the action to the next middleware or reducer, and the innermost function handles each action and returns a value.
p: Return value goes back to dispatch caller

r642.a: The action goes through each middleware in order; if it reaches the store, the root reducer computes the new state from the current state and action. The store saves the new state and notifies subscribers; React Redux runs each component's selector and re-renders those whose selected values changed.
r642.f: What happens if a middleware doesn't call next(action)?

r643.a: Organize by feature (feature folders with slices, selectors and thunks), keep state normalized, use RTK Query for server data so slices hold only client state, expose selectors as the public API of each slice, avoid cross-slice imports with shared actions or listener middleware, lazy-load reducers for code-split features, and type everything with TypeScript.
r643.f: How do you inject reducers for lazy-loaded routes?

r644.a: Let multiple slices respond to the same action via `extraReducers`, use thunks that read state with `getState` and dispatch actions to several slices, use the listener middleware to react to one slice's action by updating another, or compute combined data with selectors rather than copying it between slices.
r644.f: Why is copying data between slices a smell?

r645.a: Serializable values are those that can be converted to JSON and back without losing information: plain objects, arrays, strings, numbers, booleans and null. Redux expects state and actions to be serializable so devtools, persistence and time travel work; Promises, functions, class instances, Maps, Sets and Dates aren't (store dates as ISO strings or timestamps).
p: Store dates as strings or numbers
r645.f: Where would you keep non-serializable things like a socket instance?

r646.a: Track the latest request so stale responses are ignored: compare request ids or arguments in reducers, use `takeLatest` in sagas, use `createAsyncThunk`'s `condition` and abort signals, or rely on RTK Query, which handles deduplication and cancels outdated requests.
p: Request ids to ignore stale results
r646.f: How does takeLatest cancel the earlier task?

r647.a: Use `redux-persist` (wrap the root reducer with `persistReducer` and render with `PersistGate`) or subscribe to the store and save selected slices to storage, loading them as `preloadedState`. Persist only what's needed, version and migrate the shape, and never persist sensitive data in localStorage.
r647.f: What problems arise when the persisted state shape changes?

r648.a: Use the React Profiler to see which components re-render after actions, check selectors with Redux DevTools and `why-did-you-render`, look for selectors returning new references, very frequent actions (e.g. on every keystroke or mousemove), large non-normalized state copies, and expensive reducers. Fix with memoized selectors, batching or throttling actions, normalization and splitting components.
r648.f: How would you batch many actions dispatched in a loop?

r649.a: Store only the minimal source data in Redux (raw entities, user input, UI flags) and compute anything derivable, such as filtered lists, totals, counts or sorted views, with memoized selectors. Storing derived data duplicates state and risks it getting out of sync.
r649.f: Give an example of derived data that people often store by mistake.

r650.a: Usually not by hand. Server data has caching, refetching, deduplication and invalidation needs, so use RTK Query (which stores it in Redux for you) or TanStack Query. Put API data in regular slices only when the client heavily edits or combines it with local state.
p: RTK Query or TanStack Query for caching
r650.f: How does RTK Query invalidate cached data after a mutation?

r76.a: Redux has three principles: a single source of truth (one store holds the app state), state is read-only (the only way to change it is to dispatch an action), and changes are made with pure functions (reducers take the previous state and action and return the next state).
p: State is read-only; change via actions
r76.f: How do these principles enable time-travel debugging?

r78.a: A pure function always returns the same output for the same inputs and has no side effects (no mutation, API calls, randomness or reading the current time). Redux reducers must be pure so state updates are predictable, testable and replayable.
r78.f: Is a reducer that uses Date.now() pure?

r79.a: Redux architecture consists of the store (holds state, exposes dispatch/getState/subscribe), actions (describe events), action creators, reducers (compute next state), middleware (side effects), and selectors (read state). In React, Provider and hooks connect components.
r79.f: Which part would you change to add logging?

r80.a: The store holds the application's state tree and provides the API to work with it: `getState()` to read, `dispatch(action)` to update via reducers, and `subscribe(listener)` to be notified of changes. There's normally one store per app.
p: One store per app (per request on the server)
r80.f: Why is there usually only one store?

r81.a: `<Provider store={store}>` makes the Redux store available to all nested components through React context, so hooks like `useSelector` and `useDispatch` (or `connect`) can access it without passing the store manually.
r81.f: How do you test a component that needs the store?

r82.a: `connect(mapStateToProps, mapDispatchToProps)(Component)` is a higher-order function that connects a component to the Redux store, injecting selected state and dispatching functions as props and re-rendering the component only when those props change. Hooks (`useSelector`, `useDispatch`) are the modern alternative.
p: HOC that injects state and dispatchers
r82.f: What are the advantages of connect over hooks, if any?

r83.a: `dispatch(action)` sends an action to the store; it passes through middleware and then the reducers, which compute the new state. In components you get it with `useDispatch()` or from `connect`.
r83.f: What does dispatch return when you dispatch a thunk?
r83.c:
const dispatch = useDispatch();
<button onClick={() => dispatch(addTodo('Learn Redux'))}>Add</button>

n25.a: On open, store the currently focused element (`document.activeElement`), then focus the input in an effect via a ref (or `autoFocus`). Trap focus inside the modal while it's open. On close, in the effect cleanup or close handler, call `.focus()` on the saved trigger element. The native `<dialog>` element with `showModal()` does much of this for you.
p: Focus the input with a ref in an effect
Trap Tab focus inside the modal
n25.f: How would you implement a focus trap?

r151.a: `useRef` returns the same ref object on every render of a function component, so it keeps its value across renders. `createRef` creates a new ref object each time it's called, so it's meant for class components (created once in the constructor); using it in a function component resets the ref every render.
r151.f: What happens if you use createRef inside a function component?

r18.a: Hooks use refs (`useRef`) to keep mutable values that persist across renders without causing re-renders, such as DOM nodes, timer ids, previous values or the latest callback, which is impossible with plain variables that reset each render.
p: Store timers, previous values, latest callbacks
Escape hatch from React's data flow
r18.f: Why shouldn't you store data that affects rendering in a ref?

r199.a: `useImperativeHandle(ref, () => api, deps)` customizes what a parent receives when it attaches a ref to your component. Instead of exposing the whole DOM node, you expose a small API like `{ focus, scrollToTop }`.
p: Customizes the ref value exposed to parents
Use with ref prop (React 19) or forwardRef
r199.f: Why limit the exposed API instead of exposing the DOM node?

r235.a: `useRef(initial)` returns a mutable object `{ current }` that persists for the component's lifetime. Use it to access DOM elements (focus, measure, scroll), store values that shouldn't trigger re-renders (timer ids, previous values, latest callbacks), and integrate with imperative libraries.
p: Don't read/write during render for rendering logic
r235.f: What's the difference between useRef and a module-level variable?

r254.a: `forwardRef` lets a function component receive a `ref` from its parent and pass it to a child DOM element or component, so parents can focus or measure it. In React 19, `ref` is available as a regular prop for function components, so `forwardRef` is no longer required.
p: React 19: ref as a normal prop
r254.f: How does the React 19 version look without forwardRef?
r254.c: const TextInput = forwardRef(function TextInput(props, ref) { return <input ref={ref} {...props} />; });

r266.a: Use `useImperativeHandle` when a parent genuinely needs to trigger an imperative action on a child (focus, scroll, play/pause, open a dialog, reset a form) and you want to expose only specific methods rather than the DOM node. If it can be expressed as props, prefer props.
r266.f: How could a modal be controlled declaratively instead?

r299.a: An accessible portal modal uses `role="dialog"` with `aria-modal="true"` and `aria-labelledby`, moves focus into the dialog when it opens, traps Tab focus inside, closes on Escape, returns focus to the trigger on close, makes the background inert (the `inert` attribute or aria-hidden) and prevents background scrolling. The native `<dialog>` with `showModal()` provides most of this.
p: Focus moves in and is trapped
r299.f: Why doesn't rendering in a portal alone make it accessible?

r386.a: `react-dom` connects React to the browser DOM. It provides `createRoot` and `hydrateRoot` from `react-dom/client`, `createPortal`, `flushSync`, resource preloading APIs, `useFormStatus`, and server rendering APIs in `react-dom/server`.
r386.f: What changed between ReactDOM.render and createRoot?

Destructure the props you consume and spread only the rest intentionally.

r41.a: `forwardRef` wraps a function component so it can accept a `ref` from its parent and attach it to an inner element. You need it (before React 19) when building reusable components like inputs or buttons that parents must focus, measure or scroll, or when an HOC must pass a ref through to the wrapped component.

React 19: ref is a regular prop

Use it for modals, tooltips, popovers and toasts that need to escape `overflow: hidden` or z-index stacking contexts.
p: Render outside the parent DOM node
Still part of the React tree

r521.a: Use refs when you need to step outside React's declarative flow: managing focus, text selection or media playback, measuring or scrolling DOM elements, triggering imperative animations, integrating non-React libraries (maps, charts), and storing mutable values like timer ids that shouldn't cause re-renders.

r521.f: Why shouldn't you use a ref to show or hide an element?

r555.f: What bug happens if you show ref.current in JSX?

null before mount and after unmount

r605.f: Why not use a plain variable inside the component?

Read it during the next render

Read refs in effects or event handlers instead (an exception is lazily initializing a ref once).
p: DOM refs are null during the first render
Lazy init pattern is an accepted exception

r608.a: Common uses: accessing DOM nodes (focus, scroll, measure, media control), storing timer or interval ids, keeping the previous value of props/state, holding the latest callback to avoid stale closures, storing instances of third-party libraries, and flags like "is mounted" or "has run".

r100.a: React Router gives single-page apps client-side navigation without full page reloads, declarative route configuration, nested routes and layouts, URL parameters and query strings, programmatic navigation, history management, lazy-loaded routes, and in data mode, loaders and actions for data fetching and mutations.

</Routes>

r132.a: Yes. On the server you render with a static/memory router (`StaticRouter`, or `createStaticHandler` + `StaticRouterProvider` in data mode) using the request URL, then hydrate on the client with `BrowserRouter` or `RouterProvider`. Frameworks like React Router's framework mode or Next.js handle this for you.

Loaders run on the server first

<Route path="dashboard" element={<DashboardLayout />}>

</Route>

r136.f: Why is redirecting in a loader better than in a component effect?

Server should return a 404 status for SSR
