r139.a: `BrowserRouter` uses the HTML5 History API and clean URLs like `/users/42`, which requires the server to return index.html for all routes. `HashRouter` stores the route after `#` (`/#/users/42`), which works on static hosts without server configuration but has uglier URLs and worse SEO.
p: BrowserRouter: clean URLs, needs server fallback
Hash isn't sent to the server
r139.f: What server configuration does BrowserRouter need?

r140.a: Use the `useSearchParams()` hook, which returns a `URLSearchParams` object and a setter, so you can read values with `get` and update the query string (which also updates the URL and history).
p: Keep filters in the URL for shareable state
r140.f: How would you update one param without dropping others?

r141.a: The `location` object describes the current URL: `pathname`, `search`, `hash`, `state` (data passed during navigation) and `key`. Read it with `useLocation()` to react to route changes, track page views, or read state like "where to go after login".
r141.f: How would you redirect back to the original page after login?

r142.a: The `history` object (from the history library in v4/v5) manages the browser session history: it exposes `push`, `replace`, `go`, `goBack` and `listen`. In v6+, you use `useNavigate()` instead of accessing history directly.
p: push adds an entry, replace swaps it
r142.f: What's the difference between push and replace for UX?

r143.a: In React Router v4/v5, the `match` object told you how a route matched the URL: `params`, `isExact`, `path` and `url`. It was used for reading params and building nested routes. In v6+ you use `useParams()` and relative paths instead.
r143.f: How do you build nested links in v6 without match.url?

r144.a: `useNavigate()` returns a function to navigate programmatically, for example after a form submit or login: `navigate('/dashboard')`, `navigate(-1)` to go back, or `navigate('/login', { replace: true, state: {...} })`. It replaced `useHistory` in v6.
r144.f: Why prefer a Link over a button calling navigate?
r144.c:
const navigate = useNavigate();
async function onSubmit() { await save(); navigate('/thanks', { replace: true }); }

r145.a: In v5, `<Route>` matches a path and renders a component, but several routes can render at once. `<Switch>` wraps routes and renders only the first one that matches. In v6, `<Routes>` replaced `<Switch>`, picking the best match automatically rather than the first.
p: Switch: render only the first match
exact needed in v5, not v6
r145.f: Why did order matter so much in v5's Switch?

r176.a: `useHistory` (v5) returned the history object, and you called `history.push('/path')`. `useNavigate` (v6+) returns a `navigate` function: `navigate('/path')`, `navigate(-1)`, with options like `replace` and `state`. useNavigate also supports relative paths.
r176.f: How would you migrate history.replace to v6?

r177.a: Route parameters are dynamic URL segments declared with a colon (`/products/:id`). They let one route handle many URLs, and you read them with `useParams()` in components or `params` in loaders.
r177.f: How would you validate params in a loader?

r179.a: With server-side routing, every navigation requests a new HTML page from the server, causing a full reload. With client-side routing, JavaScript intercepts link clicks, updates the URL with the History API and renders the new view without reloading, making navigation faster but requiring JS and care for SEO and initial load.
p: Client routing: History API, no reload
Client routing is faster after load
SEO and first load need SSR/SSG
r179.f: How do frameworks combine both approaches?

r180.a: `<Switch>` (v5) rendered the first child route whose path matched, so order mattered and you often needed `exact`. `<Routes>` (v6+) chooses the best match based on route ranking, supports relative nested routes and requires `element` props instead of `component`/`render`.

r20.a: A switching component renders one of several components based on a value, like the current route or a tab. Implement it with a lookup object mapping keys to components, or use React Router's `<Routes>` to switch between pages based on the URL.
r20.f: How would you lazy-load each page in the map?
r20.c:
const pages = { home: Home, about: About, contact: Contact };
function Page({ name }) { const Component = pages[name] ?? NotFound; return <Component />; }

r200.a: `withRouter` (v4/v5) was an HOC that injected `history`, `location` and `match` props into a component that wasn't rendered by a Route, so it could access routing information. In v6 it was removed in favour of hooks: `useNavigate`, `useLocation`, `useParams`.
p: You can write your own wrapper for class components
r200.f: How would you give a class component routing props in v6?

r202.a: In React Router v5, `exact` made a route match only when the path matched the URL exactly; without it, `/` would match every URL starting with `/`. v6 removed it because routes match exactly by default.
p: Use /* for prefix matching in v6
r202.f: How do you match "this path and anything under it" in v6?

r203.a: A default route is what renders when no specific child matches: an `index` route for the default child of a parent path, a `*` route for unknown URLs, or a `<Navigate>` from `/` to a default page.
p: index route for the parent's default content
Navigate to redirect to a default page
r203.f: Why use replace when redirecting to a default route?
r203.c:
<Route path="settings" element={<Settings />}>
  <Route index element={<Navigate to="profile" replace />} />
  <Route path="profile" element={<Profile />} />
</Route>

r205.a: Wrap protected routes in a guard (layout route or loader) that checks authentication and redirects to login with `<Navigate>` or `redirect()`, remembering the original location. For authorization, check roles/permissions per route and show a 403 page. Always enforce permissions on the server too; client guards are only for UX.
p: Guard component or loader checks auth
Show loading while auth state resolves
r205.f: Why isn't a client-side guard enough for security?

r206.a: `useRouteMatch` (v5) returned the match object for the current route or for a given path, so components could check whether a path matched and read params or build nested URLs. In v6 it's replaced by `useMatch(pattern)` and relative routing.
p: Used for active checks and nested URLs
r206.f: How would you highlight a tab when its route matches in v6?

r207.a: React Router doesn't animate on its own. You animate route changes by keying the outlet by location and using an animation library (Framer Motion's `AnimatePresence`), CSS transitions, or the View Transitions API, which React Router supports with `viewTransition` on links and `useViewTransitionState`.
r207.f: Why must the outgoing route stay mounted during an exit animation?

r208.a: For large apps, lazy-load route components (`lazy` in route objects or `React.lazy`), split code per route, use loaders to fetch data in parallel with code loading, define routes as configuration objects, and use nested layouts so shared UI isn't reloaded.
p: lazy route property in data routers
r208.f: How does the lazy route property avoid waterfalls?

r22.a: Siblings shouldn't talk through the router directly. Options: lift shared state to a common parent, use context or a store, put the data in the URL (params or search params) so both routes read it, or pass navigation `state` when moving from one route to another.
p: Lift state up or use a store
URL params/search params for shareable data
Location state is lost on refresh
r22.f: Why is navigation state unreliable for important data?

r23.a: After a successful login, call `navigate('/dashboard', { replace: true })`, or return to the page the user originally requested using location state saved by the auth guard. In data mode, redirect from the login action. Use `replace` so Back doesn't return to the login page.
r23.f: What should happen if a logged-in user opens /login?

r239.a: React Router listens to the URL (via the History API), matches it against your route tree, and renders the matching elements, with nested routes rendering into `<Outlet>`s. Dynamic routing means routes are defined as components or config at runtime, can include dynamic segments, and can be generated from data or loaded lazily.
p: Routes can be generated from data
r239.f: How would you generate routes from a CMS response?

r240.a: Use the `useNavigate()` hook: `navigate('/path')`, `navigate(-1)`, `navigate('/path', { replace: true, state })`. Outside components (data mode), return `redirect()` from loaders and actions.
r240.f: Why is calling navigate during render a problem?

r241.a: Let the URL be the source of truth: use `NavLink` for active styling, `useLocation`/`useMatch` to check the current route, and nested routes so layouts know which child is active. Avoid duplicating "current page" in React state.
p: URL as the source of truth
r241.f: How would you highlight a parent menu item when a child route is active?

r243.a: In v6+, pass props directly in the element: `<Route path="/user" element={<User role="admin" />} />`. For data common to many routes, use context, the `Outlet` context (`<Outlet context={...}>` and `useOutletContext()`), or loaders.
r243.f: When is Outlet context the right tool?

r283.a: Define child routes inside a parent route; the parent renders a layout with `<Outlet />`, and child paths are relative. Read parameters from any level with `useParams()`, which merges params from all matched routes.
r283.f: How would a parent loader share data with a child route?
r283.c:
<Route path="projects/:projectId" element={<Project />}>
  <Route path="tasks/:taskId" element={<Task />} />
</Route>
// In Task: const { projectId, taskId } = useParams();

r285.a: The `history` library is a low-level package for managing session history (push, replace, listen) across browsers and environments. React Router is a routing library built on top of that idea: it matches URLs to routes, renders components, handles nested layouts, links and data loading.
p: React Router: route matching and rendering
You rarely use history directly now
r285.f: Why did React Router stop exposing history directly?

r286.a: React Router v6 provides `BrowserRouter` (HTML5 history), `HashRouter` (URL hash), `MemoryRouter` (in-memory, for tests and non-browser environments), `StaticRouter` (server rendering), plus the data routers created with `createBrowserRouter`, `createHashRouter` or `createMemoryRouter` and rendered via `RouterProvider`.
r286.f: What features require a data router?

r287.a: `push(path)` adds a new entry to the history stack, so Back returns to the previous page. `replace(path)` swaps the current entry, so Back skips it. Use replace for redirects (like after login or from a default route) to avoid loops.
r287.f: What bug appears if a redirect uses push?

r288.a: Wrap protected routes in a guard: a layout route or component that checks auth state and renders `<Outlet />` or a `<Navigate to="/login" state={{ from }} replace />`. In data mode, check auth in loaders and `throw redirect('/login')` so data isn't fetched for unauthorized users. Handle loading while auth status is unknown.
r288.f: How would you add role-based guards on top of this?

r289.a: State that someone might want to share, bookmark, refresh or navigate back to belongs in the URL: current page or route, selected item id, search queries, filters, sort order, pagination and active tabs. Ephemeral UI state (open menus, hover, unsaved input) stays in React state.
r289.f: How do you keep URL state and component state in sync?

r290.a: Declarative mode is the classic `<BrowserRouter>` with `<Routes>`, handling only URL matching and navigation. Data mode (`createBrowserRouter` + `RouterProvider`) adds loaders, actions, pending UI and lazy routes outside rendering. Framework mode (React Router v7, formerly Remix) adds file-based routing conventions, SSR, code splitting, type safety and a Vite plugin.
p: Framework: full-stack features, SSR, type-safe routes
r290.f: When would you stay with declarative mode?

r37.a: React Router is the standard routing library for React. It maps URLs to components, enables navigation without full page reloads, supports nested routes and layouts, URL parameters, search params, programmatic navigation and, in data/framework modes, loaders, actions and server rendering.
r37.f: How does React Router keep the UI in sync with the URL?

r398.a: A switching component renders one of several child components depending on a value (route, tab, status). It's usually built with an object map from keys to components, or with React Router's `<Routes>` for URLs.
r398.f: Why define the map outside the component?

r413.a: Track page views when the location changes: in a component inside the router, use `useLocation()` and an effect that sends a page_view event (gtag or GA4) with `location.pathname + location.search`. GA4's enhanced measurement can also track History API changes automatically.
p: Avoid double-counting with GA4 auto tracking
r413.f: How do privacy and consent rules affect analytics setup?

r422.a: In React Router v4, a `<Router>` could only have one child element. Rendering several routes or elements directly inside it triggered the warning. Wrap them in a single element (a `div`, `Switch` or Fragment).
r422.f: How does v6 structure routes instead?

r423.a: In v4/v5, `history.push` accepts a path and a state object, or a location object with `pathname`, `search` and `state`. The receiving component reads `location.state` or `location.search`.
r423.f: When would you use search params instead of state?

r424.a: Add a catch-all route that renders the NotFound page when nothing else matches: `<Route path="*" element={<NotFound />} />` in v6, or a path-less `<Route component={NotFound} />` as the last child of `<Switch>` in v4/v5.
p: v4/v5: last route in Switch without path
r424.f: How would you show a section-specific 404 page?

r425.a: In v4, get history via the `withRouter` HOC (props.history), the render props of a Route, or by creating your own history object with the `history` package and passing it to `<Router history={history}>` so it can be imported anywhere. v5 added the `useHistory` hook.
p: Custom history object exported from a module
r425.f: Why was a custom history object useful outside components?

r491.a: React Router v4 introduced dynamic routing: routes became regular components rendered during the app's render, instead of a static config. This allowed nested routes anywhere in the tree, responsive routes, separate packages for web and native, and a simpler mental model.
r491.f: What did v6 change compared with v4's approach?

r517.a: Route-based code splitting loads each route's component only when the user navigates to it. Use `React.lazy` with `<Suspense>` for route elements, or the `lazy` property in React Router's data routes, so the initial bundle only contains what the first page needs.
r517.f: How would you prefetch the reports route on link hover?
r517.c:
const Reports = lazy(() => import('./pages/Reports'));
<Route path="/reports" element={<Suspense fallback={<Spinner />}><Reports /></Suspense>} />

r651.a: `BrowserRouter` uses the History API for clean URLs and needs server fallback configuration. `HashRouter` keeps the route in the URL hash, which works on static hosts. `MemoryRouter` keeps history in memory without touching the address bar, useful for tests, React Native or embedded widgets.
r651.f: How would you test a component that uses useParams?

r652.a: Dynamic routes have variable segments that match many URLs, declared with a colon, like `/posts/:slug`. The matched values are route parameters, available through `useParams()` or in loaders, so one component can render any post.
r652.f: What does a splat route (*) capture?

r654.a: Create a guard (layout route or wrapper) that checks authentication: if logged in, render the child routes via `<Outlet />`; if not, redirect to login with `<Navigate>` and remember the original location. In data mode, check in loaders and throw a redirect. Enforce real authorization on the server.
p: Navigate with replace and from state
r654.f: How do you avoid flashing protected content before the auth check finishes?

r656.a: In React Router's data mode, a route can define a `loader` that fetches data before the route renders (read with `useLoaderData`), and an `action` that handles form submissions and mutations (triggered by `<Form>` or `useSubmit`). Related APIs include `useFetcher`, `useNavigation` for pending states, `redirect()` and error elements; data is revalidated automatically after actions.
r656.f: How do loaders help avoid data-fetching waterfalls?
r656.c: { path: 'todos', loader: () => fetch('/api/todos'), action: async ({ request }) => { const data = await request.formData(); await createTodo(data.get('title')); return redirect('/todos'); }, element: <Todos /> }

r72.a: React Router offers BrowserRouter (History API, clean URLs), HashRouter (hash-based URLs for static hosting), MemoryRouter (in-memory, for tests and non-browser), StaticRouter (server rendering) and NativeRouter for React Native, plus data-router equivalents created with `createBrowserRouter` etc.
r72.f: Which would you choose for an app hosted on GitHub Pages?

r73.a: An `<a href>` triggers a full page load from the server. React Router's `<Link to>` renders an `<a>` but intercepts the click, updates the URL with the History API and renders the new route without reloading, preserving app state. Use `<a>` for external links.
p: Link still renders an accessible anchor
Keeps app state and is faster
r73.f: What does a Link do with modifier-key clicks (Ctrl/Cmd+click)?

r74.a: The main pieces are a router (`BrowserRouter` or `RouterProvider`), `Routes`/`Route` for defining paths, `Link`/`NavLink` for navigation, `Outlet` for nested layouts, `Navigate` for redirects, and hooks like `useParams`, `useNavigate`, `useLocation` and `useSearchParams`.

r99.a: Install the package with `npm install react-router` (v7; `react-router-dom` for v6), then wrap your app in a router like `<BrowserRouter>` or create a router with `createBrowserRouter` and render `<RouterProvider>`.
p: Framework mode uses its own setup
r99.f: What changed in package naming in React Router v7?

The server and client rendered different output. Common causes: using `Date.now()`, `Math.random()` or locale/timezone-dependent formatting during render; reading `window`, `localStorage` or `navigator` during render; different data on server and client; invalid HTML nesting (a `
` inside `

`) that the browser rewrites; and browser extensions altering the DOM. Fix by rendering deterministic output, moving browser-only logic into effects, passing the same data to both, fixing markup, and using `suppressHydrationWarning` only for intentional differences like timestamps.
p: Different data between server and client
Read browser values in effects; same data both sides
n27.f:
Why does invalid nesting like
in

cause a mismatch?

r161.a: Popular options include Redux Toolkit (structured global store), Zustand (lightweight hook-based store), Jotai and Recoil (atomic state), MobX (observables), React context with useReducer for simple cases, and TanStack Query/SWR/RTK Query for server state. In Next.js App Router, server state increasingly lives in Server Components and caching.
r161.f: What do you have to watch out for with global stores in Next.js App Router?

r322.a: Hydration is the process where React, running in the browser, attaches event handlers and state to HTML that was rendered on the server, turning static markup into an interactive app. React expects the client render to match the server HTML; mismatches cause warnings and re-rendering.
p: Client loads JS and calls hydrateRoot
React reuses DOM and attaches listeners
r322.f: What's the cost of hydration, and how do Server Components reduce it?

r325.a: Static generation (SSG) renders pages to HTML at build time, so they can be served from a CDN instantly. It's great for content that doesn't change per request (blogs, docs, marketing). Incremental static regeneration and on-demand revalidation update pages without a full rebuild.

r328.a: Read the console error, which in React 19 shows a diff of server vs client output, then find what differs: dates, random ids, locale formatting, browser-only APIs, conditional rendering on `typeof window`, user-specific data, invalid HTML nesting or extensions. Compare view-source HTML with the rendered DOM, reproduce with extensions disabled, and move client-only logic into effects or a client-only component.
p: Use React's diff in the error message
Compare server HTML with client render
Check time, locale, random and window-based code

r336.a: Use static generation for content that's the same for everyone and changes rarely (docs, marketing, blogs). Use SSR for per-request, personalized or frequently changing data that still needs SEO or fast first paint (dashboards with SEO, product pages with live stock). Use client rendering for highly interactive, authenticated apps where SEO doesn't matter. Many apps mix them per route.
r336.f: How do Server Components change this decision?

r395.a: Render the app on the server per request with `renderToPipeableStream` (or `renderToString`), send the HTML with the client bundle, and hydrate it in the browser with `hydrateRoot`. You must handle routing on the server, fetch data before or during render, serialize it for the client, and avoid browser-only code during render. Frameworks like Next.js or React Router framework mode do this for you.
p: Fetch data and pass it to the client

r42.a: With SSR, the server renders components to HTML for each request, so users and crawlers get content immediately and JavaScript then hydrates it. With client-side rendering, the server sends an almost empty HTML page and the browser builds the UI after downloading and running JavaScript. SSR improves first paint and SEO but adds server cost and complexity.
p: SSR: HTML on the server per request
CSR: HTML built in the browser
SSR: faster first content, better SEO
CSR: simpler hosting, slower first load
r42.f: What is time-to-interactive and how can SSR affect it?

r502.a: Next.js is a React framework by Vercel. Major features: file-based routing (App Router with layouts, Server Components, streaming), multiple rendering strategies (SSR, SSG, ISR, client), built-in data fetching and caching, Server Actions, API route handlers, image/font/script optimization, middleware, and zero-config bundling with Turbopack.
r502.f: How does the App Router differ from the Pages Router?

r579.a: The Pages Router (`pages/`) uses one file per route with `getServerSideProps`/`getStaticProps` for data and renders all components as client components. The App Router (`app/`) uses nested layouts, React Server Components by default, streaming with Suspense, `loading.js`/`error.js` conventions, Server Actions and fetch-based caching.
p: Data functions vs async Server Components
Client by default vs server by default
Nested layouts and streaming in App Router
r579.f: What's the hardest part of migrating to the App Router?

r601.a: `useLayoutEffect` doesn't run on the server, because there's no DOM to measure. React used to warn when it appeared in server-rendered components. Use `useEffect` if the logic isn't layout-critical, render that part only on the client, or use an isomorphic layout effect pattern (useLayoutEffect in the browser, useEffect on the server).
p: Move layout logic to client-only components
Hydrated UI may flash before layout effects run

r632.a: `renderToString` renders the whole tree to a single HTML string synchronously and waits for nothing; it doesn't support Suspense data fetching or streaming. `renderToPipeableStream` (Node streams) streams HTML progressively: it sends the shell first, then streams Suspense boundaries as their data resolves, supports selective hydration, and offers callbacks like `onShellReady` and `onAllReady`.
p: renderToString: synchronous, one string, no streaming
r632.f: Why would you wait for onAllReady when serving a search engine crawler?

n20.a: `count` is a snapshot from the current render, so all three calls compute `0 + 1` and set the same value; React batches them into one render. Use the updater form so each call receives the latest queued value.
p: All three calls use the same old count
Same applies inside timeouts and async code
n20.f: What would setCount(count + 1) followed by setCount(c => c + 1) give?

n878.a: Change the component's `key` to force React to remount it with fresh state (for example `key={userId}`), or explicitly set the state back to initial values with a reset function. For forms, a `key` change or the native form `reset()` (for uncontrolled inputs) works well.
p: Keep initial values in a constant
Avoid syncing state with props in effects
n878.f: What are the trade-offs between a key reset and manual reset?

r165.a: Both terms describe values calculated from existing state or props rather than stored separately. "Derived state" sometimes refers to the anti-pattern of copying props into state (or `getDerivedStateFromProps`), while computed values are simply calculated during render (optionally memoized). The recommendation: don't store what you can compute.
p: Compute values from state/props during render
r165.f: What bugs does storing derived values in state cause?
r165.c: const total = useMemo(() => cart.reduce((s, i) => s + i.price * i.qty, 0), [cart]);

r174.a: Event bubbling means an event fired on an element propagates up through its ancestors, triggering their handlers too. In React, call `e.stopPropagation()` in a handler to stop it from reaching parent React handlers, and `e.preventDefault()` to stop the browser's default action (they're different).
p: Events propagate from target to ancestors
React events bubble through the React tree (including portals)
r174.f: Why is stopPropagation sometimes considered a code smell?

r214.a: Props are inputs passed to a component by its parent and are read-only inside the component. State is data a component owns and can change over time with a setter, causing re-renders. Props flow down; state lives inside and can be passed down as props.
p: State can be passed to children as props
Lift state up to share it
r214.f: Can a child change its parent's state?

r215.a: Stateless components hold no state of their own: they render purely from props (also called presentational or "dumb" components). They're simple, predictable and easy to test and reuse.
r215.f: Are components using context still stateless?

r216.a: Stateful components manage their own state (with `useState`/`useReducer` or `this.state`) and re-render when it changes. They often coordinate data and logic and pass it down to stateless children.
p: Keep state as low as practical
r216.f: How do you decide which component should own a piece of state?

r220.a: `onClick={save}` passes the function itself, so React calls it when the click happens. `onClick={save()}` calls `save` immediately during render and passes its return value (often undefined) as the handler, which runs code at the wrong time and can cause infinite render loops if it sets state.
p: Can trigger infinite loops with setState
Use an arrow to pass arguments
r220.f: How do you pass an argument to save without calling it immediately?

r224.a: React decides whether to re-render by comparing references; if you mutate an object or array in place, the reference doesn't change and React may skip the update or show stale UI. Immutability also keeps previous state intact for undo/time travel, makes memoization (`memo`, `useMemo`) work, avoids bugs where shared objects change unexpectedly, and is required for concurrent rendering to stay consistent.
p: memo and selectors rely on new references
r224.f: How can Immer help you write immutable updates?

r227.a: `setState` (or a hook setter) enqueues an update and schedules a re-render. React batches pending updates, processes them in order to compute the new state, re-renders the component and its children, reconciles the new output with the previous one, commits DOM changes and then runs effects. The current render's variables don't change.
r227.f: In class components, how do you run code after the state update is applied?

r229.a: If each call uses the current value (`setCount(count + 1)` three times), they all set the same value because `count` is fixed for this render; the result is +1 and one re-render. If you use updater functions (`setCount(c => c + 1)`), React applies them in order and the result is +3, still in one batched render.
p: count variable unchanged in this render
r229.f: How would the outcome change in React 17 inside a setTimeout?

r230.a: Copy each level you change with the spread operator, leaving other references intact, or use Immer to write it as a mutation.
p: Spread every level along the path
r230.f: Why is deeply nested state a sign to restructure?
r230.c:
setUser(u => ({ ...u, address: { ...u.address, city: 'Pune' } }));
// with Immer: setUser(produce(d => { d.address.city = 'Pune'; }));

r264.a: Make sure only the latest request can update state: in the effect, set an `ignore` flag in cleanup (or abort the previous request with `AbortController`) so earlier responses that arrive late are dropped. Data libraries like TanStack Query handle this automatically by keying on the query.
r264.f: Does aborting a fetch stop the server from doing the work?

r267.a: Use discriminated unions so certain props are only allowed together, for example a Button that's either a link with `href` or a button with `onClick`, but not both. Combine with `never` to forbid props in the other branch, so invalid combinations fail at compile time.
p: Discriminated unions with a literal tag
r267.f: How would you type a component where loading and data can't both be set?

r369.a: React event names are camelCase (`onClick` instead of `onclick`), you pass functions rather than strings, you must call `preventDefault()` explicitly instead of returning false, and React wraps native events in synthetic events delegated at the root container.
r369.f: How does event delegation in React affect stopPropagation with native listeners?

r370.a: Synthetic events are React's cross-browser wrappers around native browser events. They have the same interface (`target`, `preventDefault`, `stopPropagation`) and behave consistently across browsers; the native event is available as `e.nativeEvent`. Since React 17, events are attached to the root container rather than `document`, and event pooling was removed.
r370.f: Why did React remove event pooling?

r390.a: React events use camelCase names, take function handlers, require explicit `preventDefault()`, use synthetic event objects that normalize browser differences, and are delegated from the root container. Some events behave differently, such as `onChange` firing on every keystroke for inputs (like native `input`).
p: onChange behaves like native input event
r390.f: Why does React's onChange differ from the native change event?

r399.a: React supports Pointer Events: `onPointerDown`, `onPointerMove`, `onPointerUp`, `onPointerCancel`, `onGotPointerCapture`, `onLostPointerCapture`, `onPointerEnter`, `onPointerLeave`, `onPointerOver` and `onPointerOut`. They unify mouse, touch and pen input.

r486.a: Avoid setting state when the value hasn't changed (React bails out for identical values with `Object.is`, but mutated objects look identical), keep state minimal, avoid storing derived data, use functional updates, and in classes implement `shouldComponentUpdate` or use `PureComponent`; in function components use `React.memo` for children.
r486.f: Why does setting state to a new identical object still re-render?

r503.a: Pass the function as a prop, like `<Button onPress={handleSave} />`, and the child calls it from its own event handler. Name handler props `onSomething` and handler functions `handleSomething` by convention.
p: Functions are passed like any prop
Child calls the prop on events
Wrap in an arrow to pass arguments
useCallback if the child is memoized
r503.f: Why name props onX rather than handleX?
r503.c:
function Parent() { const handleDelete = id => remove(id); return <Item onDelete={handleDelete} />; }
function Item({ onDelete }) { return <button onClick={() => onDelete(42)}>Delete</button>; }

r504.a: Use throttling or debouncing (lodash `throttle`/`debounce` or custom hooks) for rapid events, disable the button while an async operation is in flight, or use a `once` wrapper or a ref flag to ensure a function runs only once.
p: Throttle for "at most every N ms"
Keep the debounced function stable with useMemo/useRef
r504.f: Why must a debounced function be memoized in a component?

r505.a: JSX escapes any values embedded with `{}` before rendering, converting characters like `<` and `&` into text, so user input can't inject HTML or scripts. You can still introduce XSS through `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`, `javascript:` URLs in `href`, or unsafe third-party code.
r505.f: How can an href attribute still be an XSS vector?

r562.a: Use non-mutating operations that return new arrays: spread (`[...arr, item]`), `map`, `filter`, `slice`, `concat`, and the newer `toSorted`, `toReversed`, `toSpliced` and `with`. Copy before using mutating methods like `sort`, `reverse`, `splice` or `push`, or use Immer.
p: Object.freeze in dev to catch mutations
r562.f: What's the difference between slice and splice?

r563.a: Events have a capture phase (from the root down to the target) before the bubble phase (back up). In React you handle the capture phase by adding `Capture` to the event name, like `onClickCapture`, which runs on ancestors before the target's handlers, useful for logging or intercepting events.
p: Fires even if a child stops propagation in bubble phase
r563.f: When would you use a capture handler instead of a bubbling one?

r567.a: Treat objects in state as immutable: create a new object with the spread syntax containing the changed fields (and copy nested objects you change), then pass it to the setter. Use Immer for deep structures.
r567.f: What happens if you write form.email = 'x'; setForm(form)?

r568.a: Create new arrays instead of mutating: add with `[...arr, item]`, remove with `filter`, replace with `map`, insert with `slice`/`toSpliced`, and sort a copy (`[...arr].sort()` or `toSorted`). If items are objects, copy the item you change too.
p: Update: map with a new object
r568.f: Why must you copy the object inside map as well?
r568.c: setItems(items => items.map(i => i.id === id ? { ...i, qty: i.qty + 1 } : i));

r569.a: Immer lets you write updates as if mutating a "draft" copy; it records the changes and produces a new immutable object with structural sharing. Use `produce` with `useState`, the `useImmer` hook, or Redux Toolkit, which uses Immer internally.
p: Mutate a draft, get a new immutable result
r569.f: What's the performance cost of Immer?

n29.a: Use React Testing Library with a mocked network layer (MSW or a mocked fetch). Render the component and assert the spinner appears (`getByRole('progressbar')` or text), then await the list with `findByRole`/`findByText`. For the error case, make the mock return an error and await the error message. Assert what the user sees, not implementation details.
p: Separate test for the error path
n29.f: Why is MSW better than mocking fetch directly?

r195.a: Reducers are pure functions, so test them directly: call the reducer with a state and an action and assert the returned state. Action creators can be tested by checking the returned object. For thunks, mock the API (or use MSW), dispatch to a real store and assert the resulting state rather than the exact action sequence.
p: Reducers: input state + action → expected state
Thunks: real store with mocked API
r195.f: Why test thunks with a real store instead of mocking dispatch?

r198.a: Test components that use hooks like any component: render them with React Testing Library, interact through the UI and assert results. For custom hooks, use `renderHook` from `@testing-library/react`, and wrap updates with `act` (Testing Library does this for its helpers).

r198.f: When should you test a hook directly rather than through a component?

r244.a: Use a mix of unit/component tests with Jest or Vitest plus React Testing Library (render components, interact like a user, assert visible output), integration tests across several components with mocked APIs (MSW), and end-to-end tests with Playwright or Cypress for critical user flows. Add type checking and linting as cheap safety nets.
p: Static checks with TypeScript and ESLint
r244.f: How do you decide what deserves an end-to-end test?

r245.a: Jest is a JavaScript testing framework with a test runner, assertion library (`expect`), mocking (`jest.fn`, `jest.mock`), fake timers, snapshot testing and coverage. For React it's combined with jsdom and React Testing Library to render components and assert on the output.
r245.f: How does Vitest compare with Jest?

r246.a: React Testing Library renders components into a DOM and provides queries that find elements the way users do (by role, label, text), plus utilities to fire events or simulate typing with user-event. Its philosophy is to test behaviour rather than implementation details.

r247.a: `getBy*` returns the element or throws if it's missing (use for elements that should be there now). `queryBy*` returns null if missing (use to assert absence). `findBy*` returns a promise that waits for the element to appear (use for async UI). The `*AllBy` variants return arrays.
p: getBy: must exist now, throws otherwise
queryBy: null if absent, for negative assertions
findBy: async, waits up to a timeout
r247.f: When would you use waitFor instead of findBy?

r301.a: Use `findBy*` queries or `waitFor` to wait for UI changes, mock network calls (MSW) so responses are controlled, use fake timers for timeouts and debounce, and make sure promises resolve inside `act` (Testing Library's async helpers handle this).
r301.f: What causes "not wrapped in act(...)" warnings?

r302.a: Prefer Mock Service Worker (MSW), which intercepts requests at the network level so components use their real fetching code. Alternatives are mocking `fetch`/axios with `jest.fn` or mocking your API module with `jest.mock`. Reset mocks between tests.
r302.f: How do you simulate a slow or failing network with MSW?

r303.f: How would you test a hook that depends on a context?

r304.a: Snapshot testing renders a component and saves its output (DOM or serialized tree) to a file; later runs compare against it and fail if it changed. It catches unexpected UI changes, but large snapshots are easy to approve blindly, so keep them small and focused.
p: Not a replacement for behaviour tests
r304.f: What makes a snapshot test brittle?

r305.a: Render the component inside the real provider (or a test provider) with the values you want, often via a custom `render` helper or the `wrapper` option, then assert behaviour. Avoid mocking `useContext` directly.
r305.f: How would you build a reusable renderWithProviders helper?

Wrap in Provider via a helper

r307.a: Use fake timers (`jest.useFakeTimers()` or `vi.useFakeTimers()`), type into the input, then advance time with `jest.advanceTimersByTime(delay)` inside `act`, and assert the debounced effect happened. With user-event, configure it to use the fake timers (`advanceTimers: jest.advanceTimersByTime`).

r339.a: The shallow renderer (`react-test-renderer/shallow`) rendered a component only one level deep, without rendering child components or touching the DOM, so you could assert on its direct output. It's deprecated; React Testing Library's full rendering is the recommended approach.
r339.f: Why did the community move away from shallow rendering?

r340.a: Shallow rendering renders only the component itself, leaving children as placeholders, which isolates units but tests implementation details and misses integration bugs. Full DOM rendering (React Testing Library or Enzyme's mount) renders the whole tree into a DOM, runs effects and lets you interact like a user, giving more realistic confidence.
p: Shallow: isolated, one level, no DOM
Full: entire tree, real DOM, effects run
r340.f: How would you isolate a component with an expensive child in a full render?

r341.a: `react-test-renderer` rendered React components to plain JavaScript objects without a DOM, useful for snapshot tests and React Native. It's deprecated as of React 19; use React Testing Library (or React Native Testing Library) instead.

r341.f: What's the replacement for snapshot tests built on it?

p: Any JS value, including functions and elements

r217.a: PropTypes (`prop-types` package) let you declare the expected types of a component's props and warn in development when they don't match. They're runtime-only and removed from React's core checks in React 19, so TypeScript is the recommended approach.
r217.f: What can PropTypes check that TypeScript can't?

r385.f: How would you introduce TypeScript gradually into a JS codebase?

p: Copy into state only when you need independent edits
r410.f: How do you edit a value that came in as a prop?

r463.a: Flow is a static type checker for JavaScript created by Meta. You add type annotations and it reports type errors without running the code. It's similar to TypeScript but much less widely used today.
r463.f: Why did TypeScript win over Flow in popularity?

r464.a: Flow checks types statically at build time across your whole codebase, while PropTypes checks only component props at runtime in development. Flow catches errors earlier and covers all code; PropTypes can validate data coming in at runtime but only warns.

r464.f: Is there any reason to use both?

n101.a: Walk both sorted arrays with two pointers: if the values match, add it (skipping duplicates) and advance both; otherwise advance the pointer with the smaller value. This is O(m + n) time and O(1) extra space besides the output.
p: Skip duplicates if unique output wanted
n101.f: What if one array is huge and the other tiny?

n102.a: Assign each node a column: root is 0, left child is col - 1, right child is col + 1. Do a BFS (so higher nodes come first within a column), group values by column in a map, then output columns sorted from leftmost to rightmost. O(n log n) for sorting columns, or O(n) by tracking min/max column.
n102.f: Why does DFS need extra information to produce the same order?

n103.a: The simple approach merges both arrays (O(m + n)) and picks the middle. The optimal approach binary-searches a partition in the smaller array so that left halves of both arrays contain half the elements and every left value ≤ every right value, giving O(log(min(m, n))).
p: Left max ≤ right min on both sides
n103.f: Why binary search on the smaller array?

n109.a: Implement long division on decimal strings: scale both numbers to integers (track decimal places), then divide digit by digit like on paper, using BigInt-free string arithmetic or BigInt for the integer parts, and stop at a precision limit, applying rounding and the sign at the end.
p: Stop at a precision and round
n109.f: How would you implement this without BigInt at all?

n110.a: Treat decimals as integers: remove the decimal points, multiply the digit strings (schoolbook multiplication or BigInt), then insert the decimal point at (decimals of a + decimals of b) places from the right and fix the sign.
p: Total decimal places = sum of both
n110.f: How does schoolbook multiplication on digit arrays work?

n111.a: Align both numbers on the decimal point by padding the fractional parts to equal length, compare magnitudes to decide the sign, subtract the smaller from the larger digit by digit with borrowing, then reinsert the decimal point and trim zeros.
p: Pad fractional parts to the same length
Handle negative inputs by converting to addition
n111.f: How would you do the borrow manually without BigInt?

n112.a: Pad both numbers so their integer and fractional parts have equal length, then add digits from right to left with a carry, placing the decimal point back in the same position. Handle signs by turning mixed-sign addition into subtraction.
p: Add right to left with carry
n112.f: What changes when one number is negative?

n114.a: Evaluate the expression by tokenizing numbers, operators and parentheses, then parse with operator precedence: either the shunting-yard algorithm (convert to postfix, then evaluate with a stack) or a recursive-descent parser (expression → term → factor). Handle unary minus and invalid input.
n114.f: Why should you never solve this with eval()?

n118.a: A number n > 1 is prime if no integer from 2 up to √n divides it. Handle small cases first, skip even numbers, and only test odd divisors up to the square root: O(√n).
n118.f: How would you find all primes up to N efficiently?

n126.a: The common version (LeetCode "Remove Duplicate Letters") asks for the smallest lexicographic string containing each letter once. Use a monotonic stack: for each char, skip if already in the stack; otherwise pop larger chars from the stack if they appear again later, then push. O(n).
p: Pop larger chars that appear later
n126.f: How is this different from simply keeping first occurrences?

n128.a: Serialize with a preorder traversal, writing a marker (like `#`) for null children, joined by commas. Deserialize by reading the tokens in the same preorder, recursively building left and right subtrees. Both are O(n).
p: Recursively rebuild in the same order

n129.a: Use fast exponentiation (exponentiation by squaring): x^n = (x^(n/2))² for even n and x · x^(n-1) for odd n, which takes O(log n) multiplications. Handle negative exponents by computing 1 / x^|n|, and 0 exponents as 1.
n129.f: Why use Math.floor instead of n >> 1 for large exponents?

n130.a: Use a queue (only enqueue, dequeue, peek, size). To push x, enqueue it and then rotate the queue size-1 times (dequeue and re-enqueue) so x is at the front; pop and peek then just use the front. Push is O(n), pop O(1).
n130.f: Which version would you choose if pushes are much more frequent?

n131.a: The largest difference between any two numbers is simply max − min, found in one pass (O(n)). If the problem requires the larger element to come after the smaller one (like stock profit), track the minimum so far and the best difference while scanning.
p: Handle arrays with fewer than 2 elements
n131.f: How would you avoid spreading a very large array into Math.max?

n132.a: Use a Set: for each number, check if its negation was seen before; if yes, return the pair, otherwise add it. This is O(n) time. Sorting with two pointers is the O(n log n), O(1)-space alternative.
n132.f: How does this generalize to any target sum?

n135.a: Use binary search on the integer answer between 0 and x, checking mid * mid against x, to find the floor of the square root in O(log x). For decimals, continue binary search to a precision or use Newton's method (r = (r + x/r) / 2), which converges quickly.
n135.f: How would Newton's method look for this?

n136.a: Push opening brackets onto a stack; for each closing bracket, check that the stack's top is the matching opener and pop it. The string is valid if all closers match and the stack is empty at the end. O(n).
p: Stack must be empty at the end
n136.f: How would you return the length of the longest valid substring?

n147.a: Swap every node's left and right children, recursively (or with a queue). Each node is visited once, so it's O(n) time and O(h) stack space.
n147.f: How would you check whether two trees are mirrors of each other?

n151.a: Use a sliding window with a map of each character's last index. Move the right pointer through the string; when a repeated character is inside the window, move the left pointer just past its previous position. Track the longest window. O(n).
n151.f: How does this change if you need the length of the longest substring with at most k distinct characters?

n152.a: Compute Fibonacci iteratively with two variables (O(n) time, O(1) space) rather than naive recursion, which is O(2^n). For very large n, use matrix exponentiation or fast doubling in O(log n), and BigInt to avoid precision loss.
n152.f: How would you write the memoized recursive version?

n156.a: Merge all busy intervals: sort them by start time, merge overlaps, then the gaps between merged intervals (within the day's bounds) are the free slots. O(n log n) for sorting.
n156.f: How would you require a minimum meeting length?

n157.a: To merge k sorted arrays, either repeatedly merge pairs (divide and conquer, O(N log k)) or use a min-heap holding the next element of each array (O(N log k)). For two arrays, use two pointers in O(m + n).
p: Simple concat + sort is O(N log N)
n157.f: Why is reducing pairwise from left to right slower than divide and conquer?

n163.a: Subtract two non-negative integer strings digit by digit from right to left with a borrow, assuming the first is larger (or compare first and add a minus sign), then strip leading zeros.
p: Compare magnitudes to decide the sign
Borrow when a digit is smaller
n163.f: How would you extend this to signed inputs?

n172.a: Use a Set to keep unique values in order: `[...new Set(arr)]`, O(n). For objects, keep a Set of keys and filter. If you must do it in place on a sorted array, use two pointers.
p: In-place two pointers for sorted arrays
n172.f: Does Set treat NaN and objects correctly?
n172.c:
const unique = arr => [...new Set(arr)];
const uniqueBy = (arr, key) => { const seen = new Set(); return arr.filter(x => !seen.has(x[key]) && seen.add(x[key])); };

n176.a: Add two non-negative integer strings from right to left, summing digits plus a carry, prepending each result digit and carrying 1 when the sum is 10 or more.
n176.f: How would you support negative numbers?

n183.a: Find all occurrences of the keywords (case-insensitive), merge overlapping or adjacent ranges, then build the result by wrapping each merged range in a tag like `<em>`, escaping the rest. Merging ranges avoids nested or broken tags.
p: Collect match ranges for each keyword
n183.f: Why merge adjacent ranges as well as overlapping ones?

n187.a: Find the first index of an element strictly greater than the target (upper bound) using binary search: when `arr[mid] <= target` move right, else record mid and move left. The element right after the target is at that index (or undefined if none).
p: Clarify: after last occurrence of target
n187.f: How would you write the "element right before target" variant?

n188.a: Binary search for the target, but when you find it, record the index and keep searching the right half to find a later occurrence. Returns the last index or -1, in O(log n).
p: Don't stop at the first match
Mirror version finds the first index
n188.f: How would you count occurrences of target in O(log n)?

n191.a: Options: sort and pick (O(n log n)), keep a min-heap of size k (O(n log k)), or Quickselect, which partitions like quicksort but recurses into one side only (average O(n), worst O(n²), mitigated with random pivots).
p: Min-heap of size k: O(n log k)
k-th largest = index n - k in ascending order
n191.f: When would the heap approach be better than Quickselect?

n192.a: Selection sort repeatedly finds the minimum of the unsorted part and swaps it into place at the start. It's O(n²) comparisons regardless of input but does at most n − 1 swaps; it's not stable.

n193.a: Quick sort picks a pivot, partitions the array so smaller elements go left and larger go right, then recursively sorts both parts. Average O(n log n), worst O(n²) on bad pivots (mitigate with random or median-of-three pivots); in-place and not stable.
p: Average O(n log n), worst O(n²)
n193.f: How does three-way partitioning help with many duplicates?

n194.a: Insertion sort builds a sorted prefix: take the next element and shift larger elements right until you find its spot, then insert it. O(n²) worst case, but O(n) for nearly sorted data; stable and in-place.
p: Good for small or nearly sorted arrays
n194.f: Why do hybrid sorts like Timsort use insertion sort for small runs?

n195.a: Merge sort splits the array in halves, recursively sorts each, then merges the two sorted halves. It's O(n log n) in all cases, stable, but uses O(n) extra space.
n195.f: Why is merge sort preferred for linked lists?

n196.a: Bubble sort repeatedly passes through the array swapping adjacent elements that are out of order, so the largest values "bubble" to the end. O(n²) in general; with an early exit when a pass makes no swaps it's O(n) on sorted input. Stable.
p: Largest settles at the end each pass
n196.f: Is bubble sort ever a good choice in practice?

n199.a: Binary search on a sorted array of unique values: compare the target with the middle element and discard half each step until found or the range is empty. O(log n).
n199.f: What changes if the array has duplicates and you want the first index?

n211.a: Given `items` and `newOrder` where `newOrder[i]` is the new index of `items[i]`, either build a new array (`result[newOrder[i]] = items[i]`) in O(n) with O(n) space, or do it in place by following cycles: swap items and indexes until each position holds the right element.
p: Simple: new array by target index
Swap both items and indexes together
n211.f: Why does the cycle approach terminate?

n212.a: Implement a priority queue with a binary heap stored in an array: `add` pushes to the end and sifts up, `poll` swaps the root with the last item, pops it and sifts down. Both are O(log n), `peek` is O(1). Accept a comparator for min or max ordering.
p: Sift up on insert, sift down on removal
n212.f: How would you support changing an item's priority?

n225.a: Given `isBad(version)` where all versions after the first bad one are also bad, binary search for the first bad version: if mid is bad, the answer is mid or earlier; otherwise it's later. O(log n) calls.
n225.f: What other problems reduce to "binary search on a predicate"?

n65.a: This simulates CSS Grid's auto-placement with `grid-auto-flow: row dense`: place items in order, but for each item scan from the start of the grid for the first free area big enough for its span, filling holes left by earlier items. Maintain an occupancy matrix, growing rows as needed.
p: Dense: restart search from the top-left for each item
Check that the whole span fits
Sparse mode keeps a moving cursor instead
n65.f: How does sparse placement differ from dense?

n66.a: Uncompressing strings like `3(ab2(c))` → `abccabccabcc` uses a stack: push the current string and repeat count when you see `(`, and on `)` pop and append the repeated inner string to the previous one. Multi-digit counts must be parsed fully.
n66.f: What happens if a count is missing before a parenthesis?

n70.a: This variant of LRU (like Chrome's storage eviction) evicts least recently used origins when total size exceeds a limit, rather than when an item count is exceeded. Track each entry's size and use a Map (insertion order = recency): on access, delete and re-insert; on insert, add size and evict from the oldest end until under the limit, skipping entries that are currently in use if required.
p: Handle items too large to fit
n70.f: What should happen if a single item exceeds the total quota?

n71.a: Move all zeros to the end while keeping the order of non-zero elements, in place: keep a write pointer for the next non-zero position, copy each non-zero there, then fill the rest with zeros (or swap as you go). O(n) time, O(1) space.
p: Fill or swap zeros to the end
Minimize writes by swapping only when needed
n71.f: How would you move zeros to the front instead?

n72.a: For unsorted arrays, count elements of one array in a Map, then walk the other array and collect elements whose count is positive, decrementing as you go (keeps duplicates as many times as they appear in both). O(m + n) time. For a unique result, use Sets.
n72.f: How would you do this with very limited memory?

n73.a: Validate whether a string is a valid number (integers, decimals, optional sign, exponent like `1e-5`). A regular expression is the cleanest: optional sign, digits with optional decimal part (or a leading-dot decimal), and an optional exponent with optional sign and digits. A state machine is the manual alternative.

n74.a: The common "remove characters" problem removes all `b`s and any `ac` pairs, including pairs formed after earlier removals. Use a stack: skip `b`, and when the current char is `c` and the stack top is `a`, pop instead of pushing. O(n).
n74.f: Why can't a single replace() call handle this?

n742.a: Implement a stack (LIFO) with `push`, `pop`, `peek`, `isEmpty` and `length`. A JavaScript array's `push`/`pop` already give O(1) operations at the end, so wrap one in a class.
p: push/pop at the end are O(1)
n742.f: How would you implement a min-stack with O(1) getMin?

n743.a: Count the 1 bits (Hamming weight). The neat trick is `n &= n - 1`, which clears the lowest set bit, so loop until n is 0 and count iterations. Use `>>> 0` to treat the number as unsigned.
p: n & (n - 1) clears the lowest set bit
n743.f: How would you count bits for every number from 0 to n efficiently?

n744.a: Find duplicates with a Set of seen values: when a value is already seen, add it to a duplicates set. O(n) time and space. If values are in range 1..n, you can mark visited positions by negating elements for O(1) extra space.
n744.f: How would you just return whether any duplicate exists?

n745.a: For numbers 0..n with one missing, the missing value is the expected sum n(n+1)/2 minus the actual sum, or XOR all indices and values. Both are O(n) time and O(1) space.
n745.f: How would you find two missing numbers?

n746.a: For a single buy and sell (max profit), scan once tracking the lowest price so far and the best profit `price - minPrice`. O(n) time, O(1) space.
n746.f: How would you allow unlimited transactions?

n747.a: Find indices of two numbers that add up to the target: store each number's index in a Map, and for each element check if `target - x` is already present. O(n) time.
n747.f: Why check before inserting the current number?

n748.a: Two strings are anagrams if they contain the same characters with the same counts. Compare lengths, then count characters with a map (increment for one string, decrement for the other) and check all counts are zero. O(n).
n748.f: How would you handle Unicode and case-insensitivity?

n749.a: The maximum depth of a binary tree is 1 + the larger depth of its two subtrees, with an empty tree having depth 0. Recursion is O(n); BFS counting levels avoids deep recursion.
n749.f: How would you compute the minimum depth instead?
n749.c: const maxDepth = node => node ? 1 + Math.max(maxDepth(node.left), maxDepth(node.right)) : 0;

n750.a: Flipping (inverting) a binary tree swaps each node's left and right children throughout the tree, recursively or with a queue. O(n).
n750.f: How would you check if a tree is symmetric?

n751.a: The number of ways to climb n stairs taking 1 or 2 steps follows the Fibonacci pattern: ways(n) = ways(n-1) + ways(n-2), with ways(1)=1, ways(2)=2. Compute iteratively in O(n) time and O(1) space.
n751.f: How does this change if you can take 1, 2 or 3 steps?

n752.a: Check balanced brackets with a stack: push openers, and for each closer verify it matches the top before popping. The string is balanced if every closer matched and the stack is empty at the end.
n752.f: How would you find the minimum additions to make it balanced?

n753.a: Two binary trees are equal if both are empty, or both roots have the same value and their left subtrees and right subtrees are equal, checked recursively. O(n).
n753.f: How would you check if one tree is a subtree of another?
n753.c: const isSameTree = (a, b) => !a || !b ? a === b : a.value === b.value && isSameTree(a.left, b.left) && isSameTree(a.right, b.right);

n754.a: Counting bits for every number 0..n can be done with DP in O(n): `bits[i] = bits[i >> 1] + (i & 1)`, reusing the count of i without its last bit.
n754.f: Why does i >> 1 already have a known count?

n755.a: Reverse the bits of a 32-bit unsigned integer by building the result bit by bit: shift the result left, add the lowest bit of n, shift n right, 32 times. Use `>>> 0` to keep it unsigned.

n756.a: Reverse a singly linked list iteratively with three pointers (prev, current, next): point each node's next to prev while walking the list. O(n) time, O(1) space; return the old tail as the new head.
p: Reverse the link at each step
n756.f: How would you reverse only the nodes between positions m and n?

n757.a: Check a palindrome by comparing characters from both ends moving inward, usually after normalizing (lowercase, remove non-alphanumeric). O(n) time, O(1) extra space.
p: Avoid creating reversed copies if memory matters
n757.f: How would you allow deleting at most one character?

n758.a: Use Floyd's tortoise and hare: move one pointer by one step and another by two. If they ever meet, there's a cycle; if the fast pointer reaches null, there isn't. O(n) time, O(1) space.
p: Fast reaching null means no cycle
Set of visited nodes is the O(n)-space alternative
n758.f: How do you find the node where the cycle starts?

n759.a: A tree `sub` is a subtree of `root` if, at some node in root, the tree starting there is identical to `sub`. Traverse root and run an `isSameTree` check at each node: O(m·n) worst case; serialization with string matching can make it O(m + n).
p: Traverse every node of the main tree
Null subtree is always a subtree
n759.f: Why must serialization include null markers for this to work?
n759.c:
const same = (a, b) => !a || !b ? a === b : a.value === b.value && same(a.left, b.left) && same(a.right, b.right);
const isSubtree = (root, sub) => !sub || (!!root && (same(root, sub) || isSubtree(root.left, sub) || isSubtree(root.right, sub)));

n76.a: Convert an integer to Roman numerals greedily: list values with their symbols from largest to smallest, including subtractive forms (900 CM, 400 CD, 90 XC, 40 XL, 9 IX, 4 IV), and repeatedly subtract the largest value that fits while appending its symbol.
n76.f: How would you convert Roman numerals back to integers?

n760.a: Merge two sorted linked lists by walking both with a dummy head, always attaching the smaller current node and advancing that list, then attaching whatever remains. O(m + n) time, O(1) extra space.
n760.f: How would you merge k sorted lists efficiently?

n761.a: "Meeting Calendar" usually asks whether one person can attend all meetings. Sort the intervals by start time and check whether any meeting starts before the previous one ends. O(n log n).
p: Compare each start with the previous end
n761.f: How would you find the minimum number of rooms needed instead?

n762.a: Build the result with prefix and suffix products without division: first pass stores the product of everything to the left of each index, second pass multiplies by the product of everything to the right. O(n) time, O(1) extra space besides the output.
n762.f: Why is the division approach problematic?

n764.a: Implement a binary search tree where each node's left subtree has smaller values and right subtree has larger values. Insert and search walk left or right from the root, O(h) where h is the height (O(log n) if balanced, O(n) if skewed). Deletion handles three cases: leaf, one child, two children (replace with the in-order successor).
p: Delete: leaf, one child, two children
Balanced trees (AVL, red-black) keep h = O(log n)
n764.f: How would you delete a node with two children?

n765.a: A binary tree is a structure where each node has at most two children. Typical tasks: implement node creation and traversals (pre-order, in-order, post-order with recursion, level-order with a queue), compute height, count nodes, and search.
p: BFS level order with a queue
n765.f: How would you do in-order traversal iteratively?
n765.c:
function inorder(node, out = []) { if (node) { inorder(node.left, out); out.push(node.value); inorder(node.right, out); } return out; }
function levelOrder(root) { const out = [], q = root ? [root] : []; while (q.length) { const n = q.shift(); out.push(n.value); n.left && q.push(n.left); n.right && q.push(n.right); } return out; }

n766.a: Breadth-first search explores a graph level by level using a queue: start from a node, mark it visited, then repeatedly dequeue a node and enqueue its unvisited neighbours. It finds shortest paths in unweighted graphs. O(V + E).
n766.f: Why mark nodes visited when enqueuing rather than when dequeuing?

n767.a: Depth-first search explores as far as possible along each branch before backtracking, using recursion or an explicit stack, marking nodes visited. It's used for connectivity, cycle detection, topological sort and path finding. O(V + E).
n767.f: When could recursion overflow the stack and how would you avoid it?

n768.a: Heap sort builds a max-heap from the array (heapify in O(n)), then repeatedly swaps the root (largest) with the last unsorted element and sifts the new root down. O(n log n) time, O(1) extra space, not stable.
n768.f: Why is building the heap O(n) rather than O(n log n)?

n769.a: An undirected graph with n nodes is a tree if it has exactly n − 1 edges and is fully connected (which together imply no cycles). Check the edge count, then run DFS/BFS or union-find from one node and confirm all nodes are reached.
n769.f: Why does n - 1 edges plus no cycles guarantee connectivity?

n77.a: When every number appears twice except one, XOR all numbers: pairs cancel out (x ^ x = 0) and the single number remains. O(n) time, O(1) space.
p: Hash map alternative uses O(n) space
n77.f: What if every other number appears three times?
n77.c: const singleNumber = nums => nums.reduce((a, b) => a ^ b, 0);

n770.a: For "trapping rain water", water above each bar is min(max left, max right) − height. Use two pointers from both ends, tracking leftMax and rightMax, moving the side with the smaller max and adding trapped water as you go. O(n) time, O(1) space. (If it's "container with most water", move the shorter wall inward and track the max area.)
p: Water at i = min(maxLeft, maxRight) - h[i]
Move the side with the smaller max
n770.f: Why is it safe to move the pointer on the side with the smaller height?

n771.a: Implement a FIFO queue with `enqueue`, `dequeue`, `front` and `size`. `Array.shift()` is O(n), so for efficiency keep a head index (or a linked list) so dequeue is O(1).
n771.f: How would you implement a queue with two stacks?

n772.a: Dijkstra's algorithm finds shortest paths from a source in a graph with non-negative edge weights. Keep a distance map (source 0, others Infinity) and a min-priority queue; repeatedly take the closest unvisited node and relax its edges. O((V + E) log V) with a heap.
n772.f: Why doesn't Dijkstra work with negative edge weights?

n773.a: Implement a singly linked list with nodes `{ value, next }` and operations like `insertHead`, `insertTail`, `insertAt`, `remove`, `find`, `toArray` and `length`, keeping head (and optionally tail) pointers so head/tail insertions are O(1).
n773.f: When is a linked list better than an array?

n774.a: Topological sort orders the nodes of a directed acyclic graph so every edge goes from earlier to later. Kahn's algorithm: compute in-degrees, queue nodes with in-degree 0, repeatedly output one and decrement its neighbours' in-degrees. If not all nodes are output, there's a cycle. O(V + E).
n774.f: Where do build tools use topological sorting?

n775.a: Do BFS with a queue, processing one level at a time: record the queue's current size, dequeue that many nodes into a level array, enqueuing their children. Returns a list of levels. O(n).
n775.f: How would you return the rightmost node of each level?

n776.a: Kadane's algorithm: scan the array keeping the best sum of a subarray ending at the current index (`cur = max(x, cur + x)`) and the overall best. O(n) time, O(1) space.
p: Extend or restart at each element
Track indices for the subarray itself
n776.f: How would you return the start and end indices?

n777.a: In a rotated sorted array, binary search for the minimum: compare the middle with the right end; if mid > right, the minimum is to the right of mid, otherwise it's at mid or to the left. O(log n).
n777.f: How do duplicates break the O(log n) guarantee?

n778.a: Modified binary search: at each step one half of the range is sorted. Check which half is sorted, and whether the target lies within it; if so search that half, otherwise search the other. O(log n).
p: Check if target is in the sorted half
n778.f: How would you find the rotation point first and then search?

n779.a: Track both the maximum and minimum product ending at each position, because multiplying by a negative number turns the minimum into the maximum. At each step, compute candidates from x, x·max and x·min. O(n).
n779.f: Why isn't Kadane's algorithm alone enough here?

n780.a: In-order traversal of a BST visits values in sorted order, so traverse in-order (iteratively with a stack) and stop at the k-th visited node. O(h + k) time.
p: Augment nodes with subtree sizes for repeated queries
n780.f: How would you support frequent inserts and kth queries?

n781.a: In a BST, start at the root: if both values are smaller, go left; if both are larger, go right; otherwise the current node is the lowest common ancestor. O(h).
n781.f: How would you find the LCA in a general binary tree?

n782.a: Scan the grid; whenever you find land ('1') that hasn't been visited, increment the island count and flood-fill (DFS or BFS) all connected land to mark it visited. O(rows × cols).
n782.f: How would you solve it without mutating the input?

n783.a: Use two pointers with a dummy head: move the fast pointer n steps ahead, then move both until fast reaches the end; slow is then just before the node to remove, so skip it. One pass, O(L).
p: Dummy node handles removing the head
n783.f: Why move fast n + 1 steps instead of n?

n784.a: Count paths from top-left to bottom-right moving only right or down. DP: paths to a cell = paths from above + paths from the left, first row and column are 1. O(m × n) time, O(n) space with a single row. Mathematically it's C(m+n−2, m−1).
n784.f: How would obstacles change the solution?

n785.a: If a cell is 0, set its entire row and column to 0. Record which rows and columns contain zeros (sets, or use the first row/column as markers for O(1) space), then zero them in a second pass. O(m × n).
p: O(1) space with first row/col markers
n785.f: Why can't you zero cells during the first scan?

n786.a: Sort intervals by start, then iterate: if the current interval overlaps the last merged one (start ≤ last end), extend the last end; otherwise push it as a new interval. O(n log n).
p: Compare with the last merged interval
n786.f: How would you insert a single new interval into an already merged list?

n787.a: Return the k most frequent elements: count frequencies with a Map, then either sort entries by count (O(n log n)), use a min-heap of size k (O(n log k)), or bucket sort by frequency for O(n).
p: Bucket sort by count for O(n)
n787.f: Why is the bucket approach linear?

n788.a: This is "House Robber": you can't take adjacent houses, maximize the total. DP: best at i = max(best at i−1, best at i−2 + value[i]). O(n) time, O(1) space with two variables.
n788.f: How do you handle the circular street version?

n789.a: Reorder a list L0→Ln→L1→Ln−1…: find the middle with slow/fast pointers, reverse the second half, then merge the two halves alternately. O(n) time, O(1) space.
p: Split the list cleanly at the middle
n789.f: How would you do this with an array instead, and what's the trade-off?

n790.a: Add two integers without `+` using bit operations: XOR gives the sum without carries, AND shifted left gives the carries. Repeat until there's no carry. Works for negatives with 32-bit integers in JS.
n790.f: Why does this terminate for negative numbers in JavaScript?

n791.a: Find all unique triplets summing to zero (3Sum): sort the array, fix one element, then use two pointers on the rest to find pairs summing to its negation, skipping duplicates. O(n²).
p: Fix i, two pointers for the rest
n791.f: How would you generalize this to kSum?

n792.a: Find all combinations of candidates (reusable) that sum to a target using backtracking: try each candidate from the current index onward, subtract it from the remaining target, recurse, and backtrack. Sorting lets you stop early when a candidate exceeds the remainder.
p: Reuse allowed: recurse with the same index
n792.f: How does the code change if each candidate can be used only once?

n793.a: "Course Dependency" is Course Schedule: can you finish all courses given prerequisite pairs? That's checking whether the directed graph has a cycle. Use Kahn's topological sort (count processed nodes) or DFS with visiting/visited states. O(V + E).
n793.f: How would you return a valid course order?

n794.a: Put all numbers in a Set, then for each number that starts a sequence (num − 1 isn't in the set), count upward while num + 1 exists. Each number is visited a constant number of times, so it's O(n).
p: Only start counting at sequence starts
n794.f: Why does skipping non-starts keep it linear?

n795.a: The O(n log n) approach keeps an array `tails` where tails[i] is the smallest possible tail of an increasing subsequence of length i + 1; for each number, binary-search its position and replace (or append). The array's length is the LIS length. The simpler DP is O(n²).
p: DP O(n²): dp[i] = 1 + max(dp[j]) for j < i with smaller value
n795.f: How would you reconstruct the actual subsequence?

n796.a: Minimum coins to make an amount (Coin Change): DP where dp[a] = min over coins of dp[a − coin] + 1, with dp[0] = 0 and unreachable amounts as Infinity. O(amount × coins). Return −1 if impossible.
p: Greedy fails for some coin sets
n796.f: Why doesn't the greedy approach always work?

n797.a: Count palindromic substrings by expanding around every center (each character and each gap between characters): extend outward while the ends match, counting each expansion. O(n²) time, O(1) space.
n797.f: How would you return the longest palindromic substring instead?

n798.a: "Segment Words" is Word Break: can the string be split into dictionary words? DP: dp[i] is true if some j < i has dp[j] true and s.slice(j, i) is in the dictionary. O(n²) substring checks with a Set.
p: Limit j by max word length
n798.f: How would you return all possible sentences?

n799.a: Group anagrams by a canonical key: the sorted characters of each word (O(k log k)) or a 26-letter count signature (O(k)). Use a Map from key to a list of words.
n799.f: Why is the count signature faster for long words?

n800.a: "Task Coordination" is Task Scheduler: same tasks need a cooldown of n between them; find the minimum time. The most frequent task count maxF determines frames: answer = max(tasks.length, (maxF − 1) × (n + 1) + countOfTasksWithMaxF).
p: Most frequent tasks define idle frames
n800.f: How would you output the actual schedule?

n801.a: A trie (prefix tree) stores strings character by character: each node has a map of children and an end-of-word flag. `insert` walks/creates nodes, `search` checks the path ends at a word, `startsWith` checks the path exists. Each operation is O(word length).
n801.f: How would you build autocomplete suggestions with a trie?

n802.a: The first preorder element is the root; its position in the inorder array splits left and right subtrees. Recurse with index ranges, using a Map from value to inorder index for O(1) lookups, giving O(n) overall.
n802.f: Why must you build the left subtree before the right one here?

n803.a: "Disjoint Intervals" asks for the minimum number of intervals to remove so the rest don't overlap. Greedy: sort by end time, keep an interval if it starts at or after the last kept end, otherwise remove it. O(n log n).
n803.f: Why does sorting by end time give the optimal answer?

n804.a: "End of Array Reachable" is Jump Game: each value is the max jump length; can you reach the last index? Greedy: track the furthest reachable index while scanning; if the current index is beyond it, you're stuck. O(n).
p: Jump Game II counts minimum jumps
n804.f: How would you find the minimum number of jumps?

n805.a: Expand around each center (every character and every gap), tracking the longest palindrome found. O(n²) time and O(1) space; Manacher's algorithm achieves O(n) but is rarely expected.
p: DP table alternative uses O(n²) space
n805.f: How does the DP table approach work?

n806.a: Word Search: does the word exist in the grid using adjacent cells without reuse? Backtracking DFS from every cell: match the current character, mark the cell visited, explore four neighbours for the next character, then unmark. O(R·C·4^L).
n806.f: How would you search for many words efficiently?

n807.a: Count connected components in an undirected graph with union-find (start with n components, decrement each time an edge merges two different sets) or by running DFS/BFS from each unvisited node. O(V + E).
n807.f: What does union by rank add?

n808.a: DP over prefixes: dp[i][j] is the LCS length of a[0..i) and b[0..j). If characters match, dp[i][j] = dp[i−1][j−1] + 1; otherwise max(dp[i−1][j], dp[i][j−1]). O(m × n) time, reducible to O(min(m, n)) space.
n808.f: How is this used in diff tools?

n809.a: Longest substring without repeating characters: sliding window with a map of each character's last index; when you see a repeat inside the window, move the left edge past its previous position. Track the max window length. O(n).
n809.f: Why compare the last index with left before moving?

n810.a: Longest repeating character replacement: with up to k replacements, find the longest substring of one repeated letter. Sliding window tracking counts and the max frequency in the window; if window length − maxFreq > k, shrink from the left. O(n).
p: Track max frequency in the window
n810.f: Why is it safe not to recompute maxF when shrinking?

n811.a: Rotate an n × n matrix 90° clockwise in place: transpose it (swap matrix[i][j] with matrix[j][i]), then reverse each row. O(n²) time, O(1) extra space.
p: Counter-clockwise: reverse rows then transpose (or reverse columns)
n811.f: How would you rotate a non-square matrix?

n812.a: Traverse the matrix in spiral order by maintaining four boundaries (top, bottom, left, right): walk right along top, down the right side, left along bottom, up the left side, shrinking the boundaries after each edge until they cross. O(m × n).
n812.f: Why are the extra checks needed for the bottom and left passes?

n813.a: Insert a new interval into a sorted, non-overlapping list: add all intervals ending before the new one starts, merge all that overlap by expanding the new interval's bounds, then add the rest. O(n).
p: Merge by min start and max end
n813.f: How would this change if the list weren't sorted?

n814.a: Circular House Robber: the first and last houses are adjacent, so solve the linear version twice, once excluding the first house and once excluding the last, and take the maximum. O(n).
p: First and last can't both be taken
n814.f: Why does splitting into two linear cases cover all valid choices?

n815.a: Ocean Flow is Pacific Atlantic Water Flow: find cells from which water can reach both oceans. Instead of searching from every cell, run DFS/BFS from each ocean's border moving to equal or higher neighbours (reverse flow), mark reachable cells for each ocean, and return the intersection. O(R × C).
p: Move to neighbours with height ≥ current
n815.f: Why is reversing the flow more efficient?
