n816.a: "Word Finder" is the add-and-search-words data structure: `addWord` inserts into a trie, and `search` supports `.` as a wildcard matching any letter, handled by DFS that branches into every child at a dot.
n816.f: How would you support '*' matching any sequence?

n817.a: Deep-copy a graph by traversing it (DFS or BFS) with a Map from original node to its clone: create a clone when first seen, then connect each clone's neighbours to the clones of the original neighbours. The map also prevents infinite loops on cycles. O(V + E).
n817.f: Why must the clone be stored in the map before visiting neighbours?

n818.a: Minimum meeting rooms: sort start times and end times separately, then sweep with two pointers; each start before the earliest unfinished end needs a new room, otherwise a room frees up. Alternatively use a min-heap of end times. O(n log n).
n818.f: How would the heap-based approach look?

n819.a: Implement a binary heap (min or max) backed by an array with `insert` (push and sift up), `extract` (move the last item to the root and sift down), `peek` and `size`. Insert and extract are O(log n), peek O(1); building from an array can be O(n).
p: Complete binary tree in an array
n819.f: What problems are naturally solved with heaps?

n820.a: Serialize with a preorder (or level-order) traversal including null markers, and deserialize by consuming the tokens in the same order to rebuild nodes recursively. Both O(n).
p: Rebuild with the same traversal order
n820.f: How would you make the output more compact?
n820.c:
const serialize = root => { const out = []; const go = n => { if (!n) { out.push('#'); return; } out.push(n.val); go(n.left); go(n.right); }; go(root); return out.join(','); };
const deserialize = data => { const t = data.split(','); let i = 0; const build = () => { const v = t[i++]; return v === '#' ? null : { val: Number(v), left: build(), right: build() }; }; return build(); };

n821.a: Binary Tree Maximum Path Sum: a path can start and end anywhere. Recursively compute, for each node, the best downward path gain (node value plus the better non-negative child gain), and update a global maximum with node value + left gain + right gain. O(n).
p: Gain = node + max(0, leftGain, rightGain) path downward
Update best with node + left + right
n821.f: Why can a returned path only use one child?

n822.a: Word Search II: find all dictionary words in a grid. Build a trie of the words, then DFS from each cell following trie branches, collecting words when you reach an end node; prune branches that aren't in the trie and remove found words to avoid duplicates.
p: DFS from each cell guided by the trie
Record word at end nodes and clear the flag
n822.f: Why is a trie much faster than running Word Search for each word?

n823.a: Merge k sorted linked lists by repeatedly merging pairs (divide and conquer) or using a min-heap of list heads. Both are O(N log k), where N is the total number of nodes.
n823.f: Which approach uses less extra memory?

n824.a: Minimum window substring: find the shortest substring of s containing all characters of t (with multiplicity). Sliding window with a need-count map: expand right until all needed characters are covered, then shrink from the left while still valid, recording the best window. O(|s| + |t|).
n824.f: How does need going negative represent surplus characters?

n825.a: "Extraterrestrial Language" is Alien Dictionary: given words sorted in an unknown alphabet, derive the letter order. Compare adjacent words to find the first differing letters (an edge a → b), then topologically sort the letters. Return "" if there's a cycle or an invalid prefix order.
p: Edges from first differing characters of adjacent words
Invalid if a word is followed by its own prefix
n825.f: Why is only the first differing character used from each pair?

n826.a: Find the median of a data stream with two heaps: a max-heap for the lower half and a min-heap for the upper half, keeping their sizes balanced (differ by at most one). The median is the top of the larger heap, or the average of both tops. Insert O(log n), median O(1).
n826.f: How would you handle a sliding-window median?

n87.a: Find the top k elements (largest values or most frequent): for largest values, keep a min-heap of size k (O(n log k)) or use Quickselect (average O(n)); for most frequent, count with a Map then bucket sort by frequency (O(n)). Sorting is the simple O(n log n) fallback.
n87.f: When would a heap beat sorting?
n87.c: const topKLargest = (arr, k) => [...arr].sort((a, b) => b - a).slice(0, k);

n1010.a: Arrays can be iterated with `for` loops, `for...of`, `forEach`, and transforming methods like `map`, `filter`, `reduce`, `some`, `every`, `find`, `findIndex`, `flatMap`, plus `entries()`, `keys()` and `values()`. Use `for...of` or a plain `for` loop when you need `break` or `await`.
n1010.f: Why doesn't await work as expected inside forEach?

n1013.a: Shallow copies: spread (`{...obj}`, `[...arr]`), `Object.assign`, `Array.from`, `slice`, `concat`. Deep copies: `structuredClone(value)` (handles Dates, Maps, Sets, cycles, but not functions or DOM nodes), `JSON.parse(JSON.stringify())` (loses functions, undefined, Dates become strings), or libraries like Lodash's `cloneDeep`.
p: Nested objects are shared in shallow copies
n1013.c: const copy = structuredClone({ date: new Date(), tags: new Set(['a']), nested: { x: 1 } });

n1035.a: `Intl` is the built-in internationalization API. It formats and compares values according to a locale: `Intl.NumberFormat` (numbers, currencies, units), `Intl.DateTimeFormat`, `Intl.RelativeTimeFormat` ("3 days ago"), `Intl.PluralRules`, `Intl.ListFormat`, `Intl.Collator` (locale-aware sorting) and `Intl.Segmenter` (graphemes and words).
n1035.f: Why use Intl instead of hand-written formatting?

n1094.a: Native objects are defined by the ECMAScript specification and exist in every JavaScript environment, such as `Object`, `Array`, `Function`, `Date`, `Math` and `JSON`. Host objects are provided by the environment the script runs in, such as `window`, `document` and `fetch` in browsers, or `process` and `fs` in Node.
p: Native: part of the language spec
Host: provided by browser or Node
Native objects behave the same everywhere
n1094.f: Why should you feature-detect host objects?

n1141.a: Extending built-ins (monkey-patching `Array.prototype` etc.) makes new methods available everywhere, which can be handy for polyfills. But it risks name clashes with future standard methods or other libraries, can break `for...in` loops if properties are enumerable, and makes code harder to reason about. Only add standards-compliant polyfills guarded by feature detection.
p: Con: conflicts with future standards (e.g. the "smoosh" issue)
n1141.f: How did extending built-ins cause problems in the past?

n1143.a: Mutable objects can be changed after creation (most JS objects and arrays); immutable values can't (primitives like strings and numbers, or objects frozen with `Object.freeze`). Immutability makes code predictable, enables cheap change detection and undo, and avoids shared-state bugs, at the cost of copying and memory. Achieve it with `const` plus non-mutating updates (spread, map, filter), `Object.freeze`, or libraries like Immer.

n1146.a: A `while` loop checks its condition before each iteration, so it may run zero times. A `do...while` loop runs the body first and checks the condition afterwards, so it always runs at least once.
p: while: condition first, may not run
do...while: body first, runs at least once
Use do...while for "try at least once" logic
n1146.f: Can you give a practical use case for do...while?

n1148.a: In JavaScript, apply OOP with classes or prototypes: encapsulation (private `#fields` and closures), inheritance (`extends`) used sparingly, polymorphism through shared method names, and abstraction via clear interfaces. Prefer composition over deep inheritance hierarchies, and combine OOP with functional patterns where they fit.
n1148.f: When would you choose functions and closures over classes?

n8.a: The spread operator only copies the top level; nested objects are still shared references, so changing `copy.address.city` also changes the original. Fix it by copying each nested level you change (`{...obj, address: {...obj.address, city}}`) or making a deep copy with `structuredClone(obj)`, which handles nested objects, Dates, Maps and cycles.
n8.f: When is a deep copy wasteful compared to targeted copying?

n889.a: Extending built-in prototypes can collide with future JavaScript features or other libraries, changes behaviour for all code in the page (including third-party code), can add enumerable properties that break loops, and makes debugging harder. Use standalone helpers, or polyfills that follow the spec and are added only when missing.
n889.f: How would you safely polyfill a missing method?

n894.a: For objects: `for...in` (includes inherited enumerable keys, so guard with `Object.hasOwn`), or better `Object.keys`, `Object.values` and `Object.entries` with `for...of` or array methods. For arrays: `for`, `for...of`, `forEach`, `map`/`filter`/`reduce`, and `entries()` when you need indices.
n894.f: Why can for...in be risky with arrays?
n894.c:
for (const [key, value] of Object.entries(user)) console.log(key, value);
for (const [i, item] of items.entries()) console.log(i, item);

n897.a: A mutable object can be changed after it's created (adding, removing or modifying properties). An immutable one can't. In JavaScript, primitives are immutable while objects and arrays are mutable by default; you can make objects immutable with `Object.freeze` (shallow) or by treating them as read-only and creating new copies for each change.
n897.f: Does const make an object immutable?

n941.a: Dot notation (`obj.name`) is concise but requires a valid identifier known in advance. Bracket notation (`obj['first-name']`, `obj[key]`) accepts any string or symbol and lets you use variables or computed keys.
p: Brackets needed for symbols and hyphens
n941.f: When does using bracket notation with user input become a security risk?

n943.a: A shallow copy duplicates only the top level: nested objects are still shared, so changing them affects both copies. A deep copy recursively duplicates every level, making the copies fully independent. Use spread/Object.assign for shallow and `structuredClone` (or a deep-clone utility) for deep copies.
n943.f: How would you write a simple deep clone for plain objects and arrays?

n979.a: Check that it's a plain object and has no own keys: `Object.keys(obj).length === 0` (or `Object.getOwnPropertyNames`/`Reflect.ownKeys` if non-enumerable or symbol keys matter), plus a check that it isn't null or an array.
n979.f: Why might `obj.constructor === Object` fail for objects created with Object.create(null)?
n979.c: const isEmpty = o => o != null && o.constructor === Object && Object.keys(o).length === 0;

n1014.a: Common ways: the `fetch` API (modern, promise-based), `XMLHttpRequest` (older, event-based), libraries like Axios or ky, `navigator.sendBeacon` for analytics on page unload, WebSockets or Server-Sent Events for realtime data, and in frameworks, data-fetching libraries (TanStack Query, SWR) built on top of fetch.
n1014.f: Why doesn't fetch reject on 404 or 500?

n1031.a: In Node.js, `process.nextTick` callbacks run immediately after the current operation, before promise microtasks and before the event loop continues. `setImmediate` runs in the "check" phase after I/O callbacks, and `setTimeout(fn, 0)` runs in the timers phase after at least ~1ms. In browsers only `setTimeout` exists (plus microtasks via promises/`queueMicrotask`).
p: Order of setTimeout vs setImmediate varies outside I/O callbacks
n1031.f: Why can recursive process.nextTick calls starve I/O?

n1085.a: JSONP worked around the same-origin policy before CORS: you add a `<script>` tag pointing to another domain's URL with a `callback` parameter, and the server responds with JavaScript that calls your function with the data (`myCallback({...})`). It's not Ajax because it doesn't use XHR or fetch, only supports GET, has poor error handling, and is insecure because you execute whatever script the server returns. CORS replaced it.
p: Server wraps JSON in a function call
n1085.f: Why is JSONP considered a security risk today?

n1105.a: The call stack tracks currently executing functions. When async work completes (timers, network, events), its callback is placed in a task queue. The event loop repeatedly checks: when the call stack is empty, it runs all queued microtasks (promise callbacks), then takes the next task from the task queue, possibly rendering in between. This lets single-threaded JavaScript handle concurrency without blocking.
p: Web APIs handle timers and I/O
Microtasks run before the next task
Event loop moves work when the stack is empty
n1105.f: What happens to the UI if a task runs for 2 seconds?

n4.a: Sorting 200,000 rows synchronously blocks the main thread, so the page can't paint or respond. Options: split the work into chunks scheduled with `setTimeout` or `scheduler.yield()` so the browser can paint between chunks (simple but slower overall); use `requestIdleCallback` to run chunks only when the browser is idle (good for non-urgent work, but timing is unpredictable); or move the sort to a Web Worker, which runs on a separate thread and keeps the UI fully responsive, at the cost of copying data (or transferring buffers). For large data the Worker is usually best; also consider sorting on the server or virtualizing the table.
p: Long synchronous tasks block paint and input
Chunking with setTimeout/scheduler.yield keeps UI alive
Web Worker moves work off the main thread
n4.f: How do transferable objects reduce the cost of sending data to a worker?

n857.a: The event loop is the mechanism that lets single-threaded JavaScript run asynchronous code. It runs synchronous code on the call stack; when the stack is empty, it drains the microtask queue (promise callbacks, `queueMicrotask`), lets the browser render if needed, then takes the next macrotask (timers, I/O, events) and repeats.
n857.f: Why do promise callbacks run before setTimeout callbacks?

n881.a: A synchronous function runs to completion before the next line executes, blocking the thread while it works. An asynchronous function starts an operation (timer, network request) and returns immediately; its result is delivered later through a callback, promise or `await`, so other code can run in the meantime.
n881.f: Does marking a function async make its work run in parallel?

n883.a: Ajax (Asynchronous JavaScript and XML) means using JavaScript to send HTTP requests in the background and update part of the page with the response, without a full page reload. Originally done with `XMLHttpRequest` and XML, it's now usually `fetch` with JSON. The browser sends the request, continues running, and a callback/promise handles the response to update the DOM.
p: Subject to same-origin policy and CORS
n883.f: What does the "asynchronous" part buy the user?

n884.a: Advantages: faster, smoother interactions without full reloads, less data transferred, and dynamic UIs. Disadvantages: content loaded by JS can be harder for search engines and requires JavaScript, the back button and bookmarks need extra handling (History API), more complex error and loading states, and accessibility issues if updates aren't announced.
p: Pro: no full reloads, better UX
n884.f: How do SPAs fix back-button behaviour?

n886.a: `fetch` is the modern, promise-based API with a cleaner interface, streams, `Request`/`Response` objects, and cancellation via `AbortController`; it doesn't reject on HTTP error statuses. `XMLHttpRequest` is older and event-based, supports upload progress events natively, and synchronous requests (deprecated). Fetch is preferred except where you need upload progress.
n886.f: How would you show upload progress for a file?

n887.a: Create an `AbortController`, pass its `signal` to `fetch`, and call `controller.abort()` to cancel. The fetch promise rejects with an `AbortError`, which you should handle separately from real errors. `AbortSignal.timeout(ms)` creates a signal that aborts automatically.
n887.f: How would you cancel the previous search request when a new one starts?

n909.a: Workers run JavaScript on background threads. Web Workers handle CPU-heavy work (parsing, image processing, sorting) without freezing the UI; Shared Workers can be shared between tabs; Service Workers act as network proxies for offline support, caching and push notifications. Workers communicate via `postMessage` and can't access the DOM.
n909.f: What's the difference between a Web Worker and a Service Worker?

n914.a: A callback is a function passed to another function to be called later, for example when a timer fires, a file loads or a request completes. It's the original way JavaScript handled async results. Deeply nested callbacks ("callback hell") and inconsistent error handling led to promises and async/await.
p: Function passed in and invoked later
Common in events, timers, Node APIs
n914.f: How would you convert a callback-based function to return a promise?
n914.c:
setTimeout(() => console.log('done'), 1000);
fs.readFile('a.txt', 'utf8', (err, data) => { if (err) return console.error(err); console.log(data); });

n915.a: The microtask queue holds high-priority callbacks such as promise `.then` handlers, `await` continuations, `queueMicrotask` and MutationObserver callbacks. After each macrotask (and after the main script), the event loop runs all microtasks, including ones added while running, before rendering or taking the next task.
p: Infinite microtasks can block the page
n915.f: Why can an infinite loop of microtasks freeze the page even though it's "async"?

n972.a: With promises, attach `.catch()` (or a second `.then` argument); with async/await, wrap awaits in `try/catch/finally`. Handle errors where you can respond meaningfully, rethrow otherwise, use `Promise.allSettled` when partial failure is acceptable, and add global `unhandledrejection` handlers for logging.
n972.f: Why do you need `return await` inside try for the catch to work?

n1028.a: A parameter is the variable listed in a function's definition; an argument is the actual value passed when calling it. In `function greet(name) {}`, `name` is a parameter; in `greet('Ana')`, `'Ana'` is the argument.
p: Extra arguments available via rest params/arguments
n1028.f: What happens if you pass more arguments than parameters?

n1038.a: `break` exits the nearest loop or `switch` immediately. `continue` skips the rest of the current loop iteration and moves to the next one. Both can target labeled outer loops.
p: continue skips to the next iteration
n1038.f: How would you stop iterating early with array methods?
n1038.c: for (const n of [1, 2, 3, 4]) { if (n === 2) continue; if (n === 4) break; console.log(n); } // 1 3

n1041.a: A `switch` compares one expression against several `case` values using strict equality and runs the matching block, with `break` to stop fall-through and `default` for no match. It's clearer than long `if/else` chains for many discrete values; object lookups are often an alternative.

n1067.a: Use ES modules: `export` from one file and `import` in another (natively in browsers with `type="module"` and in Node). Older approaches include CommonJS (`require`/`module.exports`) in Node, global variables via script tags, and bundlers that combine modules.
n1067.f: What's the difference between named and default exports?

n1068.a: Organize code into small modules grouped by feature, with clear responsibilities and minimal shared global state. Use ES modules, keep pure utility functions separate from side-effecting code, follow consistent naming and folder conventions, and enforce style with ESLint and Prettier. Patterns like modules, classes or functional composition depend on the problem.
p: Separate pure logic from side effects
n1068.f: How do you decide when to split a module?

n1082.a: Reproduce the issue in the affected browser, inspect computed styles with its DevTools, and check support on caniuse or MDN. Fix with standards-based approaches: normalize/reset CSS, Autoprefixer for vendor prefixes, feature queries (`@supports`) with fallbacks, avoiding browser hacks, and testing across browsers (BrowserStack, Playwright).
p: Reproduce and inspect in that browser
n1082.f: How does @supports help with progressive enhancement?

n1091.a: `undefined` means a variable was declared but not assigned (or a property doesn't exist). `null` is an intentional "no value" assigned by code. An undeclared variable was never declared, and reading it throws a ReferenceError. Check with `x === undefined`, `x === null`, `x == null` (both), and `typeof x === 'undefined'` (safe even for undeclared names).
p: typeof is safe for undeclared names
value == null catches both null and undefined
n1091.c:
let a; const b = null;
a === undefined; // true
b === null;      // true
typeof notDeclared === 'undefined'; // true, no error

n1096.a: JavaScript templating means generating HTML from data with placeholders. Libraries include Handlebars, Mustache, EJS, Pug and lit-html; today JSX (React), Vue templates, Svelte and tagged template literals cover most needs. Always ensure output is escaped to avoid XSS.
n1096.f: How do tagged template literals help build safe HTML templates?

n1099.a: "Ternary" means "composed of three parts": the conditional operator `condition ? valueIfTrue : valueIfFalse` is the only JavaScript operator that takes three operands.
n1099.f: How would you refactor nested ternaries?

n1104.a: Compile-to-JavaScript languages (TypeScript, CoffeeScript, Elm, ReasonML) can add static types, better tooling, and safer or more concise syntax. Downsides: a build step, learning curve, debugging through source maps, possible lag behind new JS features, and smaller communities for some languages. TypeScript is the dominant choice today.
p: Pros: types, tooling, earlier error detection
Pros: nicer syntax or functional guarantees
n1104.f: Why did TypeScript succeed where CoffeeScript faded?

n1139.a: Type coercion is JavaScript automatically converting values between types, for example in `==`, `+` with strings, or `if` conditions. Pitfalls: `'5' + 1` is `'51'` while `'5' - 1` is `4`, `[] == false` is true, `null == 0` is false, and `0`, `''` and `NaN` are all falsy. Use `===`, explicit conversions (`Number()`, `String()`), and be careful with truthiness checks.
p: Falsy values: 0, '', NaN, null, undefined, false

n13.a: Numbers are IEEE-754 binary floating point, which can't represent 0.1 or 0.2 exactly, so their sum is 0.30000000000000004. Compare with a tolerance (`Math.abs(a - b) < Number.EPSILON`), round for display (`toFixed`), or work in integer units such as paise/cents for money, or use a decimal library.
p: Binary floating point can't represent some decimals
n13.f: Why is storing prices as integers a common practice?
n13.c:
const equal = (a, b) => Math.abs(a - b) < Number.EPSILON;
equal(0.1 + 0.2, 0.3); // true

n856.a: `===` (strict equality) compares value and type without conversion. `==` (loose equality) converts types first using coercion rules, which leads to surprises like `'' == 0` and `null == undefined` being true. Use `===` by default; `x == null` is a common idiom to check for both null and undefined.

n893.a: JavaScript has seven primitive types: string, number, bigint, boolean, undefined, null and symbol, plus the object type, which includes plain objects, arrays, functions, dates, maps, sets and more. Primitives are immutable and compared by value; objects are compared by reference.
p: Primitives: string, number, bigint, boolean, undefined, null, symbol
n893.f: What's the difference between number and bigint?

n966.a: Use `typeof` for primitives and functions (beware `typeof null === 'object'`), `Array.isArray` for arrays, `instanceof` for class instances (within the same realm), `value === null` for null, and `Object.prototype.toString.call(value)` for a precise tag like `[object Date]`.
n966.f: Why can instanceof fail across iframes?

n968.a: Use `Number(str)` (strict: whole string must be numeric, empty string → 0), unary plus `+str` (same rules), `parseInt(str, 10)` and `parseFloat(str)` (parse leading digits and ignore the rest), and check for `NaN` with `Number.isNaN`. Always pass a radix to parseInt.

n1017.a: Closures keep references to their outer variables alive, which can cause memory leaks if long-lived callbacks capture large objects or DOM nodes, stale values when a closure captured an old variable (common in React effects and timers), and the classic `var`-in-a-loop bug. Creating closures in hot loops also has a small cost.
p: var in loops shares one binding
n1017.f: How would you find a closure-related memory leak in DevTools?

n2.a: Wrap the count in a function scope and return only the methods that change it: the variable is private because nothing outside the closure can reach it. Each counter instance keeps its own captured variable alive as long as the returned object exists, which is a small memory cost; methods are recreated per instance (classes with `#private` fields share methods via the prototype).
p: Variable in function scope is private
Each instance keeps its own closure alive
n2.f: When would a class with #count be a better choice?

n873.a: A closure is a function together with the variables from the scope where it was created; the function can still access those variables after the outer function has returned. Closures are used for data privacy, function factories, keeping state in callbacks and event handlers, memoization, partial application and module patterns.
n873.f: What is the classic closure bug with var in a for loop?

n950.a: Define variables inside a function and return functions that read or modify them. Outside code can only use the returned functions, so the variables behave like private fields. This is the basis of the module pattern.
p: Each call creates new private state
#private class fields as a modern alternative
n950.f: How does this compare with #private class fields?

n1187.a: CSS animations and transitions are declarative, simple for state changes, and the browser can run transform/opacity animations on the compositor thread even when JS is busy. JavaScript animations (Web Animations API, requestAnimationFrame, GSAP) give fine-grained control: pausing, reversing, seeking, physics, sequencing and reacting to input. Use CSS for simple UI transitions; use JS when you need dynamic control or complex choreography.
p: JS: more code, can jank if main thread is busy
n1187.f: What does the Web Animations API offer over CSS keyframes?

n43.a: Changing top/left/width affects layout, so every frame triggers layout, paint and composite on the main thread. Transform and opacity can be handled by the compositor on the GPU without relayout or repaint, so they stay smooth even when JS is busy. `will-change: transform` hints the browser to promote the element to its own layer ahead of time; use it sparingly because each layer costs memory.
p: Layout properties trigger reflow every frame
Compositor runs off the main thread
will-change promotes to a layer in advance
n43.f: How would you verify in DevTools that an animation avoids layout?
n43.c:
.card { transition: transform .3s, opacity .3s; }
.card:hover { transform: translateY(-4px) scale(1.02); }

n1060.a: Gotchas: browsers match selectors right to left, so overly generic key selectors (`div *`) and deep descendant chains cost more; avoid over-qualified selectors and excessive nesting from preprocessors; keep specificity low to avoid `!important` wars; animate only transform/opacity; avoid layout thrashing from JS; remove unused CSS; and be careful with expensive properties like large box-shadows, filters and `position: fixed` backgrounds.
p: Selectors are matched right to left
Keep selectors short and specificity low
Remove unused CSS and limit expensive effects
n1060.f: How would you find unused CSS on a site?

n1062.a: `display: none` and `visibility: hidden` hide from everyone, including screen readers. To hide visually but keep content for assistive technology, use a "visually-hidden" utility (1px clipped box). `aria-hidden="true"` does the opposite: visible but hidden from screen readers. `hidden` attribute behaves like display none. Off-screen positioning also works but can cause focus issues.
p: display: none / hidden attribute → hidden for all
visibility: hidden keeps space, hidden for all
Don't hide focusable elements from AT
n1062.f: Why must focusable elements never be inside aria-hidden content?
n1062.c: .visually-hidden { position: absolute; width: 1px; height: 1px; padding: 0; margin: -1px; overflow: hidden; clip: rect(0 0 0 0); white-space: nowrap; border: 0; }

n1077.a: A CSS sprite combines many small images into one file, and each element shows its part using `background-image` plus `background-position` with a fixed width and height. It reduced HTTP requests in the HTTP/1.1 era. Today HTTP/2, SVG icon sprites (`<use>`), icon fonts or inline SVG are generally preferred.
p: Harder to maintain and scale for retina
SVG sprites are the modern equivalent
n1077.f: Why are sprites less important with HTTP/2?
n1077.c:
.icon { background: url(sprite.png) no-repeat; width: 24px; height: 24px; }
.icon-search { background-position: -24px 0; }

n1117.a: Reproduce in the affected browser, inspect with its DevTools, check support on caniuse/MDN, then fix with standard approaches: a reset or normalize stylesheet, Autoprefixer for vendor prefixes, `@supports` feature queries with fallbacks, and progressive enhancement. Keep fixes isolated and documented, avoid UA-sniffing hacks, and add the browser to your test matrix.
n1117.f: When is a browser-specific hack ever acceptable?

n1119.a: Use `@font-face` to load web fonts in WOFF2 (with WOFF fallback if needed) from your own server or a service like Google Fonts, choose `font-display: swap` to avoid invisible text, preload the critical font, subset to needed characters, and define a sensible fallback stack (optionally with size-adjust) to reduce layout shift. Check licensing.
p: Fallback stack with size-adjust to reduce CLS
n1119.c:
@font-face { font-family: 'Brand'; src: url(/fonts/brand.woff2) format('woff2'); font-display: swap; }
body { font-family: 'Brand', system-ui, sans-serif; }

n1120.a: Common frameworks are Bootstrap, Tailwind CSS, Foundation, Bulma and Material UI. Typical improvements: ship only what you use (tree-shaking/purging), customize design tokens rather than overriding classes, reduce specificity to make overrides easy, improve accessibility defaults, and move to modern layout (Grid, custom properties) instead of legacy float/flex grids.
n1120.f: What trade-offs come with utility-first CSS?

n1122.a: Resetting (e.g. Eric Meyer's reset) removes all browser default styles so everything starts from zero. Normalizing (normalize.css) keeps useful defaults but makes them consistent across browsers and fixes bugs. Normalizing is usually preferred because it keeps sensible defaults; many projects use a small modern reset (box-sizing, margin removal) on top.
p: Choose based on design system needs
n1122.f: What would you include in a minimal modern reset?

n1124.a: Preprocessors like Sass, Less and Stylus add variables, nesting, mixins, functions, loops and partials, improving maintainability. Downsides: a build step, compiled output that can be bloated (deep nesting, mixin duplication), and debugging through source maps. Native CSS now has custom properties, nesting and `@layer`, which cover many needs.
p: Native CSS now covers much of it
n1124.f: What's the difference between Sass variables and CSS custom properties?

n1131.a: `px` is an absolute unit. `em` is relative to the parent's font size (for font-size) or the element's own font size (for other properties), so it compounds when nested. `rem` is relative to the root (`html`) font size, so it's consistent and respects the user's browser font-size setting. Prefer rem for font sizes and most spacing, em for things that should scale with the component's text.
p: em: relative to parent/own font size, compounds
rem: relative to root font size
n1131.f: Why can nested em sizes become unpredictable?

n45.a: BEM is a naming convention (no tooling) that avoids conflicts but depends on discipline. CSS Modules scope class names at build time, keeping plain CSS with no runtime cost. CSS-in-JS (styled-components, Emotion) colocates styles and supports dynamic props but adds runtime cost and SSR complexity (zero-runtime variants exist). Utility classes (Tailwind) give speed and consistency via design tokens, small CSS bundles, but verbose markup. For a large team, CSS Modules or Tailwind with a shared token system are common choices.
p: Choose based on team, SSR and performance needs
n45.f: Why have some teams moved away from runtime CSS-in-JS with React Server Components?

n913.a: Yes: SVG can be styled with presentation attributes (`fill="red"`), inline styles, or CSS (internal or external) when the SVG is inline in the HTML. Use `fill`, `stroke`, `stroke-width`, and `currentColor` to inherit text color. SVG loaded via `` or as a background can't be styled from page CSS.
p: Inline SVG can be styled with CSS
fill and stroke instead of color/background
n913.f: How would you theme icons for dark mode?

n976.a: Set inline styles via `el.style.prop` (camelCase) or `el.style.setProperty('--var', value)`, toggle classes with `classList.add/remove/toggle`, read final values with `getComputedStyle(el)`, and change CSS custom properties to restyle many elements at once. Prefer toggling classes over many inline style writes.
n976.f: Why can reading getComputedStyle in a loop be slow?

n1054.a: A floated element is taken out of normal flow and pushed to the left or right of its container; inline content and text wrap around it. Floats were used for layouts before flexbox and grid. Parent containers don't expand to contain floats unless cleared (clearfix or BFC). Today floats are mainly for wrapping text around images.
n1054.f: How do you make a parent contain its floated children?

n1063.a: Clearing techniques: an empty div with `clear: both` (old, adds markup); the clearfix `::after` pseudo-element on the parent; `overflow: auto/hidden` on the parent (creates a BFC but can clip); and `display: flow-root` (modern, no side effects). Use `flow-root` today, clearfix for older code, and `clear` on a following element when it must sit below floats.
n1063.f: Why can overflow: hidden be a problematic clearing technique?

n1075.a: A Block Formatting Context is an independent layout region in which block boxes are laid out and floats are contained. Created by `display: flow-root`, floats, absolute positioning, `overflow` other than visible, inline-block, flex/grid items and more. Inside a BFC, floats are contained, margins don't collapse with the outside, and the BFC doesn't overlap external floats.
p: Prevents margin collapse across its boundary
n1075.f: Give an example where creating a BFC fixes margin collapse.

n1123.a: Floats move an element to the left or right edge of its containing block, removing it from normal flow so text and inline content wrap around it. Block siblings ignore it (but their text wraps), the parent's height doesn't include it unless the float is cleared or the parent becomes a BFC. Use flexbox/grid for layout; floats for text wrapping.

n1130.a: A clearfix makes a parent element expand to contain its floated children by adding a pseudo-element after the content that clears the floats. Without it, the parent's height collapses and backgrounds/borders don't wrap the children. `display: flow-root` is the modern replacement.
n1130.f: Why does the clearfix use display: table?

n1133.a: Block-level elements start on a new line and take the full available width, and respect width, height and vertical margins (div, p, h1–h6, section, ul, form). Inline elements flow within text, take only the width of their content, and ignore width/height and vertical margins (span, a, strong, em, img is inline-replaced, code).
p: Examples: div, p vs span, a
n1133.f: Why can you set width on an img even though it's inline?

n44.a: In the default `content-box` model, width applies to content only, so padding and border are added: 200 + 2×20 + 2×2 = 244px total. With `border-box`, padding and border are included in the 200px, so the box is exactly 200px and the content area is 156px. border-box makes sizing predictable, especially with percentages.

n847.a: Every element is a rectangular box made of content, padding, border and margin. `box-sizing` controls how width/height are calculated: `content-box` (default, size excludes padding and border) or `border-box` (size includes padding and border). Most projects set `border-box` globally for predictable sizing.
p: Margin collapse for vertical block margins

n848.a: It makes every element use the border-box model, so the width and height you set include padding and border. This makes layouts predictable: a `width: 50%` element with padding still takes exactly half the space. Often written with `*, *::before, *::after` to include pseudo-elements.
n848.f: Why use inheritance (`html { box-sizing: border-box } * { box-sizing: inherit }`) instead?

n849.a: `display` sets how an element generates boxes: its outer role (block or inline) and its inner layout model. Examples: `block` (div-like), `inline` (span-like), `inline-block`, `none` (removes it), `flex` and `grid` (layout children), `inline-flex`, `table`, `list-item`, `contents` (box disappears, children remain) and `flow-root` (new BFC).
p: none removes from layout and a11y tree
n849.f: What accessibility issue has display: contents had?

n851.a: `block` starts on a new line and takes full width, with width/height respected. `inline` flows in text, sized by content, ignoring width/height and vertical margins. `inline-block` flows inline like text but respects width, height, padding and margins like a block.
n851.f: Why do inline-block elements show small gaps between them?

n470.a: Make font size scale with the viewport but stay within limits using `clamp(min, preferred, max)` with a viewport-based preferred value, combining rem with vw so text still respects user zoom.
p: Mix rem and vw for accessibility
n470.f: Why combine rem with vw instead of using vw alone?

n471.a: Grid layouts are built by defining columns/rows on the container and placing items with line numbers, spans or named areas. For example, a dashboard where a wide item spans two columns and a tall one spans two rows.
n471.f: How does grid-auto-flow: dense change placement?

n472.a: A basic grid layout: header across the top, sidebar and main content, footer at the bottom, using `grid-template-areas` so the structure is readable and easy to rearrange in media queries.
n472.f: How would you stack the layout on mobile?
n472.c:
.page { display: grid; min-height: 100vh; grid-template: "header header" auto "nav main" 1fr "footer footer" auto / 200px 1fr; }
header { grid-area: header; } nav { grid-area: nav; } main { grid-area: main; } footer { grid-area: footer; }

n473.a: Holy Grail: header, footer, and three columns (left nav, main, right aside) where the main column is fluid and the side columns are fixed, footer at the bottom. Grid makes it simple; flexbox also works with a column wrapper.
p: Header and footer span full width
n473.f: How would you do this with flexbox only?
n473.c:
body { display: grid; min-height: 100vh; grid-template: "h h h" auto "l m r" 1fr "f f f" auto / 180px 1fr 180px; }
@media (max-width: 700px) { body { grid-template: "h" "l" "m" "r" "f" / 1fr; } }

n474.a: Keep the footer at the bottom of the viewport when content is short but below content when it's long: make the body a column flex container with `min-height: 100vh` and let main grow with `flex: 1`, or use a grid with `grid-template-rows: auto 1fr auto`.
n474.f: What's the difference between a sticky footer and a fixed footer?
n474.c: body { min-height: 100dvh; display: grid; grid-template-rows: auto 1fr auto; }

n475.a: Style form controls with `accent-color` for checkboxes, radios, ranges and progress; `caret-color` for the text cursor; `color` and `background` for text inputs; `::placeholder` for placeholder text; and states like `:focus-visible`, `:invalid`, `:disabled`.
n475.f: When would you need appearance: none instead?
n475.c:
input { color: #111; caret-color: #7c3aed; accent-color: #7c3aed; }
input::placeholder { color: #888; }

n476.a: Apply a gradient as the background, clip it to the text with `background-clip: text`, and make the text color transparent.
n476.f: How would you animate the gradient across the text?
n476.c: .gradient-text { background: linear-gradient(90deg, #f97316, #ec4899, #8b5cf6); -webkit-background-clip: text; background-clip: text; color: transparent; }

n477.a: When an inline element wraps across lines, its padding, border and background are "sliced" by default. `box-decoration-break: clone` makes each line fragment get its own padding, border radius and background, as if styled separately.
n477.f: What does slice look like compared to clone?
n477.c: .highlight { background: #fde68a; padding: 0 .3em; border-radius: 4px; -webkit-box-decoration-break: clone; box-decoration-break: clone; }

n478.a: A typical flex layout: items in a row with spacing, some fixed and one taking the remaining space, aligned vertically and wrapping on narrow screens.
n478.c:
.row { display: flex; gap: 12px; align-items: center; flex-wrap: wrap; }
.row .grow { flex: 1; min-width: 0; }

n479.a: A doughnut chart in CSS: a `conic-gradient` for the segments on a circle, plus a radial mask (or an inner pseudo-element) to cut out the center.
p: mask or inner circle for the hole
n479.f: How would you make it accessible to screen readers?
n479.c: .donut { width: 160px; aspect-ratio: 1; border-radius: 50%; background: conic-gradient(#8b5cf6 0 40%, #ec4899 0 70%, #f59e0b 0); mask: radial-gradient(circle, transparent 55%, #000 56%); }

n480.a: Many screens can't render a half-pixel border directly, so draw a 1px border on a pseudo-element at 200% size and scale it down by 0.5, or use a 1px-high pseudo-element scaled on the Y axis, or a `box-shadow`/gradient trick. On high-DPI screens `0.5px` works in modern browsers.
n480.f: Why is this mainly a mobile concern?
n480.c:
.hairline { position: relative; }
.hairline::after { content: ''; position: absolute; inset: 0; width: 200%; height: 200%; border: 1px solid #ccc; transform: scale(.5); transform-origin: 0 0; pointer-events: none; }

n481.a: Use CSS counters: `counter-reset` on the list, `counter-increment` on items and `content: counter(name)` in a pseudo-element. `counters()` handles nested numbering like 1.2.3. `::marker` and `list-style-type` customize simple lists.
n481.f: How would you start numbering from 5?

n482.a: Build a close (×) icon with a button and two rotated pseudo-element bars, keeping a real button for accessibility with an accessible name.
n482.f: Why not just use the × character?

n483.a: Use `object-fit` on the image to control how it fills its box: `cover` fills and crops while keeping aspect ratio, `contain` fits entirely (letterboxing), `fill` stretches. `object-position` chooses the focal point.
n483.f: How would you avoid layout shift for images?
n483.c: img.thumb { width: 100%; aspect-ratio: 16 / 9; object-fit: cover; object-position: center top; }

n484.a: Use `aspect-ratio` with the golden ratio (~1.618) so the rectangle keeps its proportions at any width.
n484.f: How did people do this before aspect-ratio?

n485.a: Use CSS multi-column layout: `column-count` or `column-width`, plus `column-gap` and `column-rule`. Use `break-inside: avoid` to keep items together.
p: Good for text, not for app layouts
n485.f: Why is multi-column awkward for long content on screens?
n485.c:
.article { column-width: 18rem; column-gap: 2rem; column-rule: 1px solid #ddd; }
.article figure { break-inside: avoid; }

n486.a: A three-column social layout: fixed left nav, a center feed with a max width, and a right sidebar that hides on smaller screens; side columns sticky so they stay visible as the feed scrolls.
p: Hide right column on medium screens

n487.a: Lay out items in a row: flexbox with `gap`, alignment and distribution (`justify-content: space-between`), with `flex-wrap` or overflow scrolling when it doesn't fit.
n487.f: How would you push the last item to the right only?
n487.c: .row { display: flex; gap: 8px; align-items: center; justify-content: space-between; }

n488.a: Hide the native look with `appearance: none` and style the input itself (size, border, checked state with a pseudo-element or background), keeping the real checkbox for accessibility and keyboard support. For simple color changes, `accent-color` is enough.
n488.f: Why not hide the input and style a span instead?

n489.a: Center the modal and limit its height to the viewport with `max-height`, making the body section scrollable with a flex column so the header and footer stay visible.
n489.f: What does the native <dialog> give you for free?
n489.c:
dialog { max-height: calc(100dvh - 4rem); display: flex; flex-direction: column; padding: 0; }
dialog .body { overflow: auto; flex: 1; }

n490.a: Two columns: a fixed-width sidebar and a fluid main area, with grid (`grid-template-columns: 240px 1fr`) or flex (`flex: 0 0 240px` and `flex: 1`), collapsing to one column on small screens.
n490.f: How would you make the sidebar width adapt to its content?

n491.a: Use `-webkit-line-clamp` with `display: -webkit-box`, `-webkit-box-orient: vertical` and `overflow: hidden`, which is supported in all major browsers.
n491.f: How would you show a "Read more" toggle?

n492.a: Combine `white-space: nowrap`, `overflow: hidden` and `text-overflow: ellipsis` on a block with a constrained width. In flex children add `min-width: 0`.
n492.f: Why doesn't ellipsis work inside a flex item by default?
n492.c: .truncate { white-space: nowrap; overflow: hidden; text-overflow: ellipsis; }

n493.a: Modern options: flex (`display: flex; align-items: center; justify-content: center`), grid (`display: grid; place-items: center`), or absolute positioning with `top: 50%; transform: translateY(-50%)`. The parent needs a height.
n493.f: Which method works when the child's height is unknown?

n1058.a: Yes: Flexbox is for one-dimensional layout (a row or a column) like nav bars, toolbars and aligning items; Grid is for two-dimensional layout (rows and columns) like page layouts and galleries. Useful features include `gap`, `auto-fit`/`minmax`, grid template areas, subgrid and alignment properties.

n1134.a: Flexbox lays items along one axis and is content-driven: items size themselves and wrap. Grid is layout-driven in two dimensions: you define rows and columns and place items into them. Use Flexbox for components and alignment (navbars, button groups), Grid for page layouts and card grids where rows and columns must line up.
p: Grid for page and gallery layouts
n1134.f: Can you build a card grid with flexbox, and what's the drawback?

n38.a: Flexbox: `display: flex; justify-content: center; align-items: center` on the parent. Grid: `display: grid; place-items: center`. Absolute: parent `position: relative`, child `position: absolute; top: 50%; left: 50%; transform: translate(-50%, -50%)` (or `inset: 0; margin: auto` with a known size). Each needs the parent to have a height.
p: inset: 0 + margin: auto for fixed size
n38.f: Which approach could blur text, and why?

n46.a: Flex items have `min-width: auto` by default, meaning they won't shrink below their content's minimum width. A long unbreakable word sets that minimum, so the item overflows. Setting `min-width: 0` (or overflow other than visible) lets it shrink, and `overflow-wrap: anywhere` (or `break-word`) lets the long word break.
p: Long word sets the min content size
n46.f: Why does grid need minmax(0, 1fr) for the same reason?

n1057.a: Yes: grid systems such as Bootstrap's 12-column grid or Foundation, and now native CSS Grid. I prefer native CSS Grid with design tokens for gaps and breakpoints, because it handles two-dimensional layouts without extra markup and class soup, and use `auto-fit`/`minmax` for responsive galleries.
n1057.f: How would you implement a 12-column grid with CSS Grid?

n1128.a: Yes. CSS Grid defines rows and columns on a container (`grid-template-columns`, `grid-template-rows`, `grid-template-areas`) and places children by lines, spans or named areas. Features like `fr` units, `minmax()`, `auto-fit`, `gap` and `subgrid` make responsive two-dimensional layouts simple.
n1128.f: What's the difference between auto-fill and auto-fit?
n1128.c: .gallery { display: grid; grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fill, minmax(200px, 1fr)); gap: 1rem; }

n39.a: Use `grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(min(100%, 240px), 1fr))`. `minmax` sets a minimum card width with flexible growth, `auto-fit` creates as many columns as fit and collapses empty tracks so cards stretch, and `repeat` generates the tracks. To cap at 4 columns, base the minimum on the container width: `minmax(max(240px, (100% - 3 * gap) / 4), 1fr)`.
p: repeat(auto-fit, ...) creates as many columns as fit
minmax(min, 1fr) sets min width and growth
min(100%, 240px) avoids overflow on tiny screens
Cap columns with a max() trick
n39.f: How does auto-fill behave differently with few items?
n39.c: .cards { --gap: 16px; display: grid; gap: var(--gap); grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(max(240px, (100% - 3 * var(--gap)) / 4), 1fr)); }

n1046.a: CSS in the `<head>` lets the browser build the CSSOM early and render the page styled immediately, avoiding a flash of unstyled content. Classic scripts block HTML parsing, so placing them before `</body>` lets the page render first. Today, `defer` or `type="module"` scripts in the head achieve the same benefit while downloading earlier.
p: Scripts at end let content render
defer/async in head is the modern approach
n1046.f: When must a script stay in the head without defer?

n1076.a: `z-index` controls stacking order of positioned elements (and flex/grid items) within the same stacking context. A stacking context is a group whose children are stacked together and can't interleave with outside elements; it's created by the root, positioned elements with a z-index, `opacity` < 1, `transform`, `filter`, `isolation: isolate`, `position: fixed/sticky` and more. A child's z-index only competes within its parent's stacking context.
p: Created by transform, opacity, filter, z-index
n1076.f: Why can't a child with z-index 9999 appear above an element outside its stacking context?

n1083.a: `transform: translate()` doesn't affect layout and is composited on the GPU, so it's best for animations and smooth movement; the element keeps its original space. Absolute positioning takes the element out of flow and positions it relative to an ancestor, triggering layout when changed; it's best for static placement (tooltips, overlays). Use translate for motion, absolute for layout placement.
n1083.f: Why might translated text look blurry?

n1127.a: `static` is the default normal flow (top/left ignored). `relative` stays in flow but can be offset from its normal position and becomes a containing block for absolute children. `absolute` is removed from flow and positioned relative to the nearest positioned ancestor. `fixed` is positioned relative to the viewport and stays during scrolling (unless an ancestor has a transform).
p: absolute: out of flow, nearest positioned ancestor
n1127.f: What happens to a fixed element inside a transformed parent?

n40.a: z-index only competes within the same stacking context. If the modal is inside a parent that creates a stacking context (for example with `transform`, `opacity`, `filter`, or `position` with z-index), its huge z-index is limited to that parent's level, which may be below the sticky header's context. Fix by rendering the modal at the document root (a portal), using the native `<dialog>` with `showModal()` (top layer), or removing the property that created the stacking context.
p: z-index is local to its stacking context
Header's context outranks the modal's parent
n40.f: What is the top layer and which elements use it?

n852.a: `static`: default normal flow. `relative`: offset from its normal position, keeps its space. `absolute`: removed from flow and positioned against the nearest positioned ancestor. `fixed`: positioned against the viewport. `sticky`: acts like relative until it crosses a threshold (`top: 0`), then sticks within its scrolling container until its parent scrolls out.
p: sticky: hybrid within its scroll container
n852.f: Why does position: sticky sometimes not work?

n1053.a: Media types other than `screen` include `print` (for printed pages and print preview), `all`, and `speech`. Media features like `prefers-color-scheme`, `prefers-reduced-motion`, `hover`, `pointer` and `orientation` are also commonly used.
n1053.f: What would you change in a print stylesheet?
n1053.c: @media print { nav, .ads { display: none; } a::after { content: ' (' attr(href) ')'; } }

n1059.a: Yes: mobile-first CSS with `min-width` media queries, fluid units (rem, %, clamp), flexible layouts with Flexbox/Grid, responsive images (`srcset`, `sizes`), touch-friendly targets, the viewport meta tag, and container queries for components that adapt to their container.
n1059.f: What are container queries and why are they useful?

n1081.a: Responsive design uses one fluid layout that adapts continuously with flexible grids and media queries. Adaptive design serves several fixed layouts for specific breakpoints or devices (sometimes detected server-side). Responsive is simpler to maintain; adaptive gives more control per device but more work.
n1081.f: When might an adaptive approach make sense?

n1118.a: Use progressive enhancement: start with semantic HTML that works everywhere, add CSS and JS that enhance when supported, use feature detection (`@supports`, `'fetch' in window`), polyfills only where needed, and transpile with targets from a browserslist. Test on low-end devices and define a support matrix.
n1118.f: What's the difference between progressive enhancement and graceful degradation?

n1121.a: Yes. For high-DPI screens use SVG for icons and logos, `srcset` with `1x`/`2x` descriptors (or width descriptors with `sizes`) for raster images, `image-set()` for CSS backgrounds, and icon fonts or CSS for simple shapes. Compress larger images carefully to keep file sizes down.
n1121.f: How do width descriptors with sizes differ from density descriptors?

n1129.a: Responsive design is the goal: the site adapts to any screen. Mobile-first is a strategy for getting there: you write base styles for small screens and add complexity with `min-width` media queries. Desktop-first starts with large layouts and uses `max-width` queries to remove things. Mobile-first tends to produce leaner CSS and prioritizes core content.
n1129.f: Why does mobile-first often produce less CSS?

n1135.a: Fixed layouts use set pixel widths regardless of screen size. Fluid layouts use percentages so they stretch with the viewport but can become too wide or narrow. Responsive layouts combine fluid sizing with media queries (and flexible images) to rearrange the layout at breakpoints.
n1135.f: How do max-width and fluid widths work together?

n42.a: `px` is fixed; `em` is relative to the element's/parent's font size; `rem` to the root font size; `%` to the parent's dimension; `vw`/`vh` to 1% of the viewport width/height. Use rem for font sizes (respects user settings, ideally with `clamp()` for fluid type), rem or em for spacing (em when it should scale with the component's text), and %, fr, vw/vh (or dvh on mobile) for layout.
n42.f: Why is 100vh problematic on mobile browsers?

n1055.a: Pseudo-elements style a specific part of an element or insert generated content: `::before`/`::after` (decorative content, icons, clearfix), `::first-line`, `::first-letter` (drop caps), `::placeholder`, `::selection`, `::marker` and `::backdrop`. They use double colons and aren't real DOM nodes.
n1055.f: Why shouldn't important content be inserted with ::before?

n1078.a: Browsers match selectors from right to left: they start from the key (rightmost) selector to find candidate elements, then walk up the tree to check ancestors and other conditions. So `.nav a` first finds all `a` elements, then checks whether each has a `.nav` ancestor. Specific key selectors are cheaper to match.
n1078.f: Why do browsers match right to left?

n1126.a: `:nth-child(n)` counts all sibling elements regardless of type, then checks that the element matches; `:nth-of-type(n)` counts only siblings of the same element type. In a div with an h2 followed by paragraphs, `p:nth-child(2)` is the first p, while `p:nth-of-type(2)` is the second p.

n1132.a: A pseudo-class selects elements in a particular state or position: `:hover`, `:focus-visible`, `:checked`, `:disabled`, `:invalid`, `:first-child`, `:not()`, `:has()`. Example: `input:invalid:not(:placeholder-shown)` highlights invalid fields only after the user has typed; `.card:has(img)` styles cards containing an image.
n1132.f: What can :has() do that wasn't possible before?

n41.a: When multiple rules match, the cascade decides: first origin and importance (`!important` declarations win over normal ones), then cascade layers, then specificity (inline styles > IDs > classes/attributes/pseudo-classes > elements), and finally source order (later wins). So a `.btn.primary` rule beats `.btn` regardless of order, but two equal-specificity rules are settled by order.
n41.f: How do @layer rules change this ordering?

n850.a: Specificity is the weight the browser uses to choose between conflicting rules, calculated as (IDs, classes/attributes/pseudo-classes, elements/pseudo-elements). Compare column by column from left. Inline styles beat all selectors; `!important` overrides normal specificity. `:where()` has zero specificity, while `:is()`/`:not()` take the specificity of their most specific argument.
n850.f: How would you use :where() in a component library?

n940.a: `getElementById` looks up a single element by ID and is very fast. `querySelector` accepts any CSS selector and returns the first match; it's more flexible but slightly slower. Both return live element references; `querySelectorAll` returns a static NodeList, unlike `getElementsByClassName`'s live HTMLCollection.
p: Both return first match or null
n940.f: What's the difference between a live and a static collection?

n1186.a: ARIA (Accessible Rich Internet Applications) is a set of attributes (roles, states, properties) that add semantics to elements for assistive technologies when native HTML isn't enough. Screen readers read the accessibility tree aloud and let users navigate by headings, landmarks and controls. To make a site accessible: use semantic HTML first, label every control, provide alt text, ensure keyboard access and visible focus, keep good color contrast, manage focus in dynamic UI, and test with screen readers and tools like axe.
p: First rule of ARIA: prefer native HTML
Screen readers use the accessibility tree
n1186.f: What's an example where ARIA makes things worse?

n32.a: Use a native `<select>` if possible. If custom, follow the ARIA listbox/combobox pattern: a real `<button>` trigger with `aria-haspopup="listbox"` and `aria-expanded`, a list with `role="listbox"` and options with `role="option"` and `aria-selected`, keyboard support (Enter/Space to open, arrow keys to move, Escape to close, type-ahead), focus management with `aria-activedescendant` or roving tabindex, and a label linked with `aria-labelledby`.
p: Manage focus and label the control
n32.f: What's the difference between roving tabindex and aria-activedescendant?

n33.a: Use empty alt (`alt=""`) for decorative images, or images whose information is already in nearby text, so screen readers skip them. Use descriptive alt for informative images (describe the meaning, not "image of"), functional images like linked logos or icon buttons (describe the action/destination), and complex images (short alt plus a longer description nearby).
p: Complex charts → short alt + long description
n33.f: What would good alt text be for a logo that links to the home page?

n1048.a: `data-*` attributes store custom data on HTML elements without non-standard attributes. They're read in JS via `element.dataset` (camelCased) and in CSS via attribute selectors or `attr()`. Used for configuration, IDs for event delegation and test hooks. Don't store sensitive data or replace proper semantics/ARIA.
n1048.f: Why is data-testid used in testing libraries?

n35.a: Auth token: prefer an HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookie so JavaScript can't read it (protects against XSS theft), with CSRF protection. Cart: localStorage for persistence across sessions (or server-side for logged-in users); sessionStorage if it should end with the tab. Offline data: IndexedDB, which is asynchronous, stores large structured data and works with service workers. localStorage is synchronous, string-only and ~5MB, and any XSS can read it.
p: Cookies: sent with requests; HttpOnly protects tokens
Never put tokens where XSS can read them if avoidable
n35.f: How does SameSite help against CSRF?

n960.a: Iframes communicate with `window.postMessage(message, targetOrigin)`; the receiver listens for `message` events and must check `event.origin`. Same-origin frames can access each other's `contentWindow` directly. `MessageChannel` creates a dedicated port pair, and `BroadcastChannel` works between same-origin contexts.
n960.f: Why is using '*' as targetOrigin dangerous?
n960.c:
iframe.contentWindow.postMessage({ type: 'theme', value: 'dark' }, 'https://widget.example.com');
window.addEventListener('message', e => { if (e.origin !== 'https://app.example.com') return; handle(e.data); });

n1047.a: HTML5 as a platform includes: semantic elements (header, nav, article, section), forms with new input types and validation, multimedia (`<audio>`, `<video>`), graphics (`<canvas>`, SVG, WebGL), storage (localStorage, IndexedDB), offline (service workers), connectivity (WebSockets, SSE, fetch), device access (geolocation, camera), performance (Web Workers) and CSS3 styling.
n1047.f: Which of these do you use most often and why?

n31.a: Give every input a visible `<label for>`; group related controls (radio groups, address blocks) with `<fieldset>` and `<legend>`; mark required fields with the `required` attribute and a visible indicator; show error messages as text linked with `aria-describedby` and set `aria-invalid="true"`; announce errors (focus the first invalid field or use a live region summary); use proper input types and `autocomplete`.
p: Move focus to errors, use autocomplete
n31.f: Why are placeholders not a substitute for labels?
n31.c: Enter a valid email address.

n1112.a: Stylesheets in the head let the browser render styled content as early as possible (avoiding FOUC). Classic scripts block parsing, so putting them at the end lets the content render first. Exceptions: scripts that must run before render (feature detection like Modernizr, theme/dark-mode setters to avoid flashing, analytics snippets) belong in the head; and with `defer`/`async`/modules, scripts can go in the head while still not blocking.
p: CSS early for styled first render
Exceptions: theme setters, polyfills, feature detection
n1112.f: How do you prevent a dark-mode flash on load?

n1113.a: `srcset` provides multiple image candidates so the browser picks the most appropriate for the device: with density descriptors (`1x`, `2x`) it uses the device pixel ratio; with width descriptors (`400w`, `800w`) plus `sizes`, it computes the image's display width from `sizes` (media conditions), multiplies by the pixel ratio, and picks the smallest candidate that's large enough. It may also consider network conditions and cache.
p: Width descriptors + sizes for fluid images
Browser picks based on slot size × DPR
Use <picture> for art direction or formats
n1113.f: When would you use <picture> instead of srcset?

n34.a: `loading="lazy"` defers offscreen images/iframes until near the viewport (don't use on the LCP image). `<link rel="preload">` fetches a critical resource for the current page early (hero image, fonts). `<link rel="prefetch">` downloads low-priority resources likely needed for the next navigation. `fetchpriority="high"|"low"` adjusts the priority of a fetch, e.g. high on the LCP image, low on carousel images.
n34.f: What happens if you preload resources you don't use?

n862.a: A plain `<script>` blocks HTML parsing while it downloads and executes. `async` downloads in parallel and executes as soon as it's ready, pausing parsing, in no guaranteed order — good for independent scripts like analytics. `defer` downloads in parallel and executes in document order after parsing finishes, before DOMContentLoaded — good for app scripts that need the DOM. Module scripts are deferred by default.
p: defer: run after parsing, in order
n862.f: Which would you use for a script that depends on another script?

n1030.a: `innerHTML` gets/sets the HTML markup inside an element, parsing tags (so setting it with user input risks XSS). `textContent` gets/sets only text, treating everything as plain text, and is faster and safer. `innerText` is similar but layout-aware (respects CSS visibility) and slower.
n1030.f: How would you safely insert user-generated content?

n1080.a: Build with progressive enhancement: semantic HTML that works without JS or modern CSS, then enhance with feature detection (`@supports`, checking APIs), polyfills loaded only when needed, transpiling to a browserslist target, responsive images, and graceful fallbacks. Test on the oldest supported browsers.
p: Define and test a support matrix
n1080.f: How would you load polyfills only for browsers that need them?

n1115.a: Canvas is a raster bitmap drawn with JavaScript; it's fast for many objects (games, charts with thousands of points, image manipulation) but has no DOM for individual shapes, so interactivity and accessibility must be built manually. SVG is vector markup in the DOM: resolution-independent, styleable with CSS, has events per element and is accessible, but slows down with very many elements.
p: Choose by object count and interactivity
n1115.f: Which would you use for a chart with 100,000 points?

n1116.a:
Empty (void) elements have no content and no closing tag, e.g. `
`, `
`, ``, ``, ``, ``, ``, ``, ``, ``, `` and ``. The trailing slash (`
`) is optional in HTML.
p: br, hr, img, input, meta, link
n1116.f: Why does JSX require while HTML doesn't?

n30.a: Use `<header>` for the site/page header, `<nav>` for main navigation, `<main>` for the unique main content (one per page), `<article>`/`<section>` for content groups with headings, `<aside>` for the sidebar, and `<footer>` for the footer. Semantic HTML creates landmarks screen-reader users can jump between, improves SEO, makes code readable, and provides built-in behaviors.
n30.f: When should you use section vs article vs div?

n36.a: `<button>` performs an action on the page (submit, open a dialog, toggle) and is focusable with Enter/Space support. `<a href>` navigates to a URL and supports open-in-new-tab, history and link semantics. A `<div>` with a click handler has no role, isn't focusable and doesn't respond to the keyboard, so it should be avoided; recreating a button needs `role`, `tabindex` and key handling.
p: div has no semantics or keyboard support
Don't use a without href as a button
Native elements give accessibility for free
n36.f: What attributes would a div need to behave like a button?

n963.a: Create with `document.createElement` and insert with `append`, `prepend`, `before`, `after`, or `insertAdjacentElement`; remove with `el.remove()`; modify with `textContent`, `setAttribute`, `classList`, `style` or `replaceWith`. Use `DocumentFragment` or `replaceChildren` for many changes at once.
n963.f: Why is building elements safer than concatenating innerHTML strings?

n1071.a: Watch for: text expansion (German can be ~30% longer), right-to-left languages (`dir="rtl"`, logical CSS properties), fonts supporting all scripts, not putting text in images, locale-aware date/number/currency formats (Intl), pluralization rules, string concatenation that breaks grammar, culturally sensitive colors/icons, and proper `lang` attributes for screen readers and SEO.
p: No text in images; full-sentence translations
n1071.f: What are CSS logical properties and why do they help?

n1072.a: Detect language from the URL (e.g. `/en/`, `/fr/` or subdomains) rather than only `Accept-Language`, let users switch manually, set `<html lang>`, add `<link rel="alternate" hreflang>` tags for SEO, serve translated content from translation files or a CMS, and use an i18n library for formatting and pluralization.
n1072.f: Why is relying only on IP or Accept-Language a bad idea?

n1073.a: The doctype (`<!DOCTYPE html>`) tells the browser which HTML standard to use and triggers standards mode. Without it, browsers fall into "quirks mode", emulating old buggy behaviors (e.g. different box model), causing inconsistent rendering.
n1073.f: How can you check whether a page is in quirks mode?

n1114.a: Yes: Handlebars/Mustache (logic-less), EJS, Pug/Jade (indentation-based), Nunjucks/Jinja, and in modern frameworks JSX, Vue templates and Svelte. Key considerations: auto-escaping to prevent XSS, how much logic is allowed, and server vs client rendering.
p: Pick based on stack and SSR needs
n1114.f: Why is auto-escaping essential in templating?

n1170.a: Good practices: semantic HTML with one h1 and logical headings, unique titles and meta descriptions, canonical URLs, descriptive URLs, structured data (JSON-LD), fast Core Web Vitals, mobile friendliness, server-side or static rendering for JS-heavy sites, image alt text, an XML sitemap and robots.txt, internal linking, and HTTPS.
n1170.f: How does client-side rendering affect SEO?

n37.a: For SEO: `<title>`, `<meta name="description">`, `<link rel="canonical">` to avoid duplicate content, `<meta name="robots">` (noindex/nofollow), and viewport. For link previews: Open Graph tags (`og:title`, `og:description`, `og:image`, `og:url`, `og:type`) used by Facebook, LinkedIn, Slack; and Twitter/X cards (`twitter:card`, `twitter:title`, `twitter:image`). Meta keywords is ignored.
n37.f: Why must og:image be an absolute URL?
n37.c:
<link rel="canonical" href="https://example.com/post/1">
<meta property="og:title" content="Post title">
<meta property="og:image" content="https://example.com/og.png">
<meta name="twitter:card" content="summary_large_image">

n1029.a: `preventDefault()` stops the browser's default action for the event (following a link, submitting a form, checking a box) but the event still propagates. `stopPropagation()` stops the event from bubbling/capturing to other elements but the default action still happens. They're independent; use both if you need both.
p: stopPropagation: stops travel through the DOM
stopImmediatePropagation also stops other listeners on the same element
n1029.f: Why can overusing stopPropagation break event delegation and analytics?

n1032.a: `window` is the global object for the browser tab: it represents the browser window and holds globals, timers, location, history, `localStorage`, and the `document`. `document` is the DOM of the loaded page (`window.document`), used to query and manipulate elements.
p: window: global object and browser environment
document is a property of window
Each iframe has its own window and document
n1032.f: What happens to global var declarations relative to window?

n1033.a: The DOM (Document Object Model) is the browser's tree representation of an HTML document as objects. The `document` is the root; elements, text nodes and comments are nodes with parent/child/sibling relationships. JavaScript reads and changes this tree, and the browser re-renders accordingly.
n1033.f: What's the difference between a node and an element?

n1045.a: Attributes are defined in HTML markup and are always strings (`getAttribute`). Properties live on the DOM object and can be any type, reflecting current state. Many attributes initialize properties: `input.value` reflects what the user typed, while `getAttribute('value')` still returns the original value. Some are synced both ways (id), others not (value, checked).
n1045.f: How do the checked attribute and checked property differ?

n1050.a: Feature detection checks whether a feature exists before using it (`if ('IntersectionObserver' in window)`) and is the reliable approach. Feature inference assumes that if one feature exists, another does too (unreliable). UA-string sniffing parses the user agent to guess the browser; it's easily spoofed, breaks with new versions, and should be a last resort.
n1050.f: When might UA detection still be justified?

n1066.a: `DOMContentLoaded` fires when the HTML is fully parsed and deferred scripts have run, without waiting for stylesheets, images or iframes. `load` fires on window when everything, including images and subresources, has finished loading. Use DOMContentLoaded for initializing UI, load for things that need dimensions of images.
n1066.f: How do you run code safely if the event already fired?

n1089.a: Almost never. `document.write()` writes into the document stream during parsing; calling it after load wipes the whole page. It blocks parsing and is discouraged (Chrome blocks it for cross-origin scripts on slow connections). Old uses were third-party ad and analytics snippets. Use DOM APIs instead.
p: After load it replaces the page
n1089.f: Why does document.write after load clear the page?

n10.a: Use event delegation: attach one listener to the list container and use `event.target.closest('[data-row]')` to find which row was clicked. This avoids 5,000 listeners (memory and setup time), automatically works for rows added later, and keeps cleanup simple. For very long lists, virtualize rendering so only visible rows exist.
n10.f: Which events don't bubble and so can't be delegated directly?

n1149.a: `event.target` is the element where the event originated (the deepest element clicked). `event.currentTarget` is the element whose listener is currently running. With delegation, target might be a span inside a button, while currentTarget is the list with the listener.
n1149.f: Why is currentTarget null when logged asynchronously?

n11.a: Reflow (layout) recalculates element sizes and positions; triggered by changes to geometry (width, font size, adding elements) and by reading layout values (offsetHeight, getBoundingClientRect) after a write. Repaint redraws pixels without geometry changes (color, background). Layout thrashing happens when you alternate reads and writes in a loop, forcing synchronous layout each time. Batch all reads first, then all writes (or use requestAnimationFrame / FastDOM).
p: Reading layout after writes forces sync layout
n11.f: How can DevTools reveal forced synchronous layouts?

n858.a: Event delegation attaches a single listener to a common ancestor instead of each child, relying on event bubbling. In the handler, check `event.target` (or `closest()`) to see which child triggered it. Benefits: fewer listeners, works for dynamically added elements, simpler cleanup.
p: Some events don't bubble (focus → use focusin)
n858.f: How does React use delegation internally?

n876.a: Event bubbling: after an event fires on the target element, it propagates up through its ancestors to the document and window, triggering their listeners for that event. This allows delegation. `stopPropagation()` stops it. Some events (focus, blur, mouseenter, load) don't bubble.
n876.f: What's the bubbling equivalent of focus?

n877.a: Event capturing is the first phase of propagation: the event travels from window down through ancestors to the target. Listeners registered with `{ capture: true }` (or `true` as the third argument) run during this phase, before bubbling listeners. It's useful for intercepting events before children handle them.
n877.f: Give a use case where capturing is useful.

n879.a: `mouseover` fires when the pointer enters an element or any of its children, and bubbles, so it fires repeatedly while moving across children. `mouseenter` fires only once when the pointer enters the element itself, and doesn't bubble. Same for `mouseout` vs `mouseleave`.
n879.f: Which would you use for a hover card on a complex element?

n888.a: Polyfills are code that implement a newer standard feature in older environments that lack it, so you can use modern APIs everywhere (e.g. `Array.prototype.includes`, `fetch`, `Promise`). They check whether the feature exists first and only define it if missing. Syntax features (arrow functions, optional chaining) need transpiling rather than polyfills.
n888.f: Why can't you polyfill optional chaining?

n948.a: DOM events go through three phases: capturing (from window down to the target's parent), target (at the element itself), and bubbling (from the target back up to window). `event.eventPhase` indicates the current phase. Listeners run in capture phase only if registered with `capture: true`.
n948.f: In what order do capture and bubble listeners on the same ancestor fire?

n962.a: Use `forEach((item, index) => ...)`, `map`/`filter` (the callback's second argument), a classic `for` loop, or `for (const [index, item] of arr.entries())`.
n962.f: Why is entries() handy when you need break?

n964.a: Add: `push` (end), `unshift` (start), `splice(i, 0, x)` (middle). Remove: `pop`, `shift`, `splice(i, 1)`, or `filter`. Update: `arr[i] = x` or `splice`. Non-mutating versions: spread, `toSpliced`, `with(i, x)`, `filter`, `map` — preferred in React state.
n964.f: Why must React state arrays be updated immutably?

n965.a: Use `Object.hasOwn(obj, 'key')` (own properties, modern), `obj.hasOwnProperty('key')` (fails for null-prototype objects), or the `in` operator (`'key' in obj`, includes inherited properties). Checking `obj.key !== undefined` fails when the value is undefined.

n970.a: JavaScript can't detect its own absence, so use `<noscript>` to show content when JS is disabled, or render a fallback by default and remove/replace it with JS (e.g. add a `js` class to `<html>` early and style accordingly). Server-side you can infer it if an expected JS-made request never arrives.
n970.f: Why is progressive enhancement the real solution?

n971.a: Use `URLSearchParams` with `window.location.search`: `new URLSearchParams(location.search).get('q')`. `getAll` returns repeated keys, and `Object.fromEntries(params)` gives an object.
n971.f: How would you update the query string without reloading?
n971.c:
const params = new URLSearchParams(location.search);
const page = Number(params.get('page') ?? 1);

n977.a: Call `event.preventDefault()` in the event listener, e.g. to stop form submission, link navigation or a checkbox toggle. For passive listeners (scroll/touch by default in some cases) it's ignored. Returning false only works in inline handlers or jQuery.
n977.f: What does { passive: true } promise to the browser?

n980.a: `history.pushState(state, '', url)` adds a new history entry and changes the URL without reloading; `replaceState` replaces the current entry; `back()`, `forward()` and `go(n)` navigate; and the `popstate` event fires when the user navigates via back/forward so you can render the right view. Client-side routers use this.
