n981.a: The Constraint Validation API uses HTML attributes (`required`, `pattern`, `min`, `type=email`) and exposes `el.validity` (flags like valueMissing, typeMismatch), `checkValidity()`, `reportValidity()`, `setCustomValidity(msg)` for custom errors, and `validationMessage`. Use `novalidate` on the form to show custom UI while still using the API.
n981.f: Why must you reset setCustomValidity to an empty string?

n989.a: Event listeners are functions registered with `addEventListener(type, handler, options)` that run when an event happens on an element (click, input, keydown). Options include `once`, `capture`, `passive` and `signal` (an AbortSignal to remove it). Remove with `removeEventListener` using the same function reference.
n989.f: Why does removeEventListener with an inline arrow function not work?

n121.a: Implement delegation: one listener on a parent that runs a handler when the event originated inside an element matching a selector, using `closest` and making sure the match is within the parent.
p: Call handler with match as context
n121.f: How would you support events that don't bubble, such as focus?

n125.a: Virtual DOM I: convert a real DOM tree to a plain object representation ({ type, props, children }) and back. Serialize recursively: text nodes become strings; elements become objects with tag, attributes and children. Render does the reverse with createElement.
n125.f: How would you diff two virtual trees?

n134.a: Traverse the DOM breadth-first using a queue of elements, returning them level by level (or in level order). Use `children` to skip text nodes.
n134.f: How would you return nodes grouped by depth?

n149.a: Find the element immediately to the right of a target at the same depth in the tree (not necessarily a sibling). Do a BFS level by level; when you find the target, return the next node in the same level or null.
p: Next node in the same level
n149.f: How can you do it without scanning whole levels, by walking up and down?

n170.a: Return all distinct tag names in a DOM tree (lowercase), by traversing every element and collecting `tagName` in a Set.
n170.f: How would you implement it recursively without querySelectorAll?

n180.a: The height of a DOM tree is 1 + the maximum height among its children's subtrees (0 for null). Compute recursively or with BFS counting levels.
n180.f: How would you avoid stack overflow for very deep trees?

n217.a: Given two identical DOM trees A and B and a node in A, find the corresponding node in B. Record the path from the node up to root A (child indexes), then follow the same path down from root B. Or traverse both trees in parallel.
p: Build index path to the root
Replay the path in the other tree

n219.a: Create a store that maps DOM elements to values, like a Map but implemented without using Map (e.g. tagging the element with a unique hidden property or symbol), with set, get and has. WeakMap is the real-world answer since it doesn't leak.
p: Without Map: attach a unique key to the node
n219.f: Why is WeakMap the ideal production solution?

n221.a: Wrap an element in an object whose methods return `this`, so calls can be chained: e.g. `$(el).css('color', 'red').css('fontSize', '20px')`.
n221.f: How would you support a collection of elements?

n583.a: Return all elements under a root whose computed style property equals a given value. Traverse elements and compare `getComputedStyle(el).getPropertyValue(prop)` (computed values are normalized, e.g. colors in rgb()).
p: Can be slow on large trees
n583.f: Why might '#fff' not match the computed value?

n600.a: `$(selector).css(prop)` returns the style value of the first element; `$(selector).css(prop, value)` sets it and returns the wrapper for chaining. Setting undefined/empty removes the style.
n600.f: Should the getter read inline or computed styles?

n604.a: Find all descendants whose class list contains every class in a space-separated string. Traverse elements and check `classList.contains` for each class; exclude the root itself.
n604.f: Why is the native version live and yours not?

n605.a: Generate a nested table of contents from the headings (h1–h6) in a document: walk headings in order, nest lists based on heading level, and link to IDs.
n605.f: How would you handle heading levels that skip (h2 then h4)?

n606.a: Serialize a tree of objects ({ tag, children }) into indented HTML: recursively output the opening tag, children (strings as text), and the closing tag, with indentation per depth.
n606.f: What escaping would you add to make it safe?

n640.a: `jQuery.contains(a, b)` returns true if b is a descendant of a (not the same node). Walk up from b via parentNode until reaching a or null, or use `a !== b && a.contains(b)`.

n648.a: Return the visible text content of an element's subtree in reading order, ignoring hidden elements (display none etc.) — a DFS that collects text nodes and skips elements hidden via styles.
n648.f: How would visibility: hidden differ from display: none here?

n679.a: Return all descendant elements with a given tag name (case-insensitive), excluding the root, in document order.
n679.f: How would you support the '*' wildcard?

n681.a: Implement `$(el).toggleClass(names, state?)`, `addClass` and `removeClass` that accept space-separated class names and are chainable.
n681.f: What does classList.toggle's second argument do?

n683.a: Given a set of elements, find the lowest (deepest) common ancestor whose hiding would hide all of them: compute ancestor chains and pick the deepest shared node.
p: Lowest common ancestor in a DOM tree
Collect ancestors of the first node
Walk up others until a shared ancestor
n683.f: What's the complexity, and how could you improve it?

n685.a: A node registry stores data against DOM nodes and lets entries disappear when nodes are removed. Use a WeakMap keyed by node so garbage collection cleans up automatically, with set/get/has/delete.
n685.f: Why can't you get the size of a WeakMap?

n699.a: Find the corresponding node in another, structurally identical document/page: compute the child index path from the node to its root, then follow it from the other root.
p: Replay downward in the other tree
n699.f: What breaks if structures differ slightly?

n69.a: Generate a unique CSS selector from a root to a target element: walk up from the target, using `#id` if available, otherwise `tag:nth-child(n)`, joined with `>`.
n69.f: Why are nth-child selectors fragile for test automation?

n708.a: Return the text content between two nodes in document order: use a Range (`range.setStartAfter(a); range.setEndBefore(b); range.toString()`) or a TreeWalker collecting text nodes after the start until the end.
p: Range API for spans of the document
n708.f: How would you handle the end node appearing before the start node?

n712.a: A focus trap keeps keyboard focus inside a container (like a modal): find focusable elements, focus the first on open, and on Tab/Shift+Tab wrap from last to first and vice versa; restore focus to the trigger on close. The `inert` attribute on the rest of the page is a modern alternative.
n712.f: What does showModal() on <dialog> do for focus?

n713.a: Sanitize HTML by parsing it into an inert document (DOMParser), walking the tree, keeping only allowlisted tags and attributes, dropping dangerous URLs (`javascript:`), and serializing the result. Use DOMPurify or the Sanitizer API in production.
n713.f: Why is a denylist approach unsafe?

n721.a: Reading Order II extends the visible-text traversal to respect layout ordering: hidden elements (display none, visibility hidden, aria-hidden) are skipped, and text is returned in the order a reader would encounter it, typically DOM order with block boundaries producing separate entries.
n721.f: How could CSS order or flex-direction: row-reverse change visual reading order?

n730.a: Implement `getElementsByTagNameHierarchy(root, 'div span')`: return elements matching the last tag that have ancestors matching the previous tags in order (like a descendant selector).
p: Check ancestors for earlier tags in order
n730.f: How would you solve it top-down with recursion instead?

n736.a: Convert a rich-text model (text with formatting ranges, e.g. bold/italic spans) into HTML: split the text at every range boundary, determine which formats apply to each segment, and wrap segments in the corresponding tags (escaping text).
p: Wrap with tags in a consistent order
n736.f: How would you merge adjacent segments with the same formatting?

n81.a: Find the element immediately to the left of a target at the same depth in the DOM tree (not necessarily a sibling). BFS by levels, returning the previous element in the target's level or null.
p: Find target's index in its level
n81.f: Can you solve it by walking up to the parent and then down the previous subtree?

n85.a: Two-way binding keeps a state object and an input in sync: changing the input updates state, and setting state updates the input. Use `Object.defineProperty` (or a Proxy) on the state with a setter that writes to the input, and an input listener that writes to state.
n85.f: Why do React apps prefer one-way data flow instead?

n1011.a: Built-in error types: `Error` (base), `SyntaxError` (invalid code or JSON.parse failure), `ReferenceError` (undeclared variable or TDZ access), `TypeError` (wrong type, like calling undefined), `RangeError` (value out of range, e.g. invalid array length, too much recursion), `URIError`, `EvalError`, and `AggregateError` (multiple errors, from Promise.any). You can also define custom errors by extending Error.
n1011.f: Which error does accessing a let variable before its declaration throw?

n1039.a: `finally` runs after `try` and `catch` regardless of the outcome — success, thrown error or even return — so it's used for cleanup like closing connections, hiding spinners or releasing locks. A `return` in finally overrides earlier returns, which should be avoided.
n1039.f: What does `try { return 1 } finally { return 2 }` return?
n1039.c: try { setLoading(true); await save(); } catch (e) { showError(e); } finally { setLoading(false); }

n12.a: `forEach` doesn't await async callbacks: it calls each one, gets a promise back, and ignores it. Rejections from those promises aren't connected to the surrounding try/catch, so they become unhandled rejections, and the code after forEach runs before they finish. Use `for...of` with `await` for sequential work, or `await Promise.all(items.map(async ...))` for parallel work; both propagate errors to try/catch.
p: Code continues before the work finishes
n12.f: When would you prefer allSettled here?

n908.a: Browser DevTools (breakpoints, conditional and logpoints, the debugger statement, call stack and scope inspection, Network and Performance panels), `console` methods (log, table, trace, time), React/Redux DevTools, source maps, error monitoring (Sentry), and Node's `--inspect`. Approach: reproduce reliably, isolate (binary search, git bisect), form hypotheses and verify.
n908.f: How does git bisect help find regressions?

n912.a: JavaScript engines use automatic garbage collection based on reachability: anything reachable from roots (globals, the call stack, closures) is kept; everything else is freed. Modern engines use mark-and-sweep with generational collection (young objects collected often, old ones less). Leaks happen when you unintentionally keep references (globals, listeners, timers, caches, detached DOM nodes).
n912.f: Why doesn't reference counting work for cycles?

n922.a: When an error is thrown, it propagates up the call stack until it's caught by a try/catch; if nothing catches it, it becomes an uncaught error. In async code, a rejected promise propagates down the `.then` chain to the next `.catch`, or through `await` into the caller's try/catch. Errors can be rethrown or wrapped (with `cause`) to add context.
p: Promises propagate to the next catch
n922.f: What happens to an error thrown inside a setTimeout callback?
n922.c: try { await loadUser(); } catch (e) { throw new Error('Profile page failed to load', { cause: e }); }

n952.a: Extend the built-in `Error` class, call `super(message)`, set `this.name`, and add extra fields. Custom errors let callers distinguish error types with `instanceof` and carry useful data.

n973.a: Wrap code that may throw in `try`, handle errors in `catch (err)`, and put cleanup in `finally`. Only catch where you can handle the error; otherwise rethrow. With async/await, try/catch handles rejected promises. The catch binding is optional (`catch {}`).
n973.f: Why doesn't try/catch catch errors thrown in a callback scheduled later?
n973.c:
try { const data = JSON.parse(input); use(data); }
catch (err) { if (err instanceof SyntaxError) showInvalidJson(); else throw err; }

n1006.a: Spread makes copying and combining concise: clone arrays/objects (`[...arr]`, `{...obj}`), merge objects with later properties overriding, concatenate arrays, convert iterables (Set, NodeList, strings) to arrays, pass array elements as function arguments, and create immutable updates for state.
n1006.f: What's the risk of spreading a very large array into function arguments?

n1015.a: Inside an ES module, `import.meta` provides metadata about the module: `import.meta.url` (the module's URL), `import.meta.resolve()` (resolve a specifier), and in Node `import.meta.dirname`/`filename`; bundlers add fields like `import.meta.env` (Vite) and `import.meta.hot` (HMR).
n1015.c: const worker = new Worker(new URL('./worker.js', import.meta.url), { type: 'module' });

n1070.a: ESM is the standard: static imports enable tree-shaking and static analysis, it works natively in browsers and Node, supports top-level await and async loading. CommonJS (`require`) is synchronous, dynamic, and Node-only, still widespread in older packages. New code should use ESM; interop between them (dual packages, require of ESM) can be painful.
n1070.f: Why does static import structure enable tree-shaking?

n1090.a: AMD (RequireJS) was designed for browsers: asynchronous loading with `define`/`require` and callbacks, but verbose. CommonJS was designed for servers (Node): synchronous `require`, simple syntax, but not suitable for browsers without bundling. Both are largely replaced by ES modules, which are standard and support static analysis.

n1092.a: `forEach` runs a callback for each element for side effects and returns undefined. `map` creates a new array from the callback's return values without mutating the original. Use `map` when transforming data (and chaining), `forEach` when you only need side effects.
p: Don't use map without using its result
n1092.f: Which would you use to render a list in React and why?

n1109.a: Template literals use backticks and allow embedded expressions with `${}`, multi-line strings without `\n`, and tagged templates for custom processing.
n1109.f: How would a tagged template escape HTML in interpolations?
n1109.c:
const user = { name: 'Ana', items: 3 };
const msg = `Hi ${user.name}, you have ${user.items} item${user.items === 1 ? '' : 's'} in your cart.`;

n892.a: CommonJS (`require`, `module.exports`) loads modules synchronously at runtime, exports are value copies made when assigned, and it's Node's original system. ES modules (`import`/`export`) are static (analyzed before running), load asynchronously, provide live read-only bindings, support top-level await and tree-shaking, run in strict mode, and work natively in browsers and Node.
p: ESM in browsers natively; CJS needs bundling
n892.f: What does "live binding" mean for an exported counter?

n895.a: Spread (`...`) expands an iterable or object into individual elements/properties (in array literals, object literals and function calls): copy, merge, pass arguments. Rest (`...`) does the opposite: collects remaining elements/properties into an array or object (in function parameters and destructuring). Same syntax, opposite direction, determined by position.
n895.f: Why must the rest element be last?
n895.c:
const sum = (...nums) => nums.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0); // rest
sum(...[1, 2, 3]);                                         // spread
const { password, ...safeUser } = user;                     // rest in destructuring

n896.a: An iterator is an object with a `next()` method returning `{ value, done }`; an iterable implements `[Symbol.iterator]()` returning an iterator, which is what `for...of`, spread and destructuring use. Generators (`function*`) create iterators easily: `yield` pauses execution and returns a value, resuming on the next call. Used for lazy sequences, infinite streams, custom iteration of data structures, and (historically) async control flow.
n896.f: How would you make a class iterable?
n896.c:
function* range(start, end, step = 1) { for (let i = start; i < end; i += step) yield i; }
[...range(0, 5)]; // [0, 1, 2, 3, 4]

n898.a: Map accepts any key type (objects, functions) while objects use strings/symbols only; Map preserves insertion order and has `size`, is directly iterable, has no prototype key collisions, and performs better for frequent additions/removals. Plain objects suit fixed records and JSON serialization.
n898.f: How would you serialize a Map to JSON?

n899.a: WeakMap/WeakSet hold their keys (objects only) weakly: if nothing else references a key, it can be garbage-collected and the entry disappears. Because of that they aren't iterable and have no size or clear. Map/Set hold strong references, accept primitives, and are iterable. Use WeakMap for metadata/caches attached to objects (DOM nodes, private data) without leaks.
p: Entries vanish when keys are collected

n921.a: Destructuring unpacks values from arrays (by position) or properties from objects (by name) into variables, with defaults, renaming, nesting and rest. It's common in function parameters, React props and hooks.
n921.f: Why does `useState` return an array instead of an object?

n930.a: A tagged template calls a function with the template's string parts and interpolated values: `tag\`Hello ${name}\`` calls `tag(['Hello ', ''], name)`. The function can process values (escape HTML, build SQL safely, styled-components CSS, GraphQL queries) and return anything. `strings.raw` gives raw strings.
p: Function receives strings array and values
n930.c:
const html = (strings, ...vals) => strings.reduce((out, s, i) => out + s + (i < vals.length ? String(vals[i]).replace(/[&<>"]/g, c => `&#${c.charCodeAt(0)};`) : ''), ''); html`

${'

n961.a: Sets and Maps use SameValueZero equality: primitives compare by value (and NaN equals NaN, +0 equals -0), but objects compare by reference. Two different objects with the same content are different keys; you must use the same object reference to look them up.
p: NaN treated as equal to NaN
Serialize to string keys for value equality
n961.f: How would you dedupe objects by id?
n961.c:
const s = new Set([{ id: 1 }, { id: 1 }]);
s.size; // 2

n967.a: Use spread `[...set]` or `Array.from(set)` (which can also map in one step).
n967.f: How would you dedupe while preserving the last occurrence?

n974.a: Use `export` for named exports (`export const x`, `export function f`) or `export default`; import with `import { x } from './a.js'`, `import def from './a.js'`, `import * as ns from`, rename with `as`, and load lazily with `import()` which returns a promise. Re-export with `export { x } from`.
n974.f: What are the downsides of barrel files?

n987.a: Default parameters give a parameter a value when the argument is `undefined` (not when it's null). Defaults are evaluated at call time, can reference earlier parameters, and work with destructuring.
n987.f: What happens to the default if you pass null?
n987.c: function createUser(name, role = 'viewer', createdAt = new Date()) { return { name, role, createdAt }; }

n991.a: Modules are files with their own scope that explicitly export what others can import. They avoid global namespace pollution, make dependencies explicit, enable reuse and encapsulation, allow tree-shaking and code splitting, and make large codebases maintainable.
n991.f: How do modules help bundlers split code?

n995.a: A `Set` stores unique values of any type, with `add`, `has`, `delete`, `size` and iteration — great for deduplication and fast membership checks. A `Map` stores key–value pairs with keys of any type, preserving insertion order, with `set`, `get`, `has`, `delete`, `size` — great for lookups keyed by objects and frequently changing collections.
n995.f: What do Set.prototype.union and intersection add?
n995.c:
const visited = new Set(); visited.add(nodeId);
const cache = new Map(); cache.set(userObj, profile);

n9.a: Choose Map over an object when keys aren't strings (objects, DOM nodes), keys are added/removed frequently, you need size and ordered iteration, or keys come from user input (no prototype collisions like `__proto__`). Example: a cache of fetch results keyed by request objects, or counting word frequencies. Choose WeakMap over Map when keys are objects whose lifetime you don't control and you don't want to keep them alive: e.g. storing metadata for DOM elements or memoizing computations per object, so entries disappear when the element/object is garbage collected.
p: Map: non-string keys, frequent changes, size, ordering
WeakMap: per-DOM-node data, memoization per object
n9.f: When would a WeakRef be used instead?
n9.c:
const tooltipData = new WeakMap();
tooltipData.set(buttonEl, { text: 'Save' }); // gone when buttonEl is removed and unreferenced

n1008.a: Currying and partial application let you create specialized functions from general ones by fixing some arguments, improving reuse and readability (e.g. `const logError = log('error')`), enable point-free composition pipelines, and make configuration-then-use APIs clean. Drawbacks: harder debugging and readability if overused.
n1008.f: Show an example where currying improves a filter call.

n1021.a: Currying transforms a function with multiple arguments into a sequence of functions each taking one argument: `f(a, b, c)` becomes `f(a)(b)(c)`. A generic curry collects arguments until it has as many as the function's length, then calls it.
p: Returns functions until all args are supplied
n1021.f: Why doesn't fn.length work with default or rest parameters?

n1025.a: Recursion is a function calling itself with a smaller subproblem until it hits a base case. Used for tree/graph traversal (DOM, file systems, nested comments), divide-and-conquer algorithms, and nested data (deep clone, flatten). Watch for missing base cases and stack overflow on deep inputs; convert to iteration with an explicit stack when needed.
p: Natural for trees and nested data
n1025.f: Does JavaScript have tail-call optimization in practice?
n1025.c: const flatten = arr => arr.reduce((out, x) => out.concat(Array.isArray(x) ? flatten(x) : x), []);

n14.a: Debounce waits until calls stop for a set delay, then runs once with the last call — ideal for a search box (call the API 300ms after typing stops), window resize recalculation after resizing ends, or autosave. Throttle runs at most once per interval while calls keep coming — ideal for scroll handlers (update a progress bar every 100ms), mousemove/drag, or infinite-scroll checks. For a button double-click, use a leading-edge debounce/throttle or simply disable the button while the request is pending.
p: Throttle: run at a fixed max rate
Double submit → leading edge or disable button
n14.f: Why might you prefer requestAnimationFrame over throttle for scroll-driven visuals?
n14.c:
function debounce(fn, ms) { let t; return (...a) => { clearTimeout(t); t = setTimeout(() => fn(...a), ms); }; }
function throttle(fn, ms) { let last = 0; return (...a) => { const now = Date.now(); if (now - last >= ms) { last = now; fn(...a); } }; }

n871.a: Anonymous functions are functions without a name, typically used inline as callbacks (`arr.map(x => x * 2)`, event handlers, `setTimeout`), in IIFEs to create a private scope, and when returning functions from other functions. Downsides: less helpful stack traces and you can't remove an anonymous event listener easily.
n871.f: How does naming a function expression help debugging?

n874.a: A higher-order function either takes a function as an argument or returns a function (or both). Examples: `map`, `filter`, `reduce`, `setTimeout`, `addEventListener`, `debounce`, React HOCs, middleware.
n874.f: How are HOCs in React related to higher-order functions?
n874.c: const withLogging = fn => (...args) => { console.log('calling', fn.name, args); return fn(...args); };

n920.a: Both limit how often a function runs during rapid events. Debouncing delays the call until events stop for a given time (only the last call runs) — for search input, resize-end, autosave. Throttling ensures the function runs at most once per interval during continuous events — for scrolling, mousemove, resize updates.
n920.f: How would you add a cancel method to debounce?

n928.a: Partial application fixes some arguments of a function, producing a new function that takes the remaining ones. `Function.prototype.bind` does it natively (`multiply.bind(null, 2)`), or a helper `partial(fn, ...preset)`.
n928.f: How does lodash support placeholders in partial?

n959.a: Currying turns an n-ary function into n nested unary functions, applied one argument at a time, and is automatic until all args are provided. Partial application fixes any number of arguments at once and returns a function that takes the rest, once. A curried function makes partial application trivial.
p: Currying: one arg per call, chain of functions
Partial: fix some args at once
Partial produces a single new function
n959.f: Is `add(1, 2)(3)` currying or partial application with a flexible curry?

n985.a: Examples: event handlers that need extra data (`onClick={handleSelect(id)}` via a curried handler), logging (`const logWarn = log('warn')`), API helpers (`const getUsers = request('GET', '/users')`), validation (`const minLength = n => s => s.length >= n`), and reusable array predicates (`items.filter(byCategory('books'))`).
n985.f: What's a downside of creating curried handlers in every render?

n1026.a: The Command pattern wraps an action in an object with an `execute` (and often `undo`) method, decoupling the code that triggers it from the code that performs it. Used for undo/redo stacks, queuing and logging operations, keyboard shortcut and menu systems, and macro recording.
p: Encapsulate an action as an object

n1027.a: The Decorator pattern adds behaviour to an object or function by wrapping it, without changing the original: e.g. wrapping a function with logging, caching, retry or auth checks. In JS this is often done with higher-order functions; TypeScript/ES decorators (`@log`) apply it to classes and methods.
n1027.f: How do decorators differ from inheritance for adding behaviour?
n1027.c:
const withRetry = (fn, tries = 3) => async (...args) => { for (let i = 1; ; i++) { try { return await fn(...args); } catch (e) { if (i >= tries) throw e; } } };
const fetchUserSafe = withRetry(fetchUser);

n1034.a: The Factory pattern creates objects through a function or method instead of calling constructors directly, choosing which type to create based on input and hiding construction details. Used for creating UI components by type, API clients per environment, or parsers per file format.
n1034.f: How does a factory help with testing?

n1036.a: The Module pattern uses a closure (often an IIFE) to keep variables private and return a public API object, encapsulating state and avoiding global pollution. ES modules now provide the same benefits natively: anything not exported is private.
n1036.c: const Counter = (() => { let count = 0; return { inc: () => ++count, get: () => count }; })();

n1093.a: I organize code into ES modules by feature (components, hooks, services, utils per feature), keep business logic in pure functions separate from UI and side effects, favour composition and small functions over deep class hierarchies, use classes where state + behaviour fit naturally, and enforce consistency with TypeScript, ESLint and Prettier.
p: Pure logic separate from side effects
n1093.f: How do you prevent circular dependencies between modules?

n16.a: Implement an event bus with a Map of event name to a Set of handlers: `subscribe` adds a handler and returns an unsubscribe function, `publish` calls all handlers for that event. To avoid leaks, always call the returned unsubscribe when a widget is destroyed (e.g. in a React effect cleanup or disconnectedCallback), use AbortSignal-based subscriptions, and use `once` for one-time listeners.
p: publish iterates a copy of handlers
n16.f: Why iterate over a copy of the handlers when publishing?

n932.a: The Prototype pattern creates new objects by cloning or linking to an existing object (the prototype) instead of instantiating a class. In JavaScript it's built in: `Object.create(proto)` creates an object that delegates to `proto`, and all objects share methods through their prototype chain.
n932.f: How is delegation different from copying properties?
n932.c:
const carProto = { drive() { return `${this.name} is driving`; } };
const car = Object.create(carProto, { name: { value: 'Tesla' } });

n933.a: A Singleton ensures only one instance of something exists and provides a global access point: e.g. a config store, logger, or API client. In JS, an ES module that exports an instance is naturally a singleton. Downsides: hidden global state, harder testing and coupling.
p: ES module export acts as singleton
n933.f: How would you reset a singleton between tests?

n935.a: The Strategy pattern defines a family of interchangeable algorithms behind a common interface and selects one at runtime, instead of large if/else blocks. Examples: payment methods, sorting options, validation rules, pricing calculations.
n935.f: How does Strategy support the open/closed principle?
n935.c:
const shipping = { standard: w => 5 + w * 0.5, express: w => 15 + w, free: () => 0 };
const cost = shipping[selectedOption](weight);

n949.a: The Observer pattern lets a subject maintain a list of observers and notify them automatically on state changes. Use cases: DOM event listeners, pub/sub event buses, state management stores (Redux subscribe), RxJS observables, data binding and real-time updates.
p: Subject keeps a list of observers
n949.f: How is Observer different from Pub/Sub?

n988.a: Design patterns are proven, reusable solutions to common software design problems, such as Singleton, Factory, Observer, Strategy, Decorator and Module. They give teams a shared vocabulary, encourage maintainable and flexible code, and help avoid reinventing solutions — but should be applied only when they fit the problem.
n988.f: Which patterns do you see most in frontend frameworks?

n1019.a: `async` functions always return a promise; `await` pauses inside the function until a promise settles, returning its value or throwing its rejection. This makes asynchronous code read like synchronous code, uses normal try/catch for errors, and avoids long `.then` chains. Run independent work in parallel with `Promise.all` instead of sequential awaits.
n1019.f: What's the cost of awaiting independent calls one after another?

n1044.a: `Promise.all(iterable)` runs promises concurrently and resolves with an array of results in the same order once all fulfil; it rejects immediately when any promise rejects (the others keep running but their results are ignored). Used for parallel independent requests.
p: allSettled when partial failure is OK
n1044.f: How do you limit concurrency when you have 1000 requests?

n1103.a: I use promises daily via fetch and async/await, combinators (`all`, `allSettled`, `race`, `any`), cancellation with AbortController, and wrapping callback APIs (`new Promise`, `util.promisify`). Polyfills (core-js, es6-promise) were needed for IE11; today native support is universal, but implementing a Promise polyfill is a common exercise to understand states, then chaining and microtask scheduling.
n1103.f: How would you implement Promise.all yourself?

n1147.a: A promise is an object representing the eventual result of an asynchronous operation: pending, then fulfilled with a value or rejected with a reason. You chain `.then`, `.catch` and `.finally`, or use `await`. Use them for network requests, timers, file I/O, and wrapping callback APIs.
n1147.f: What happens if you call resolve twice?
n1147.c:
const sleep = ms => new Promise(resolve => setTimeout(resolve, ms));
await sleep(500);

n5.a: `Promise.all` rejects as soon as one fails: use it when all results are required (e.g. a page that can't render without every piece) — the user sees an error state. `Promise.allSettled` waits for all and reports each outcome: use it for independent widgets — the user sees four widgets and an error message for the failed one. `Promise.any` resolves with the first success and only rejects if all fail: use it for redundant sources (mirrors/CDNs) — the user sees the fastest successful result.
p: allSettled: partial results with per-item status
race: first to settle (success or failure)
n5.f: When would Promise.race be the right choice?
n5.c:
const results = await Promise.allSettled(urls.map(u => fetch(u).then(r => r.json())));
results.forEach((r, i) => r.status === 'fulfilled' ? renderWidget(i, r.value) : renderError(i, r.reason));

n6.a: Out-of-order responses cause stale data. Fixes: cancel the previous request with AbortController when a new query starts; or tag each request with an incrementing id/the query and ignore responses that aren't the latest; in React, use an `ignore` flag in the effect cleanup; or use libraries like TanStack Query that key results by query. Debouncing reduces requests but doesn't fix the race alone.
p: Ignore stale responses with a request id

n7.a: Use `AbortSignal.timeout(ms)` (or a controller aborted by setTimeout) so the fetch rejects with a TimeoutError after the deadline. A plain `Promise.race` with a timer only stops waiting — the request keeps running in the background. AbortController actually cancels the network request; a timeout is just one reason to abort, while manual cancellation is triggered by user actions or component unmounts. `AbortSignal.any` combines both.
n7.f: What should the UI show for a timeout vs a user cancel?

n882.a: Pros: avoid callback hell with flat chaining, centralized error handling with catch, composition with all/race/allSettled, guaranteed async resolution (no sync/async ambiguity), and enable async/await. Cons: a promise settles only once (not for repeated events), can't be cancelled by itself, slight overhead, and forgotten catch leads to unhandled rejections.
n882.f: What would you use for a stream of values instead?

n946.a: A promise is pending initially, then becomes either fulfilled (resolved with a value) or rejected (with a reason). Once fulfilled or rejected it is settled and immutable: further resolve/reject calls are ignored. A promise resolved with another promise follows that promise's state.
p: Resolving with a promise adopts its state
n946.f: Can you check a promise's state synchronously?

n984.a: `Promise.all` resolves with an array of values when all fulfil and rejects immediately on the first rejection. `Promise.allSettled` always waits for every promise and resolves with an array of `{ status: 'fulfilled', value }` or `{ status: 'rejected', reason }` objects; it never rejects.
n984.f: How would you write allSettled using Promise.all?

n1022.a: `Object.freeze(obj)` makes an object immutable at the top level: no adding, removing or changing properties (silently ignored, or TypeError in strict mode), and property descriptors can't be changed. It's shallow: nested objects remain mutable unless frozen recursively. Use it for constants and to prevent accidental mutation.

n1023.a: `Object.preventExtensions(obj)` prevents adding new properties, but existing properties can still be changed and deleted. Check with `Object.isExtensible`. It's the weakest of the three restrictions (preventExtensions < seal < freeze).
n1023.f: Can you change the prototype of a non-extensible object?

n1024.a: `Object.seal(obj)` prevents adding or deleting properties and makes all properties non-configurable, but existing writable properties can still be changed. Check with `Object.isSealed`.
n1024.f: When would seal be preferable to freeze?

n1037.a: Every object has an internal link (`[[Prototype]]`) to another object. When you access a property, JavaScript looks at the object itself, then its prototype, then the prototype's prototype, and so on until it finds the property or reaches `null` (returning undefined). This chain is how methods are shared (e.g. arrays get `map` from `Array.prototype`).
n1037.f: What's the performance cost of long prototype chains?

n1040.a: `new` calls a function as a constructor: it creates a new empty object, sets its prototype to the constructor's `prototype`, runs the constructor with `this` bound to the new object, and returns that object (unless the constructor explicitly returns another object).
p: Arrow functions can't be used with new
n1040.f: What happens if you forget new with a function constructor?

n15.a: `new Person('Ana')`: (1) create a new empty object; (2) set its `[[Prototype]]` to `Person.prototype`; (3) call `Person` with `this` set to the new object and the arguments; (4) return the object unless the function returns another object. With `class Person { constructor(name) { this.name = name } greet() {} }`, the constructor body becomes the function, methods go on `Person.prototype`, and `extends` sets up both `Child.prototype → Parent.prototype` and `Child → Parent` (for statics). Classes add strict mode, non-enumerable methods and require `new`.
p: Class syntax is sugar over the same chain
n15.f: Why must super() be called before using this in a derived class?

n868.a: Objects inherit directly from other objects: each object has a prototype it delegates to for missing properties. Constructor functions and classes set the prototype of instances to `Constructor.prototype`, so methods defined there are shared by all instances. Inheritance is a chain of these links (e.g. `Dog.prototype → Animal.prototype → Object.prototype`).
p: class extends sets up the chain
n868.f: How do you check if an object is in another's prototype chain?

n872.a: Object literals `{}`, constructor functions with `new`, ES6 classes, `Object.create(proto)` (custom prototype, or null), factory functions returning objects, `Object.assign`/spread to compose, `Object.fromEntries`, and `structuredClone`/JSON for copies.

n875.a: Classes are mostly syntactic sugar over constructor functions, but differ: classes must be called with `new`, class bodies run in strict mode, class declarations are hoisted but in the TDZ (not usable before definition), methods are non-enumerable, `extends` handles prototype setup and `super`, and classes support private `#fields`, static blocks and fields.
n875.f: How would you do inheritance with ES5 constructors?

n901.a: Static members belong to the class itself, not instances: use them for utility functions related to the class (`Date.now`, `Array.from`), factory methods (`User.fromJSON`), constants and configuration, and shared caches or counters across instances.
n901.f: Are static members inherited by subclasses?

n902.a: Symbols are unique, immutable primitive values used as property keys that won't collide with other keys, ideal for hidden/meta properties and library internals. Well-known symbols customize language behaviour: `Symbol.iterator` (iteration), `Symbol.asyncIterator`, `Symbol.toPrimitive`, `Symbol.toStringTag`. `Symbol.for` creates global shared symbols.
p: Not enumerated by for...in or JSON
n902.f: How would you make an object iterable using Symbol.iterator?

n904.a: Each property has a descriptor: data properties have `value`, `writable`, `enumerable`, `configurable`; accessor properties have `get`, `set`, `enumerable`, `configurable`. Read them with `Object.getOwnPropertyDescriptor` and define with `Object.defineProperty`. Flags default to false when using defineProperty.
n904.c:
Object.defineProperty(user, 'id', { value: 7, writable: false, enumerable: false });
Object.getOwnPropertyDescriptor(user, 'id');

n905.a: Getters and setters define computed properties accessed like normal fields: a getter computes a value on read (e.g. fullName), a setter runs code on write (validation, normalization, triggering updates). They provide encapsulation while keeping a simple property API.
n905.f: What happens if you define a getter without a setter and assign to it?

n906.a: A `Proxy` wraps an object and intercepts operations through handler "traps" (get, set, has, deleteProperty, apply, construct). Used for validation, logging, default values, negative array indexes, reactivity systems (Vue 3, MobX), access control and mocking. `Reflect` provides default behaviours inside traps.
n906.f: How does Vue 3 use proxies for reactivity?

n924.a: `class Child extends Parent` sets Child's prototype chain to Parent; the constructor must call `super(...)` before using `this`; methods can be overridden and call `super.method()`; static members are inherited too. You can extend built-ins like Error and Array.
p: extends sets up the prototype chain
n924.f: What happens if a derived constructor doesn't call super()?
n924.c:
class Shape { constructor(name) { this.name = name; } area() { return 0; } }
class Circle extends Shape { constructor(r) { super('circle'); this.r = r; } area() { return Math.PI * this.r ** 2; } }

n939.a: Classical inheritance (Java, C++) uses classes as blueprints; instances are created from classes and inheritance is defined between classes at compile time. Prototypal inheritance (JavaScript) has objects inherit directly from other objects through prototype links at runtime, which is more flexible (you can change prototypes, mix in behaviour). JS `class` syntax mimics the classical style on top of prototypes.
p: JS classes are sugar over prototypes
Composition and mixins are natural in JS
n939.f: What's a mixin and how would you implement one?

Disadvantages: can break old code relying on sloppy behaviours, and concatenating strict/non-strict scripts can cause issues. Modules and classes are strict automatically.

n854.a: Hoisting is JavaScript's behaviour of processing declarations before executing code: `var` declarations are hoisted and initialized to undefined; function declarations are hoisted with their body (callable before definition); `let`, `const` and `class` are hoisted but not initialized, so accessing them before declaration throws a ReferenceError (temporal dead zone).

n855.a: `var` is function-scoped, hoisted and initialized as undefined, can be redeclared, and creates a property on window at global level. `let` is block-scoped, in the TDZ until declared, can't be redeclared in the same scope, and can be reassigned. `const` is like let but must be initialized and can't be reassigned (the object it points to can still be mutated).

n869.a: `function Person(){}` is a function declaration. `const person = Person()` calls it as a normal function: `this` is undefined (strict) or global, and since it returns nothing, `person` is undefined. `const person = new Person()` calls it as a constructor, creating a new object linked to `Person.prototype` and assigning it to `person`.

n870.a: `function foo() {}` is a declaration: both name and body are hoisted, so `foo` can be called before the line. `var foo = function() {}` is an expression assigned to a variable: only the `var` is hoisted (as undefined), so calling `foo()` before the assignment throws a TypeError ("foo is not a function").

n880.a: Strict mode is an opt-in restricted variant of JavaScript (`'use strict'` at the top of a file or function) that turns silent errors into thrown errors, makes `this` undefined in standalone function calls, disallows undeclared variables, `with`, duplicate parameters and octal literals, and reserves future keywords. ES modules and classes are strict by default.

n923.a: Function declarations are hoisted completely (name and body), so you can call them before they appear. Function expressions and arrow functions assigned to variables follow the variable's hoisting: `var` gives undefined (TypeError when called), `let`/`const` give a TDZ ReferenceError.

n927.a: Lexical (static) scoping means a function's access to variables is determined by where it is written in the source code, not where it's called. Inner functions can access variables of their outer functions; this is what makes closures possible.

n929.a: Scope determines where variables are accessible. JavaScript has global scope, module scope, function scope and block scope (let/const in `{}`). Scopes nest, and lookup goes from inner to outer scopes (the scope chain). Inner scopes can shadow outer variables.
n929.f: What's variable shadowing and when is it a problem?

n942.a: Global scope variables are accessible everywhere. Function scope (var, and everything declared in a function) is accessible only within that function. Block scope (let, const, class within `{}` blocks like if/for) is accessible only within that block. `var` ignores block scope.

n945.a: All three are hoisted. `var` is initialized with undefined, so reading it before the assignment gives undefined. `let` and `const` are hoisted but uninitialized; accessing them before the declaration throws a ReferenceError (temporal dead zone).
n945.f: Why does `typeof x` throw for a let in the TDZ but not for undeclared variables?

n983.a: Function declarations are hoisted with their bodies, so they're callable anywhere in their scope. Function expressions (including arrows) are only as hoisted as the variable they're assigned to: with var, the name is undefined before the assignment (calling throws TypeError); with let/const, accessing early throws ReferenceError.

n1136.a: `this` is determined by how a function is called: method call (`obj.fn()`) → obj; plain call → undefined in strict mode (global otherwise); `new` → the new instance; `call/apply/bind` → explicitly set; event handlers → the element. n866.a: An arrow function assigned in the constructor (or as a class field) captures the instance's `this` lexically, so the method stays bound when passed as a callback (event handlers, setTimeout, React props) without calling bind. Trade-off: each instance gets its own copy of the function instead of sharing one on the prototype, and it can't be overridden via the prototype.

n947.a: Four rules plus arrows: default binding (plain call → undefined in strict, global otherwise), implicit binding (method call → the object before the dot), explicit binding (`call`, `apply`, `bind`), and `new` binding (the new instance). n47.a: Both describe object shapes. `interface` can be extended with `extends`, supports declaration merging (useful for augmenting libraries), and gives clearer error messages for object types. `type` aliases can represent anything: unions, intersections, primitives, tuples, mapped and conditional types. n48.a: `any` disables type checking — anything goes (avoid; use for migration only). `unknown` is the type-safe top type: you can assign anything to it but must narrow it before use — ideal for `JSON.parse` results, catch errors and external input. `never` is the bottom type for values that can't exist: functions that always throw, and exhaustive checks in switch statements.

n1111.a: Spread expands an iterable or object into its parts (copying arrays/objects, merging, passing array elements as arguments), while rest collects multiple elements into one array/object (function parameters, destructuring). n1151.a: Under HTTP/1.1, browsers limited parallel connections per domain (about six), so spreading assets across several domains ("domain sharding") increased parallel downloads; cookie-free domains also avoided sending cookies with static requests. n1153.a: Long-polling: the client sends a request the server holds open until data is available, then the client immediately reconnects — works everywhere but has overhead. WebSockets: a persistent full-duplex TCP connection for two-way, low-latency messaging (chat, games). Server-Sent Events: a one-way stream from server to client over HTTP with automatic reconnection and event IDs, great for notifications and live feeds.

n1154.a: `Expires`: absolute date after which a response is stale (older, overridden by Cache-Control max-age). `Date`: when the response was generated. `Age`: seconds the response has been in a shared cache. `If-Modified-Since`: conditional request; server returns 304 if unchanged since `Last-Modified`. `DNT`: the user's do-not-track preference (deprecated). `Cache-Control`: caching directives (max-age, no-cache, no-store, public, private, immutable). `Transfer-Encoding`: how the body is encoded for transfer, e.g. chunked. `ETag`: a version identifier for conditional requests via `If-None-Match`. `X-Frame-Options`: whether the page may be framed (DENY/SAMEORIGIN), protecting against clickjacking (now CSP frame-ancestors).

n1179.a: With HTTP/1.1, browsers open about 6 parallel connections per host (exact number varies), so requests beyond that queue. Exceptions: HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 multiplex many concurrent requests over a single connection, and different hosts get their own connection pools.

n56.a: `Cache-Control: max-age=N` lets clients reuse a response for N seconds without asking the server. `immutable` tells the browser the file will never change, so don't revalidate even on reload. `ETag` is a version identifier: after expiry the browser sends `If-None-Match`, and the server replies 304 Not Modified if unchanged. For a hashed bundle like `app.3f9a1c.js`: `Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable` — new content gets a new filename. For `index.html`: `Cache-Control: no-cache` (always revalidate with ETag) so users get new bundle references immediately after a deploy.

n57.a: Browsers enforce the same-origin policy: JavaScript can't read responses from a different origin (scheme, host or port) unless the server allows it via CORS headers. For "non-simple" requests (JSON content type, custom headers like Authorization, PUT/DELETE), the browser first sends an OPTIONS preflight. The server must respond with `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` (your origin), and for preflights `Access-Control-Allow-Methods`/`Allow-Headers`; with cookies, `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true` and a specific (non-*) origin. It's fixed on the server (or via a same-origin proxy), not in the frontend.
p: Same-origin policy blocks reading cross-origin responses
n57.f: Why does a request succeed in Postman but fail in the browser?

n861.a: Cookies (~4KB) are sent with every HTTP request to the domain, can be HttpOnly/Secure/SameSite, and have an expiry — used for sessions and server-readable data. localStorage (~5–10MB) persists until cleared, is per origin, and is accessible only from JS (not sent to the server). sessionStorage is like localStorage but scoped to a single tab and cleared when it closes. Both storages are synchronous and string-only.
p: Cookies: sent to server, small, can be HttpOnly
Never store secrets accessible to XSS
n861.f: Why is HttpOnly important for session cookies?

n903.a: Server-Sent Events let a server push a stream of text events to the browser over a single long-lived HTTP connection. In the browser, `new EventSource(url)` receives `message` (and named) events, automatically reconnects, and resumes with `Last-Event-ID`. It's one-way (server → client); use WebSockets for bidirectional needs.
p: Great for notifications, live feeds, AI token streaming
n903.f: How do LLM chat UIs often use streaming responses?
n903.c:
const es = new EventSource('/api/notifications');
es.addEventListener('message', e => showToast(JSON.parse(e.data)));

n916.a: Caching stores copies of data or computations so repeated requests are served faster. Layers: browser HTTP cache (Cache-Control, ETag), service worker caches (offline, stale-while-revalidate), CDN edge caches, application/in-memory caches (memoization, React Query), and server caches (Redis). The challenge is invalidation: hashed filenames, TTLs and revalidation.

n936.a: WebSocket provides a persistent, full-duplex connection between browser and server over a single TCP connection, started via an HTTP upgrade. Both sides can send messages at any time with low overhead, ideal for chat, multiplayer games, collaborative editing and live dashboards. You handle reconnection, heartbeats and message formats yourself.
n936.f: How would you handle reconnection with backoff?

n955.a: Reduce the number and size of requests: bundle and code-split, compress (Brotli/gzip), use modern formats (WebP/AVIF), cache with proper headers and a CDN, use HTTP/2/3, preconnect/preload critical resources, lazy-load non-critical assets, debounce and dedupe API calls, paginate, batch requests, and use GraphQL or BFFs to avoid over-fetching.
n955.f: How does request deduplication work in data-fetching libraries?

n975.a: Call `fetch(url, options)`, which returns a promise of a Response. Check `res.ok`, parse with `res.json()` (or text/blob), and for POST pass `method`, `headers` and a `body` (JSON.stringify). Handle network errors with try/catch, and cancel with AbortController.
p: Check res.ok (fetch doesn't reject on HTTP errors)
n975.f: How do you send cookies with a cross-origin fetch?

n994.a: Rest parameters (`...args`) collect any number of remaining arguments into a real array. They must be last, replace the old `arguments` object (which isn't an array and isn't available in arrow functions), and work well for variadic functions.
p: Collects remaining args into an array
n994.f: How does fn.length treat rest parameters?

n1001.a: Batch DOM reads and writes; change classes instead of many inline styles; modify elements off-DOM (DocumentFragment) or hidden then show; avoid layout-triggering reads in loops; animate only transform and opacity; use `will-change` sparingly; virtualize long lists; use `content-visibility: auto` for offscreen content; and contain layout with CSS `contain`.

n1004.a: Chrome DevTools Performance panel (flame charts, long tasks), Lighthouse and PageSpeed Insights, WebPageTest, the Performance and Memory panels for leaks, `performance.now()`/`performance.mark()`/`measure()`, the web-vitals library for real user metrics, React Profiler, bundle analyzers (webpack-bundle-analyzer, source-map-explorer), and RUM tools (Sentry, Datadog).
n1004.f: Why are lab and field data both needed?

n1007.a: Module bundlers (Vite/Rollup, webpack, esbuild) resolve imports into optimized files: they combine modules, tree-shake unused code, minify, split code into chunks for lazy loading, handle assets (CSS, images), transpile modern syntax, add content hashes for caching, and provide dev servers with HMR.
n1007.f: Why is bundling still useful with native ES modules?

n1018.a: Web Workers run scripts on a background thread, communicating with the main thread via `postMessage`. Moving CPU-heavy work (parsing big JSON, image processing, sorting/filtering large data, crypto, syntax highlighting) to a worker keeps the main thread free for rendering and input, preventing jank. Workers can't touch the DOM; transferables (ArrayBuffer) avoid copying costs; libraries like Comlink simplify the API.
n1018.f: What data can't be sent to a worker?

n1049.a: Progressive rendering shows content to the user as soon as possible rather than waiting for everything: streaming HTML (SSR streaming, flushing the head early), lazy-loading images below the fold, prioritizing above-the-fold content and critical CSS, skeleton screens, and loading async chunks after the initial render.
n1049.f: How does React's streaming SSR with Suspense implement this?

n1158.a: Chrome DevTools Performance panel (record, look for long tasks, layout thrashing, forced reflows), Lighthouse, the Memory panel for leaks (heap snapshots, allocation timelines), Network panel with throttling, React DevTools Profiler for unnecessary renders, `performance.mark/measure` for custom timings, and RUM data (web-vitals) to see real-user impact.
n1158.f: How do you find a detached DOM node leak?

n1159.a: Use passive event listeners for scroll/touch, throttle or use requestAnimationFrame for scroll handlers, prefer IntersectionObserver over scroll calculations, animate only transform/opacity, avoid expensive paint effects on large areas (heavy shadows, filters, fixed backgrounds), virtualize long lists, use `content-visibility`, and reduce DOM size.
n1159.f: Why do passive listeners help scrolling?

n1160.a: Layout (reflow) calculates the size and position of each element. Paint fills in pixels — text, colors, images, borders, shadows — into layers. Compositing combines layers in the right order (on the GPU) to draw the final frame. Changing geometry triggers all three; changing color triggers paint and composite; changing transform or opacity often only needs compositing.
n1160.f: What creates a new compositing layer?

n1169.a: Examples: optimized images (responsive sizes, WebP/AVIF, lazy loading), code splitting and tree-shaking, caching with hashed assets and a CDN, critical CSS and deferred scripts, font optimization, reducing third-party scripts, SSR/SSG for faster first paint, virtualization for long lists, memoization to reduce re-renders, and monitoring Core Web Vitals.
n1169.f: Which optimization gave you the biggest measurable gain?

n1178.a: Minify and compress (Brotli/gzip) CSS/JS/HTML; bundle and code-split; tree-shake; optimize and resize images in modern formats with srcset; subset and preload fonts; use a CDN and long-term caching with hashed filenames; remove unused CSS/JS and heavy dependencies; lazy-load non-critical resources; and audit third-party scripts.
p: Remove unused code and third parties
n1178.f: How would you find the biggest dependencies in a bundle?

n1180.a: 1) Optimize the critical rendering path: inline critical CSS, defer non-critical JS. 2) Reduce payload: compress and resize images, code-split, remove unused code. 3) Cache and deliver efficiently with a CDN and HTTP caching. Perceived load: skeleton screens, progressive rendering, and prioritizing above-the-fold content.
n1180.f: What's the difference between actual and perceived performance?

n1185.a: FOUC (Flash of Unstyled Content) happens when HTML renders before its CSS loads, briefly showing unstyled content. Avoid it by linking CSS in the head (render-blocking by design), inlining critical CSS, avoiding `@import` chains, not injecting styles late with JS, and for CSS-in-JS ensuring SSR extracts styles. Similar flashes happen with fonts (FOUT) and theming.
n1185.f: How would you prevent a dark-mode flash?

n53.a: Diagnose: identify the LCP element (Lighthouse, Performance panel, web-vitals attribution) and break LCP into TTFB, resource load delay, load duration and render delay. Fixes: reduce TTFB (CDN, caching, SSR/SSG); make the LCP image discoverable in HTML (not via JS/CSS background), add `fetchpriority="high"` or preload it, never lazy-load it; compress and serve the right size (srcset, AVIF/WebP); eliminate render-blocking CSS/JS (critical CSS, defer); and avoid client-side rendering delays for the hero content. Verify with field data.
p: Break into TTFB, load delay, load time, render delay
Make the image discoverable and high priority
n53.f: Why does client-side rendering often hurt LCP?

n54.a: LCP (Largest Contentful Paint) measures load speed of the main content (good ≤ 2.5s); bad scores come from slow servers, render-blocking resources, large or lazy-loaded hero images, and client-side rendering. INP (Interaction to Next Paint) measures responsiveness to user input (good ≤ 200ms); bad scores come from long JS tasks, heavy event handlers, and large re-renders. CLS (Cumulative Layout Shift) measures visual stability (good ≤ 0.1); bad scores come from images/ads without dimensions, injected content, and web fonts swapping.
p: LCP killers: slow TTFB, blocking resources, big images
INP: long tasks; CLS: missing dimensions, late content

n926.a: Lazy loading defers loading resources until they're needed: images and iframes with `loading="lazy"` or IntersectionObserver, JavaScript via dynamic `import()` and `React.lazy` for routes/heavy components, and data loaded on scroll. It reduces initial payload, speeds up first load and saves bandwidth. Don't lazy-load above-the-fold content.
n926.f: How do you avoid layout shift with lazy images?

n938.a: Tree shaking removes unused exports from the final bundle by statically analyzing ES module imports/exports. It requires ESM (static structure), side-effect-free modules (declared with `"sideEffects": false` in package.json), and named imports. CommonJS and side-effectful code limit it.
n938.f: Why can `import _ from 'lodash'` defeat tree shaking?

n954.a: Minimize DOM access and size: batch reads/writes, use DocumentFragment or `replaceChildren` for many insertions, update classes instead of individual styles, use event delegation, avoid layout thrashing, debounce frequent updates, use requestAnimationFrame for visual changes, and virtualize long lists.
n954.f: Why can a frameworks' virtual DOM still be slower than targeted DOM updates?

n998.a: Common bottlenecks: long tasks blocking the main thread, large bundles and heavy dependencies, excessive re-renders in frameworks, layout thrashing and expensive DOM operations, memory leaks (listeners, timers, detached nodes), inefficient algorithms on large data, unoptimized images, too many network requests, and third-party scripts.
n998.f: How would you break up a long task?

n1002.a: Tools: npm audit / Snyk / Dependabot for vulnerable dependencies, ESLint security plugins and static analysis (Semgrep, CodeQL, SonarQube), DAST scanners (OWASP ZAP, Burp Suite), CSP reports, browser security headers checkers, and manual code reviews against the OWASP Top 10. Techniques: threat modeling, penetration testing, and dependency pinning with lockfiles.
n1002.f: How do supply-chain attacks via npm packages happen?

n1020.a: XSS is when an attacker injects malicious script into a page that runs in other users' browsers, stealing cookies/tokens or acting as the user. Types: stored, reflected and DOM-based. Prevent it by escaping output (frameworks like React escape by default), avoiding `innerHTML`/`dangerouslySetInnerHTML` with untrusted data (or sanitizing with DOMPurify), validating URLs (block `javascript:`), using a strict Content Security Policy, HttpOnly cookies, and Trusted Types.
p: Injected scripts run as the victim
n1020.f: How can a React app still be vulnerable to XSS?

n1086.a: The same-origin policy prevents scripts from one origin (scheme + host + port) from reading data from another origin — DOM of other windows/iframes, responses of cross-origin requests, storage. It isolates sites so a malicious page can't read your bank data. Controlled exceptions: CORS, postMessage, and embedding resources (images, scripts) which can be loaded but not read.
p: CORS and postMessage as controlled exceptions
n1086.f: Why can a page load a cross-origin image but not read its pixels without CORS?

n1171.a: Examples: preventing XSS with output escaping, sanitization and CSP; protecting session cookies with HttpOnly/Secure/SameSite; CSRF tokens; avoiding storing tokens in localStorage; Subresource Integrity for CDN scripts; clickjacking protection with frame-ancestors; keeping dependencies patched (supply-chain attacks); and removing secrets from frontend bundles.

n1188.a: CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing) is an HTTP-header-based mechanism that lets a server tell browsers which other origins may read its responses. It addresses the restriction of the same-origin policy, enabling legitimate cross-origin API calls (e.g. app.example.com calling api.example.com) while keeping other origins blocked.
n1188.f: Does CORS protect your server from attacks?

n55.a: Rendering user text with innerHTML treats it as HTML, so a comment like `` executes for every visitor (stored XSS): session theft, defacement, actions as the user. Fix: render as text with `textContent` (or React's default `{text}` escaping); if formatting is needed, sanitize with DOMPurify against an allowlist; add a Content Security Policy and HttpOnly cookies as defense in depth; validate/encode on the server too.
p: Sanitize with DOMPurify when HTML is needed
CSP and HttpOnly as defense in depth
n55.f: Why doesn't `<script>` inserted via innerHTML execute while onerror does?

n918.a: Content Security Policy is an HTTP header (or meta tag) that tells the browser which sources of scripts, styles, images, frames etc. are allowed. A strict CSP (nonces or hashes for scripts, no `unsafe-inline`/`unsafe-eval`) blocks injected scripts even if an XSS bug exists, and `frame-ancestors` prevents clickjacking. Use `Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only` to roll it out safely.

n919.a: CSRF tricks a logged-in user's browser into sending an unwanted request to a site where they're authenticated (cookies are sent automatically), e.g. a hidden form that transfers money. Mitigations: SameSite cookies (Lax/Strict), anti-CSRF tokens (synchronizer or double-submit), checking Origin/Referer headers, requiring re-authentication for sensitive actions, and never changing state with GET requests.
n919.f: Why are token-in-header APIs (Authorization) less exposed to CSRF?

n925.a: Input validation checks that data matches expected types, formats, lengths and ranges before using it. Client-side validation improves UX but can be bypassed, so the server must always validate. It reduces injection attacks, data corruption and crashes; combine allowlists (what's allowed) with proper output encoding and parameterized queries.
n925.f: Why isn't input validation alone enough to prevent XSS?

n953.a: Authentication: use a proven provider or protocol (OAuth 2.0/OIDC with PKCE), store sessions in HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookies rather than localStorage, enforce HTTPS, short-lived tokens with refresh rotation, MFA, and rate limiting. Authorization: enforce permissions on the server for every request (frontend checks are only for UX), use role/attribute-based access control, and least privilege.
n953.f: Why can't you rely on hiding admin buttons for security?

n956.a: Clickjacking embeds your site in an invisible iframe to trick users into clicking. Prevent it with the `Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'none'` (or `'self'`) header, the older `X-Frame-Options: DENY/SAMEORIGIN`, and SameSite cookies; frame-busting JavaScript is a weak fallback.
n956.f: How would you allow embedding only on partner sites?

n957.a: SQL injection happens server-side (e.g. Node.js) when user input is concatenated into SQL. Prevent it with parameterized queries/prepared statements, ORMs or query builders that parameterize, input validation, least-privilege database accounts, and never building queries with template strings. Same idea for NoSQL injection (validate types, avoid passing raw objects to queries).
n957.c:
// unsafe: db.query(`SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = '${email}'`)
const { rows } = await db.query('SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = $1', [email]);

n996.a: Don't put secrets (API keys, private tokens) in frontend code — everything shipped is public. Use HTTPS, keep auth tokens in HttpOnly cookies, avoid storing sensitive data in localStorage or logs, minimize data kept client-side, clear it on logout, mask inputs, disable autocomplete for sensitive fields where appropriate, and validate everything server-side.
n996.f: How would you call a third-party API that requires a secret key?

n999.a: `Content-Security-Policy` (restrict sources, mitigate XSS), `Strict-Transport-Security` (force HTTPS), `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff` (stop MIME sniffing), `X-Frame-Options`/CSP `frame-ancestors` (clickjacking), `Referrer-Policy` (limit referrer leakage), `Permissions-Policy` (restrict APIs like camera), and `Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy`/`Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy` (isolation).

n1000.a: Jest and Vitest (unit/integration test runners with mocking), Mocha + Chai, Jasmine, React Testing Library and Vue Test Utils (component testing), Playwright and Cypress (end-to-end), Storybook test runner, and MSW for API mocking.
n1000.f: Why has Vitest become popular in Vite projects?

n1003.a: Test runners (Jest, Vitest, Mocha), assertion libraries (Chai, expect), component testing (Testing Library), E2E (Playwright, Cypress, WebdriverIO), mocking (MSW, Sinon), coverage (Istanbul/c8), visual regression (Chromatic, Percy), accessibility testing (axe), and CI integration.
n1003.f: Which tests would you run on every commit vs nightly?

n1012.a: Unit tests (individual functions/components), integration tests (modules working together), end-to-end tests (full user flows in a real browser), plus regression, smoke, performance/load, accessibility, visual regression, security, contract and user acceptance testing.
n1012.f: How do you decide the right balance (testing pyramid vs trophy)?

n1161.a: Advantages: catch bugs early, safe refactoring, living documentation, better design (testable code), confidence to deploy often. Disadvantages: time to write and maintain, slower CI, brittle tests that test implementation details, and false confidence from poor tests or high coverage numbers.

n1164.a: A linter (ESLint, Stylelint) analyzes code for potential bugs (unused variables, missing dependencies in hooks), bad patterns and style violations, enforcing consistent conventions across a team and catching issues before review. Formatting is usually delegated to Prettier, while linting focuses on correctness.

n1190.a: Mention concrete sources: MDN, web.dev, official framework blogs/docs, newsletters (JavaScript Weekly, Frontend Focus), CSS-Tricks / Smashing Magazine, conference talks, GitHub and TC39 proposals, podcasts, and building small experiments.
n1190.f: How do you evaluate whether a new technology is ready for production?

n917.a: Code coverage measures what percentage of code (statements, branches, functions, lines) is executed by tests, using tools like Istanbul/c8. It shows untested areas, but high coverage doesn't mean good tests — assertions may be weak. Use it as a guide (e.g. branch coverage on critical logic), not a target to game.
p: Not a measure of test quality
n917.f: How can you have 100% coverage and still have bugs?

n931.a: TDD is writing a failing test first, writing the minimal code to make it pass, then refactoring while keeping tests green (red → green → refactor). It drives design toward testable, small units, gives fast feedback and a safety net, but can slow initial development and is harder for exploratory UI work.
n931.f: When have you found TDD most useful?

n944.a: Unit tests check a single function or component in isolation (fast, many). Integration tests check that several units work together (component + hooks + mocked API). End-to-end tests run the whole app in a real browser through user flows (login, checkout) with real or staging backends — slowest and most brittle but highest confidence.
n944.f: Where would you test a checkout form validation?

n958.a: Return or await the promise in the test (`async` test functions with `await`), use `expect(promise).resolves/rejects`, use fake timers (`vi.useFakeTimers()`, `jest.advanceTimersByTime`) for setTimeout/debounce, mock network requests (MSW or mocked fetch), and in UI tests use `findBy*`/`waitFor` to wait for async updates.
n958.f: What goes wrong if you forget to await an async assertion?

n982.a: Use a runner like Vitest or Jest: group related tests with `describe`, write `test`/`it` cases following Arrange-Act-Assert, use `expect` matchers, mock dependencies, and cover normal cases, edge cases and errors. Keep tests independent and fast.
n982.f: How do you test a function that depends on the current date?

n990.a: Test doubles replace real dependencies. A stub returns canned values so the code under test can run (e.g. an API returns a fixed user). A mock also records how it was called so you can assert on interactions (called once with these arguments). Spies wrap real functions to record calls. Fakes are lightweight working implementations (in-memory DB). Use them to isolate units, but don't over-mock.
p: Spy: records calls on real functions
n990.f: Why mock at the network level (MSW) instead of mocking fetch functions?

n997.a: Test behaviour, not implementation details (query by role/text like a user); keep tests independent, deterministic and fast; use clear names and Arrange-Act-Assert; avoid excessive mocking; use factories for test data; one concept per test; cover edge cases; keep E2E tests for critical flows; and run them in CI.
n997.f: Why is getByRole preferred over getByTestId?

n494.a: Nested checkboxes: a tree where checking a parent checks all descendants, and a parent shows checked when all children are checked, indeterminate when some are, unchecked when none. Model the tree as data (id, label, children), store checked state for leaves, derive parent state, and set the DOM `indeterminate` property on parents.
n494.f: Why derive parent state instead of storing it?

n495.a: Tic-Tac-Toe design: state is a 9-cell array plus the current player (or derived from move count) and a history for undo. Compute the winner from the 8 winning lines after each move; disable moves after a win or draw. Render a grid of buttons with accessible labels ("Row 1, column 2, X"), announce status in a live region, and support an N×N board with a configurable win length for extensibility.
n495.f: How would you add an AI opponent?

n496.a: An analytics script: a tiny async snippet that queues calls (`window.ga = window.ga || function(){ (ga.q = ga.q || []).push(arguments) }`) before the full library loads, then the library processes the queue. Collect page views and events with context (URL, referrer, viewport, session/user IDs from first-party cookies), batch events, and send with `navigator.sendBeacon` (or fetch keepalive) so they survive page unload. Respect consent and Do Not Track, sample high-volume events, handle SPA route changes via History API hooks, and keep the script small and non-blocking.
p: Async loader with a command queue
Privacy, consent, and minimal performance impact
n496.f: Why does sendBeacon matter for exit events?
n496.c:
(function (w, d, s) { w.track = w.track || function () { (w.track.q = w.track.q || []).push(arguments); }; const el = d.createElement('script'); el.async = true; el.src = s; d.head.appendChild(el); })(window, document, 'https://cdn.example.com/a.js');
track('pageview', location.pathname);

n497.a: A slider (range input): use native `<input type="range">` if possible. A custom one needs a track and thumb, `role="slider"` with `aria-valuemin/max/now/valuetext`, pointer events with pointer capture for dragging, keyboard support (arrows, Page Up/Down, Home/End), configurable min/max/step, controlled and uncontrolled APIs, onChange vs onChangeEnd callbacks, range (two thumbs) support, RTL and vertical orientation.
n497.f: How would you prevent two thumbs from crossing?

n498.a: CodeSandbox: an online IDE. Components: a file tree and editor (Monaco/CodeMirror with multiple tabs), a bundler running in the browser (in a Web Worker or a sandboxed iframe, transpiling with esbuild-wasm/Babel and resolving npm packages from a CDN with caching), a preview iframe on a separate origin for security, console capture via postMessage, persistence (autosave to the server, versioning), sharing/forking, and real-time collaboration (CRDTs over WebSockets). Heavy projects can run in cloud VMs/containers instead.
p: Sandboxed preview on a different origin
n498.f: Why must the preview run on a separate origin?

n499.a: A WYSIWYG editor: avoid raw `contenteditable` + `execCommand` for anything serious; instead keep a structured document model (blocks and inline marks) and render it, intercepting input via `beforeinput` events to apply changes to the model (as ProseMirror, Lexical, Slate do). Features: toolbar for formatting, selection handling, undo/redo history, paste sanitization, keyboard shortcuts, serialization to HTML/Markdown/JSON, plugins, accessibility, and collaboration via OT/CRDT.

n500.a: YouTube frontend: pages for home feed, watch, search, channel. Watch page: an adaptive streaming video player (HLS/DASH with Media Source Extensions, bitrate switching, captions, keyboard controls), metadata, comments loaded lazily, and recommendations. Performance: SSR for first paint, lazy-load below-the-fold, image thumbnails with srcset and lazy loading, prefetch on hover, and a mini-player that persists across SPA navigation. Data: paginated APIs with cursors, caching (normalized store or query cache), optimistic likes/subscribes. Also: accessibility, i18n, analytics for watch time, and ad insertion.
n500.f: How would you keep the video playing during navigation?

n501.a: BFE.dev-style coding practice site: problem list with filters and progress; problem page with description, a code editor (Monaco), and a run/submit flow. Run tests safely in a sandboxed iframe or Web Worker with timeouts (or on a server sandbox for other languages), show results and console output. Persist drafts locally and to the server, track submissions, discussions, and solution reviews. SSR/SSG problem descriptions for SEO, lazy-load the editor, and keep the UI responsive.
n501.f: How would you stop infinite loops in user code from freezing the page?

n502.a: QR code login: the desktop page requests a login session from the server and displays a QR code containing a one-time session ID. The desktop listens for status (WebSocket, SSE or long polling). The logged-in mobile app scans it, shows a confirmation with device/location info, and on approval sends the session ID with its auth token to the server. The server marks the session approved and issues a session to the desktop, which completes login. Security: short expiry and refresh of codes, single use, binding to the browser, confirmation prompt to prevent QR phishing, HTTPS.
p: Server issues a one-time session ID
n502.f: How would an attacker abuse QR login, and how do you mitigate it?

n503.a: Twitter web app: timeline feed with cursor pagination and virtualization, real-time new-tweet indicator (SSE/WebSocket or polling), compose box with character counting, media upload and drafts, optimistic likes/retweets, normalized client cache (tweets, users), routing (timeline, profile, thread, search), SSR for shareable tweet pages and SEO, image/video lazy loading, accessibility (keyboard shortcuts, alt text), offline handling and error states.
p: SSR for public pages, media optimization
n503.f: Why show "N new posts" instead of inserting them automatically?

n504.a: Carousel widget: API (items, autoplay, interval, loop, slidesPerView, onChange), rendering a track with transform or scroll-snap, lazy-loading offscreen images, prev/next controls and indicators, keyboard and swipe support, autoplay that pauses on hover/focus and respects prefers-reduced-motion, accessible markup (region with label, slide "x of n" labels, live region when not autoplaying), and responsive behaviour.
p: ARIA carousel pattern and reduced motion
n504.f: How would you implement infinite looping without visible jumps?

n506.a: Star widget: props for max stars, value, onChange, readOnly and allowHalf. Render buttons or a radio group (best for accessibility: each star a radio labelled "3 stars"), show hover preview, keyboard arrows to change, and allow clearing. Use SVG stars with fill controlled by CSS; for half stars, clip the fill.
