n506.f: How would you support half-star ratings?

n507.a: A great TODO app: add/edit/delete/complete tasks, filters (all/active/done), drag-to-reorder, due dates and tags, keyboard shortcuts, undo for deletions, persistence (localStorage/IndexedDB offline-first plus server sync with conflict resolution), optimistic updates, accessibility (labels, focus management after add/delete, live announcements), and performance with virtualization for huge lists.
n507.f: How would you resolve sync conflicts between devices?

n508.a: Typeahead: debounce input (~250ms), cancel stale requests (AbortController) or ignore out-of-order responses, cache results per query (LRU) and optionally prefetch popular queries, show loading/empty/error states, highlight matches, keyboard navigation (up/down/enter/escape) with the ARIA combobox pattern (`role="combobox"`, `aria-expanded`, `aria-activedescendant`, listbox options), virtualize long lists, and make the fetcher and renderer configurable.
n508.f: When would you filter on the client instead of calling the server?

n509.a: API progress bar (like page-loading bars): track in-flight requests globally (fetch wrapper or interceptor incrementing a counter), show the bar when the count > 0 after a short delay to avoid flicker, animate progress asymptotically toward ~90% since total time is unknown (or use real progress from upload/download events), complete to 100% and fade out when all requests finish, and handle errors.
p: Delay before showing to avoid flicker
Real progress via XHR events when available
n509.f: How do you get real download progress with fetch?

n510.a: Messenger: conversation list and chat view; real-time messaging over WebSockets with reconnection and backoff; optimistic sending with client-generated IDs and states (sending, sent, delivered, read); message ordering by server timestamps/sequence numbers; pagination of history (load older on scroll up, virtualized list anchored at bottom); typing indicators and presence; offline queue in IndexedDB; notifications; attachments upload; end-to-end encryption considerations; accessibility.
n510.f: How do you avoid duplicate messages after reconnecting?

n511.a: Infinite scroller: use an IntersectionObserver sentinel near the end to load the next page via cursor-based pagination, guard against concurrent loads, show loading/error/end states, virtualize the list (render only visible items) to keep the DOM small, preserve scroll position on navigation back, provide a "load more" button fallback for accessibility, and keep the footer reachable.
n511.f: Why is cursor pagination better than offset pagination for feeds?
n511.c:
const io = new IntersectionObserver(([entry]) => { if (entry.isIntersecting && !loading && hasMore) loadMore(); }, { rootMargin: '600px' });
io.observe(sentinel);

n512.a: Instagram web: feed with cursor pagination and virtualization, image-heavy so serve responsive, compressed images (srcset, AVIF/WebP, blur placeholders, lazy loading), stories carousel with preloading of next items, post detail modal with route-based URLs, optimistic likes/comments, upload flow with client-side resize and progress, profile grid, notifications, SSR for public profiles/posts, and offline/error handling.
p: Upload with client resize and progress
n512.f: How would you preload the next story without wasting bandwidth?

n513.a: Facebook.com: news feed with heterogeneous post types (rendered via a component registry), cursor pagination and virtualization, real-time updates for comments and notifications, optimistic reactions, a normalized GraphQL client cache (Relay) with fragments colocated with components, code splitting per route and per post type, SSR/streaming for first load, chat dock, accessibility and i18n at scale, and performance budgets.
p: Normalized cache with colocated data needs
n513.f: Why colocate data requirements with components (fragments)?

n59.a: Requirements: suggestions as you type, fast, works for millions. Client: debounce (~200–300ms) and a minimum query length; cancel stale requests with AbortController or ignore out-of-order responses (request IDs); cache results in an in-memory LRU (and optionally prefetch top queries), serving cached prefixes instantly; server responses via CDN-cacheable GET endpoints. UI: combobox ARIA pattern (`role="combobox"`, `aria-expanded`, `aria-controls`, `aria-activedescendant`), arrow keys/Enter/Escape, highlighted matches, loading/empty/error states, announcement of result counts via a live region. Performance: virtualize long lists, keep bundle small. Extensibility: pluggable data source and result renderer, analytics on selections.
n59.f: How would you handle very slow networks?

n60.a: Data: cursor-based pagination (stable with new inserts), normalized cache of posts/users, prefetch the next page before reaching the end. Rendering: virtualize the list with dynamic heights (measure and cache), reserve image space with aspect ratios to avoid CLS, lazy-load images with srcset and blur placeholders. Interactions: optimistic likes/comments with rollback on failure, comments loaded on demand. Updates: "new posts" banner via polling/SSE instead of shifting content. Also: scroll restoration, error/retry states, accessibility (feed role, keyboard navigation), and performance monitoring.
n60.f: How do you keep scroll position stable when items above change height?

n827.a: News feed (Facebook-style). Requirements: infinite feed of mixed posts, create posts, react/comment. Architecture: server-rendered first page, then client navigation; a normalized store. API: `GET /feed?cursor=` returning posts plus next cursor; `POST /posts`; reactions endpoints. Rendering: virtualization, component per post type, lazy-load media, skeletons. Interactions: optimistic reactions/comments, composer with drafts and media upload. Real-time: badge for new posts. Performance: code split rich post types, image optimization. Accessibility: `role="feed"` with `aria-setsize/posinset`, keyboard navigation. i18n and error handling.
n827.f: How would you handle post types the client doesn't know yet?

n828.a: Autocomplete as a reusable component: API with props for data source (async fetch function), debounce duration, min query length, result limit, renderItem, onSelect, and caching strategy. Internals: input + listbox following the combobox pattern, debounced fetching with cancellation of stale requests, an LRU cache keyed by query, keyboard navigation and highlight, loading/empty/error states, and virtualization for many results. Consider mobile (full-screen results), i18n (IME composition events) and analytics.
p: Handle IME composition and mobile UX

n829.a: Pinterest: a masonry grid of pins with varying heights. Layout: compute positions in JS (place each item in the shortest column) using known image aspect ratios from the API so there's no layout shift; recompute on resize; virtualize by rendering only items in view (positions are known). Data: cursor pagination with prefetch; images via srcset, dominant-color placeholders, lazy loading. Pin detail opens as a modal with its own URL; save/board actions optimistic. SSR for SEO on pin pages.
p: Aspect ratios from API avoid CLS
Modal routes and SSR for SEO
n829.f: Why not use CSS columns for the masonry?

n830.a: Rich text editor: a document model (tree of blocks with inline text and marks) independent of the DOM; a view layer rendering the model into a contenteditable; input handling via `beforeinput` events mapped to transactions; selection mapping between DOM and model; history (undo/redo by inverting transactions); commands and toolbar state; paste handling with sanitization and conversion; plugins (mentions, links, embeds); serialization (JSON/HTML/Markdown); accessibility; and performance for large documents.

n831.a: Google Docs: a rich text editor plus real-time collaboration. Collaboration via Operational Transformation (server orders and transforms ops) or CRDTs (e.g. Yjs) over WebSockets; local edits apply immediately and sync in the background; presence (cursors, selections) as ephemeral state; offline editing with an IndexedDB queue and later merge. Rendering: custom layout for pagination (Docs uses canvas-based rendering), virtualized pages. Also: comments anchored to ranges, version history (snapshots + ops), permissions and sharing, autosave status.
p: OT or CRDT for concurrent edits
n831.f: OT vs CRDT: what are the trade-offs?

n832.a: Drawing tool (Figma/Excalidraw): a scene graph of shapes (id, type, transform, style) in a normalized store; rendering on canvas (or WebGL) with a viewport (pan/zoom transforms), dirty-rect or full redraws via requestAnimationFrame; hit testing with spatial indexing (R-tree/quadtree); tools as a state machine (select, draw, text); undo/redo via commands; selection handles and snapping; real-time collaboration with CRDTs; export to PNG/SVG; and large-file performance with culling and layer caching.
n832.f: Why use canvas instead of DOM/SVG for large designs?

n833.a: Netflix-style streaming: browse pages of rows of titles (horizontal virtualized carousels, lazy-loaded artwork, hover previews), search, title details, and the player. Player: adaptive bitrate streaming (DASH/HLS via Media Source Extensions), DRM via Encrypted Media Extensions, buffering strategy, subtitles/audio tracks, resume position sync, keyboard controls. Performance: SSR for the first screen, image CDNs, prefetching likely next content, TV/device constraints. Personalization data drives rows; analytics for QoE (startup time, rebuffering).
n833.f: What metrics define video quality of experience?

n834.a: E-commerce (Amazon): product listing with filters/sort reflected in the URL, server-rendered for SEO and speed; product detail page (images gallery, variants, price, reviews loaded lazily, structured data); cart (persisted locally and server-side, optimistic updates); checkout (multi-step forms, address/payment validation, accessibility, secure payment iframes, idempotent order submission); search with autocomplete; performance (Core Web Vitals impact conversions), i18n/currency, and A/B testing.
n834.f: How do you prevent double orders when the user clicks pay twice?

n835.a: Travel booking (Airbnb): search with location autocomplete, date-range picker and guest count in the URL; results list synced with an interactive map (markers clustering, bounds-based search with debounce); listing pages with photo galleries, availability calendar, pricing breakdown; booking flow with holds and payment; SSR for SEO; image optimization; i18n, currencies, and time zones; accessibility of date pickers and maps.
n835.f: How would you avoid excessive requests while the user pans the map?

n836.a: Chat app (Messenger): see n510 — WebSocket connection with heartbeat and reconnection, optimistic send with client IDs and status ticks, ordered message history with pagination and bottom-anchored virtualization, unread counts and read receipts, typing/presence indicators, attachments, notifications (Push API), offline queue, search, and normalized storage (conversations, messages, users) possibly in IndexedDB for instant load.
n836.f: How do you keep unread counts consistent across tabs?

n837.a: Photo sharing (Instagram): feed with cursor pagination and virtualization; heavy image optimization (CDN resizing, srcset, AVIF/WebP, blurhash placeholders, lazy loading); upload flow (client resize/crop, filters via canvas/WebGL, chunked/resumable upload with progress); stories with preloading; optimistic likes/comments; profile grids; SSR for public pages; accessibility (alt text prompts).
n837.f: How would you implement resumable uploads?

n838.a: Music streaming (Spotify): a persistent player that keeps playing across SPA navigation (player state in a global store outside routes), queue management, gapless playback with preloading of the next track, Media Session API for OS controls, offline caching (with DRM limits), library/playlists with optimistic edits, search, virtualized long track lists, and syncing playback state across devices via WebSockets.
n838.f: How does the Media Session API improve UX?

n839.a: Video conferencing (Zoom): WebRTC for media (getUserMedia, RTCPeerConnection) via an SFU server for multi-party calls; signaling over WebSockets; adaptive layouts (grid/speaker views) with only visible videos at high resolution (simulcast); controls for mute, camera, screen sharing (getDisplayMedia); network quality indicators and reconnection; chat, reactions, captions; device selection; performance (limit decoded streams, use requestVideoFrameCallback/WebCodecs for effects); permissions and accessibility.
n839.f: Why use an SFU instead of peer-to-peer mesh for large meetings?

n840.a: Google Sheets: a virtualized grid (render only visible rows/columns, often on canvas for performance) with frozen headers; a cell data model stored sparsely (Map keyed by cell); a formula engine with parser, dependency graph and topological recalculation (detect cycles), possibly in a Web Worker; selection ranges, copy/paste, fill handle; undo/redo; collaboration via OT/CRDT; formatting; and large-sheet performance.
p: Recalculate in topological order, detect cycles
n840.f: How do you recalculate efficiently when one cell changes?

n841.a: Dropdown menu component: trigger button with `aria-haspopup="menu"` and `aria-expanded`; menu with `role="menu"` and `menuitem`s; keyboard support (Enter/Space/ArrowDown to open, arrows to move, Home/End, type-ahead, Escape to close and return focus); close on outside click; positioning with collision detection (flip/shift, e.g. Floating UI) and rendering in a portal; submenus; configurable API (items vs composable children).
n841.f: When should you use a menu versus a listbox/select?

n842.a: Image carousel component: API (images with alt, autoplay, loop, startIndex, onChange), track rendering with transforms or scroll-snap, lazy-load and preload adjacent images, controls and indicators, swipe via pointer events, keyboard support, autoplay that pauses on interaction and honours reduced motion, accessibility (carousel roledescription, slide labels, live region), and responsive image sizes.
n842.f: What are the accessibility problems with auto-rotating carousels?

n843.a: Modal dialog component: use native `<dialog>` with `showModal()` (top layer, inert background, Escape handling) or implement `role="dialog"` + `aria-modal="true"` with focus trap, background inert, scroll lock and Escape/overlay click to close; label with `aria-labelledby`; move focus into the dialog and restore it on close; render in a portal; support stacking, animations and configurable close behaviour.
n843.f: Why is restoring focus after close important?

n844.a: Data table component: column definitions (accessor, header, sortable, width, renderer), sorting, filtering, pagination (client or server), row selection, resizable/reorderable columns, sticky headers, virtualization for large data, loading/empty/error states, accessible table semantics (`<table>`, `aria-sort`, captions), and a headless API (like TanStack Table) so styling is flexible. Server-side mode for large datasets.
n844.f: When would you choose server-side sorting and pagination?

n845.a: Poll widget: embeddable component taking a poll ID, fetching the question and options; voting with optimistic updates and results shown as percentages/bars; prevent duplicate votes (server-side by user/session, client flag in storage); live result updates via polling or SSE; accessible radio group and results with text percentages; small bundle (or iframe/web component for embedding in third-party pages) with theming.
n845.f: Would you embed it as an iframe or a script? Why?

n846.a: Email client (Outlook): three-pane layout (folders, message list, reading pane), virtualized message list with cursor pagination, threading, search with filters, compose with rich text editor, attachments, drafts autosave, offline support (IndexedDB cache and outbox), sync via push/WebSocket, keyboard shortcuts, sanitizing email HTML and rendering it in a sandboxed iframe, accessibility, and performance for huge mailboxes.
n846.f: Why render emails in a sandboxed iframe?

n514.a: Counter: a button that displays a count and increments it on click; in React, store count in state and update with the functional setter.
n514.f: Why use the functional update form?

n515.a: Todo list: an input and Add button (in a form so Enter submits), a list of tasks each with a Delete button. Keep tasks in state as `{ id, label }`, trim input and ignore empty, clear input after adding, and delete by id. Add labels for accessibility.
n515.f: Why not use the array index as key?

n516.a: Job board: fetch the list of job IDs from the Hacker News API, then fetch details for the first page (e.g. 6) in parallel with Promise.all; render title, poster and date with links; a "Load more" button fetches the next page; show loading states and avoid duplicate fetches.
p: Fetch details per page in parallel
n516.f: How would you prevent double clicks on Load more from fetching twice?
n516.c:
const ids = await fetch('https://hacker-news.firebaseio.com/v0/jobstories.json').then(r => r.json());
const page = await Promise.all(ids.slice(0, 6).map(id => fetch(`https://hacker-news.firebaseio.com/v0/item/${id}.json`).then(r => r.json())));

n517.a: Contact form: fields name, email, message with labels, `required` and type="email" validation, submit via fetch POST (or native form action), disable the button while submitting, show success/error messages in a live region, and reset on success.
n517.f: How do you make validation errors accessible?

n518.a: Tabs: a list of tab buttons and panels; state holds the active tab; clicking a tab shows its panel and hides others.
n518.f: Why keep inactive panels in the DOM with hidden instead of unmounting?

n519.a: Tabs II adds accessibility: `role="tablist"`, `role="tab"` with `aria-selected` and `aria-controls`, `role="tabpanel"` with `aria-labelledby`, and unique IDs via `useId` so multiple instances don't clash.
p: Only active tab in tab order
n519.f: Why is tabIndex -1 used on inactive tabs?

n520.a: Tabs III adds keyboard navigation per the WAI-ARIA pattern: Left/Right arrows move to and activate the previous/next tab (wrapping), Home/End go to first/last, and focus moves with the selection (roving tabindex).
n520.f: What's the difference between automatic and manual activation?

n521.a: Accordion: a list of sections each with a header button and a panel; clicking toggles that section's visibility; multiple sections can be open. Store open section IDs in a Set.
n521.f: How would you allow only one section open at a time?

n522.a: Accordion II adds accessibility: header buttons with `aria-expanded` and `aria-controls`, panels with `role="region"` and `aria-labelledby`, unique IDs via `useId`.
n522.f: Why wrap the button in a heading?
n522.c: {contents}

n523.a: Accordion III adds keyboard navigation: ArrowDown/ArrowUp move focus between headers (wrapping), Home/End jump to first/last; Enter/Space toggle (native button behaviour).
n523.f: Does arrow navigation change which panel is open?

n524.a: Holy Grail layout in a component: header, footer, left nav, main and right aside, with fixed-width side columns, fluid main, equal heights and a footer at the bottom. Use CSS grid with template areas and `min-height: 100vh`.
n524.f: How would this change on mobile?
n524.c: .app { display: grid; min-height: 100vh; grid-template: "header header header" 60px "nav main aside" 1fr "footer footer footer" 100px / 100px 1fr 100px; }

n525.a: Progress bars: an "Add" button appends a new bar; each bar animates from 0% to 100% over 2 seconds when it appears. Use a CSS transition triggered after mount (set width to 100% in an effect or use a keyframes animation).
p: Array of bar ids in state
n525.f: Why delay setting the width until after mount?

n526.a: Star rating: render `max` stars, highlight up to the hovered star (or the current value when not hovering), click to set the value via onChange. Use buttons/radios for accessibility.
p: Fill stars up to hover || value
n526.f: Why is a span-based star not accessible?
n526.c: {Array.from({ length: max }, (_, i) => setHover(i + 1)} onMouseLeave={() => setHover(0)} onClick={() => onChange(i + 1)}>{i < (hover || value) ? '★' : '☆'})}

n527.a: Stopwatch: start/stop and reset. Track elapsed time accurately with timestamps (`Date.now()` / `performance.now()`) rather than counting intervals; use a ref for the interval ID; display mm:ss.ms.
n527.f: Why does counting setInterval ticks drift?

n528.a: Like button: shows liked/unliked state, on click sends a POST request with the action, shows a spinner and disables during the request, toggles state on success, and shows an error message on failure.
p: Update on success only (or optimistic with rollback)
n528.f: How would you make it optimistic?

n529.a: Image carousel: show one image at a time from a list, with previous/next buttons (wrapping) and page dot buttons to jump to an image; fixed container size with `object-fit: cover`.
n529.f: How would you add keyboard support?
n529.c:
const next = () => setI(i => (i + 1) % images.length);
const prev = () => setI(i => (i - 1 + images.length) % images.length);

n530.a: Image carousel II adds sliding transitions: render all images in a horizontal track and translate it by `-index * 100%` with a CSS transition; buttons and dots update the index.
p: All images in a flex track
n530.f: Why does wrapping from last to first animate backwards, and how to fix it?
n530.c: {images.map(img => )}

n531.a: Image carousel III adds seamless infinite looping: clone the first and last slides at the ends; when transitioning onto a clone, after the transition ends, jump without animation to the real slide. Alternatively, render only current and next images and animate those.
p: Disable transition and jump on transitionend
n531.f: What race conditions appear with rapid clicks?

n532.a: Traffic light: cycle green → yellow → red with different durations, using a config object and a `setTimeout` in an effect that advances to the next state when the current duration elapses.
n532.f: Why setTimeout instead of setInterval here?
n532.c:
const config = { green: { next: 'yellow', ms: 3000 }, yellow: { next: 'red', ms: 500 }, red: { next: 'green', ms: 4000 } };
useEffect(() => { const t = setTimeout(() => setLight(config[light].next), config[light].ms); return () => clearTimeout(t); }, [light]);

n533.a: Digital clock: show current time hh:mm:ss updating every second; use an interval in an effect with cleanup; format with padStart; use `<time>` for semantics.
n533.f: How would you avoid the clock lagging behind real seconds?

n534.a: File explorer: render a nested folder/file tree recursively; folders can be expanded/collapsed (state per folder), directories listed before files and sorted alphabetically, with indentation per depth.
n534.f: How would you lazy-load a folder's children?

n535.a: Tic-tac-toe: a 3×3 grid of buttons, X and O alternate, detect a winner or draw after each move, show status, disable moves after game over, and a reset button. Derive winner from the board instead of storing it.
n535.f: How would you generalize to N×N with M in a row?

n536.a: Transfer list: two lists with checkboxes; buttons move selected items left/right and move all items in either direction. Store each side as an array (or Map of item → checked), disable buttons when no items/selection.
p: Two lists of items with checked state
n536.f: Why store checked state per item rather than separately?
n536.c: const moveSelected = (from, setFrom, setTo) => { setTo(t => [...t, ...from.filter(i => i.checked).map(i => ({ ...i, checked: false }))]); setFrom(f => f.filter(i => !i.checked)); };

n537.a: Transfer List II adds: a "select all" checkbox per list (with indeterminate state), a count of selected items, and an input to add new items to each list.
n537.f: Why must indeterminate be set via a ref?
n537.c: <input type="checkbox" ref={el => el && (el.indeterminate = some && !all)} checked={all} onChange={() => setItems(items.map(i => ({ ...i, checked: !all })))} />

n538.a: Nested checkboxes in React: render a tree recursively; toggling a node sets all descendants to the same value; then recompute ancestors' state (checked if all children checked, indeterminate if some). Keep checked state for leaves and derive parents.
n538.f: How would you compute ancestor states efficiently?

n539.a: Modal dialog: a component with `open`, `title`, `children` and `onClose` props, rendered in a portal over an overlay. Simplest robust version uses `<dialog>` with `showModal()` in an effect when `open` changes.
n539.f: What does the native dialog's cancel event do?

n540.a: Modal Dialog II adds accessibility: `role="dialog"`, `aria-modal="true"`, `aria-labelledby`/`aria-describedby` with unique IDs from `useId`.
n540.f: Why does aria-modal matter for screen readers?

n541.a: Modal Dialog III adds closing behaviours: Escape key closes, clicking the overlay (outside the content) closes, and the close button closes. Listen for keydown on document while open and compare click target with the overlay.
n541.f: Why compare target and currentTarget for overlay clicks?
n541.c:
useEffect(() => { if (!open) return; const onKey = e => e.key === 'Escape' && onClose(); document.addEventListener('keydown', onKey); return () => document.removeEventListener('keydown', onKey); }, [open, onClose]);
e.target === e.currentTarget && onClose()}>…

n542.a: Modal Dialog IV adds focus management: on open, focus the first focusable element (or the dialog); trap Tab/Shift+Tab inside; on close, return focus to the element that opened it.
n542.f: How would you handle a dialog with no focusable elements?

n543.a: Data table: display a list of users with columns and client-side pagination: page size selector (5/10/20), previous/next buttons, page indicator, slicing the data per page.
n543.f: Why reset to page 1 when the page size changes?
n543.c:
const pages = Math.ceil(users.length / size);
const rows = users.slice((page - 1) * size, page * size);

n544.a: Data table II adds sorting: clicking a column header sorts by that column, toggling ascending/descending; sort a copy of the data (numbers numerically, strings with localeCompare) before paginating, and show `aria-sort` on the header.
n544.f: Should sorting happen before or after pagination?
n544.c: const sorted = [...users].sort((a, b) => { const x = a[field], y = b[field]; const r = typeof x === 'number' ? x - y : String(x).localeCompare(String(y)); return dir === 'asc' ? r : -r; });

n545.a: Data table III makes the table generic: accept a `columns` config (label, key, renderCell, comparator) and `data`, so the same component sorts and paginates any dataset.
n545.f: How would you type columns with TypeScript generics?
n545.c: function DataTable({ data, columns }) { /* sort with columns.find(c => c.key === field).comparator, render with column.renderCell(row) */ }

n546.a: Undoable counter: buttons for /2, −1, +1, ×2, plus Undo, Redo and Reset; a history table of operations (op, old, new). Keep a history stack and a redo stack; each operation pushes to history and clears redo; undo pops history and pushes to redo.
n546.f: How does this relate to the Command pattern?
n546.c:
const apply = (label, fn) => { setHistory(h => [{ label, prev: value, next: fn(value) }, ...h]); setValue(fn); setRedo([]); };
const undo = () => { const [last, ...rest] = history; setValue(last.prev); setHistory(rest); setRedo(r => [last, ...r]); };

n547.a: Connect Four: a 7×6 grid; clicking a column drops a disc to the lowest empty row; players alternate; after each move check four in a row horizontally, vertically and both diagonals from the placed disc; detect draws when the board fills; reset button.
n547.f: Why check only from the last placed disc?
n547.c:
const dirs = [[0,1],[1,0],[1,1],[1,-1]];
const wins = (b, r, c, p) => dirs.some(([dr, dc]) => { let n = 1; for (const s of [1, -1]) for (let k = 1; b[r + dr*k*s]?.[c + dc*k*s] === p; k++) n++; return n >= 4; });

n548.a: Users database (CRUD): a list of users with a filter input, selecting a user loads their first/last name into inputs; Create, Update, Delete and Cancel buttons enabled appropriately depending on mode (creating vs editing) and validity.
n548.f: How would you prevent losing unsaved edits when selecting another user?

n549.a: Whack-a-mole: a 3×3 grid where moles randomly appear for a short time; clicking a visible mole scores a point; a game timer (e.g. 15s) counts down; Start resets score and timer. Use intervals/timeouts cleaned up on stop/unmount.
p: Random visible moles on an interval
n549.f: How would you ensure a mole can't be scored twice?

n550.a: Memory game: shuffle pairs of emoji cards face down; clicking reveals a card; after two flips, keep them if they match, otherwise flip back after a delay (blocking clicks meanwhile); win when all matched; restart reshuffles.
n550.f: Why is sort(() => Math.random() - 0.5) a bad shuffle?
n550.c: const shuffle = a => { a = [...a]; for (let i = a.length - 1; i > 0; i--) { const j = Math.floor(Math.random() * (i + 1)); [a[i], a[j]] = [a[j], a[i]]; } return a; };

n551.a: Selectable cells: a grid where dragging the mouse selects a rectangular range of cells from the mousedown cell to the current hovered cell; mouseup ends selection. Track start and end cells in state and compute selection by min/max row/col.
n551.f: How would you support touch devices?

n552.a: Wordle: 6 guesses of a 5-letter word; typed via physical or on-screen keyboard; on Enter validate the guess (length, word list), color each letter: green (correct position), yellow (in word elsewhere, respecting counts), gray (absent); update keyboard colors; win/lose states.
p: Grid of guesses and current input

n553.a: Flight booker: select one-way or return flight, departure date (and return date for return), validate that dates aren't in the past and return ≥ departure, and show a confirmation message on submit.
p: Return date only for return trips
n553.f: How do time zones affect "today" here?

n554.a: Generate table: inputs for rows and columns; on submit render a table where numbers go down column 1, then up column 2, etc. (snake/zig-zag vertical order). Cell value = col * rows + (col even ? row : rows - 1 - row) + 1.
n554.f: How would you test the cell formula?
n554.c: const value = (r, c, rows) => c * rows + (c % 2 === 0 ? r : rows - 1 - r) + 1;

n555.a: Progress bar: takes a value 0–100, clamps it, fills the bar to that width and shows the percentage; use `role="progressbar"` with aria-valuenow/min/max.
n555.f: Why use transform: scaleX instead of width for animation?

n556.a: Temperature converter: two inputs (Celsius, Fahrenheit); typing in one updates the other: F = C × 9/5 + 32, C = (F − 32) × 5/9; leave the other blank when input isn't a number; round to 4 decimals.
n556.f: Why store both strings in state rather than one number?

n557.a: Mortgage calculator: inputs for loan amount, annual interest rate and term in years; monthly payment M = P·r(1+r)^n / ((1+r)^n − 1) with monthly rate r and n months; show monthly payment, total payment and total interest formatted as currency; validate inputs and handle 0% interest.
p: Monthly rate and number of payments
n557.f: How would you show an amortization schedule?
n557.c: function monthlyPayment(P, annualRate, years) { const r = annualRate / 100 / 12, n = years * 12; return r === 0 ? P / n : (P * r * (1 + r) ** n) / ((1 + r) ** n - 1); }

n558.a: Tweet component: avatar, name, handle, timestamp, text content and action buttons (reply, retweet, like, share) with counts; semantic markup (`<article>`), accessible labels, and CSS layout with flexbox.
p: Action buttons with labels and counts
n558.f: How would you render links and hashtags safely in tweet text?

n559.a: Analog clock: a circle with hour, minute and second hands rotated by CSS transforms based on the current time (updated every second): seconds 6° per second, minutes 6° per minute plus seconds fraction, hours 30° per hour plus minutes fraction.
p: transform: rotate with origin at bottom
n559.f: How do you avoid the hand spinning backwards from 354° to 0°?
n559.c:
const s = now.getSeconds(), m = now.getMinutes() + s / 60, h = (now.getHours() % 12) + m / 60;
const hands = { hour: h * 30, minute: m * 6, second: s * 6 };

n560.a: Dice roller: input for number of dice (1–12), Roll button, display the results as dice faces in a grid with random values 1–6 each.
n560.f: How would you draw dice faces with CSS grid?

n561.a: File Explorer II adds accessibility: use `role="tree"`, `treeitem` with `aria-expanded` on folders, `aria-level`, and `group` for children; or use nested lists with buttons and aria-expanded.
n561.f: Why must treeitems not contain other interactive controls?

n562.a: File Explorer III adds keyboard navigation per the tree pattern: Up/Down move between visible items, Right expands a folder or moves to first child, Left collapses or moves to parent, Home/End, Enter activates; roving tabindex with a flattened list of visible nodes.
n562.f: How do you compute the visible node list efficiently?

n563.a: Grid lights: a 3×3 grid (with the center cell empty); clicking cells activates them (green) and records the order; when all are activated, they deactivate one by one in reverse order of activation at intervals; clicks are disabled during deactivation.
p: Pop in reverse with an interval
n563.f: How would you make the grid configurable?
n563.c: useEffect(() => { if (!deactivating) return; const id = setInterval(() => setOrder(o => { const n = o.slice(0, -1); if (!n.length) { clearInterval(id); setDeactivating(false); } return n; }), 300); return () => clearInterval(id); }, [deactivating]);

n564.a: Progress Bars II: bars are added by a button, but only one fills at a time — the next bar starts filling after the previous completes (sequential queue). Track the index of the currently filling bar and advance on completion (transitionend or timer).
n564.f: Why might relying on transitionend be fragile?

n565.a: Progress Bars III: up to 3 bars fill concurrently; additional bars wait until a slot is free. Track each bar's progress in state and on each tick advance the first N incomplete bars.
n565.f: How does this relate to a promise pool?
n565.c: setBars(bars => { let slots = 3; return bars.map(p => (p < 100 && slots-- > 0 ? Math.min(100, p + 1) : p)); });

n566.a: Birth year histogram: fetch random birth years (e.g. from an API), bucket them by decade, and render a bar chart with bars proportional to counts, axes and labels; a refresh button refetches.
n566.f: How would you make the chart accessible?
n566.c: const buckets = years.reduce((m, y) => { const d = Math.floor(y / 10) * 10; m[d] = (m[d] || 0) + 1; return m; }, {});

n567.a: Pixel art: a grid of cells; choose a color from a palette and a mode (draw/erase); click or drag to paint cells; state is a 2D array (or Map) of colors.
n567.f: Why use pointer events instead of mouse events?

n568.a: Signup form: username, email, password, confirm password with client-side validation (required, formats, password rules, match), inline accessible errors, disabled submit while sending, POST to the API, and display server errors (e.g. username taken).
n568.f: Why validate on blur rather than on every keystroke?

n569.a: Auth code (OTP) input: N single-character inputs; typing a digit moves focus to the next, Backspace on empty moves back, arrow keys navigate, pasting a full code fills all inputs; only digits allowed; submit when complete. Use `inputMode="numeric"` and `autocomplete="one-time-code"`.
n569.f: Why might a single input be better for accessibility?
n569.c: function onPaste(e) { const digits = e.clipboardData.getData('text').replace(/\D/g, '').slice(0, n).split(''); if (digits.length) { e.preventDefault(); setCode(c => c.map((_, i) => digits[i] ?? '')); refs.current[Math.min(digits.length, n - 1)].focus(); } }

n570.a: Progress Bars IV: concurrent filling (limit 3) plus Start/Pause controls: pausing stops the interval but keeps progress; resuming continues. Keep the interval in an effect controlled by a running flag.
n570.f: How would you persist progress across page reloads?

n571.a: Data Table IV adds filtering per column: text inputs for string columns and min/max range inputs for numbers; apply filters before sorting and pagination, resetting to page 1 when filters change. Column config defines filter type.
n571.f: When should filtering move to the server?

n408.a: Unique removes duplicate elements from a tuple type, keeping first occurrences. Recurse through the tuple with an accumulator; append the head only if it isn't already in the accumulator (using an exact equality check).
n408.f: Why use Equal rather than `extends` to compare elements?

n409.a: Prefix<T, P> adds a string prefix P to each key of an object type T (or to a string union). Use key remapping in a mapped type with a template literal.
n409.f: How would you write a Suffix type?
n409.c:
type Prefix<T, P extends string> = { [K in keyof T as K extends string ? `${P}${K}` : never]: T[K] };
type R = Prefix<{ a: 1; b: 2 }, 'x_'>; // { x_a: 1; x_b: 2 }

n410.a: UndefinedToNull<T> replaces `undefined` with `null`, recursively through objects and arrays (as when serializing to JSON).
n410.f: Why does the mapped type also work for tuples?
n410.c:
type UndefinedToNull<T> = T extends undefined ? null : T extends object ? { [K in keyof T]: UndefinedToNull<T[K]> } : T;
type R = UndefinedToNull<{ a: undefined; b: [string, undefined] }>; // { a: null; b: [string, null] }

n411.a: MapStringUnionToObjectUnion<U> turns a union of strings into a union of objects `{ value: S }`. Conditional types distribute over unions automatically.
n411.c:
type MapStringUnionToObjectUnion<U extends string> = U extends any ? { value: U } : never;
type R = MapStringUnionToObjectUnion<'a' | 'b'>; // { value: 'a' } | { value: 'b' }

n412.a: Diff<A, B> returns the keys/properties present in exactly one of two object types (symmetric difference). Use Omit with the union of keys minus the shared keys.
p: B minus keys of A & B
Values taken from whichever has them
n412.f: Why use A & B as the base?
n412.c:
type Diff<A, B> = Omit<A & B, keyof A & keyof B>;
type R = Diff<{ a: 1; b: 2 }, { b: 2; c: 3 }>; // { a: 1; c: 3 }

n413.a: ObjectPaths<O> produces a union of all dot-separated property paths of a nested object.
n413.f: How would you type a get(obj, path) function using this?
n413.c:
type ObjectPaths<O> = O extends object
  ? { [K in keyof O & (string | number)]: `${K}` | (O[K] extends object ? `${K}.${ObjectPaths<O[K]>}` : never) }[keyof O & (string | number)]
  : never;
type R = ObjectPaths<{ a: { b: { c: 1 } }; d: 2 }>; // 'a' | 'a.b' | 'a.b.c' | 'd'

n414.a: Abs<N> returns the absolute value of a number literal type as a string-free number: convert to a string, strip a leading `-`, and convert back with `infer ... extends number`.
p: infer X extends number converts back
n414.f: How did people convert strings to numbers before TS 4.8?
n414.c:
type Abs<N extends number> = `${N}` extends `-${infer P extends number}` ? P : N;
type R = Abs<-5>; // 5

n415.a: StringToNumber<S> converts a numeric string literal to a number literal type.
p: Older: build tuples digit by digit
n415.f: How would you do it with tuple lengths?
n415.c:
type StringToNumber<S extends string> = S extends `${infer N extends number}` ? N : never;
type R = StringToNumber<'42'>; // 42

n416.a: CamelCase<S> converts snake_case to camelCase: find `_x` and replace with uppercase X recursively.
n416.f: How would you convert kebab-case too?
n416.c:
type CamelCase<S extends string> = S extends `${infer H}_${infer T}` ? `${H}${CamelCase<Capitalize<T>>}` : S;
type R = CamelCase<'big_front_end'>; // 'bigFrontEnd'

n417.a: SnakeCase<S> converts camelCase to snake_case: process characters; when a character is uppercase (it differs from its lowercase), emit `_` plus the lowercase letter.
n417.f: How should a leading uppercase letter be handled?

n418.a: Split<S, D> splits a string type by a delimiter into a tuple type, like `String.prototype.split`.
n418.f: Why special-case the non-literal string type?
n418.c:
type Split<S extends string, D extends string> =
  string extends S ? string[] :
  S extends '' ? (D extends '' ? [] : ['']) :
  S extends `${infer H}${D}${infer T}` ? [H, ...Split<T, D>] : [S];
type R = Split<'a-b-c', '-'>; // ['a', 'b', 'c']

n419.a: Capitalize<T> uppercases the first character of a string type. Infer the first character and the rest, uppercase the first with Uppercase.
n419.f: Which string intrinsics does TypeScript provide?
n419.c:
type MyCapitalize<T extends string> = T extends `${infer F}${infer R}` ? `${Uppercase<F>}${R}` : T;
type R = MyCapitalize<'hello'>; // 'Hello'

n420.a: Sort<T> sorts a tuple of non-negative number literals ascending. Use a comparison type (SmallerThan via tuple lengths) and a recursive selection/insertion sort.
p: Insert each element into a sorted accumulator
n420.f: Why does this approach hit recursion limits for large numbers?

n421.a: Implement an assertion function `assertsNever(arg: never)` used in exhaustive checks: if any union member isn't handled, the remaining type isn't never and TypeScript reports an error at compile time; at runtime it throws.
n421.f: What error appears when you add a 'triangle' kind?

n422.a: Divide<A, B> performs integer division on non-negative number literal types by repeatedly subtracting B (as tuples) and counting.
n422.f: How would you return the remainder too?

n423.a: Multiply<A, B> multiplies non-negative number literals by concatenating A-length tuples B times.
n423.f: Why does the result type need `& number` in some versions?

n424.a: Subtract<A, B> for non-negative literals: build a tuple of length A and remove B elements; if B > A, return never.
n424.f: How would you support negative results?

n425.a: Slice<A, S, E> mimics Array.prototype.slice on tuple types (supporting non-negative indexes, with E defaulting to the length): walk the tuple with an index counter, including elements whose index is ≥ S and < E.
n425.f: How would you support negative start and end?

n426.a: ReplaceAll<S, F, T> replaces every occurrence of substring F with T in a string type, without re-scanning the replaced text.
p: Replace and recurse on the rest only
n426.f: Why recurse only on R rather than the whole new string?

n427.a: Trim<T> removes leading and trailing whitespace (spaces, newlines, tabs) from a string type.
n427.f: Why match one whitespace character at a time?

n428.a: Equal<A, B> checks exact type equality, including distinguishing `any`, `readonly` modifiers and unions. The well-known trick compares two generic function types, which TypeScript only considers identical when A and B are identical.
n428.f: Why does `[A] extends [B]` fail as an equality check?

n429.a: FindIndex<T, E> returns the index of the first element in tuple T exactly equal to E, or never if absent.
n429.f: Why is exact equality needed here?

n430.a: UnionToIntersection<U> turns `A | B` into `A & B` by placing the union in a contravariant position (function parameter); inferring a type from multiple candidates in a contravariant position yields their intersection.
n430.f: What do covariance and contravariance mean here?
n430.c:
type UnionToIntersection<U> = (U extends any ? (arg: U) => void : never) extends (arg: infer I) => void ? I : never;
type R = UnionToIntersection<{ a: 1 } | { b: 2 }>; // { a: 1 } & { b: 2 }

n431.a: ToNumber<T> converts a numeric string type to a number type. With TS 4.8+, use `infer N extends number`; otherwise count up with a tuple until its length stringified equals T.
n431.f: What happens with a non-numeric input in the counting version?
n431.c:
type ToNumber<T extends string, C extends any[] = []> = T extends `${C['length']}` ? C['length'] : ToNumber<T, [...C, 0]>;
type R = ToNumber<'12'>; // 12

n432.a: Add<A, B> adds non-negative number literals by concatenating tuples of lengths A and B and taking the length.
p: Build tuples of length A and B
n432.f: How large can the numbers be before TS gives up?

n433.a: SmallerThan<A, B> returns true if A < B for non-negative integers: count up with a tuple; whichever number the counter reaches first is the smaller.

n434.a: LargerThan<A, B> returns true if A > B: count up; if the counter reaches A first (or A equals B), false; if it reaches B first, true.
n434.f: How would you compare numbers digit by digit for big values?

n435.a: Filter<T, A> keeps tuple elements assignable to A.
p: Wrap in [] to avoid distribution issues
n435.f: What would change with exact matching instead of assignability?
n435.c:
type Filter<T extends any[], A> = T extends [infer F, ...infer R] ? ([F] extends [A] ? [F, ...Filter<R, A>] : Filter<R, A>) : [];
type R = Filter<[1, 'a', 2, false], number>; // [1, 2]

n436.a: Repeat<T, C> creates a tuple containing T repeated C times.
n436.f: How would you build a fixed-length array type for function params?
n436.c:
type Repeat<T, C extends number, Acc extends any[] = []> = Acc['length'] extends C ? Acc : Repeat<T, C, [...Acc, T]>;
type R = Repeat<'a', 3>; // ['a', 'a', 'a']

n437.a: TupleToString<T> concatenates a tuple of string literals into one string.
n437.f: How would you add a separator like join(',')?
n437.c:
type TupleToString<T extends string[]> = T extends [infer F extends string, ...infer R extends string[]] ? `${F}${TupleToString<R>}` : '';
type R = TupleToString<['a', 'b', 'c']>; // 'abc'

n438.a: RepeatString<T, C> repeats a string literal C times.

n439.a: Push<T, I> appends an element to a tuple type using variadic tuple spread.
n439.c:
type Push<T extends any[], I> = [...T, I];
type R = Push<[1, 2], 3>; // [1, 2, 3]

n440.a: IsAny<T> detects `any`: `any` is the only type for which `0 extends 1 & T` is true, because `1 & any` is any.
p: 1 & T collapses to any only for any

n441.a: Shift<T> removes the first element of a tuple.
n441.c:
type Shift<T extends any[]> = T extends [any, ...infer R] ? R : [];
type R = Shift<[1, 2, 3]>; // [2, 3]

n442.a: IsEmptyType<T> checks whether T is exactly `{}` (an empty object literal type), not object, unknown or a type with properties. Check that it has no keys, that `{}` is assignable to it, and that it isn't `unknown`/`object`.
n442.f: Why is `{}` not the same as an empty object in TypeScript?

n443.a: Flat<T> recursively flattens nested tuple types.
p: If element is an array, flatten it
n443.f: How would you flatten only one level?
n443.c:
type Flat<T extends any[]> = T extends [infer F, ...infer R] ? (F extends any[] ? [...Flat<F>, ...Flat<R>] : [F, ...Flat<R>]) : [];
type R = Flat<[1, [2, [3]], 4]>; // [1, 2, 3, 4]

n444.f: Why might an accumulator version handle longer tuples?
n444.c:
type ReverseTuple<T extends any[]> = T extends [infer F, ...infer R] ? [...ReverseTuple<R>, F] : [];
type R = ReverseTuple<[1, 2, 3]>; // [3, 2, 1]

n445.a: UnwrapPromise<T> extracts the resolved type of a Promise; if T isn't a Promise, it's an error/never. TypeScript's built-in Awaited also unwraps nested promises and thenables.
n445.c:
type UnwrapPromise<T> = T extends Promise<infer R> ? R : never;
type R = UnwrapPromise<Promise<string>>; // string

n446.a: LengthOfString<T> computes the length of a string literal type by converting it to a tuple of characters and taking its length.
n446.f: Why can't you just use T['length']?
n446.c:
type LengthOfString<T extends string, C extends any[] = []> = T extends `${string}${infer R}` ? LengthOfString<R, [...C, 0]> : C['length'];
type R = LengthOfString<'hello'>; // 5

n447.a: LengthOfTuple<T> returns a tuple's length using the `length` property, which is a literal for tuples.
n447.f: What does it return for string[]?
n447.c:
type LengthOfTuple<T extends readonly any[]> = T['length'];
type R = LengthOfTuple<[1, 2, 3]>; // 3

n448.a: StringToTuple<T> splits a string literal into a tuple of characters.
n448.c:
type StringToTuple<T extends string> = T extends `${infer F}${infer R}` ? [F, ...StringToTuple<R>] : [];
type R = StringToTuple<'abc'>; // ['a', 'b', 'c']

n449.a: LastItem<T> returns the last element of a tuple, or never for an empty tuple.
n449.f: How would you write it without variadic tuples?
n449.c:
type LastItem<T extends any[]> = T extends [...any[], infer L] ? L : never;
type R = LastItem<[1, 2, 3]>; // 3

n450.a: IsNever<T> checks whether T is never. Wrap in a tuple to prevent distribution: a naked `T extends never` with T = never distributes over an empty union and returns never.
n450.f: Why does `T extends never ? true : false` give never for never?
n450.c:
type IsNever<T> = [T] extends [never] ? true : false;
type R = IsNever<never>; // true

n451.a: FirstItem<T> returns the first element of a tuple, or never for an empty tuple.
n451.c:
type FirstItem<T extends any[]> = T extends [infer F, ...any[]] ? F : never;
type R = FirstItem<[1, 2]>; // 1

n452.a: TupleToUnion<T> converts a tuple's element types into a union via indexed access with `number`.
n452.f: Why is `as const` needed for the roles example?

n453.a: LastChar<T> returns the last character of a string literal type by recursing until one character remains.
n453.f: Why can't you infer the last char directly with `${string}${infer L}`?
n453.c:
type LastChar<T extends string> = T extends `${infer F}${infer R}` ? (R extends '' ? F : LastChar<R>) : never;
type R = LastChar<'abc'>; // 'c'

n454.a: FirstChar<T> returns the first character of a string literal type.
n454.f: Why does the first infer match only one character?
n454.c:
type FirstChar<T extends string> = T extends `${infer F}${string}` ? F : never;
type R = FirstChar<'abc'>; // 'a'

n455.a: OmitThisParameter<T> removes the `this` parameter from a function type: if the function has a this parameter, return a function with the same params and return type; otherwise T unchanged.
n455.f: Why does bind return an OmitThisParameter type?

n456.a: ThisParameterType<T> extracts the type of a function's `this` parameter, or unknown if none.
n456.f: Why use never for the args in the pattern?

n457.a: InstanceType<T> gets the instance type produced by a constructor type.
p: typeof Class gives the constructor type

n458.a: ReturnType<T> extracts the return type of a function type.
n458.c:
type MyReturnType<T extends (...args: any) => any> = T extends (...args: any) => infer R ? R : never;
type R = MyReturnType<() => Promise<number>>; // Promise<number>

n459.a: ConstructorParameters<T> extracts a constructor's parameter types as a tuple.
n459.f: How would you use this to write a typed factory function?

n460.a: Parameters<T> extracts a function type's parameters as a tuple.
n460.f: How would you type a debounce that preserves parameters?
n460.c:
type MyParameters<T extends (...args: any) => any> = T extends (...args: infer P) => any ? P : never;
type R = MyParameters<(a: string, b?: number) => void>; // [a: string, b?: number]

n461.a: NonNullable<T> removes null and undefined from T. Modern TS defines it as `T & {}`; the classic version uses a distributive conditional type.
n461.c:
type MyNonNullable<T> = T extends null | undefined ? never : T;
type R = MyNonNullable<string | null | undefined>; // string

n462.a: Extract<T, U> keeps union members of T assignable to U, using a distributive conditional type.
n462.f: How would you extract members of a discriminated union by kind?
n462.c:
type MyExtract<T, U> = T extends U ? T : never;
type R = MyExtract<'a' | 'b' | 1, string>; // 'a' | 'b'

n463.a: Exclude<T, E> removes union members of T that are assignable to E.
n463.f: Why does never disappear from unions?
n463.c:
type MyExclude<T, E> = T extends E ? never : T;
type R = MyExclude<'a' | 'b' | 'c', 'a'>; // 'b' | 'c'

n464.a: Omit<T, K> constructs a type with all properties of T except keys K: Pick the keys excluding K, or use key remapping.
p: Pick remaining or remap with as never
n464.f: Why doesn't Omit work well on union types, and how would DistributiveOmit fix it?
n464.c:
type MyOmit<T, K extends keyof any> = { [P in keyof T as P extends K ? never : P]: T[P] };
type R = MyOmit<{ a: 1; b: 2; c: 3 }, 'a'>; // { b: 2; c: 3 }

n465.a: Pick<T, K> constructs a type with only the properties K of T.
n465.f: Why does Pick preserve optional and readonly modifiers?
n465.c:
type MyPick<T, K extends keyof T> = { [P in K]: T[P] };
type R = MyPick<{ a: 1; b: 2 }, 'a'>; // { a: 1 }

n466.a: Record<K, V> constructs an object type whose keys are K and values are V.
n466.f: What's the difference between Record<string, T> and an index signature?
n466.c:
type MyRecord<K extends keyof any, V> = { [P in K]: V };
type R = MyRecord<'a' | 'b', number>; // { a: number; b: number }

n467.a: Readonly<T> makes all properties of T readonly (shallow).
n467.f: Does readonly prevent mutation at runtime?
n467.c:
type MyReadonly<T> = { readonly [K in keyof T]: T[K] };
type DeepReadonly<T> = { readonly [K in keyof T]: T[K] extends object ? DeepReadonly<T[K]> : T[K] };

n468.a: Required<T> makes all properties required by removing the optional modifier with `-?`.
p: Also removes undefined from optional props
n468.f: How would you make only some keys required?
n468.c:
type MyRequired<T> = { [K in keyof T]-?: T[K] };
type R = MyRequired<{ a?: number }>; // { a: number }

n469.a: Partial<T> makes all properties optional using the `?` modifier in a mapped type.
n469.c:
type MyPartial<T> = { [K in keyof T]?: T[K] };
type R = MyPartial<{ a: number; b: string }>; // { a?: number; b?: string }

n1199.a: `foo` is the string "1020". When `+` has a string operand, the number is converted to a string and the two are concatenated.
p: Other arithmetic operators convert to numbers

n1200.a: It logs `false`. 0.1 + 0.2 is 0.30000000000000004 in IEEE-754 binary floating point, which isn't exactly 0.3.
n1200.f: Which other languages show the same result?

n1201.a: Make `add` return the sum when called with two arguments, and return a function waiting for the second argument when called with one (a simple form of currying).
p: Return a closure for partial calls
n1201.f: How would you generalize this with a curry helper?

n1202.a: It returns "goh angasal a m'i" — split into characters, reverse the array, and join back, reversing the string.
n1202.f: Why does this break with emoji, and how do you fix it?
n1202.c: "i'm a lasagna hog".split('').reverse().join(''); // "goh angasal a m'i"

n1203.a: The classic snippet is `( window.foo || ( window.foo = "bar" ) );` — `window.foo` becomes "bar". If foo is undefined (falsy), the right side of `||` runs, assigning "bar"; if it already had a truthy value, it stays unchanged.
p: Right side runs only when left is falsy

n1204.a: The first alert shows "Hello World" because the IIFE can read the outer `foo` and its own `bar`. The second line throws a ReferenceError ("bar is not defined") because `bar` is scoped to the function, so the second alert never shows.
p: Inner scope can read outer variables
Outer scope can't read inner variables
n1204.f: What would change if bar were declared without var inside the function in sloppy mode?

n1205.a: `foo.length` is 2: the array is mutated by two pushes even though it's declared with var/const — length reflects the number of elements.

n1206.a: `foo.x` is undefined. In `foo.x = foo = {n: 2}`, the left reference `foo.x` is resolved first to the original object (which `bar` also points to). Then `foo = {n: 2}` reassigns foo, and the result is assigned to the old object's x. So `bar.x` is `{n: 2}`, while the new `foo` has no x.
p: Assignment targets evaluated left to right
foo.x refers to the old object
foo rebound to a new object
New foo has no x property
n1206.f: How would you rewrite this to be clear?

n1207.a: It prints `one`, `four`, `three`, `two`. Synchronous logs run first; the promise callback is a microtask, run right after the current script; the setTimeout callback is a macrotask, run afterwards.
n1207.f: Where would a queueMicrotask callback appear?

n1208.a: (1) Returns the promise from doSomethingElse, so the chain waits for it and the next then receives its result. (2) Calls doSomethingElse but doesn't return it, so the chain doesn't wait and the next then gets undefined (errors aren't propagated). (3) Calls doSomethingElse immediately (before doSomething finishes) and passes its result (a promise) to then, which ignores non-functions — so the chain continues with doSomething's result. (4) Passes the function itself, so it's called with doSomething's result as its argument and the chain waits for its promise.
n1208.f: Which version is a common source of bugs in real code?

n1209.a: No. `foo1` returns the object `{ bar: "hello" }`. `foo2` returns `undefined`, because automatic semicolon insertion adds a semicolon right after `return` when the line ends there; the following block is parsed as a block statement with a label, never reached.
p: return followed by newline returns undefined
Keep the brace on the same line
n1209.f: What other statements are affected by ASI this way?

n235.a: Tests grapheme vs code unit length: strings are UTF-16, so `'😀'.length` is 2 and composed emoji like a family or flag are even longer, while users see one character. `[...str].length` counts code points (still not graphemes for joined emoji); `Intl.Segmenter` with granularity 'grapheme' counts user-perceived characters.
p: ZWJ sequences combine several code points
n235.f: How would you truncate a string without splitting an emoji?

n236.a: Tests `Object.groupBy(items, fn)`: it returns a null-prototype object whose keys are the callback's return values (converted to strings) and values are arrays of items in original order. `Map.groupBy` keeps keys as any type. Because the object has no prototype, methods like `hasOwnProperty` aren't available on it.

n237.a: Tests how values convert to strings: objects use `toString` (giving "[object Object]" unless overridden), arrays join elements with commas (nested arrays flatten, null/undefined become empty), and `Symbol.toPrimitive`/`valueOf` take priority in some contexts (e.g. `+` uses valueOf first with hint "default").
p: Template literals use the string hint
n237.f: What's the order of valueOf and toString for `obj + ''`?

n238.a: The classic "banana" trick: `('b' + 'a' + + 'a' + 'a').toLowerCase()` gives "banana". The `+ 'a'` with unary plus converts 'a' to NaN, which is then concatenated as the string "NaN".
n238.f: What would `'b' + 'a' + 'a'` give without the extra plus?

n239.a: Tests `return await` vs `return` inside async functions with try/catch: `return promise` inside try doesn't catch its rejection (the function returns before it settles), while `return await promise` waits inside the try, so the catch block handles the rejection. Outside try/catch they behave the same (modern engines even optimize timing).
n239.f: Is `return await` ever a performance problem?

n240.a: Tests async function execution order: an async function runs synchronously until its first `await`; the rest continues as a microtask after the awaited value resolves. So logs before the await appear synchronously, and logs after it appear after the current synchronous code but before timers.
n240.f: What if f awaited a promise that resolves after setTimeout?

n241.a: Tests function declarations vs expressions and name binding: a named function expression's name is only available inside the function and is read-only there (assignments silently ignored in sloppy mode), and the outer variable can be reassigned independently.
p: Named function expression name is local
n241.f: What happens in strict mode when assigning to g?

n242.a: Tests timers with different delays and nesting: callbacks run in order of their expiry times, not registration order; nested setTimeouts are scheduled when the outer callback runs; microtasks inside a timer callback run before the next timer.
n242.f: Why does a timer with delay 0 not run immediately?

n243.a: Tests JSON.stringify edge cases: undefined, functions and symbols are omitted in objects but become null in arrays; NaN and Infinity become null; Dates become ISO strings via toJSON; Map/Set become {}; BigInt throws; and `toJSON` methods are used if present.
n243.f: How would you serialize a Map?
n243.c:
JSON.stringify({ a: undefined, b: () => {}, c: NaN, d: new Date(0) }); // '{"c":null,"d":"1970-01-01T00:00:00.000Z"}'
JSON.stringify([undefined, () => {}]); // '[null,null]'

n244.a: Tests property order of `Object.keys`: integer-like keys come first in ascending numeric order, then string keys in insertion order (symbols are excluded). Non-enumerable and inherited properties are excluded.
p: Then string keys in insertion order
Same order for for...in own keys
n244.f: Is '01' treated as an integer key?

n245.a: Tests control flow in try/catch/finally: finally always runs; a `return` in finally overrides any return or throw from try/catch; if finally doesn't return, the try/catch return value is kept (even if finally changes the variable, the already-evaluated value is returned).
p: Throw in finally replaces earlier errors
n245.f: Why is return in finally considered harmful?

n246.a: Tests the comma operator: it evaluates each operand left to right and returns the last one. In contexts like `var a = (1, 2, 3)` a is 3; without parentheses in a declaration, commas separate declarators instead.
n246.f: Why does `const a = 1, 2;` throw a SyntaxError?

n247.a: Tests `return` inside generators: a return statement produces `{ value: returnValue, done: true }` from next(), but for...of and spread ignore the return value (they stop when done is true), so only yielded values appear.
p: return gives done: true with a value
Further next() → { value: undefined, done: true }
n247.f: How can you get the return value of a generator used with yield*?

n248.a: Tests the iterable protocol: an object is iterable if it has a `[Symbol.iterator]` method returning an iterator with `next()`. Spread, for...of, destructuring, Array.from and Promise.all use it; plain objects aren't iterable, so spreading one into an array throws a TypeError.

n249.a: Tests `generator.return(value)`: it finishes the generator immediately, returning `{ value, done: true }`, but if the generator is paused inside a try with a finally, the finally block runs first (and can yield or override).
n249.f: When does for...of call return() automatically?

n250.a: Tests `structuredClone`: it deep-copies objects, arrays, Dates, Maps, Sets, RegExps, typed arrays and circular references, but throws a DataCloneError for functions, DOM nodes and symbols as values; class instances lose their prototype (become plain objects), and getters are evaluated into values.
n250.f: How does it differ from JSON.parse(JSON.stringify())?

n251.a: Tests `this` in nested functions and arrow functions inside object methods: a regular function called plainly loses `this` (undefined/global), while an arrow function inside a method inherits the method's `this`. An arrow function defined directly as an object property takes `this` from the surrounding (module/global) scope, not the object.
p: Object literals don't create a this scope
n251.f: What is `this` at the top of an ES module?

n252.a: Tests strict mode differences: assigning to undeclared variables throws ReferenceError, `this` in plain function calls is undefined, writing to read-only properties throws TypeError, deleting non-configurable properties throws, and duplicate parameter names are syntax errors. Strict mode applies per function or file and can't be turned off inside.
n252.f: Can a strict function make its caller strict?

n253.a: Tests `parseInt` coercion: it converts the argument to a string first, then parses leading digits. So `parseInt(0.0000005)` is 5 (string "5e-7"), `parseInt(null, 36)` is 1112745 ("null" in base 36), and `parseInt('Infinity')` is NaN. The radix can change the result dramatically.
n253.f: Why use Math.trunc or Number for numeric conversion instead?

n254.a: Tests the `constructor` property: it's inherited from the prototype (`Fn.prototype.constructor === Fn`). If you replace a function's prototype with a new object literal, instances' `constructor` becomes `Object` unless you restore it. Primitives access it via wrapper objects.
n254.f: How do classes avoid this problem?

n255.a: Tests `Array.prototype.push`: it mutates the array and returns the new length (not the array). Pushing an array adds it as a single element. It works generically on array-like objects, setting `length`.
n255.f: How would you append all elements of another array?

n256.a: Tests Symbols: every `Symbol()` is unique even with the same description; `Symbol.for(key)` returns the same symbol from a global registry; symbol-keyed properties are skipped by Object.keys, for...in and JSON.stringify but appear in `Object.getOwnPropertySymbols`/`Reflect.ownKeys`; symbols can't be implicitly converted to strings (`'' + sym` throws), only explicitly.
n256.f: What are well-known symbols used for?
n256.c:
Symbol('a') === Symbol('a');          // false
Symbol.for('a') === Symbol.for('a');  // true
`${Symbol('x')}`;                      // TypeError

n257.a: Tests falsy values: the falsy values are `false`, `0`, `-0`, `0n`, `''`, `null`, `undefined` and `NaN` (plus `document.all`). Everything else is truthy, including `'0'`, `'false'`, `[]`, `{}` and `new Boolean(false)`.
n257.f: Why is `[] == false` true even though [] is truthy?
n257.c: [0, '', null, NaN, '0', [], {}].map(Boolean); // [false, false, false, false, true, true, true]

n258.a: Tests `yield` as an expression: the value passed to `next(value)` becomes the result of the paused `yield` expression. The first `next()` argument is ignored because no yield is waiting yet.
p: next(v) resumes with v as yield's result
n258.f: How did libraries like co use this for async flow?

n259.a: Tests global `isNaN` vs `Number.isNaN`: global isNaN converts its argument to a number first, so `isNaN('abc')` and `isNaN(undefined)` are true; `Number.isNaN` returns true only for the actual NaN value. NaN is the only value not equal to itself.
n259.f: How would you check NaN without either function?
n259.c:
isNaN('abc');        // true
Number.isNaN('abc'); // false
isNaN('');           // false ('' → 0)

n260.a: Tests property key coercion: object keys are strings or symbols, so other values are converted to strings. Using objects as keys makes them all "[object Object]", so they overwrite each other; numbers become strings ('1' and 1 are the same key).
p: Arrays as keys stringify with commas

n261.a: Tests `this` with method extraction and callbacks: assigning `obj.method` to a variable or passing it to setTimeout/array methods loses the receiver; `this` becomes undefined (strict) or the global object. Calling through property access with parentheses (`(obj.method)()`) keeps this, but `(0, obj.method)()` or `(obj.method = obj.method)()` doesn't.
p: Receiver is decided at call time
n261.f: Why does grouping keep `this` but the comma operator doesn't?

n262.a: Tests Promise.all edge cases: non-promise values are treated as already resolved; results keep input order regardless of completion order; an empty array resolves immediately with []; the first rejection rejects the whole thing while other promises keep running.
n262.f: What does Promise.all do with a rejection after it has already rejected?
n262.c:
Promise.all([1, Promise.resolve(2), new Promise(r => setTimeout(() => r(3), 10))]).then(console.log); // [1, 2, 3]
Promise.all([]).then(console.log); // []

n263.a: Tests typeof results: 'undefined', 'boolean', 'number', 'bigint', 'string', 'symbol', 'function', and 'object' for objects, arrays and null. typeof on undeclared variables returns 'undefined' without throwing, but throws for let/const in the TDZ. `typeof typeof x` is 'string'.
n263.f: How do you reliably detect arrays?
n263.c:
typeof null;        // 'object'
typeof [];          // 'object'
typeof class {};    // 'function'
typeof typeof 1;    // 'string'

n264.a: Tests prototype-based inheritance: properties found on an instance shadow those on the prototype; changing the prototype object affects existing instances (they share it), but replacing `Fn.prototype` with a new object only affects instances created afterwards.
p: Replacing prototype affects only new ones

n265.a: Tests ordering among multiple promise chains: each `.then` callback is queued as a microtask only when its previous promise settles, so two chains interleave one step at a time. Returning a promise from a then adds extra ticks (about two) before the next then runs.
p: Each then waits for its predecessor
Returning a promise adds extra ticks
n265.f: What changes if the first then returns Promise.resolve()?

n266.a: Tests arrow functions further: they don't have their own `arguments` (they see the enclosing function's), can't be used with `new`, have no `prototype`, and their `this` can't be changed with call/apply/bind.
n266.f: How do you access arguments in an arrow function?

n267.a: Tests loose equality edge cases: `==` converts objects to primitives (valueOf/toString), booleans to numbers, and strings to numbers when comparing with numbers; null equals only undefined. So `[] == ![]` is true ([] → '' → 0 and ![] → false → 0), while `null == 0` is false.
p: Strings convert when compared to numbers

n268.a: Tests var vs let: var is function-scoped and hoisted with undefined, so loops share one binding; let is block-scoped with a fresh binding per loop iteration and a TDZ before declaration. Closures in loops log the final var value but each iteration's let value.
p: var: function scope, single loop binding
n268.f: Does var at top level create a window property?
n268.c:
for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) setTimeout(() => console.log(i)); // 3 3 3
for (let j = 0; j < 3; j++) setTimeout(() => console.log(j)); // 0 1 2

n269.a: Tests closures capturing variables by reference, not value: functions created in a scope see the current value of the variable when they run, and each call of the outer function creates a separate environment with independent state.
p: Loop closures depend on var vs let
n269.f: How would you capture a snapshot value instead?

n270.a: Tests Promise executor behaviour: the executor runs synchronously; only the first resolve/reject call counts (later ones are ignored); code after resolve still runs; a throw after resolve is ignored; a throw before resolving rejects the promise.
n270.f: What if resolve is called with a rejected promise?

n271.a: Tests `this` with method chaining and returned functions: a method that returns a regular function loses `this` when that function is called standalone; returning `this` enables chaining; arrow functions returned from methods keep the method's this.
p: Returned regular functions use default binding
n271.f: How do builder APIs use this pattern?
n271.c:
const calc = { n: 0, add(x) { this.n += x; return this; } };
calc.add(1).add(2).n; // 3

n272.a: Tests relational comparison coercion: `<`/`>` convert both sides to primitives; if both are strings they compare lexicographically by code units ('10' < '9' is true), otherwise numerically ('10' < 9 is false). null becomes 0 in relational comparisons (`null >= 0` is true even though `null == 0` is false); undefined becomes NaN (always false).
n272.f: Why do relational and equality operators treat null differently?
n272.c:
'10' < '9';   // true
'10' < 9;     // false
null >= 0;    // true
null == 0;    // false

n273.a: Tests number literal parsing: `1.toString()` is a SyntaxError because the dot is parsed as a decimal point; `1..toString()`, `1 .toString()` and `(1).toString()` work. Also numeric separators (`1_000`), octal/hex/binary prefixes, and that `0.1.toFixed(2)` is fine.
p: First dot after an integer is the decimal point

n274.a: Tests emoji/UTF-16 behaviour: emoji outside the BMP use two code units, so `length` is 2, indexing returns lone surrogates, `split('')` breaks them, and `reverse` produces garbage; spread/Array.from and for...of iterate by code point; some emoji combine multiple code points with ZWJ.
n274.f: How would you reverse a string containing emoji safely?

n275.a: Tests string immutability and methods: strings are immutable, so assigning to an index silently does nothing (throws in strict mode); methods like toUpperCase return new strings; `str[i]` returns a character or undefined; `'abc' < 'abd'` compares lexicographically.
n275.f: How would you change one character?

n276.a: Tests NaN: it's the only value not equal to itself, typeof NaN is 'number', arithmetic with NaN gives NaN, `[NaN].includes(NaN)` is true (SameValueZero) but `[NaN].indexOf(NaN)` is -1 (strict equality), and `Object.is(NaN, NaN)` is true.

n277.a: Tests the maximum array length: valid indexes go up to 2^32 − 2 (length max 2^32 − 1). Assigning at index 2^32 − 1 or larger creates a normal string property, not an element, so length doesn't change.
p: Setting length too large throws RangeError

n278.a: Tests array keys with holes: `Object.keys` skips holes (only existing indexes), while `arr.keys()` iterates every index from 0 to length − 1 including holes; for...in also skips holes and includes added non-index properties.
n278.f: How do forEach and map handle holes?

n279.a: Tests let and the temporal dead zone: let bindings are hoisted to the top of their block but uninitialized, so reading them earlier in the block — even when an outer variable has the same name — throws ReferenceError (the inner binding shadows the outer one from the block start).
n279.c:
let x = 1;
{ console.log(x); let x = 2; } // ReferenceError

n280.a: Tests try/catch scoping and flow: the catch parameter is block-scoped (shadows outer variables only inside the catch); `var` declared inside catch is hoisted to the function; errors thrown inside catch propagate unless caught again; asynchronous errors (in setTimeout) aren't caught by an outer try.
p: Catch param scoped to the block
var inside catch hoists to function
n280.f: Why doesn't try/catch around setTimeout catch the callback's error?

n281.a: Tests `instanceof` details: it checks whether `Fn.prototype` is in the object's prototype chain, so changing Fn.prototype afterwards breaks it; primitives aren't instances (`'a' instanceof String` is false); `Symbol.hasInstance` can customize it; and objects from other realms fail.
n281.f: How does Array.isArray avoid the realm problem?
n281.c:
'a' instanceof String;              // false
Object.create(null) instanceof Object; // false

n282.a: Tests setTimeout with loops and clearTimeout: timers scheduled in a loop with var share the same variable; clearTimeout prevents a callback only if called before it fires; setTimeout returns an ID; extra arguments are passed to the callback.
p: Timer IDs are numbers in browsers
n282.f: How does Node's setTimeout return value differ?
n282.c: for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) setTimeout(n => console.log(n), 0, i); // 0 1 2

n283.a: Tests `String.raw`: as a tag it returns the raw template string with escape sequences left unprocessed (backslashes kept) and substitutions interpolated; called as a function with `{ raw: [...] }` it interleaves strings with arguments.
p: Useful for regex and Windows paths
Can be called with a raw object
n283.f: Why is it handy for building regular expressions?

n284.a: Tests `Array.prototype.sort` defaults: without a comparator it converts elements to strings and sorts by UTF-16 code units, so `[10, 9, 1].sort()` gives [1, 10, 9]; undefined values go to the end; it sorts in place and returns the same array; the sort is stable.
p: Numbers sort incorrectly without a comparator
Mutates and returns the same array

n285.a: Tests increment operators: `x++` returns the old value then increments; `++x` increments then returns the new value. Combinations like `x + ++x` evaluate left to right; `++` on non-numbers converts them to numbers (`'5'` → 6); `x+++y` parses as `(x++) + y`.
n285.f: Why do linters discourage ++ in expressions?
n285.c:
let x = 1;
const r = x++ + ++x; // 1 + 3 = 4, x is 3

n286.a: Tests Proxy traps more deeply: operations not covered by a trap fall through to the target; `has` intercepts `in`; `ownKeys` affects Object.keys; invariants must hold (e.g. a non-configurable property can't be reported as missing, or a TypeError is thrown); the proxy identity differs from the target.
p: Missing traps forward to the target
n286.f: Why can proxies break private class fields (#x)?

n287.a: Tests setTimeout with closures and changing variables: the callback reads the variable's value when it runs, not when it was scheduled; if the variable changes before the timer fires, the new value is logged.
p: Read current value at run time

n288.a: Tests a basic Proxy get trap: every property read goes through the trap, including reads of methods and `Symbol.toPrimitive` during coercion or console logging, so a trap returning a fixed value affects all properties; Reflect.get gives default behaviour.
n288.f: Where are proxies used in frameworks?
n288.c:
const p = new Proxy({}, { get: (t, k) => (typeof k === 'string' ? k.toUpperCase() : Reflect.get(t, k)) });
p.hello; // 'HELLO'

n289.a: Tests more `==` and `===` edge cases: objects are compared by reference in both; `'1' == 1` is true; `true == '1'` is true (both → 1); `[1, 2] == '1,2'` is true via toString; `{} == '[object Object]'` is true.

n290.a: Tests regex quirks: special characters must be escaped (`.` matches any char); the `g` flag makes `test`/`exec` stateful via `lastIndex`; `String.prototype.replace` with a string pattern replaces only the first occurrence; and `$&`/`$1` in replacement strings have special meaning.
n290.f: How do you safely build a regex from user input?

n291.a: Tests `['1', '2', '3'].map(parseInt)`: map passes (value, index), so parseInt gets the index as radix: parseInt('1', 0) → 1 (radix 0 means default), parseInt('2', 1) → NaN (invalid radix), parseInt('3', 2) → NaN ('3' isn't binary). Result: [1, NaN, NaN].
n291.f: Why is passing functions point-free to map sometimes risky?

n292.a: Tests const: the binding can't be reassigned (TypeError), but objects/arrays it points to can be mutated; it must be initialized at declaration; it's block-scoped with TDZ; in for...of each iteration gets a new const binding, but in a classic for loop `i++` on const throws.
p: Works in for...of, not classic for with ++
n292.f: How do you make the object itself immutable?
n292.c:
const arr = [1]; arr.push(2); // fine
arr = [];                     // TypeError
for (const x of [1, 2]) {}    // fine

n293.a: Tests silly coercion chains: e.g. `[] + []` is '' (both become empty strings), `[] + {}` is '[object Object]', `{} + []` at statement start is 0 in the console (block + unary plus), `true + true` is 2, `'3' - - '3'` is 6. Unary/binary operators convert operands via ToPrimitive then ToNumber or ToString.
p: + concatenates if either side is a string after ToPrimitive
n293.f: Why does `{} + []` differ between console and an expression context?

n294.a: Tests typed array lengths: a typed array's length is fixed at creation (pushing isn't available; setting length is ignored), values are coerced and wrapped to the type (Uint8 wraps 256 to 0, Uint8Clamped clamps), and out-of-range index writes are ignored.
n294.f: When would you use typed arrays in frontend code?

n295.a: Tests `window.name`: in browsers, `name` at global scope refers to the special `window.name` property, which always converts values to strings and persists across navigations in the same tab. So `var name = 123` makes `typeof name` 'string', and `name = [1, 2]` becomes '1,2'. With `let name` in a script, a separate binding is created.
