p: Persists across page loads in the tab
n295.f: Why could window.name be a security concern?
n295.c:
var name = 123;
typeof name; // 'string' (in a browser script)

n296.a: Tests array length: setting `length` smaller truncates the array; setting it larger creates holes; assigning to an index beyond length extends it; length is always one more than the highest index, not the count of elements.
n296.f: How do you empty an array referenced elsewhere?

n297.a: Tests two-way generator communication: values passed into `next()` become the result of the paused yield; you can compute with them and yield results back. The first next() starts the generator; its argument is discarded.
n297.f: How does throw() send errors into a generator?

n298.a: Tests function declarations inside blocks and hoisting: function declarations hoist with their body to the top of their scope; when two declarations share a name, the last wins; a later variable assignment with the same name overwrites the function at runtime.
p: var with same name doesn't override until assigned
Block-level functions behave differently in strict mode
n298.f: How do function declarations in blocks behave in sloppy mode?

n299.a: Tests undefined: it's a global property that's read-only in modern engines but can be shadowed as a local variable name; `void 0` always yields undefined; missing properties, missing arguments, and functions without return all give undefined; `undefined == null` is true but `=== null` false.

n300.a: Tests function declarations inside if blocks: in sloppy mode, a function declared inside a block is hoisted as a `var` (undefined) to the function scope and assigned when the block executes; if the block doesn't run, calling it throws TypeError. In strict mode it's block-scoped and not visible outside.
p: Sloppy: var-like hoisting, assigned when block runs
n300.f: How do you write conditional functions clearly?

n301.a: Tests if conditions with function expressions: `if (function f() {})` is truthy, but the named function expression's name `f` isn't defined outside it, so `typeof f` is 'undefined' afterwards.
p: Named function expression name is local
n301.f: Where else are function expressions evaluated in conditions?

n302.a: Tests the comma operator in different contexts: `(a, b)` returns b; in `for` loops commas allow multiple updates; in array literals extra commas create holes; trailing commas in arrays/objects/params are allowed and ignored.

n303.a: Tests the `name` property of functions: declarations and named expressions use their name; anonymous functions assigned to variables infer the variable name; methods use the property key; bound functions are 'bound f'; getters are 'get x'; `name` is read-only (assignment ignored).
p: Named expressions keep their own name
n303.f: Why is name useful for debugging?
n303.c:
const a = function () {}; a.name;        // 'a'
const b = function c() {}; b.name;       // 'c'
a.bind(null).name;                       // 'bound a'

n304.a: Tests reference types: objects and arrays are assigned and passed by sharing a reference, so mutating via one variable affects others; reassigning a parameter or variable doesn't affect the original. Comparisons with === check identity.
p: Parameters get a copy of the reference

n305.a: Tests the `in` operator: it checks property existence including the prototype chain, works with array indexes (`0 in [1]` true, holes false), requires an object on the right (throws for primitives like strings), and finds inherited methods like 'toString'.
p: Right side must be an object
n305.c:
'toString' in {};   // true
1 in [1, , 3];      // false
'length' in 'abc';  // TypeError

n306.a: Tests MessageChannel timing: `port.postMessage` delivers messages asynchronously as macrotasks (tasks), so they run after synchronous code and after microtasks (promises), typically before setTimeout callbacks of comparable time. React's scheduler uses MessageChannel for this reason.

n307.a: Tests click handlers: `element.onclick = fn` replaces any previous handler (only one), while addEventListener can register many; `this` in a regular onclick function is the element; returning false from an onclick property prevents the default action; `el.click()` dispatches synchronously, so listeners run before the next line.
n307.f: Why does a user click run microtasks between listeners but el.click() doesn't?
n307.c:
btn.addEventListener('click', () => console.log('listener'));
btn.click(); console.log('after'); // listener, after

n308.a: Tests window.postMessage timing: messages are delivered asynchronously as tasks, after current synchronous code and microtasks; the message data is structured-cloned, so the receiver gets a copy (mutations after sending don't affect it).

n309.a: Tests overriding an inherited setter: if the prototype defines a setter for a property, assigning to that property on an instance calls the setter instead of creating an own property; defining a data property on a subclass/instance with defineProperty does override it.
p: Setter runs instead of creating own property
Getter-only prototype property makes assignment fail silently
n309.f: Why do class fields shadow parent accessors?

n310.a: Tests getters/setters inherited through classes: `this` in an inherited getter/setter refers to the instance, so state set via the setter lives on the instance; overriding only the getter in a subclass removes the inherited setter for that property (accessors are defined together).
p: Overriding only get hides parent set
n310.f: How would you fix B so that the setter still works?

n311.a: Tests non-writable properties: assignments to a property with `writable: false` are silently ignored in sloppy mode and throw TypeError in strict mode; inherited non-writable properties also block creating an own property by assignment.
p: defineProperty can still define own property
n311.f: How does Object.freeze relate to writable?
n311.c:
const o = {}; Object.defineProperty(o, 'x', { value: 1, writable: false });
o.x = 2; o.x; // 1

n312.a: Tests object-to-primitive conversion: `Symbol.toPrimitive(hint)` takes precedence; otherwise for hint 'number'/'default' valueOf is tried first then toString, and for hint 'string' toString first. `+obj` uses number, template literals use string, and `obj + ''` uses default.
n312.f: Why do Dates behave differently with +?

n313.a: Tests sparse arrays: holes are skipped by forEach, map (kept as holes), filter, reduce and some/every, but treated as undefined by for...of, spread, Array.from, join (empty), and find/findIndex/includes.
n313.f: How can you create a dense array of a given length?
n313.c:
const a = [1, , 3];
a.map(x => x * 2);  // [2, empty, 6]
[...a];             // [1, undefined, 3]
a.includes(undefined); // true

n314.a: Tests `setTimeout(fn, 0)`: the callback waits for current synchronous code and all microtasks, and browsers clamp nested timers (after 5 levels) to at least 4ms. Timers with equal delay run in scheduling order.
p: Runs after sync code and microtasks
n314.f: Why are background tab timers throttled?

n315.a: Tests prototype mutations and lookups: methods added to the prototype after instances are created are still available to them; own properties shadow prototype ones; deleting the own property reveals the inherited value again.
n315.f: What happens if you mutate an array stored on the prototype?

n316.a: Tests requestAnimationFrame timing: rAF callbacks run before the next repaint, after the current task and its microtasks; relative to setTimeout(0) the order varies (it depends on frame timing), but microtasks always run first. Callbacks registered during a rAF run in the following frame.
p: Order vs setTimeout is not guaranteed
n316.f: How do you run code after the next paint?

n317.a: Tests object method shorthand vs regular function properties vs arrows: method shorthand can use `super` and isn't constructible (`new obj.method()` throws); a function property is constructible; arrows take lexical this.
n317.f: When would you need super inside an object literal?

n318.a: Tests async/await ordering: code after each await resumes as a microtask; awaiting a non-promise still yields one tick; two async functions interleave at each await; synchronous logs happen first.
n318.f: What if a awaited a function that itself awaits?

n319.a: Tests `this` with call/apply/bind precedence: a bound function ignores later call/apply/bind with a new this; `new` overrides bind's this (but keeps bound arguments); arrow functions ignore all of them.

n320.a: Tests prototype basics: `Object.getPrototypeOf(instance) === Ctor.prototype`, functions have a `prototype` property while instances don't, `Ctor.prototype.constructor === Ctor`, and `__proto__` is an accessor on Object.prototype.

n321.a: Tests mixing promises, async functions and timers: synchronous logs first; then microtasks in queue order (promise thens, async continuations), including microtasks queued by microtasks; then macrotasks (setTimeout) one at a time, each followed by its own microtasks.
p: Microtasks scheduled by microtasks run in the same drain
n321.f: How does Node's event loop phase ordering differ?

n322.a: Tests implicit coercion with objects and arrays in arithmetic: `[2] * [3]` is 6 (arrays → '2' → 2), `[1, 2] * 2` is NaN, `null + 1` is 1, `undefined + 1` is NaN, `'5' * '2'` is 10, `true + '1'` is 'true1'.

n323.a: Tests hoisting combined with function parameters and inner declarations: a var declared inside a function with the same name as a parameter doesn't reset it (the declaration is ignored, only an assignment changes it); a function declaration with that name does override the parameter at the start.

n324.a: Tests calling functions with the wrong number of arguments: missing arguments are undefined, extra ones are ignored but available via `arguments` or rest params; default parameters apply only for undefined; `fn.length` counts parameters before the first default/rest.
n324.f: Why does fn.length matter for curry implementations?

n325.a: Tests JSON.stringify basics: it outputs strings with double quotes; only own enumerable properties; nested objects; key order follows Object.keys order; the replacer (array or function) filters/transforms; the space argument indents; circular references throw TypeError.
n325.f: How does the replacer function see the root value?

n326.a: Tests hoisting with nested functions and shadowing: inside a function, a `var` with the same name as an outer variable is hoisted to the top of that function, so reading the name before the declaration gives undefined, not the outer value.
p: Shadows outer variable from the start
Use let/const to get errors instead
n326.f: What would happen with let x inside f?

n327.a: Tests `this` inside callbacks of array methods: callbacks are called without a receiver, so `this` is undefined (strict) unless you pass the optional `thisArg` (second argument of forEach/map), or use arrows inside methods to inherit this.
n327.f: Does thisArg work with arrow callbacks?
n327.c:
const obj = { factor: 2, scale(arr) { return arr.map(function (x) { return x * this.factor; }, this); } };
obj.scale([1, 2]); // [2, 4]

n328.a: Tests `RegExp.prototype.test` with the global flag: a /g regex remembers `lastIndex`, so calling test repeatedly on the same string alternates true/false; also `test()` with no argument tests the string "undefined".
n328.f: How do you avoid this bug when reusing a regex?
n328.c:
const re = /a/g;
re.test('a'); // true
re.test('a'); // false (lastIndex was 1)
/undef/.test(); // true

n329.a: Tests var specifics: var is function-scoped (visible outside if/for blocks), can be redeclared, is hoisted as undefined, and at the top level of a classic script creates a property on window.
n329.f: Does var at the top of an ES module create a global?

n330.a: Tests hoisting priority between function declarations and var: function declarations are hoisted before vars; a later `var` declaration of the same name without assignment doesn't overwrite the function, but an assignment does once executed.
p: Function declarations win at hoist time
n330.f: What if two function declarations share the name?

n331.a: Tests push and unshift return values and order: both return the new length; unshift inserts multiple arguments in the given order at the front (`[3].unshift(1, 2)` → [1, 2, 3]) — different from calling unshift one at a time.
n331.f: Which non-mutating alternative would you use in React state?

n332.a: Tests `Promise.prototype.finally`: its callback receives no arguments; it passes through the original value or rejection unchanged (its return value is ignored) unless it throws or returns a rejected promise, which replaces the outcome; it waits for a returned promise.
n332.f: How does this differ from then(fn, fn)?

n333.a: Tests coercion with `==` and objects with custom valueOf/toString: objects are converted via ToPrimitive before comparison, so an object with `valueOf() { return 1 }` equals 1 and `'1'`; the famous `a == 1 && a == 2 && a == 3` trick uses a valueOf that increments.
n333.f: Could the same trick work with ===?
n333.c:
const a = { i: 1, valueOf() { return this.i++; } };
a == 1 && a == 2 && a == 3; // true

n334.a: Tests operator precedence: e.g. `typeof` binds tighter than `+` (`typeof 1 + 1` → 'number1'), `!` binds tighter than `==`, `&&` before `||`, `??` can't be mixed with `||`/`&&` without parentheses, and assignment is right-associative.
n334.f: Why does `a ?? b || c` throw a SyntaxError?
n334.c:
typeof 1 + 1;          // 'number1'
!'' == true;           // true
true || false && false; // true

n335.a: Tests `this` when a method is assigned to another object: `this` refers to whichever object the function is called on, not where it was defined; so copying a method to another object makes it use that object's properties.
p: Borrowed methods use the new receiver
n335.f: How does Array.prototype method borrowing rely on this?

n336.a: Tests hoisting in nested blocks with let/const and functions: let/const are hoisted to their block with TDZ; functions declared inside blocks are block-scoped in strict mode and also var-hoisted in sloppy mode, so outside the block they may be undefined until the block runs.
n336.f: Why do different engines once behave differently here?

n337.a: Tests Math quirks: `Math.max()` with no args is -Infinity and `Math.min()` is Infinity; any NaN argument gives NaN; `Math.round(-0.5)` is -0 and `Math.round(2.5)` is 3 (rounds toward +Infinity at .5); `Math.max([1, 2])` is NaN-ish (array coerced) unless spread.

n338.a: Tests equality between different types: `null == false` is false (null only equals undefined), `undefined == 0` is false, `'' == []` is true, `NaN == NaN` is false, `0 == '0'` true and `0 == []` true but `'0' == []` false (not transitive).
n338.f: What does non-transitivity imply for code reviews?

n339.a: Tests hoisting of function expressions: `var f = function(){}` hoists only `var f` (undefined), so calling f before the line throws "f is not a function"; named function expression names aren't hoisted at all.
n339.f: What error with const instead of var?
n339.c:
try { f(); } catch (e) { console.log(e.constructor.name); } // TypeError
var f = function () {};

n340.a: Tests hoisting across function scopes: variables declared inside a function aren't visible outside; assigning without declaration in sloppy mode creates a global; and inner var hoisting creates a separate local binding.
n340.f: How does strict mode prevent accidental globals?

n341.a: Tests basic var hoisting: reading a var before its declaration returns undefined (declaration hoisted, assignment not); reading an undeclared variable throws ReferenceError.
n341.f: What does `typeof b` give for undeclared b?

n342.a: Tests truthiness vs equality to true: `if ([])` runs (arrays are truthy) but `[] == true` is false ([] → '' → 0 vs 1); `'0'` is truthy but `'0' == false` is true; `!!'false'` is true; `new Boolean(false)` is truthy.
n342.f: Why should you avoid `x == true` in conditions?
n342.c:
Boolean([]);     // true
[] == true;      // false
'0' == false;    // true
!!new Boolean(false); // true

n343.a: Tests +0 and -0: `0 === -0` is true but `Object.is(0, -0)` is false; `1 / -0` is -Infinity; `-0` prints as 0 via String but `Object.is` or `1/x` reveals it; `Math.round(-0.4)` gives -0; JSON.stringify(-0) is '0'.
p: Sets/Maps treat them as the same

n344.a: Tests equality algorithms: `==` (loose, coercion), `===` (strict; NaN ≠ NaN, +0 = -0), `Object.is` (SameValue; NaN equals NaN, +0 ≠ -0), and SameValueZero used by includes, Map and Set (NaN equals NaN, +0 = -0).
n344.c:
[NaN].includes(NaN);   // true
Object.is(NaN, NaN);   // true
NaN === NaN;           // false
new Set([0, -0]).size; // 1

n345.a: Tests Promise.all ordering and rejection: results are in input order even if later promises settle first; with a rejection, the then handler is skipped and catch gets the first rejection reason; values passed directly are included as-is.
n345.f: How would you get all results even if some fail?

n346.a: Tests Math.min/Math.max edge cases with arguments: `Math.min()` is Infinity, `Math.max()` is -Infinity (identity values for reductions); string numbers are coerced; null is 0; undefined is NaN; arrays must be spread.
n346.f: Why might spreading a huge array into Math.max fail?
n346.c:
Math.min();                // Infinity
Math.max(null, -1);        // 0
Math.min(1, undefined);    // NaN
Math.max(...[1, 5, 3]);    // 5

n347.a: Tests basic array behaviours: `typeof []` is 'object'; arrays compare by reference (`[] === []` false); `[1, 2, 3] + ''` is '1,2,3'; `new Array(3)` creates 3 holes while `new Array(3, 4)` creates [3, 4]; `Array(3).map(...)` does nothing on holes.
p: Array constructor quirk with one number
n347.c:
new Array(3).length;     // 3 (holes)
new Array(3, 4);         // [3, 4]
Array(3).map(() => 1);   // [empty × 3]
Array.from({ length: 3 }, () => 1); // [1, 1, 1]

n348.a: Tests names of function expressions: in a named function expression, the name is a read-only binding visible only inside the function body; reassigning it inside silently fails (sloppy) and outside the name is undefined. The variable holding it can have a different name.
p: Name scoped to the function itself
n348.f: Why use a named expression for recursion instead of the variable?

n349.a: Tests `this` basics: in a method call `obj.fn()` this is obj; in a standalone call it's undefined (strict) or globalThis; arrow functions inside methods inherit; nested object property access uses the immediate owner (`a.b.fn()` → this is a.b).
p: Nested access uses the last object
n349.f: What changes if fn is an arrow function?
n349.c:
const a = { name: 'a', b: { name: 'b', fn() { return this.name; } } };
a.b.fn(); // 'b'

n350.a: Tests Promise executor exceptions and async code inside: a synchronous throw inside the executor rejects the promise, but a throw inside a setTimeout within the executor is not caught (it's an uncaught error) and the promise stays pending unless resolved/rejected explicitly.
n350.f: How would you correctly reject from inside the timeout?
n350.c:
new Promise(() => { throw new Error('sync'); }).catch(e => console.log('caught', e.message));
new Promise(() => { setTimeout(() => { throw new Error('async'); }); }); // uncaught, promise pending forever

n351.a: Tests `reduce` details: without an initial value it uses the first element as the accumulator and starts at index 1; on an empty array without an initial value it throws TypeError; holes are skipped; the callback receives (acc, value, index, array).
p: Without it, first element is the start
Always provide an initial value for safety
n351.f: What's the difference between reduce and reduceRight?
n351.c:
[1, 2, 3].reduce((a, b) => a + b);    // 6
[].reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0);        // 0
[].reduce((a, b) => a + b);           // TypeError

n352.a: Tests parseInt basics: it parses leading digits and stops at the first invalid character ('12px' → 12), ignores leading whitespace, returns NaN if the first character is invalid, treats '0x' as hexadecimal, and truncates decimals ('3.9' → 3).

n353.a: Tests instanceof basics: it checks the prototype chain, so instances are instances of their class and all ancestors including Object; functions are instances of Function and Object; `Object.create(null)` objects aren't instances of Object; primitives return false.
n353.f: How would you check a value is a plain object?

n354.a: Tests addition vs unary plus: binary `+` concatenates when either operand (after ToPrimitive) is a string; unary `+` always converts to number. So `'1' + 1` is '11', `+'1' + 1` is 2, `1 + + '1'` is 2, `'1' - - '1'` is 2.
p: Mixed expressions evaluated left to right

n355.a: Tests operator precedence and associativity: `**` is right-associative (`2 ** 3 ** 2` = 512); unary minus before `**` is a SyntaxError without parentheses; comparison chains like `3 > 2 > 1` evaluate left to right (true > 1 → 1 > 1 → false); `1 < 2 < 3` is true for the same reason.
n355.f: How do you write a correct range check?

n356.a: Tests the `arguments` object: it's array-like (not an array), reflects the passed arguments (not defaults), and in sloppy mode with simple parameters it's linked to named parameters (changing one changes the other); in strict mode or with default/rest params, it's not linked. Arrow functions don't have it.
n356.f: How do you convert arguments to a real array?

n357.a: Tests coercion in string concatenation and comparisons with null/undefined: `null + ''` is 'null', `undefined + ''` is 'undefined', `[null] + ''` is '' (array join converts null to empty), `[undefined] == ''` is true, `{} + 'x'` in an expression is '[object Object]x'.
n357.f: Why do arrays treat null and undefined as empty strings?

n358.a: Tests basic equality: `==` converts types (`1 == '1'` true, `0 == false` true, `null == undefined` true), `===` doesn't (`1 === '1'` false); objects compare by identity in both; NaN equals nothing.
n358.f: Name the one common idiom where == is preferred.

n359.a: Tests null vs undefined: `typeof null` is 'object', `typeof undefined` is 'undefined'; `null == undefined` true but `===` false; `null + 1` is 1 while `undefined + 1` is NaN; JSON keeps null but drops undefined; default parameters apply to undefined only.
n359.f: When should an API use null rather than undefined?
n359.c:
null + 1;        // 1
undefined + 1;   // NaN
JSON.stringify({ a: null, b: undefined }); // '{"a":null}'

n360.a: Tests implicit coercion basics: `'2' * '3'` is 6, `'2' + 3` is '23', `true + 1` is 2, `[] + 1` is '1', `{} + 1` in an expression is '[object Object]1', `'b' - 1` is NaN.

n361.a: Tests increment operators with coercion: `++` converts its operand to a number first, so `let s = '1'; s++` makes s 2 (number) and returns 1; `let x = null; x++` gives x = 1; incrementing undefined gives NaN; `++` on a const throws.
n361.f: Why is old a number and not '1'?

n362.a: Tests arrow functions basics: object literals must be wrapped in parentheses (`() => ({ a: 1 })`) or braces are parsed as a block (returning undefined); single-expression bodies return implicitly; `this` is lexical.
n362.f: Why isn't `() => { value: 1 }` a syntax error?
n362.c:
const a = () => { value: 1 };   // returns undefined (label + expression)
const b = () => ({ value: 1 }); // returns { value: 1 }

n363.a: Tests scope resolution: an identifier resolves to the nearest enclosing scope where it's declared (lexical scoping), regardless of where the function is called; inner declarations shadow outer ones.
n363.f: What would dynamic scoping return here?

n364.a: Tests then callbacks with non-function arguments and return values: non-function arguments to then are ignored (value passes through); returning a value passes it to the next then; throwing passes to the next catch; catch returning a value continues the chain resolved.
p: Throws go to the next catch
n364.f: Why does then(2) not change the value?

n365.a: Tests promise executor synchronicity: the executor function runs immediately when the promise is created, so its synchronous logs appear before code after the constructor; only then/catch callbacks are async.
p: Logs order: executor, sync code, thens
n365.f: Is anything asynchronous about resolve() itself?

n366.a: Tests a classic event loop order mixing sync logs, setTimeout, Promise.then and async functions: sync code first (including promise executors and async function bodies up to the first await), then microtasks (then callbacks and await continuations in queue order), then timers.
p: Async body runs until first await
Order of queueing determines order within a queue
n366.f: Why does 'after await' come before 'then' here?

n1101.a: Loop from 1 to 100; check divisibility by 15 first (both 3 and 5), then 3, then 5, else print the number.
p: Building the string avoids ordering issues
n1101.f: How would you make the rules configurable?

n100.a: `_.partial(fn, ...args)` returns a function with some arguments pre-filled; placeholders (`_.partial.placeholder`) mark positions to fill later. Replace placeholders with incoming args in order, then append the rest.
n100.f: How does bind differ from partial with placeholders?

n104.a: Wrap localStorage so each item is stored with an expiry timestamp; `getItem` returns null and removes the entry when expired.
p: Optional: no expiry when maxAge missing
n104.f: How would you clean up expired items proactively?

n105.a: Implement a `document.myCookie` getter/setter that mimics cookies with `max-age` support: setting parses "name=value; max-age=N", storing value and expiry; getting returns "a=1; b=2" for non-expired entries.
n105.f: How would max-age=0 delete a cookie in your implementation?

n106.a: For "HH:mm", minute hand angle = 6 × minutes; hour hand angle = 30 × (hour % 12) + 0.5 × minutes. The angle is the absolute difference, taking the smaller one (≤ 180) and rounding.
p: Hour hand: 30° per hour + 0.5° per minute
n106.f: At what times do the hands overlap?

n107.a: `_.chunk(arr, size)` splits an array into groups of `size`; the last group holds the remainder. Size < 1 returns [].
n107.f: How would you chunk a stream lazily with a generator?

n108.a: LazyMan(name, log) logs a greeting and supports chained `eat(food)`, `sleep(sec)` and `sleepFirst(sec)`. Queue tasks, schedule execution with setTimeout(0) so all chained calls register first; sleepFirst goes to the front of the queue.

n113.a: `classNames(...args)` joins truthy class names: strings and numbers are included, objects contribute keys with truthy values, arrays are flattened recursively; falsy values ignored.
n113.f: How would you dedupe repeated class names?

n115.a: `finally(cb)` runs cb on fulfillment or rejection, waits for its returned promise, then passes through the original value or reason (unless cb throws).
p: Wait for cb's result via Promise.resolve
n115.f: Why does cb receive no arguments?

n116.a: memoizeOne caches only the most recent call: if called with the same `this` and arguments (shallow equality, or a custom isEqual) as last time, return the cached result.
n116.f: Why is caching only one result often enough for UI?

n117.a: The "look-and-say" sequence: '1', '11', '21', '1211', '111221'... each term describes the previous one (counts of consecutive digits). Generate the nth term by iterating and run-length encoding.
n117.f: Why does the sequence never contain digits above 3?

n119.a: Tokenize an arithmetic expression string (e.g. ' 1 * (20 - 300 ) ') into tokens: numbers, operators and parentheses, skipping whitespace. A generator yielding tokens works well.
n119.f: How would you evaluate the tokens next?

n120.a: Implement `createElement(type, props, ...children)` returning a virtual node, and `render(vnode)` that converts it into real DOM, handling text children, className and nested elements.
n120.f: How would you handle event props like onClick?

n122.a: `Object.is` is like === except NaN equals NaN and +0 doesn't equal -0. Detect -0 via 1/x and NaN via x !== x.
n122.f: Where does SameValue matter in practice?

n123.a: Divide two (possibly negative) integer strings, truncating toward zero, without BigInt: long division digit by digit, using string subtraction/comparison to compute each quotient digit.
n123.f: How would you return the remainder as well?

n124.a: Multiply two integer strings (with signs) using grade-school multiplication: multiply each digit pair into a result array at position i + j + 1, carrying as you go, then strip leading zeros.
p: Result array of length m + n
n124.f: What's Karatsuba multiplication and when does it help?

n133.a: Return the first character that appears more than once (the earliest second occurrence), or null. Scan once with a Set.
n133.f: How would you find the first non-repeating character instead?

n137.a: Wrap a `getAPI(path, config)` so identical concurrent/recent calls (same path and config) share one promise: cache by a stable key (path + sorted-key JSON of config) for a short period (e.g. 1s), and clear the cache when needed.
p: Cache the promise, not the result
n137.f: Why should failed requests be evicted?

n139.a: Extract all `...` element strings from an HTML string. A regex works for this exercise (case-insensitive, tolerant of attributes); in real code use DOMParser.
n139.f: Why is regex parsing of HTML fragile in general?

n140.a: Validate IPv4 (four decimal parts 0–255, no leading zeros) and IPv6 (eight groups of 1–4 hex digits, here without the :: shorthand).
n140.f: How would you support the IPv6 :: shorthand?

n141.a: Compress runs of repeated characters into char + count ('aaab' → 'a3b'), leaving single characters without a count.
n141.c:
const compress = s => s.replace(/(.)\1*/g, run => run[0] + (run.length > 1 ? run.length : ''));
compress('aaabba'); // 'a3b2a'

n142.a: Count the number of 1 bits in an integer's binary form. Brian Kernighan's trick: `n &= n - 1` clears the lowest set bit each iteration; count iterations. For large numbers beyond 32 bits, use division.
n142.f: How would you count bits for numbers above 2^32?

n143.a: Remove leading and trailing whitespace: find the first and last non-whitespace indexes and slice, or use a regex.

n144.a: `Object.create(proto)` creates an object whose prototype is proto. Implement with a temporary constructor whose prototype is proto; throw TypeError if proto isn't an object or null.
n144.f: Why can't this approach create a null-prototype object?

n145.a: Return the nth Fibonacci number using recursion; add memoization so it's O(n) instead of O(2^n).
n145.f: How would you avoid stack overflow for large n?

n146.a: `throttlePromises(funcs, max)` runs promise-returning functions with at most `max` in flight, resolving with results in order (rejecting on first error).
n146.f: How would you make it return allSettled-style results?

n148.a: `myInstanceOf(obj, Ctor)` walks obj's prototype chain checking for `Ctor.prototype`; primitives return false.

n150.a: Wrap an array in a Proxy so negative indexes count from the end (arr[-1] is the last element), for both get and set, while normal operations keep working on the original array.
n150.f: Why do proxy keys arrive as strings?

n153.a: `_.get(obj, path, defaultValue)` reads a nested value by a path string ('a.b[0].c') or array, returning defaultValue if any segment is missing (undefined).
p: Return default when result is undefined
n153.f: Why check undefined rather than falsy for the default?

n154.a: A fake timer for setInterval: replace global setInterval/clearInterval and Date.now with versions driven by a virtual clock; `tick()` advances time and runs due callbacks in order, rescheduling intervals.
p: Queue of { id, at, fn, interval }
tick advances and runs due timers
n154.f: Why do intervals need a time limit when ticking?

n155.a: Create `mySetInterval(fn, delay, period)` where each next call waits `delay + period * count` (an increasing interval), plus `myClearInterval(id)`. Use chained setTimeouts and map our ID to the current timeout.
n155.f: Why use chained setTimeout instead of setInterval here?

n158.a: Implement URLSearchParams: parse a query string (with or without '?') into ordered key/value pairs with decoding ('+' as space), and support get, getAll, has, set, append, delete, sort, forEach, keys/values/entries and toString.
p: Store an ordered list of pairs

n159.a: Convert snake_case to camelCase: replace an underscore followed by a letter with the uppercase letter, but keep leading/trailing underscores and double underscores unchanged.
n159.f: Why does the lookbehind-free regex need overlapping care for 'a_b_c'?

n160.a: Convert a HEX color (#RGB, #RGBA, #RRGGBB, #RRGGBBAA) to an 'rgba(r,g,b,a)' string: expand shorthand, parse pairs as hex, alpha divided by 255 (rounded), and throw on invalid input.
n160.f: How would you convert back from rgba to hex?

n161.a: Subtract two signed integer strings without BigInt: rewrite a − b as a + (−b) and reuse signed addition (which handles mixed signs via magnitude comparison and subtraction).
n161.f: What are the cases a signed add must handle?
n161.c: function subtract(a, b) { return add(a, b.startsWith('-') ? b.slice(1) : '-' + b); } // add() from the signed addition problem

n162.a: Add two signed integer strings: if signs match, add magnitudes and keep the sign; otherwise subtract the smaller magnitude from the larger and take the larger's sign. Normalize '-0' to '0'.
n162.f: How would you test these functions thoroughly?

n164.a: Implement Observable operators like `map` and `filter` (and others) as functions returning a new Observable that subscribes to the source and forwards transformed values, propagating errors and completion.
p: Operator returns a function source → new Observable
n164.f: How would you implement pipe() for these operators?

n165.a: `fromEvent(element, eventName, capture)` returns an Observable that adds an event listener on subscribe and removes it on unsubscribe, emitting each event.

n166.a: `interval(period)` returns an Observable emitting 0, 1, 2... every period ms, clearing the interval on unsubscribe.
n166.f: How is a cold observable different from a hot one here?

n167.a: A Subject is both an Observable and an Observer: it keeps a list of subscribers and multicasts next/error/complete to all of them.
n167.f: What do BehaviorSubject and ReplaySubject add?

n168.a: `Observable.from(input)` creates an Observable from an Observable, array, array-like, iterable or promise: emit each item then complete, or the promise's value then complete (error on rejection).
n168.f: Why wrap the iteration in try/catch?

n169.a: Deep equality for plain objects and arrays: same type, same keys and recursively equal values; handle primitives with Object.is semantics (or ===), and circular references with a WeakMap of compared pairs.
n169.f: How would you extend it to Dates, Maps and Sets?

n171.a: Implement a Promise: states (pending/fulfilled/rejected), executor run synchronously, resolve handling thenables (adoption), then returning a new promise with callbacks run as microtasks, catch, finally and static resolve/reject.
p: then returns new promise; handle thenable results
n171.f: Why must then callbacks always run asynchronously?

n173.a: Format a number with thousands separators: split integer and decimal parts, insert commas every three digits from the right in the integer part, keep sign and decimals.
n173.f: Why is Intl.NumberFormat better for real apps?

n174.a: `fetchWithAutoRetry(fetcher, maximumRetryCount)` calls fetcher and, on rejection, retries up to the max number of times, rejecting with the last error.
p: Only retry retryable errors in production
n174.f: How would you add exponential backoff with jitter?

n175.a: Deep clone plain objects and arrays (and primitives), preserving circular references with a WeakMap, copying symbol keys and prototypes as needed.
n175.f: When is structuredClone the better choice?

n177.a: Implement `Function.prototype.mycall(thisArg, ...args)`: temporarily attach the function to thisArg (boxed with Object(), defaulting to globalThis) under a unique Symbol key, call it, then delete the key.
n177.f: How else could you implement it without mutating thisArg?

n178.a: `myNew(Ctor, ...args)` emulates `new`: create an object linked to Ctor.prototype, call Ctor with it as this, return the result if it's an object (or function), otherwise the new object.
n178.f: How does Reflect.construct let you handle classes?

n179.a: BrowserHistory with `visit(url)`, `goBack()`, `forward()` and `current`: keep an array and an index; visiting truncates forward history.
p: Array of URLs and current index
Back/forward move the index within bounds
n179.f: How does this mirror the real History API?

n181.a: An Observable wraps a subscriber function; subscribe accepts a function or observer object, returns a subscription with unsubscribe; after error/complete/unsubscribe no more values are delivered, and the teardown runs.
n181.f: Why run the teardown immediately if the setup completed synchronously?

n182.a: Given a paginated API `fetchList(since?)` returning `{ items }` (oldest last), fetch up to `amount` items by repeatedly calling with the last item's id as cursor until enough items or an empty page.
p: Stop on empty page or enough items
n182.f: How would you write it as an async iterator?

n184.a: A thunk is a function taking a callback `(error, result) => {}`; a thunk may return another thunk as its result. `flattenThunk(thunk)` returns a thunk that keeps calling returned thunks until a non-function result, forwarding errors.
n184.f: How does this relate to promise adoption?

n185.a: `myExtends(SuperType, SubType)` returns a constructor that calls both constructors on the instance and sets up prototypes so instances inherit from SubType.prototype then SuperType.prototype, plus static inheritance.
p: Call SuperType then SubType with this
n185.f: What's the ES5 way of linking prototypes without setPrototypeOf?

n186.a: A middleware system: `use(fn)` registers middlewares `(req, next)` or error handlers `(error, req, next)`; `start(req)` runs them in order. Calling `next()` proceeds; calling `next(error)` or throwing skips to the next error handler.
p: Errors go to handlers that take three arguments
n186.f: How does Express distinguish error middleware?

n190.a: `once(fn)` returns a function that calls fn only the first time and returns the cached result afterwards.
n190.f: Should a failed (throwing) first call count as called?

n197.a: `range(from, to)` returns an iterable of integers from..to inclusive, usable with for...of and spread. A generator is simplest.
n197.f: How would you make it an object with Symbol.iterator instead?
n197.c:
function* range(from, to) { for (let i = from; i <= to; i++) yield i; }
[...range(1, 4)]; // [1, 2, 3, 4]

n198.a: `spyOn(obj, methodName)` replaces the method with a wrapper that records calls (arguments) and calls the original, returning a spy with `calls`.

n200.a: A fake timer for setTimeout: install replaces setTimeout, clearTimeout and Date.now with a virtual clock; `tick()` runs all pending timers in order of their scheduled time (and creation order for ties), advancing the clock, including timers created during the tick.
p: Queue sorted by time then id
n200.f: Why sort by id for equal times?

n201.a: `Promise.race(promises)` settles with the first promise to settle, fulfilled or rejected. Wrap each value with Promise.resolve and attach resolve/reject; later settlements are ignored.
n201.f: How would you implement a timeout with race?

n202.a: `Promise.any(promises)` resolves with the first fulfilled value; if all reject, it rejects with an AggregateError containing all reasons (in input order). Empty input rejects immediately.
n202.f: When would you use any instead of race?

n203.a: `Promise.allSettled(promises)` waits for all and resolves with `{ status, value }` / `{ status, reason }` objects in input order; never rejects.
n203.f: How would you write it using Promise.all?

n204.a: `Promise.all(promises)` resolves with an array of values in input order once all fulfil, rejects on the first rejection; empty input resolves to [].
n204.f: Why count completions instead of checking out.length?

n205.a: Async helper `race(funcs)`: funcs are callback-style async functions `(callback, data)`; return a function that runs all with the same data and calls the final callback with the first one that finishes (error or result), ignoring the rest.
n205.f: How would you convert these helpers to promises?

n206.a: Async helper `parallel(funcs)`: run all callback-style functions with the same data at once; call the final callback with an array of results in order when all finish, or with the first error (only once).

n207.a: Async helper `sequence(funcs)`: run callback-style functions one after another, passing each result as the next function's data; stop on the first error.

n208.a: `clearAllTimeout()` cancels all timers created with setTimeout. Wrap setTimeout to record IDs in a Set (removing them when they fire or are cleared), then clear them all.
n208.f: What are the risks of monkey-patching globals?

n209.a: `completeAssign(target, ...sources)` copies the property descriptors of enumerable own string and symbol keys (so getters and setters are kept) rather than values, unlike Object.assign which invokes getters.
n209.f: Why does Object.assign flatten getters into values?

n210.a: `Object.assign(target, ...sources)` copies own enumerable string and symbol properties from sources to target using assignment (so setters on target run, and a non-writable target property throws), skipping null/undefined sources.
n210.f: What happens when assigning to a frozen target?

n213.a: `sum(1)(2)(3) == 6`: return a function that accumulates and override valueOf (or Symbol.toPrimitive) so comparisons and arithmetic yield the running total.
p: Each call returns a new function

n214.a: Implement JSON.parse with a recursive descent parser: parse values (object, array, string with escapes, number, true/false/null), skipping whitespace, and throw on invalid syntax or trailing characters.
n214.f: How would you add support for a reviver function?

n215.a: Implement JSON.stringify for primitives, arrays and plain objects: strings quoted and escaped, NaN/Infinity → null, undefined/functions/symbols omitted in objects and null in arrays, toJSON honoured, Dates via toJSON, BigInt throws.
n215.f: How would you detect circular references?

n216.a: `detectType(value)` returns a precise lowercase type: 'null', 'array', 'date', 'map', 'set', 'arraybuffer', 'function', 'number', etc. Use typeof for primitives and functions, and Object.prototype.toString for objects (falling back to 'object' for custom classes).
p: Boxed primitives map to primitive names
n216.f: How can Symbol.toStringTag spoof this check?

n218.a: The "Improve a function" problem: an `excludeItems(items, excludes)` filter that loops over excludes for every item is O(n·m). Precompute a Map of key → Set of excluded values so each item check is O(k) (number of keys).
n218.f: How do you explain the complexity improvement in an interview?

n222.a: `memo(fn, resolver)` caches results by key: default key is the arguments joined (or the first argument); a resolver can compute custom keys. Store results in a Map, and preserve `this`.

n223.a: An immutability helper `update(data, command)` like React's legacy helper: commands `$push`, `$set`, `$merge`, `$apply` applied at nested paths, returning new objects along the changed path and sharing unchanged parts.
p: Recursive descent through the command object

n224.a: `pipe(funcs)` composes functions left to right: the output of each is the input of the next. Use reduce over the functions starting with the input.
n224.f: How would you support async functions in a pipe?
n224.c:
const pipe = funcs => input => funcs.reduce((acc, fn) => fn(acc), input);
pipe([x => x + 1, x => x * 2])(3); // 8

n226.a: Decode a message hidden in a 2D character grid: start at top-left, move diagonally down-right; when hitting the bottom edge, switch to up-right, bouncing between edges until reaching the last column; collect characters.
n226.f: How would you encode a message into such a grid?

n227.a: Shuffle an array uniformly in place with the Fisher–Yates algorithm: iterate from the end, swapping each element with a random index ≤ current.
n227.f: How would you test that a shuffle is uniform?

n228.a: Debounce with options `{ leading, trailing }`: leading calls immediately when no timer is pending; trailing calls with the latest args after the wait if there were calls during the wait (and not already handled by leading).
p: Leading fires on first call of a burst
Avoid double call when only one call happened
n228.f: What happens with both leading and trailing false?

n229.a: Basic debounce: delay calling func until `wait` ms have passed since the last call, using the latest arguments and this.
n229.f: How would you add a flush method?

n230.a: Throttle with `{ leading, trailing }`: with leading, call immediately at the start of a window; during the window, store the latest args; at the end, if trailing and there are stored args, call with them and start a new window.
p: Trailing call at window end starts new window
n230.f: Why restart the timer after a trailing call?

n231.a: Basic throttle: call func immediately, then ignore calls during the next `wait` ms, but remember the latest call and run it when the window ends (trailing), starting a new window.
n231.f: When would you prefer throttle over debounce for a resize handler?

n232.a: `flat(arr, depth = 1)` flattens nested arrays up to depth levels, skipping holes like the native method.
n232.f: How would you implement it iteratively?

n233.a: Curry with placeholders: arguments equal to `curry.placeholder` reserve positions to be filled by later calls; call the function once the first fn.length arguments are all non-placeholders.
p: Merge new args into placeholder slots
Check first n args for placeholders
n233.f: Why must the completeness check look only at the first fn.length args?

n234.a: `curry(fn)` returns a function that collects arguments across calls until it has fn.length of them, then calls fn.
n234.f: Why does curry struggle with functions using default parameters?

n572.a: Flatten a nested array of any depth into a single-level array, without using Array.prototype.flat.
n572.f: What's the time cost of shift/unshift here and how could you avoid it?

n573.a: Debounce delays invoking a function until `wait` ms have passed since the last call; each call resets the timer. Keep `this` and the latest arguments.
n573.f: Why does using an arrow function inside setTimeout preserve this?

n574.a: Debounce II adds `cancel()` (drop the pending call) and `flush()` (run the pending call immediately) methods.
n574.f: When is flush useful (e.g. before page unload)?

n576.a: Implement `Array.prototype.myFilter(callback, thisArg)`: return a new array of elements for which the callback returns truthy, skipping holes, passing (value, index, array) and thisArg.

n577.a: Classnames II: like classNames but with deduplication and support for falsy overrides — later arguments can turn off earlier classes (`{ foo: false }` removes 'foo'), and functions/nested arrays are handled. Collect into an ordered Set, adding or deleting as you go.
p: Objects add or delete per value

n580.a: Throttle ensures func runs at most once per `wait` ms: call immediately if not throttled, then ignore calls until the timer expires.
n580.f: What calls are lost with this leading-only version?

n581.a: `mapAsync(iterable, callbackFn)` applies an async callback to each item in parallel and resolves with results in order; rejects if any rejects.
n581.f: How would you limit the concurrency?
n581.c: const mapAsync = (iterable, callbackFn) => Promise.all(Array.from(iterable, x => callbackFn(x)));

n582.a: EventEmitter with `on(event, listener)`, `off(event, listener)` and `emit(event, ...args)`: store listeners per event in arrays (allowing duplicates), off removes one occurrence, emit calls a copy of the list and returns whether any listeners existed; on/off return this for chaining.
n582.f: Why iterate over a copy during emit?

n584.a: Deep clone JSON-serializable values (objects, arrays, primitives) recursively so nested structures are independent copies.

n587.a: `setCancellableInterval(callback, delay, ...args)` behaves like setInterval but returns a function that cancels it.
n587.f: How would you do the same with AbortSignal?

n589.a: A Backbone-like Model: stores attributes, `get(attr)`, `set(attr, value)` emitting 'change' events with (attr, newValue, oldValue) only when the value changes, `has`, `unset` (emits 'unset'), and `on/off` for subscriptions.
p: set emits change only when different
n589.f: How do modern state libraries differ from this pattern?

n590.a: `listFormat(items, { sorted, length, unique })` formats a list like 'a, b and c': filter empty strings, optionally dedupe and sort, optionally show only `length` items followed by 'and N other(s)'.
n590.f: How does Intl.ListFormat handle this natively?

n591.a: `mapAsyncLimit(iterable, callbackFn, size)` maps items with an async callback with at most `size` running concurrently, preserving result order; rejects on the first error.
n591.f: Why is next++ safe here without locks?

n593.a: `compose(...fns)` returns a function that applies functions right to left: compose(f, g)(x) = f(g(x)). With no functions it returns the identity.
n593.f: Why do Redux enhancers use compose?
n593.c:
const compose = (...fns) => x => fns.reduceRight((acc, fn) => fn(acc), x);
compose(x => x + 1, x => x * 2)(3); // 7

n595.a: `selectData(sessions, { user, minDuration, merge })` filters an array of session records by user and minimum duration; with merge, combine sessions of the same user (sum durations, union equipment sorted) keeping the order of most recent occurrence, then apply filters.
p: Then filter by user and minDuration

n596.a: Type utilities: `isBoolean`, `isNumber`, `isNull`, `isString`, `isSymbol`, `isUndefined` checking primitive types precisely with typeof/strict equality.

n597.a: `deepOmit(obj, keys)` removes the given keys at every level of a nested structure of objects and arrays, returning a new value.
p: Recurse into arrays and plain objects
n597.f: Why check for arrays before objects?

n599.a: Promisify II: like promisify, but if the function has a custom promisified version under `Symbol.for('util.promisify.custom')`, return that instead; otherwise convert `(err, value)` callback style to a promise.
n599.f: Why do some Node APIs need custom promisified versions?

n601.a: `memoize(func)` caches results of a single-argument function keyed by that argument in a Map, preserving this.
n601.f: How would you add an LRU size limit?

n602.a: `squashObject(obj)` flattens a nested object into one level with dot-separated keys; arrays use their indexes as keys; empty keys are skipped in the path.
p: Arrays treated as objects with index keys
n602.f: What happens to empty nested objects?

n603.a: `unsquashObject(obj)` reverses squashObject: split each dot-separated key and build nested objects, creating arrays when the next segment is a numeric index (or objects in a simple version).
n603.f: How would you handle conflicting keys like 'a' and 'a.b'?

n607.a: JSON.stringify II: also handle cycles (throw TypeError), nested toJSON, and the rules for undefined/functions/symbols, NaN/Infinity, Dates, and keys order. Track ancestors in a stack to detect circular structures.
p: Cycle detection with a Set of ancestors
n607.f: Why remove the value from the stack after serializing it?

n608.a: `promiseMerge(p1, p2)` resolves with the merged result of two promises: numbers are added, strings concatenated, arrays concatenated, plain objects shallow-merged; mismatched types reject with 'Unsupported data types'; any rejection rejects.
n608.f: Should rejecting with a string or an Error be preferred?

n61.a: An AsyncTaskQueue runs async tasks with a concurrency limit: `add(task)` enqueues a function returning a promise and returns a promise for its result; the queue starts tasks while running < limit and starts the next when one finishes.
n61.f: How would you add priorities or cancellation?

n610.a: `clamp(number, lower, upper)` restricts a number to the inclusive range.
n610.f: Where is clamp handy in UI code?
n610.c: const clamp = (number, lower, upper) => Math.min(upper, Math.max(lower, number));

n611.a: `functionLength(fn)` returns the number of parameters a function expects — simply `fn.length`, which counts parameters before the first default or rest parameter.
n611.f: Why is length unreliable for curry in some cases?
n611.c:
const functionLength = fn => fn.length;
functionLength((a, b = 1, c) => {}); // 1

n612.a: `makeCounter(initialValue = 0)` returns a function that returns the current value then increments it on each call (closure state).
n612.f: How would you add reset and decrement?

n613.a: `mean(array)` returns the average of numbers, NaN for an empty array.
n613.f: How would you compute a running mean without storing all values?
n613.c: const mean = array => array.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0) / array.length;

n614.a: `numberOfArguments(...args)` returns how many arguments were passed — use rest parameters and return their length.
n614.f: How is this different from fn.length?

n615.a: `sleep(duration)` returns a promise that resolves after duration ms, used with await to pause async functions.
n615.f: How is this different from a busy-wait loop?
n615.c: const sleep = duration => new Promise(resolve => setTimeout(resolve, duration));

n616.a: `Array.prototype.square()` returns a new array with each element squared.
n616.f: Why is extending Array.prototype discouraged in production?
n616.c:
Array.prototype.square = function () { return this.map(x => x * x); };
[1, 2, 3].square(); // [1, 4, 9]

n617.a: `setCancellableTimeout(callback, delay, ...args)` behaves like setTimeout but returns a cancel function.
n617.f: Why do APIs often return disposer functions?

n618.a: `compact(array)` removes falsy values (false, null, 0, '', undefined, NaN) from an array.
n618.f: What if you want to keep 0?

n619.a: `difference(array, values)` returns elements of array not present in values (SameValueZero), preserving order.
n619.f: How would you implement differenceBy with an iteratee?

n62.a: Parse Twitter-style mentions: find `@username` tokens in text where usernames are alphanumeric/underscore and the @ isn't part of an email (preceded by start or a non-word character). Return usernames or render links.
n62.f: How would you render mentions as links safely?
n62.c:
const mentions = text => [...text.matchAll(/(?<![\w@])@(\w{1,15})/g)].map(m => m[1]);
mentions('hi @ana and @bo_b, mail me a@b.com'); // ['ana', 'bo_b']

n620.a: `dropRightWhile(array, predicate)` removes elements from the end while the predicate returns truthy.
n620.f: How does this differ from filter?

n621.a: `dropWhile(array, predicate)` removes elements from the start while the predicate returns truthy.

n622.a: `fill(array, value, start = 0, end = array.length)` mutates elements from start up to (not including) end with value, supporting negative indexes.
n622.f: Why is `new Array(3).fill([])` a common bug?

n623.a: `findIndex(array, predicate, fromIndex = 0)` returns the first index where predicate is truthy, starting at fromIndex (negative counts from end), or -1.
n623.f: How do find and findIndex treat holes?

n624.a: `findLastIndex(array, predicate, fromIndex = array.length - 1)` searches backwards from fromIndex (negative supported, clamped) and returns the index or -1.
p: Return first match from the end
n624.f: When is searching from the end useful?

n625.a: `fromPairs(pairs)` turns an array of [key, value] pairs into an object (later pairs override earlier ones).
n625.c: const fromPairs = pairs => { const obj = {}; for (const [k, v] of pairs) obj[k] = v; return obj; };

n626.a: Implement `Function.prototype.myApply(thisArg, argArray)`: call the function with thisArg and arguments from an array (or array-like); null/undefined args mean no arguments.
p: Use call with spread or a temporary property
n626.f: How would you implement it without using call?

n627.a: Implement `Function.prototype.myCall(thisArg, ...args)` — e.g. via bind (`this.bind(thisArg)(...args)`) or by temporarily attaching the function to the object with a Symbol key.
n627.f: What's the difference between this and the Symbol approach for primitives?

n628.a: `intersection(...arrays)` returns unique values present in every array, in the order of the first array.
n628.f: How would you optimize by starting from the smallest array?

n629.a: `maxBy(array, iteratee)` returns the element whose iteratee value is largest (first one on ties), ignoring elements where iteratee returns null/undefined.

n63.a: `Object.groupBy(items, callback)` groups items into a null-prototype object keyed by the callback's return value (converted to a property key), preserving item order within groups.

n630.a: `minBy(array, iteratee)` returns the element with the smallest iteratee value, skipping null/undefined values, first on ties.
n630.f: How would you support a property-name shorthand iteratee?

n631.a: `mapObject(obj, fn)` returns a new object with the same keys and values transformed by fn(value, key, obj), with `this` inside fn bound to the object.
n631.f: How would you map keys instead of values?

n632.a: `promiseReject(reason)` returns a promise rejected with reason (without unwrapping thenables).
p: Attach catch to avoid unhandled rejections
n632.f: Why doesn't Promise.reject unwrap a promise reason?
n632.c: const promiseReject = reason => new Promise((_, reject) => reject(reason));

n633.a: `rangeRight(start = 0, end, step = 1)` creates numbers from start up to (not including) end, in descending output order (like lodash): if only one argument, it's end with start 0; step sign adjusts; returns reversed range.
n633.f: Why does step 0 need special handling?

n634.a: A Singleton exposes one shared instance: a module-level instance with `getInstance()` that lazily creates it, e.g. a GlobalMap with get/set.
n634.f: How would you reset it in tests?

n635.a: `uniqueArray(array)` returns a duplicate-free version keeping first occurrences.
n635.f: How would you dedupe objects by a key?

n636.a: `Array.prototype.myAt(index)` returns the element at an index, supporting negative indexes from the end; out-of-range → undefined.
n636.f: How does at() differ from bracket access?

n637.a: `Array.prototype.myWith(index, value)` returns a copy of the array with one element replaced (negative index supported), throwing RangeError when out of range.
n637.f: Why are these copying methods useful for React state?

n638.a: `cycle(...values)` returns a function that returns the next value in sequence each call, looping back to the start.
n638.f: How would you implement this with a generator?

n639.a: Implement `Function.prototype.myBind(thisArg, ...boundArgs)`: return a function that calls the original with thisArg and concatenated args; when called with new, ignore thisArg and construct, preserving the prototype.
n639.f: Why should new ignore the bound this?

n64.a: `undefinedToNull(arg)` recursively converts all undefined values in nested objects and arrays to null (e.g. before JSON serialization).
n64.f: Why does JSON.stringify drop undefined object properties?

n641.a: `meanBy(array, iteratee)` returns the mean of iteratee values for each element.
n641.f: How would you support a property-name shorthand?
n641.c: const meanBy = (array, iteratee) => array.reduce((sum, x) => sum + iteratee(x), 0) / array.length;

n642.a: `size(collection)` returns the number of elements: length for arrays and strings, size for Map/Set, number of own enumerable keys for plain objects, 0 for null/undefined/other.
n642.f: How should array-like objects (arguments) be handled?

n643.a: `String.prototype.myRepeat(count)` returns the string repeated count times; throws RangeError for negative or infinite counts. Doubling the string halves iterations.
n643.f: Why is the doubling approach faster?

n644.a: `sum(value)` returns a function that keeps accepting values and returns the total when called with no arguments: sum(1)(2)(3)() === 6.
n644.f: How would you make sum(1)(2) == 3 work without the final call?

n645.a: Type utilities II: `isArray`, `isFunction`, `isObject` (any non-null object or function), and `isPlainObject` (prototype is Object.prototype or null).
n645.f: Why does isPlainObject matter for deep merge?

n649.a: Make Counter II: `makeCounter(initialValue)` returns an object with `get`, `increment`, `decrement` and `reset` methods sharing closure state.
n649.f: How would you implement the same with a class and private fields?

n650.a: `negate(predicate)` returns a function that returns the logical opposite of predicate's result, preserving this and arguments.
n650.f: Why might you prefer negate over writing an inline arrow?
n650.c:
const negate = predicate => function (...args) { return !predicate.apply(this, args); };
[1, 2, 3, 4].filter(negate(n => n % 2 === 0)); // [1, 3]

n651.a: `Array.prototype.myConcat(...items)` returns a new array with the original elements followed by items, spreading array arguments one level (respecting holes) and appending non-arrays as single elements.

n652.a: `countBy(array, iteratee)` returns an object whose keys are iteratee results and values are counts.
n652.f: How would you return a Map instead?

n653.a: `groupBy(array, iteratee)` groups elements into an object keyed by iteratee results, each mapping to an array.
n653.f: How would you support a string iteratee like 'length'?

n654.a: `isEmpty(value)` returns true for null/undefined, empty arrays/strings/array-likes, empty Maps/Sets, and objects without own enumerable keys.

n655.a: `limit(func, n)` returns a function that invokes func at most n times; later calls return the result of the last invocation.
n655.f: How does this relate to once()?

n656.a: `promiseTimeout(promise, duration)` resolves/rejects like the promise if it settles within duration ms, otherwise rejects with 'Promise timeout'; clear the timer once settled.
n656.f: Why doesn't timing out stop the original request?

n657.a: `promiseResolve(value)` returns value if it's a native promise, otherwise a new promise resolved with value (adopting thenables).

n658.a: `promiseWithResolvers()` returns `{ promise, resolve, reject }`, exposing the resolver functions outside the executor.
n658.f: Give a use case for a deferred promise.

n659.a: A Turtle class tracks position and direction on a grid: `forward(n)`, `backward(n)`, `left()` and `right()` turn 90°, and `position()` returns [x, y]. Store direction as an index into a list of vectors.
n659.f: How would you support arbitrary angles?

n660.a: `unionBy(iteratee, ...arrays)` returns unique values across arrays, uniqueness determined by iteratee results, keeping the first occurrence.
p: Track seen iteratee values in a Set
n660.f: How would you implement union without an iteratee?

n67.a: `Math.clz32(x)` counts leading zero bits in the 32-bit unsigned representation of x. Convert with `>>> 0`, then count by shifting, or use the binary string length.

r2.a: React makes UIs predictable and composable: you describe what the UI should look like for a given state and React updates the DOM efficiently. Advantages include reusable components, one-way data flow that's easy to reason about, a huge ecosystem (routing, data fetching, testing), strong tooling (DevTools, TypeScript support), server rendering and Server Components through frameworks, and React Native for mobile.
p: Huge ecosystem, SSR and React Native
r2.f: Which of these advantages matters most for a large team?

r3.a: React is a UI library, not a full framework, so you choose routing, data fetching and state tools yourself (or adopt a framework like Next.js). JSX and the component model have a learning curve, hooks have rules and pitfalls (stale closures, dependency arrays), client-only rendering hurts SEO and initial load without SSR, bundle size can grow, and the ecosystem moves fast.
p: CSR needs SSR for SEO and speed
r3.f: How do frameworks like Next.js address some of these limitations?

n1210.a: `componentDidMount` runs once, right after the component is first inserted into the DOM — used for initial data fetching, subscriptions and DOM measurements. `componentDidUpdate(prevProps, prevState)` runs after every re-render (not the first) — used to react to changes, e.g. refetch when an id prop changes; compare with previous values to avoid infinite loops. In hooks, `useEffect(fn, [])` covers mount and `useEffect(fn, [deps])` covers updates.
p: setState in didUpdate needs a condition
n1210.f: What happens if you call setState unconditionally in componentDidUpdate?

n1211.a: Class lifecycles split logic by time (mount, update, unmount), so related code for one concern (like a subscription) is scattered across methods. `useEffect` groups logic by concern: one effect sets up and returns its own cleanup, re-running when its dependencies change. Effects run after paint (useLayoutEffect runs before paint), capture values from the render they belong to (closures), and in Strict Mode development they mount, unmount and remount to surface missing cleanups. Think "synchronize with external systems" rather than "lifecycle events".
p: Organized by concern, not by lifecycle phase
Each render's effect sees that render's values
n1211.f: Why does React run effects twice in Strict Mode during development?

n1212.a: Use a client-side router (React Router, or the router of a framework like Next.js) that maps URLs to components and updates the URL with the History API without full page reloads. Use `<Link>`/`NavLink` for navigation links, `useNavigate()` for programmatic navigation (after form submit), route params (`useParams`) and search params for state in the URL, nested routes with layouts, redirects and protected routes for auth, lazy-loaded route components for code splitting, and handle 404s, scroll restoration and focus management for accessibility.
p: Code splitting, protected routes, focus/scroll management
n1212.f: Why should you use Link instead of a plain <a> for internal navigation?
n1212.c:
<Routes>
  <Route path="/" element={<Layout />}>
    <Route index element={<Home />} />
    <Route path="users/:id" element={<User />} />
    <Route path="*" element={<NotFound />} />
  </Route>
</Routes>

n1213.a: Thinking declaratively means describing what the UI should look like for each state, rather than writing step-by-step instructions to change the DOM. You identify the visual states (empty, typing, submitting, success, error), decide what state variables drive them, and let React render the right output; event handlers only update state. This removes whole classes of bugs where the DOM gets out of sync, makes components easier to test, and keeps logic in one place.
p: Event handlers update state, not the DOM
n1213.f: How would you model a form's states to avoid impossible combinations?

n1214.a: Keep the minimal state needed and derive the rest during render: if a value can be computed from props or other state (full name, filtered list, counts), don't store it. Group related values that change together, avoid contradictions (use a single status instead of several booleans), avoid redundant and duplicated state (store ids instead of copies), and place state in the closest common parent of the components that use it (lifting state up); use context or a store when many distant components need it, and the URL for shareable state.
p: Single status instead of conflicting booleans
Context, stores or URL for wider sharing
n1214.f: When is it acceptable to store derived data (e.g. for performance)?

n1215.a: Duplicated state (the same object stored in two places) gets out of sync when one copy is updated. Deeply nested state is hard to update immutably because every level must be copied. Normalize it: store entities in flat lookup tables keyed by id (`{ byId: {...}, allIds: [...] }`), refer to related entities by id, and keep selected items as ids. This makes updates simple, avoids inconsistency and is how Redux Toolkit's entity adapter and normalized caches work.
p: Nested updates require copying every level
Selected item = id, not a copy
n1215.f: How does normalization interact with server cache libraries like TanStack Query?

n1216.a: React attaches handlers via props like `onClick` and delegates events at the root, passing a SyntheticEvent that wraps the native event with a consistent cross-browser API. Pass a function, not a call (`onClick={() => remove(id)}` to pass arguments). Use `e.preventDefault()` to stop default behaviour (form submit) and `e.stopPropagation()` to stop bubbling through React's tree; capture-phase handlers use the `Capture` suffix (`onClickCapture`). Events propagate through the React component tree, including through portals.
p: Events bubble through the React tree, even portals
n1216.f: Why do events from a portal bubble to React ancestors but not DOM ancestors?

n1217.a: Keep field values in state (or use uncontrolled inputs with FormData / a library like React Hook Form), with a single `status` ('idle' | 'submitting' | 'success' | 'error'). Validate on blur/submit (required, email format, password rules, matching confirmation) and show errors next to fields linked with `aria-describedby`. On submit: preventDefault, validate, set status to submitting (disable the button), call the API, show success or map server errors to fields, and always reset loading. Use proper labels, input types and autocomplete attributes; with React 19 you can also use form actions and `useActionState`.
p: State for values or uncontrolled + FormData
Map server errors back to fields
n1217.f: When would you choose a form library instead of hand-written state?

n1218.a: Approaches: (1) fetch in `useEffect` with local state — simple but you must handle loading/error, race conditions (ignore flag or AbortController), caching and request waterfalls yourself; (2) a server-state library (TanStack Query, SWR) — caching, deduplication, background refetching, retries and pagination out of the box; (3) framework/route loaders (React Router loaders, Next.js) — fetch before rendering the route, avoiding waterfalls and enabling SSR; (4) React Server Components — fetch on the server close to the data with no client JS; plus Suspense with `use()` for promises. Choose based on SSR needs, caching requirements and app complexity.
n1218.f: What is a request waterfall and how do loaders avoid it?
n1218.c: const { data, isPending, error } = useQuery({ queryKey: ['user', id], queryFn: () => fetch(`/api/users/${id}`).then(r => r.json()) });

n1219.a: Common expectations: composition with `children` and slot props; container/presentational separation; compound components (Tabs, Select) sharing state via context; render props and higher-order components (mostly legacy, still seen in libraries); custom hooks to reuse stateful logic (the modern default); controlled vs uncontrolled components; provider pattern with context; state reducer and prop getters for flexible components; and error boundaries for failures. Be ready to explain trade-offs and when hooks replace older patterns.
p: Render props and HOCs (legacy, know them)
Controlled vs uncontrolled, providers, error boundaries
n1219.f: Why did custom hooks largely replace HOCs and render props?

n1220.a: React started with class components (lifecycle methods, mixins, then HOCs and render props for reuse). Hooks (2019) made function components first-class, with logic reuse through custom hooks. Concurrent rendering (React 18) added transitions, automatic batching and streaming SSR with Suspense. The recommended way to start is now a framework (Next.js, React Router/Remix), and React Server Components let parts of the tree render on the server with no client JS; React 19 added Actions, `useActionState`, `use()` and the React Compiler for automatic memoization. Interviewers ask about this to check you understand why patterns changed, can work in legacy codebases, and know current best practices.
p: Frameworks as the default starting point
n1220.f: What problems in class components did hooks solve?

n1221.a: Compound components are a set of components that work together and share implicit state, like `<Tabs>`, `<Tabs.List>`, `<Tabs.Tab>` and `<Tabs.Panel>`. The parent holds state and provides it through context; children read it with a hook. This gives users a flexible, declarative API (they control markup and order) without prop drilling. Add accessibility (roles, aria-selected, keyboard support) inside the subcomponents.
n1221.f: How would you make Tabs support both controlled and uncontrolled usage?

L1.a: For reference types `==` compares references by default (unless the type overloads the operator, as `string` does), while `.Equals()` is a virtual method that types override to compare values. For value types both compare values. Strings are the classic case: both `==` and `Equals` compare content because `string` overloads both.
p: `==` is resolved at compile time from the static type; `Equals` is virtual and resolved at runtime
Override `Equals` and `GetHashCode` together for value semantics
L1.f: Why must you override GetHashCode when you override Equals?

L2.a: The C# compiler turns source into Intermediate Language (IL) plus metadata inside an assembly. At runtime the CLR loads the assembly, verifies it, and the JIT compiler converts each method's IL to native machine code the first time it is called, caching it for later calls. The CLR also provides garbage collection, type safety and exception handling.
p: CLR loads assemblies and manages memory via the GC
JIT compiles methods on first call; tiered compilation re-optimizes hot code
ReadyToRun and Native AOT precompile to cut startup time
L2.f: What is the difference between JIT and Native AOT?

L3.a: `IEnumerable<T>` runs queries in memory with LINQ to Objects: the data is pulled first, then filtered by C# delegates. `IQueryable<T>` builds an expression tree that a provider such as EF Core translates (for example to SQL), so filtering happens in the database. Calling `.AsEnumerable()` or `.ToList()` too early moves filtering into memory and loads too much data.
p: IQueryable: expression trees translated by a provider
Use IQueryable for database queries so WHERE/ORDER BY/paging run server-side
L3.f: What happens if you call a custom C# method inside an IQueryable Where clause?

L4.a: Most LINQ operators (Where, Select, OrderBy) don't run when you write them; they build a query that runs only when you enumerate it, with `foreach`, `ToList()`, `ToArray()`, `Count()`, `First()` and similar. Each enumeration runs the query again, so materialize with `ToList()` when you need a stable snapshot or will iterate several times.
p: Deferred: Where, Select, OrderBy, Skip, Take
Immediate: ToList, ToArray, ToDictionary, Count, Sum, First, Any
Re-enumerating a deferred EF query hits the database again
Changes to the source collection before enumeration are reflected in results

L5.a: `throw;` rethrows the current exception and keeps its original stack trace. `throw ex;` resets the stack trace to the current line, hiding where the error actually happened. Preserving the trace is essential for debugging production logs, so use `throw;` or wrap with `throw new MyException("context", ex)` to keep the inner exception.
p: `throw ex;` restarts it at the catch block
Wrap with an inner exception to add context
`ExceptionDispatchInfo.Capture(ex).Throw()` rethrows elsewhere while keeping the trace
L5.f: When would you catch an exception at all instead of letting it bubble up?

L6.a: No. `async`/`await` does not create threads by itself. An awaited I/O operation (HTTP call, DB query, file read) releases the current thread while waiting, and the continuation resumes later on a thread-pool thread (or the captured context). Only work you explicitly offload, such as `Task.Run`, uses another thread.
p: I/O-bound async frees threads instead of blocking them
CPU-bound work needs `Task.Run` or parallelism to run elsewhere
`ConfigureAwait(false)` avoids resuming on the captured context in libraries
Blocking with `.Result`/`.Wait()` can deadlock or starve the pool
L6.f: Why is `async void` dangerous outside event handlers?

L7.a: Singleton creates one instance for the whole application lifetime. Scoped creates one instance per scope, which in ASP.NET Core means per HTTP request. Transient creates a new instance every time it is requested. Pick by state: stateless helpers can be transient or singleton, per-request state like a DbContext is scoped, and shared caches or configuration are singletons.
p: Singleton: one for the app; must be thread-safe
Scoped: one per request; DbContext is scoped by default
Transient: new each resolve; good for lightweight stateless services
Never inject a scoped service into a singleton (captive dependency)
L7.f: How would you use a scoped service from inside a singleton background service?

L8.a: By default EF Core tracks entities it loads, keeping snapshots so `SaveChanges()` can detect and write changes. `AsNoTracking()` skips that bookkeeping, which is faster and uses less memory. Use tracking when you will modify and save the entities; use `AsNoTracking()` for read-only queries such as lists, reports and API GET endpoints.
p: Tracking enables change detection and identity resolution
AsNoTracking is faster for read-only data
You can set `QueryTrackingBehavior.NoTracking` as the context default
L8.f: How do you update an entity that was loaded with AsNoTracking?

L9.a: An access token is short-lived (minutes) and sent with every API request to prove the caller is authorized. A refresh token is long-lived and used only to get a new access token when the old one expires. This keeps the frequently sent token low-risk if leaked while the user doesn't have to log in again constantly.
p: Access token: short expiry, sent in the Authorization header
Refresh token: long expiry, sent only to the token endpoint, ideally in an httpOnly cookie
Rotate refresh tokens and revoke them on logout or reuse
Expiry limits the damage of a stolen access token
L9.f: How do you handle many parallel requests failing with 401 at the same time?

L10.a: After login the server issues a token (often a signed JWT) describing the user and their permissions. The client stores it and attaches it to requests, usually as `Authorization: Bearer <token>`. The server verifies the signature and expiry on each request without a session lookup, and a refresh flow issues new access tokens when they expire.
p: Login → server signs a token with claims and expiry
Client sends the token with each API call
Server validates signature, expiry, audience and scopes
Store carefully: httpOnly cookies resist XSS; memory storage avoids persistence
L10.f: What are the trade-offs between storing tokens in localStorage and in cookies?

L11.a: Cookies are small key-value strings the server sets with `Set-Cookie`, and the browser sends them back automatically on matching requests. They are used for sessions and login state, preferences and tracking. Attributes control security: `HttpOnly` hides them from JavaScript, `Secure` restricts them to HTTPS, `SameSite` limits cross-site sending, plus `Domain`, `Path` and expiry.
p: About 4 KB per cookie, sent with every matching request
HttpOnly + Secure + SameSite protect session cookies
