Session cookies vanish when the browser closes; persistent ones have Expires/Max-Age
L11.f: How does SameSite=Lax help against CSRF?

L12.a: Authentication verifies who you are (login with a password, OTP or SSO). Authorization decides what you are allowed to do once identified (roles, permissions, resource ownership). Authentication always comes first; a 401 means not authenticated and a 403 means authenticated but not authorized.
p: Authentication: identity, e.g. credentials, OAuth/OIDC login
Authorization: permissions, e.g. roles, scopes, policies
Enforce authorization on the server; UI checks are only for UX
L12.f: How would you implement role-based access in a React app?

L13.a: Hoisting means declarations are processed before code runs: `var` declarations are hoisted and initialized to `undefined`, and function declarations are hoisted with their body. `let`, `const` and `class` are hoisted too but stay uninitialized until their declaration line runs; the period before that is the Temporal Dead Zone, and accessing them there throws a ReferenceError.
p: Function declarations can be called before they appear
The TDZ also applies within blocks and default parameters
L13.f: Are function expressions assigned to var hoisted?

L14.a: Keep the product list in state and update it immutably: add with a spread, update with `map`, delete with `filter`. A single form handles both create and edit by tracking which id is being edited.
p: Never mutate state arrays; return new arrays
Reuse one form for add and edit
Lift state up if other components need the list
L14.f: How would you add validation and an optimistic API save?

L15.a: Initialise state lazily from localStorage and write it back in an effect whenever it changes. Wrap reads in try/catch because storage can be unavailable or contain bad JSON, and version the key so you can migrate the shape later.
p: Lazy initial state avoids reading storage on every render
Save in useEffect keyed on the data
localStorage is synchronous and ~5 MB; use IndexedDB for large data
Listen to the `storage` event to sync across tabs
L15.f: Why shouldn't you store auth tokens this way?

L16.a: AWS, Azure and GCP provide compute, storage, databases and networking on demand. A frontend is usually built in CI and deployed as static files to object storage behind a CDN (S3 + CloudFront, Azure Static Web Apps, Firebase Hosting) or to a platform like Vercel or Netlify, with separate dev, staging and production environments that use their own configuration.
p: Environments: dev → staging/QA → production, each with its own env variables
CI/CD builds, tests and deploys on merge
CDNs cache static assets close to users; cache-bust with hashed file names
Monitoring and rollbacks matter as much as deployment
L16.f: How do you inject different API URLs per environment in a React build?

L17.a: Store the latest value in state, set a timeout whenever it changes, and clear the timeout in the effect cleanup so only the last change survives the delay.
p: Cleanup cancels the pending timer on every new value
Use the debounced value as an effect dependency for API calls
Pair with AbortController to cancel stale requests
L17.f: How is this different from debouncing the callback with useCallback?

L18.a: Make it controlled (`value` array + `onChange`), filter options by a search query, and render the list in a popover with keyboard support and ARIA roles. Keep generic props like `options`, `getLabel` and `multiple` so teams can reuse it.
p: Controlled API: value, onChange, options, multiple
Filter with a memoised query; virtualise long lists
Keyboard: arrows, Enter to toggle, Escape to close; `role="listbox"` and `aria-selected`
Close on outside click; show selected items as removable chips
L18.f: How would you make it work with thousands of options?

L19.a: Split the app by feature (domain folders with their own routes, components, hooks and API calls), lazy-load each route, and share a design system and layout shell. Keep server data in a cache like React Query, global client state small, and enforce consistency with TypeScript, lint rules and shared table, filter and chart components.
p: Feature-based structure and route-level code splitting
Shared UI kit plus layout, auth and permission guards
Server state in React Query with caching; little global state
Performance budgets, virtualised tables, monitoring of Web Vitals
L19.f: When would you consider micro-frontends for this dashboard?

L20.a: Respect the server's 429 responses and `Retry-After` header, retry with exponential backoff and jitter, and reduce calls in the first place by debouncing input, caching responses and deduplicating identical requests. Show the user a friendly "try again shortly" state instead of failing silently.
p: Cache and dedupe with React Query/SWR
Queue or batch requests; limit concurrency
L20.f: How would you implement a client-side request queue with a max of 5 calls per second?

L21.a: Build it as a versioned package with a clear API: accessible primitives, design tokens for theming, documentation in Storybook, and automated tests including visual regression. Publish with semantic versioning and changelogs, and treat breaking changes carefully with deprecations and codemods.
p: Design tokens + theming; accessible components by default
Storybook docs, unit, a11y and visual tests
Tree-shakeable builds and minimal peer dependencies
L21.f: How do you balance flexibility vs consistency in component APIs?

L22.a: CSR renders in the browser after the JS loads, which suits logged-in, highly interactive apps like dashboards. SSR renders HTML per request on the server, giving fast first paint and SEO for dynamic, personalised pages. SSG renders HTML at build time and serves it from a CDN, which is fastest for content that rarely changes, such as blogs and docs.
p: CSR: simple hosting, slower first paint, weaker SEO
SSR: fresh per request, more server cost, needs hydration
SSG: fastest, but data is only as fresh as the last build (ISR helps)
Frameworks like Next.js mix them per route
L22.f: What is ISR and when does it help?

L23.a: Serve static assets from a CDN, keep the bundle small with code splitting, render critical pages with SSR or SSG, and make the frontend resilient: caching, retries, graceful degradation and feature flags. Observe everything with real-user monitoring, error tracking and performance budgets, and deploy gradually with canaries and quick rollbacks.
p: SSR/SSG for public pages; lazy-load the rest
RUM, Web Vitals, error tracking (e.g. Sentry)
L23.f: How would you handle a backend outage without breaking the whole UI?

L24.a: Make debt visible and measurable, then tie it to business impact: slower delivery, bugs, incidents. Fix debt that blocks upcoming features as part of that work, reserve a regular slice of capacity for the rest, and prioritise by risk and cost of delay rather than taste.
p: Track debt items with impact and effort
Bundle refactors with related feature work
Escalate debt that causes incidents or security risk
L24.f: Give an example where you chose to ship with debt deliberately.

L25.a: Start by understanding their constraints and goals, then discuss options with data: user impact, effort, performance or technical limits. Propose alternatives or a prototype, agree on a decision owner, and document the outcome so it doesn't reopen. Keep it about the product, not people.
p: Offer trade-offs instead of a flat no
L25.f: Tell me about a time you changed your mind after such a discussion.

L26.a: Lead with the outcome and why it matters to them (cost, risk, timeline, user impact), use analogies instead of jargon, and present two or three options with clear trade-offs and a recommendation. Visuals and short written summaries help, and check understanding by inviting questions.
p: Start with the decision and impact
Show options, trade-offs and a recommendation
L26.f: How would you explain a migration to a new framework to a product manager?

L28.a: Open a WebSocket or Server-Sent Events connection once (for example in a provider), push incoming notifications into state or a store, and show them with a badge and toasts. Handle reconnection, deduplicate by id, mark items read via the API, and fall back to polling if needed.
p: One connection in a context/provider; clean up on unmount
SSE is enough for server→client only
Dedupe by id; reconnect with backoff
Persist read status on the server; optionally use browser Notifications
L28.f: When would you choose WebSockets over SSE here?

L29.a: Use a single real-time connection (WebSocket or SSE) shared through a store or context so every page and chart subscribes to the same stream. Throttle or batch updates (for example once per animation frame or second), keep only a rolling window of points, and update charts incrementally rather than re-rendering everything.
p: One shared connection; components subscribe to slices
Memoise charts and use canvas for many points
L29.f: How would you keep inactive tabs from wasting resources?

L30.a: WebSockets give a persistent, full-duplex connection, so server and client can both push messages instantly with little overhead after the initial handshake. They fit chat, live collaboration, multiplayer games, trading tickers, live dashboards and notifications.
p: Low latency, no repeated HTTP headers
Needs reconnection, heartbeats and scaling for many connections
SSE is simpler when only the server pushes
L30.f: How do you scale WebSocket servers horizontally?

L31.a: Likely causes: the message handler is registered twice (for example a socket listener added in a useEffect without cleanup, or Strict Mode running effects twice), the send happens twice (double submit or optimistic append plus server echo), or the server broadcasts to the sender as well. Fix by cleaning up listeners, deduplicating by message id, and reconciling optimistic messages with the server ack.
p: Don't append both optimistically and on echo without reconciling
Disable the send button while sending
L31.f: How would you reproduce and confirm the root cause?

L32.a: Memoisation isn't free: it costs memory, adds comparison work every render, makes code harder to read and is easy to break with unstable dependencies. Use it when profiling shows a real problem: expensive calculations, props to memoised children, values used as effect dependencies, or large lists. Otherwise let React re-render; it is usually fast.
p: Costs: extra memory, dependency comparisons, complexity
Useless if dependencies change every render
Measure with the React Profiler first
The React Compiler can automate much of this
L32.f: Why does passing an inline object to a React.memo child defeat memoisation?

L33.a: A stale closure happens when a function created during an earlier render keeps reading the state or props from that render, because it closed over those values. It shows up in effects with missing dependencies, intervals, and event listeners registered once. Fix it with correct dependencies, functional updates (`setX(x => x + 1)`), or a ref holding the latest value.
p: Each render has its own props and state
Callbacks capture the values of the render that created them
Functional updates or refs avoid stale reads
L33.f: How does useEffectEvent help with this?

L34.a: Common issues are missing dependencies (stale values), objects, arrays or functions created during render as dependencies (the effect runs every render or loops forever), setting state the effect depends on (infinite loops), and over-including values that trigger unwanted reruns. Fix by following the lint rule, moving objects inside the effect, memoising, or using functional updates.
p: New object/function each render → effect runs every time
Updating a dependency inside the effect → loop
Use useCallback/useMemo or move values inside the effect
L34.f: Is it ever OK to disable the exhaustive-deps lint rule?

L35.a: If the effect runs once and the interval callback reads `count`, it always sees the initial value, so the counter gets stuck (for example at 1). Fix it with a functional update so you don't read state at all, or include the value in dependencies and recreate the interval, or read from a ref.
L35.f: How would you write a reusable useInterval hook?

L36.a: Lighthouse is Google's automated audit for performance, accessibility, SEO and best practices. Run it from Chrome DevTools, PageSpeed Insights, the CLI or Lighthouse CI in your pipeline, before releases or after performance changes. It runs in mobile mode (throttled CPU and network, small viewport) or desktop mode, so test both. It is lab data; compare with real-user field data from CrUX or RUM.
p: DevTools > Lighthouse tab, PageSpeed Insights, CLI, Lighthouse CI
Mobile simulates a slow device and network
Scores vary run to run; average several runs in incognito
L36.f: Why might a page score 95 in Lighthouse but still have poor INP for users?

L37.a: HTTPS is HTTP over TLS: the connection is encrypted, the server's identity is verified with a certificate, and data can't be read or modified in transit. Plain HTTP sends everything in clear text. Modern features (HTTP/2, service workers, secure cookies, geolocation) and SEO all expect HTTPS.
p: TLS gives encryption, integrity and authentication
Certificates from a CA (e.g. Let's Encrypt)
L37.f: What happens during a TLS handshake?

L38.a: localStorage is readable by any JavaScript on the page, so an XSS bug exposes everything in it. Store only non-sensitive data there: UI preferences, cached public data, drafts. Don't store passwords, personal data or long-lived tokens; keep session tokens in httpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookies or in memory.
p: It is synchronous and persists until cleared
Encryption in the browser doesn't help if the key is also in JS
L38.f: Where would you keep an access token in a single-page app?

L39.a: It logs `false`. Objects are compared by reference, and two object literals are two different objects, even if they look identical.
p: Compare contents with a deep-equal function

L43.a: `false == "0"` is true because both convert to the number 0. `false === "0"` is false because the types differ. `null == undefined` is true by a special rule of loose equality. `null === undefined` is false because they are different types.
p: Loose equality converts booleans and strings to numbers
null and undefined are only loosely equal to each other
Prefer `===` except `x == null` to test both

L44.a: It logs `undefined`. Setting an array's `length` to 0 truncates it, deleting all elements, and `const` only prevents reassigning the variable, not mutating the array.
p: Assigning a smaller length removes elements
`const` protects the binding, not the contents
`arr.length = 0` is a common way to clear an array in place
Other references to the same array see it emptied too

L45.a: Swap elements from both ends moving inward (in place, O(n) time, O(1) space), or build a new array by iterating from the end.
p: Two pointers meet in the middle
In place mutates the input; copy first if needed
L45.f: How would you reverse only part of the array between two indexes?

L46.a: Track the largest value seen in one pass. `Math.max(...arr)` works for small arrays but can overflow the call stack for very large ones.
p: `reduce((m, x) => x > m ? x : m)` is equivalent
L46.f: How would you find the second largest in one pass?

L47.a: Accumulate with a loop or `reduce`, starting from 0 so an empty array returns 0.
p: Validate numbers if input may be mixed
L47.f: How would you sum only the numbers in a mixed array?
L47.c:
const sum = arr => arr.reduce((s, x) => s + x, 0);
sum([1, 2, 3]); // 6

L48.a: Insertion sort is simple to write by hand: walk left to right and insert each element into the sorted part before it. It is O(n²) but fine for small arrays; mention merge sort or quicksort for O(n log n).
p: Insertion sort: stable, in place, O(n²)
Merge sort: O(n log n), stable, extra memory
Quicksort: O(n log n) average, O(n²) worst
Built-in sort needs a comparator for numbers

L49.a: Normalise k with `k % n`, then take slices; or do it in place with three reversals (whole array, first k, rest) in O(n) time and O(1) space.
p: Right rotation by k = last k elements move to the front

L50.a: Compare elements from both ends moving inward; if any pair differs it isn't a palindrome.
p: Two pointers, O(n) time, O(1) space
Use a deep compare if elements are objects
Empty and single-element arrays are palindromes
Same approach works for linked lists with extra steps
L50.f: How would you check a linked list in O(1) extra space?

L51.a: Normalise the string (lowercase, remove non-alphanumerics if required) and compare characters from both ends.
p: Two pointers avoid building a reversed copy
Decide whether to ignore case and punctuation

L52.a: Use object spread or `Object.assign` for a shallow merge (later keys win). For nested objects write a recursive deep merge.
L52.f: How should arrays be merged: replaced or concatenated?

L53.a: `JSON.stringify` turns an object into a string and `JSON.parse` turns it back. It drops functions, `undefined` and symbols, turns Dates into strings, and fails on circular references, BigInt, Map and Set, so use a replacer/reviver or `structuredClone` when you need those.
p: `JSON.parse(str, reviver)` restores Dates or custom types
Wrap parse in try/catch for untrusted input
L53.f: How would you serialize a Map?
L53.c:
const s = JSON.stringify({ d: new Date() });
const o = JSON.parse(s, (k, v) => k === "d" ? new Date(v) : v);

L54.a: Recursively compare: same primitive value (use `Object.is`), or both objects with the same keys and deep-equal values. Handle arrays and null explicitly.
p: Compare key counts, then each key
Arrays are objects with index keys
L54.f: How would you support Dates, Maps and circular references?

L55.a: Use `reduce` or `Object.fromEntries` with `map` to key each item by a property, such as id.
p: Use a Map for non-string keys
L55.f: How would you group items when keys repeat?

L56.a: Use `class` and `extends`; call `super()` in the child constructor before using `this`, and override methods, optionally calling `super.method()`.
L56.f: How would you write the same thing with constructor functions?

L57.a: Turn the object into entries, filter them, and build a new object with `Object.fromEntries`.
p: The predicate gets key and value
Works for picking or omitting keys
L57.c:
const filterObj = (obj, fn) => Object.fromEntries(Object.entries(obj).filter(([k, v]) => fn(v, k)));
filterObj({ a: 1, b: 5 }, v => v > 2); // { b: 5 }

L58.a: Use `sort` with a comparator: subtract for numbers, `localeCompare` for strings. Copy first if you shouldn't mutate.
p: Comparator returns negative, zero or positive
L58.f: How would you sort by several keys?
L58.c:
const byPrice = [...items].sort((a, b) => a.price - b.price);
const byName = items.toSorted((a, b) => a.name.localeCompare(b.name));

L59.a: Use closures (variables inside a factory function that only returned methods can reach) or class private fields with `#`, which are truly private at the language level.
p: WeakMap keyed by instance is an older pattern
L59.f: Can subclasses access a parent's #private fields?

L60.a: Split into characters, reverse, join. Use `[...s]` rather than `s.split("")` so emoji and other surrogate pairs aren't broken.
p: A loop from the end works without built-ins
Strings are immutable, so you always build a new one
Combining characters may still need Intl.Segmenter
L60.f: Reverse the words in a sentence but not the letters.

L61.a: Normalise both strings, then compare character counts with a map (O(n)) or compare the sorted strings (O(n log n)).
p: Count with one map: increment for a, decrement for b
L61.f: Group a list of words into anagram groups.

L62.a: Split on spaces, uppercase the first letter of each word, and join; or use a regex replace on word boundaries.
p: Decide whether to lowercase the rest
Handle empty strings and multiple spaces
L62.f: How would you keep small words like "and" lowercase?
L62.c:
const titleCase = s => s.replace(/\b\w/g, c => c.toUpperCase());
titleCase("hello world"); // "Hello World"

L63.a: B is a rotation of A if they have the same length and B appears inside A + A.
p: Works for arrays with join and a separator
L63.f: Why is the length check necessary?
L63.c: const isRotation = (a, b) => a.length === b.length && (a + a).includes(b);

L64.a: Use recursion/backtracking: for each character, fix it and permute the rest. There are n! permutations; use a Set or skip duplicate characters if the input repeats letters.
L64.f: How would you generate them in lexicographic order?

L65.a: If the string is longer than the limit, cut it so the result including "…" fits the limit.
p: Count the ellipsis in the length
Optionally cut at the last space
L65.f: How would you truncate to N lines in CSS?
L65.c: const truncate = (s, n) => s.length > n ? s.slice(0, n - 1) + "…" : s;

L66.a: Use a regular expression with a character class anchored at both ends, or check each character against a Set of allowed characters.
p: A Set check avoids regex escaping issues
L66.f: How would you return the first invalid character?

L67.a: Repeatedly search with `indexOf` starting after the previous match. Decide whether overlapping matches count; advancing by 1 counts overlaps, advancing by the substring's length doesn't.
p: Regex with `g` flag also works (escape the input)
L67.f: How many times does "aa" occur in "aaaa" with and without overlaps?

L68.a: Generator functions (`function*`) can pause with `yield` and resume later. Calling one returns an iterator; each `next()` runs until the next `yield` and returns `{ value, done }`. They are useful for lazy sequences, custom iterators and infinite streams.
L68.c:
function* ids() { let i = 1; while (true) yield i++; }
const g = ids(); g.next().value; // 1

L69.a: Recursively walk the object and build dotted keys for nested values, stopping at primitives (and usually arrays).

L70.a: Dependencies must list every reactive value the effect uses, which can make effects rerun more often than you want, especially with objects or functions recreated each render. Leaving them out causes stale data, and the rule pushes logic into effects that often belongs in event handlers or derived values.
p: Unstable references cause reruns or loops
Hard to express "run only when X changes but read Y"
Use event handlers, useMemo, or useEffectEvent to fix
L70.f: When should logic move out of an effect into an event handler?

L71.a: Keep an auth slice (user, token status, roles), a profile slice, and feature slices for app data, with async thunks or RTK Query for API calls. Store tokens in httpOnly cookies rather than Redux persistence, clear all slices on logout, and gate routes and UI by selectors on the auth slice.
p: Separate slices: auth, profile, feature data
RTK Query or createAsyncThunk for fetching and caching
L71.f: How do you refresh an expired token inside an RTK Query base query?

L73.a: Authenticate on the server: use a library such as Auth.js (NextAuth) or your provider's SDK, keep the session in an httpOnly cookie, and read it in middleware, server components and route handlers. Protect routes in middleware, fetch user data on the server, and pass only what the client needs.
p: Read the session in server components and actions
Check authorization in every API route
L73.f: Why isn't hiding a link enough to protect a page?

L74.a: Use HTTPS (TLS) for everything; that already encrypts payloads in transit. Extra client-side encryption rarely adds security because the key must ship to the browser. Instead minimise sensitive data sent, use short-lived tokens, validate and authorise on the server, and encrypt sensitive data at rest on the server.
p: Never put secrets or keys in frontend code
Send only needed fields; mask data in responses
Payload signing (HMAC) can ensure integrity when required
L74.f: When would end-to-end encryption in the browser make sense?

L75.a: Pick a tool per kind of state: local UI state with useState/useReducer, server data with React Query, rarely changing app-wide values (theme, user) with Context, and complex shared client state with Redux Toolkit or Zustand. Keep global state minimal and colocate state with the components that use it.
p: Server state: React Query/RTK Query (caching, refetching)
Local first; lift only when needed
Redux Toolkit/Zustand for complex shared client state
L75.f: How would you prevent context re-renders in a large app?

L76.a: Organise by feature, not file type: each feature folder owns its routes, components, hooks, API client and tests. Put API calls in a service layer, server data in React Query, shared client state in a small store, and wrap the app in error boundaries with central logging. Test with unit tests for logic, React Testing Library for components and a few end-to-end flows.
p: Service layer isolates HTTP and mapping
Route-level code splitting and error boundaries per area
Lint rules or boundaries to stop features importing each other's internals
L76.f: How would you share code between two features without coupling them?

L77.a: Render public pages with SSR or SSG and serve everything through a CDN with long-lived cache headers on hashed assets. Shrink bundles with code splitting, tree shaking and lazy-loaded images, cache API data on the client and edge, and watch Core Web Vitals from real users so regressions are caught after each release.
p: Code splitting, modern image formats, font loading
RUM for LCP, INP and CLS with performance budgets in CI
L77.f: Which metric would you fix first if INP is poor?

L78.a: A `setTimeout` callback captures the state from the render that scheduled it. If you click "+1" three times and a timeout later does `setCount(count + 1)`, every callback uses the old `count`, so updates are lost. Use the functional form `setCount(c => c + 1)` or read the latest value from a ref.
p: Each render's callbacks see that render's state
Functional updates always get the latest state
Refs give the current value without re-rendering
L78.f: Why does alert(count) in a timeout show the old value?
L78.c:
// stale: setTimeout(() => setCount(count + 1), 1000)
setTimeout(() => setCount(c => c + 1), 1000);

L79.a: An effect that sets state which is also one of its dependencies, or that depends on an object or function recreated each render, reruns forever. Prevent it by using correct but stable dependencies, moving objects inside the effect, memoising with useMemo/useCallback, using functional updates, or deriving the value during render instead of syncing it with an effect.
p: Objects/functions in deps change every render
No dependency array runs after every render
Often the fix is: you don't need an effect
L79.f: How would you compute a filtered list without an effect?

L80.a: `useRef` returns a mutable `{ current }` object that persists across renders without causing re-renders; attach it to an element with `ref` to access the DOM node. To let a parent reach a child's DOM node, pass the ref down: in React 19 `ref` is a normal prop; earlier versions need `forwardRef`. Use `useImperativeHandle` to expose only specific methods.
p: Refs persist values and DOM nodes without re-rendering
Parent creates the ref, child attaches it
`useImperativeHandle` limits what the parent can call
L80.f: Why shouldn't you read ref.current during render?
L80.c:
function Input({ ref, ...p }) { return <input ref={ref} {...p} />; }
function Form() { const r = useRef(null); return <><Input ref={r} /><button onClick={() => r.current.focus()}>Focus</button></>; }

L81.a: `^1.2.3` allows any compatible 1.x.x update (minor and patch, from 1.2.3 up to below 2.0.0). `~1.2.3` allows only patch updates (1.2.x, below 1.3.0). An exact version like `1.2.3` pins it. The lockfile records the exact installed versions either way.
L81.f: What does npm ci do differently from npm install?

L82.a: Run independent calls in parallel with `Promise.all`, cache and dedupe them, and render each section as its data arrives instead of waiting for everything. Ask the backend for an aggregated endpoint (BFF or GraphQL) when the page always needs the same combination, and prefetch on navigation intent.
p: Cache with React Query; avoid duplicate calls
Aggregate on the server to cut round trips
L82.f: How do you handle one of those calls failing?

L83.a: 1,000 rows is manageable: keep the raw data once, compute the filtered list with `useMemo`, debounce text input or use `useDeferredValue` so typing stays responsive, and memoise row components. Virtualise the table if rows are heavy, and move filtering to the server if data grows much larger.
p: Derive filtered rows, don't store them in state
Debounce or defer the filter input
L83.f: When would you switch to server-side filtering?

L84.a: Get the user's roles or permissions from the server after login, keep them in an auth context, and check them through a `can(permission)` helper. Wrap routes in a guard that redirects unauthorised users and hide or disable UI they can't use, while the API enforces the same rules.
p: Prefer permissions over raw role names
Route guard component or loader checks
Server-side authorization is the real protection
L84.f: How would you handle permissions changing while the user is logged in?

L85.a: `position: sticky` behaves like `relative` until the element reaches a threshold you set (such as `top: 0`) inside its scrolling container, then sticks there like `fixed` until its parent scrolls out of view. Unlike `fixed`, it stays in normal flow and is limited to its parent.
p: Needs a threshold: top, bottom, left or right
Sticks only within its parent's bounds
Breaks if an ancestor has overflow hidden/auto in the wrong place
Common for table headers and section titles
L85.f: Why might position: sticky not work?

L86.a: A state update schedules a render. React calls your component functions to produce new elements (render phase), reconciles them with the previous fiber tree to find changes, then in the commit phase applies DOM updates, runs layout effects, lets the browser paint, and finally runs passive effects (useEffect).
p: Trigger: setState or a parent render
Render phase: pure, interruptible in concurrent mode
Commit phase: DOM mutations, refs, useLayoutEffect
L86.f: Why must the render phase be free of side effects?

L87.a: Queries read data, asking for exactly the fields you need. Mutations change data and return the updated result. Subscriptions keep a long-lived connection (usually WebSocket) so the server pushes updates. Fragments are reusable sets of fields shared between queries so components can declare their own data needs.
p: Fragments → reuse field selections and colocate with components
L87.f: How does a GraphQL client normalise its cache?

L88.a: N+1 happens when you load a list (1 query) and then make another query per item (N queries), for example GraphQL resolvers or ORM lazy loading fetching each post's author separately. Fix it by batching (DataLoader), joins or eager loading, or fetching related records with one `WHERE id IN (...)` query.
p: Symptom: query count grows with list size
GraphQL: DataLoader batches and caches per request
Monitor query counts in logs or APM
L88.f: How does DataLoader batch requests within one tick?

L89.a: Use `apollo3-cache-persist` (or write your own) to save the InMemoryCache to localStorage or IndexedDB and restore it before rendering the app. Set a size limit, version the key so schema changes clear old data, and still refetch fresh data with a cache-and-network policy.
p: Version and purge on schema or user change
L89.f: What should happen to the persisted cache on logout?

L90.a: Model cart items in the normalised Apollo cache. For quantity changes send a mutation with an `optimisticResponse` so the UI updates instantly, and update related fields (totals) in the `update` function. If the mutation fails Apollo rolls back the optimistic layer; show a toast with retry. For undo, keep the previous state and send a compensating mutation within a short window.
p: Automatic rollback of optimistic data on error
Undo = store the previous quantity and re-mutate
Debounce rapid quantity clicks; keep server as the source of truth
L90.f: How would you prevent out-of-order responses from overwriting newer quantities?

L91.a: Assign users to variants consistently (by user id hash) via a feature-flag or experimentation service, render the variant, and log exposure and conversion events. Decide the metric and sample size up front, avoid flicker by assigning on the server or edge, and keep experiments isolated so they don't interfere.
p: Stable bucketing, ideally server- or edge-side
Clean up losing variants and flags afterwards
L91.f: How do you prevent layout flicker when the variant loads late?

L92.a: Mock the API (for example with MSW) and assert the UI changes immediately after the action, before the request resolves. Then test both outcomes: on success the server data replaces the optimistic data; on failure the UI rolls back and shows an error. Control timing with delayed handlers or fake timers.
p: Failure path: rollback and error message
Test rapid repeated actions for ordering bugs
L92.f: How would you test it end-to-end with Playwright?

L93.a: Store the cart on the server tied to the user account, not only in localStorage. Each device reads it on load and after changes; push updates with WebSockets or SSE, or refetch on focus. Merge a guest cart into the account cart on login and resolve conflicts with timestamps or versions.
p: Server is the source of truth
Real-time push or refetch on window focus
Version numbers to handle concurrent edits
L93.f: How would you handle offline edits?

L94.a: `setTimeout(fn, 0)` only queues `fn` as a macrotask after at least 0 ms. It runs once the current synchronous code finishes and all microtasks (promise callbacks) are processed, and browsers may clamp nested timers to about 4 ms. So it runs "as soon as possible after now", not immediately.
p: Call stack must be empty first
Microtasks run before the next macrotask
Nested timeouts clamp to ~4 ms; background tabs throttle further
L94.f: What would requestAnimationFrame print relative to these?

L95.a: Structure your answer: what the product does and who uses it, the frontend stack (framework, state management, routing, UI library), how it talks to the backend (REST/GraphQL, auth, gateway), the backend services and data stores, and how modules communicate (APIs, events, shared packages). Finish with your own contributions and one hard problem you solved.
p: Your role, impact and a concrete challenge
L95.f: What would you change in that architecture if you started again?

L96.a: Record an interaction in the React DevTools Profiler with "why did this render" enabled to see which components re-render and why. Then reduce the blast radius: move filter state closer to the components that use it, split contexts, memoise expensive children with stable props, and derive filtered data with useMemo.
p: Profiler + highlight updates to find wasted renders
Colocate state; avoid page-level state for a single filter
L96.f: How do URL search params change this design?

L97.a: Use a form library such as React Hook Form with a schema validator (Zod or Yup), split the form into section components that register their own fields, and keep one source of truth for values. Validate per field and per section, show errors near fields, and save drafts if the form is long.
p: Uncontrolled inputs with RHF for performance
Schema validation shared with the backend
L97.f: How would you handle fields that depend on other fields?

L98.a: Disable the button and show a loading state while the request is in flight, guard the handler with an in-flight flag, and make the API idempotent with an idempotency key so retries can't create duplicates. Debouncing alone isn't enough for slow networks.
p: Ref-based in-flight guard against double clicks
Idempotency key header for the server
L98.f: How does the server use the idempotency key?

L99.a: For frequent, continuous updates WebSockets (or Server-Sent Events if data only flows to the client) beat polling: lower latency and no wasted requests. Polling is fine when updates are slow (every 30–60 s) or infrastructure can't hold connections. Add throttled rendering, reconnection and a polling fallback.
p: Polling: simple, but wasteful and laggy
SSE: one-way push over HTTP, auto-reconnect
L99.f: How would you scale this for 10,000 concurrent viewers?

L100.a: First add tests around current behaviour (characterisation tests), then refactor in small steps: extract custom hooks for logic, split the JSX into presentational components, move API calls to a service layer, and use TypeScript to catch breakages. Ship each step separately and verify with tests and review.
p: Small PRs, feature flags if risky
L100.f: How do you decide where to draw component boundaries?

L101.a: Fire all five in parallel with `Promise.allSettled` so one failure doesn't discard the others, render sections whose data succeeded, and show an inline error with retry for the failed one. If a call is truly required for the page, treat its failure as a page error; add timeouts and retries with backoff.
p: allSettled instead of all when partial data is useful
L101.f: How would you show a skeleton for each section independently?
L101.c:
const results = await Promise.allSettled(urls.map(u => fetch(u).then(r => r.json())));
const data = results.map(r => r.status === "fulfilled" ? r.value : null);

L102.a: Generally no: don't send or process thousands of records on the client if you can avoid it. Ask the API for pagination, filtering, sorting and aggregation server-side, or use infinite scrolling with virtualised rendering. If you must process them, do it in a Web Worker and render with virtualisation.
p: Only request the fields you need
L102.f: Cursor vs offset pagination: which would you choose?

L103.a: Look at the Lighthouse opportunities and the Web Vitals that fail: large JS bundles, render-blocking resources, unoptimised images and slow server response are the usual causes. Fix with code splitting, lazy loading, compressing and resizing images, preloading critical assets, caching, and SSR for the first view; then re-measure.
p: Check LCP element, TBT/INP and CLS first
Verify with field data, not only lab scores
L103.f: What usually causes CLS and how do you fix it?

L104.a: Reproduce it and record a Performance profile in DevTools to find the long task and the function responsible. Then reduce the work: better algorithm or caching, debouncing or throttling frequent calls, splitting work into chunks that yield to the browser, moving heavy computation to a Web Worker, and avoiding forced layout reads in loops.

L105.a: Both pass arguments by reference. A `ref` argument must be initialised before the call and the method may read and change it. An `out` argument needn't be initialised, but the method must assign it before returning; it is used to return extra values, as in `int.TryParse(s, out var n)`.
p: ref: in and out, caller initialises
out: output only, callee must assign
Prefer tuples for multiple return values in new code
L105.f: Why can't async methods have ref or out parameters?

L106.a: `async` marks a method that contains `await`; it returns `Task`, `Task<T>` or `ValueTask`. `await` pauses the method until the awaited task completes without blocking the thread, then continues. This keeps UIs responsive and lets servers handle more requests with the same thread pool.
p: Async all the way down; avoid .Result/.Wait()
L106.f: What is the difference between Task.WhenAll and awaiting tasks one by one?

L107.a: A thread is an independent path of execution with its own stack, scheduled by the OS. Parallel programming in .NET uses multiple threads to do CPU-bound work at the same time, through the Task Parallel Library (`Task.Run`, `Parallel.For`, `Parallel.ForEachAsync`) and PLINQ, which use the thread pool and handle partitioning for you.
p: Concurrency ≠ parallelism; async is mostly about I/O
TPL and PLINQ for CPU-bound work
Shared state needs locks, Interlocked or concurrent collections
Too many threads cause context switching overhead
L107.f: When would Parallel.ForEach make a web API slower?

L108.a: A JSON Web Token is a signed string of three base64url parts: header (algorithm), payload (claims such as user id, roles, expiry) and signature. The server signs it at login; the client sends it with requests; the server verifies the signature and expiry without storing sessions. The payload is readable, not encrypted, so never put secrets in it.
p: Signature proves it wasn't tampered with
Revocation is hard; use short lifetimes or deny-lists
L108.f: HS256 vs RS256: when would you use each?

L109.a: Middleware are components in the request pipeline. Each receives the HttpContext, can act before and after calling the next component, or short-circuit the request. The order they are added in Program.cs is the order requests flow through, and responses flow back in reverse: exception handling, HTTPS redirection, static files, routing, authentication, authorization, endpoints.
p: Order matters: auth must come before endpoints
Custom middleware for logging, correlation ids, headers
L109.f: What happens if UseAuthorization comes before UseRouting?
L109.c: app.Use(async (ctx, next) => { var sw = Stopwatch.StartNew(); await next(); logger.LogInformation("{ms}ms", sw.ElapsedMilliseconds); });

L110.a: An interface defines a contract (members without implementation) that classes implement. Code that depends on an interface instead of a concrete class is loosely coupled: the DI container supplies the implementation, so you can swap it (for example a fake in tests or a different provider) without changing the consumer.
p: Default interface methods exist but use sparingly
L110.f: Abstract class vs interface: when would you choose each?

L111.a: Rate limiting caps how many requests a client can make in a time window to protect the API from abuse and overload. ASP.NET Core 7+ has built-in middleware: add a policy (fixed window, sliding window, token bucket or concurrency) with `AddRateLimiter`, call `UseRateLimiter`, and apply it with `RequireRateLimiting` or `[EnableRateLimiting]`. It returns 429 when exceeded.
p: Algorithms: fixed/sliding window, token bucket, concurrency
Partition by user, API key or IP
Use a gateway or Redis for limits across multiple servers
L111.f: Why doesn't in-memory rate limiting work behind a load balancer?

L112.a: Take the maximum salary below the overall maximum, or rank salaries with DENSE_RANK so ties are handled and it generalises to the Nth highest.
p: Returns NULL/no row if there's no second salary
L112.f: How do you get the Nth highest salary per department?

L113.a: ACID describes reliable transactions. Atomicity: all statements succeed or none do. Consistency: the database moves from one valid state to another, respecting constraints. Isolation: concurrent transactions don't see each other's partial work. Durability: once committed, data survives crashes.
L113.f: What anomalies can occur at READ COMMITTED isolation?

L114.a: Group by the columns that define a duplicate and keep groups with a count above one. To see or delete the extra rows, number them with ROW_NUMBER.
p: ROW_NUMBER() PARTITION BY the duplicate columns
Delete rows with rn > 1 to dedupe
L114.f: How would you keep the newest row instead of the oldest?

L115.a: Join employees to their salaries and departments, then rank within each department, or compare to the department's MAX.
p: Window function handles ties with RANK
GROUP BY dept with MAX gives only the value, not the person
L115.f: How would you return the top 3 per department?
L115.c:
SELECT d.name, e.name, s.amount
FROM (SELECT employee_id, amount, RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY e.dept_id ORDER BY amount DESC) r, e.dept_id
      FROM Salary s JOIN Employee e ON e.id = s.employee_id) s
JOIN Employee e ON e.id = s.employee_id
JOIN Department d ON d.id = s.dept_id
WHERE s.r = 1;

L116.a: An index is a separate data structure (usually a B-tree) that keeps column values sorted with pointers to rows, so the database can find matching rows without scanning the whole table. It speeds up WHERE, JOIN, ORDER BY and GROUP BY at the cost of storage and slower writes.
p: Clustered index defines row order (one per table)
Too many indexes hurt inserts and updates
L116.f: When would the optimizer ignore an index?

L117.a: REST is an architectural style where resources are identified by URLs and manipulated with HTTP methods (GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE), statelessly, with standard status codes. In ASP.NET Core you build it with `[ApiController]` controllers or Minimal APIs, attribute routes like `[HttpGet("{id}")]`, model binding and validation, and return results such as `Ok`, `CreatedAtAction` or `NotFound`.
p: Resource URLs, HTTP verbs, status codes
L117.f: What status code should a successful POST return?

L118.a: Use HTTPS and authenticate every request: JWT bearer tokens issued by an identity provider via OAuth 2.0/OpenID Connect for users, client credentials or API keys for services. Authorise with policies and roles, validate input, rate limit, configure CORS narrowly, and keep secrets in a vault.
p: API keys only for server-to-server, rotated regularly
L118.f: Why shouldn't a SPA use the client credentials flow?

L119.a: `IActionResult` can return any result type but carries no information about the success payload's type. `ActionResult<T>` lets you return either a `T` directly or another result (`NotFound()`), giving type safety and better OpenAPI documentation.
p: IActionResult for endpoints with many result types

L120.a: Version via URL segment (`/api/v1/orders`), query string, header or media type. The `Asp.Versioning` package adds `[ApiVersion]`, routing by version, reporting supported versions and deprecations. Keep old versions running until clients migrate and document each version in OpenAPI.
p: URL versioning is the most visible
Only bump major versions for breaking changes
L120.f: What counts as a breaking API change?

L121.a: Middleware runs for every request in the pipeline and knows only HttpContext, so it suits cross-cutting concerns like logging, exception handling and headers. Filters run inside MVC around actions, with access to action arguments, model state and results, so they suit action-specific concerns like validation, caching or authorization.
p: Filter types: authorization, resource, action, exception, result
L121.f: Where would you put request timing: middleware or filter?

L122.a: Code-first: you write C# entity classes and EF creates and evolves the database with migrations. Database-first: you scaffold classes from an existing database. Model-first (EF6 only) used a visual designer to generate both. EF Core supports code-first and database-first (scaffolding).
p: Code-first suits new projects and version-controlled schema
Database-first suits existing or DBA-owned schemas
L122.f: How do you keep a database-first model in sync after schema changes?

L123.a: Eager loading fetches related data in the same query with `Include`. Lazy loading fetches it automatically the first time you access a navigation property (requires proxies), which can cause N+1 queries. Explicit loading fetches it on demand with `Entry(x).Collection(...).Load()`.
p: Lazy: convenient but risky for performance
L123.f: What is a cartesian explosion and how does AsSplitQuery help?

L124.a: `ObjectContext` was the original EF (EF4) API, heavy and tightly tied to EDMX models. `DbContext` (EF 4.1+) is a lighter wrapper with a simpler API (DbSet, change tracking, code-first) and is the only one in EF Core.
p: DbContext exposes underlying ObjectContext in EF6 via IObjectContextAdapter
L124.f: How do you configure a DbContext's lifetime in ASP.NET Core?

L125.a: `SaveChanges()` already wraps its changes in a transaction. For several operations together, use `await using var tx = await db.Database.BeginTransactionAsync();`, do the work, then `CommitAsync()` (rollback happens if you dispose without committing). TransactionScope or execution strategies help with distributed or retrying scenarios.
p: Explicit transactions for multiple SaveChanges or raw SQL
Use the execution strategy with retries
L125.f: How do you handle concurrency conflicts?

L126.a: Migrations version your database schema from your model. After changing entities run `dotnet ef migrations add Name` to generate a migration class with Up/Down, then apply it with `dotnet ef database update` or generate an idempotent SQL script for production.
p: Use SQL scripts or bundles for production deploys
Review generated migrations for data loss
L126.f: How do you seed data with migrations?

L127.a: `IEnumerable<T>` is a read-only, forward-only sequence evaluated in memory. `IQueryable<T>` extends it with expression trees that a provider translates (SQL) so filtering runs at the data source. `List<T>` is a concrete in-memory collection that's already materialised, supports indexing and modification.
p: Return IQueryable from repositories carefully: it leaks query building
L127.f: Why might returning IQueryable from a repository be a bad idea?

L128.a: Deferred execution means the query runs only when it's enumerated, using the source's current data each time. Immediate execution runs it right away and stores the result: methods like `ToList`, `ToArray`, `Count`, `First`, `Sum`, `Max`.
p: Reuse a deferred query and it re-runs
Materialise once to avoid repeated DB hits
L128.f: What bug can deferred execution cause in a loop?

L129.a: `join ... on ... equals` performs an inner join. A left join uses `join ... into g` (group join) plus `from x in g.DefaultIfEmpty()`. A group join returns each outer item with a collection of matching inner items. In EF Core, navigation properties often replace explicit joins.
p: Inner: `join o in Orders on c.Id equals o.CustomerId`
L129.f: How would you join on multiple keys?

L130.a: Filter and project in the database: keep queries as IQueryable until the end, select only the columns you need, avoid N+1 with Include or projections, use AsNoTracking for reads, paginate, and check the generated SQL. In memory, avoid repeated enumeration and use dictionaries for lookups.
p: Avoid client evaluation and calling ToList early
Inspect SQL with logging; add indexes
L130.f: How do you view the SQL EF Core generates?

L131.a: `SelectMany` projects each element to a sequence and flattens the results into one sequence. Use it for one-to-many flattening (all order lines across orders), cross joins, or combining nested lists.
p: Overload with a result selector keeps the parent
L131.f: What SQL does SelectMany produce in EF Core?
L131.c: var lines = orders.SelectMany(o => o.Lines, (o, l) => new { o.Id, l.Product });

L132.a: .NET Framework is Windows-only and in maintenance mode. .NET Core (now just .NET 5+) is cross-platform, open source, much faster, supports side-by-side versions and containers, and has a modular, unified ASP.NET Core with built-in DI. New development should target modern .NET.
p: Some legacy APIs (WebForms, WCF server) aren't in modern .NET
L132.f: How would you plan a migration from .NET Framework to .NET 8?

L133.a: `IHostedService` runs background work with the app's lifetime: `StartAsync` when the host starts and `StopAsync` on shutdown. `BackgroundService` is a convenient base class where you implement `ExecuteAsync` for long-running loops such as queue consumers, scheduled jobs or cache warm-up.
p: Honour the stoppingToken for graceful shutdown
Create scopes to use scoped services like DbContext

L134.a: Kestrel is ASP.NET Core's built-in, cross-platform, high-performance web server. It can face the internet directly or sit behind a reverse proxy such as Nginx, IIS or a cloud load balancer that handles TLS termination, load balancing and static files.
p: Configure endpoints and limits in appsettings or code
L134.f: Why use a reverse proxy in front of Kestrel?

L135.a: Configuration is layered: appsettings.json, then appsettings.{Environment}.json, user secrets, environment variables and command-line arguments, with later sources overriding earlier ones. Read raw values with `IConfiguration`, or bind sections to typed classes with the Options pattern: `IOptions<T>` (singleton snapshot), `IOptionsSnapshot<T>` (per request) and `IOptionsMonitor<T>` (live changes).
p: Environment variables override JSON (use `__` for nesting)
Options pattern gives typed, validated settings
Secrets belong in user-secrets or a vault

L136.a: Minimal APIs (.NET 6+) let you define HTTP endpoints with lambdas directly in Program.cs, without controllers: `app.MapGet("/items/{id}", (int id, IRepo r) => ...)`. They have less ceremony and good performance, with route groups, filters, validation and OpenAPI support for structuring larger apps.
p: Controllers still suit large, convention-heavy APIs
L136.f: How would you organise 100 minimal API endpoints?

L137.a: Use the built-in `ILogger<T>` abstraction injected via DI, with providers (console, debug, EventSource) or libraries like Serilog or NLog for sinks such as files, Seq or Elasticsearch. Use structured logging with message templates, appropriate log levels configured per category, and correlation ids for tracing requests.
p: Configure levels in appsettings Logging section
Structured sinks for search and dashboards
Don't log secrets or personal data
L137.f: What is the benefit of structured logging over string concatenation?

L138.a: Program.cs is the entry point: it builds the host, registers services and configures the middleware pipeline. Before .NET 6, Startup.cs held `ConfigureServices` (DI registrations) and `Configure` (pipeline) while Program.cs only created the host; since .NET 6 the minimal hosting model puts everything in Program.cs, though Startup can still be used.
L138.f: How would you organise service registrations in a large app?

L139.a: Immutability makes strings thread-safe, lets them be safely shared and used as dictionary keys (their hash can't change), enables string interning, and avoids surprising side effects. Every "modification" creates a new string, so use StringBuilder for heavy concatenation in loops.

L140.a: Use a record for immutable data with value semantics: DTOs, messages, events, configuration values. Records give value-based equality, `with` expressions for copies, deconstruction and a readable ToString. Use a class for entities with identity and mutable behaviour.
p: EF Core entities are usually classes

L141.a: `Span<T>` is a stack-only view over contiguous memory (arrays, strings, stack memory, native memory). Slicing a span doesn't allocate or copy, so parsing and processing data with spans avoids garbage and GC pressure, which speeds up hot paths.
p: ref struct: can't be boxed, stored in fields or used across await
L141.f: Why can't you use Span<T> inside an async method across an await?

L142.a: `Task<T>` always allocates an object. `ValueTask<T>` is a struct that avoids the allocation when the result is often available synchronously, such as cached values, which reduces GC pressure in hot paths. It has rules: await it only once and don't await it concurrently.
p: Await only once; convert with AsTask() if needed
Use in hot paths and library APIs
Plain Task is simpler for most code
L142.f: When is ValueTask slower than Task?

L143.a: DbContext is not thread-safe and tracks changes for a unit of work. Scoped (one per HTTP request) gives each request its own instance with consistent tracking, and disposes it at the end. Singleton would share it across concurrent requests (bugs, memory growth); transient would split one request's work across instances.
p: One unit of work per request
Disposed automatically at the end of the scope
Use DbContextFactory or pooling in background services and Blazor
L143.f: How do you use DbContext in a BackgroundService?

L144.a: Middleware runs in the order registered, and each can short-circuit, so exception handling must wrap everything, authentication must run before authorization, and routing before endpoints. Use custom middleware for concerns that apply to every request regardless of MVC, and an action filter when you need action context like arguments, model state or specific controllers.
p: Wrong order → auth bypassed or errors unhandled
L144.f: Where would you validate an API key: middleware or filter?

L145.a: Controllers should only handle HTTP concerns: binding input, calling the application layer, mapping results to responses. Business logic in controllers is hard to test, reuse (from jobs or other endpoints) and maintain, and mixes transport details with rules. Put it in services or domain classes.
p: Reuse across APIs, jobs and messaging
L145.f: How do you decide what belongs in the domain vs the application service?

L146.a: EF Core runs DetectChanges to compare tracked entities with their snapshots, orders the inserts, updates and deletes, generates SQL (batched where possible), executes it inside a transaction, then updates generated keys and resets entity states to Unchanged. It returns the number of affected rows.
p: Interceptors and SaveChanges overrides can add auditing
L146.f: How would you add CreatedAt/UpdatedAt automatically?

L147.a: With tracking, EF stores each entity in the change tracker, takes a snapshot of its values and performs identity resolution. `AsNoTracking()` skips all of that, so it allocates less memory and does less CPU work, which matters for large read-only result sets.
p: Entities can't be saved without attaching
Ideal for queries that return DTOs or views
L147.f: When would AsNoTracking return duplicate objects for the same row?

L148.a: N+1 in EF Core comes from lazy loading or querying related data inside a loop: one query for the parent list plus one per item. Fix it with Include for the related data, or better, with a `Select` projection to a DTO that pulls only the needed columns in one query. Projections are preferable when you only need some fields or are building API responses; Include suits loading full graphs you'll modify.
p: Symptoms: many similar queries in logs
L148.f: How do you detect N+1 queries in development?

L149.a: Every INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE must also update each index on the table, which means extra I/O, page splits and locking. More indexes mean faster reads but slower writes and more storage, so index for real query patterns only.
p: Each index is another structure to maintain
Updates to indexed columns are costlier
L149.f: How do you find unused indexes?

L150.a: Look at the actual execution plan to see where time goes: table scans, missing indexes, bad joins, key lookups, sorts spilling to disk, or wrong row estimates from stale statistics. Check wait stats and locking, and test with realistic data, then fix with indexes, query rewrites or updated statistics.

L151.a: A covering index contains every column a query needs (in the key or as INCLUDE columns), so the database answers the query from the index alone without looking up the table rows. This removes key lookups and can make queries dramatically faster.
p: Key columns for filters/sorts; INCLUDE for selected columns
Larger indexes cost storage and writes
Design for your most important queries
L151.f: Why does SELECT * defeat covering indexes?
L151.c: CREATE INDEX IX_Orders_Customer ON Orders(CustomerId, OrderDate) INCLUDE (Total);

L152.a: Without pagination the server reads, serialises and sends all rows, and the client renders them all, wasting CPU, memory and bandwidth. Paging returns a small slice, keeping response times stable as data grows. Keyset (cursor) pagination scales better than large OFFSETs.
p: OFFSET gets slower on deep pages
Keyset: WHERE id > @last ORDER BY id
L152.f: How would you implement cursor-based pagination?

L153.a: Production differs in data volume, traffic, concurrency, network latency and configuration. Before optimising, gather evidence: latency percentiles (p95/p99), throughput, error rates, CPU and memory, GC pauses, thread pool queue length, database query times and external dependency latency, using APM and distributed tracing.
p: Bigger data → slow queries, missing indexes
Config: logging levels, debug builds, connection limits
Measure with APM/traces before changing code
L153.f: How would you reproduce a production-only slowdown safely?

L154.a: Symptoms are rising latency while CPU stays low, and growing request queues. Check thread pool metrics with `dotnet-counters` (thread count climbing, queue length), take a dump or trace with `dotnet-trace`/`dotnet-dump` to find many threads blocked in `.Result`, `.Wait()` or locks. Fix by going async all the way and removing sync-over-async.
p: Dumps show threads blocked on tasks
Short-term: raise min threads; real fix: async
L154.f: Why does the thread pool inject threads slowly?

L155.a: Use Redis (a distributed cache) when you run multiple app instances that must share the cache, when the cache must survive restarts, or when it's too large for process memory. In-memory caching is fastest and simplest for a single instance or per-node data that can be stale.
p: In-memory: fastest, per instance, lost on restart
Cache invalidation across nodes needs a distributed cache
L155.f: How do you avoid a cache stampede?

L156.a: JWTs are stateless, so you need some server-side state to revoke one early: keep a deny-list of revoked token ids (jti) until they expire, store a per-user token version or "valid after" timestamp and reject older tokens, or keep access tokens very short-lived and revoke the refresh token instead.
p: Deny-list jti in Redis until expiry
Token version / security stamp per user
Short access token + revocable refresh token
Rotate signing keys only in emergencies (logs everyone out)
L156.f: What's the cost of checking a deny-list on every request?

L157.a: A JWT payload is only base64url-encoded, not encrypted, so anyone holding the token can read it. Tokens also end up in logs, browser storage and proxies. Keep claims minimal (ids, roles, expiry) and fetch sensitive data from the server; use JWE if you truly need encrypted tokens.
p: Decode any JWT at jwt.io: payload is readable
Tokens leak via logs, URLs and storage
Never include passwords, PII or secrets

L158.a: Require authentication or API keys, apply rate limiting and quotas per client, validate and size-limit all input, and put it behind a gateway/WAF with bot protection. Monitor for unusual traffic, return generic errors, paginate responses, and use CAPTCHAs or proof-of-work on abuse-prone endpoints like sign-up.
L158.f: How would you rate-limit fairly behind a load balancer?

L159.a: The Framework Class Library is .NET's standard library of reusable types: collections, I/O, networking, LINQ, threading, text, XML/JSON, security and more, organised in namespaces such as `System`, `System.Collections.Generic` and `System.IO`. The Base Class Library (BCL) is its core subset.
L159.f: What's the difference between the BCL and the FCL?

L160.a: Static classes group members that don't need instance state, such as utility functions and extension methods; they can't be instantiated or inherited. They can have a static constructor (run once before first use) but no instance constructors and no non-static members.
p: Sealed and abstract under the hood
Extension methods must be in static classes
L160.f: When is a static class a design smell?

L161.a: The CLR manages memory automatically. Value types live inline (on the stack or inside objects); reference types are allocated on the managed heap and freed by a generational garbage collector (gen 0, 1, 2, plus the large object heap). Unmanaged resources (files, connections) are released deterministically with `IDisposable` and `using`.
p: Generational GC: most objects die young in gen 0
Finalizers are a last-resort safety net
L161.f: What causes memory leaks in a garbage-collected app?

L162.a: An extension method is a static method in a static class whose first parameter is marked with `this`; it can then be called as if it were an instance method of that type. LINQ is built this way.
p: Static class + `this` on the first parameter
Import the namespace to use it
Instance methods win over extensions with the same signature
L162.f: Can you write extension methods for interfaces?

L163.a: The compiler rewrites an async method into a state machine. At each `await` it checks whether the awaited task is complete; if not, it registers the rest of the method as a continuation and returns an incomplete Task to the caller, freeing the thread. When the operation finishes, the continuation is scheduled (via the SynchronizationContext or thread pool) and the state machine resumes at the next state.
p: No thread is held during I/O waits
Exceptions are stored in the Task and rethrown on await
L163.f: What does ConfigureAwait(false) change in this flow?

L164.a: Don't insert row by row. Stream the file with a library like ExcelDataReader or ClosedXML/EPPlus, validate rows in batches, and bulk-load with `SqlBulkCopy` (or EF Core bulk extensions) into a staging table, then merge into the real tables in one transaction. Run it as a background job and report progress and row errors to the user.
p: Stream reading to keep memory low
L164.f: How would you handle a file where 2% of rows are invalid?

L165.a: Normalise both strings, then compare character counts with an array or dictionary, or compare sorted characters.
p: Sorting is O(n log n) but short
L165.f: How would you group a list of words into anagram sets?

L166.a: Encapsulation hides internal state behind methods (a bank account exposes Deposit, not a public balance field). Abstraction exposes only what matters (you drive a car with a steering wheel, not by managing the engine). Inheritance reuses and specialises behaviour (SavingsAccount is an Account). Polymorphism lets one call behave differently per type (`shape.Area()` for circles and squares).
L166.f: Why is composition often preferred over inheritance?

L167.a: Compile-time (static) polymorphism is method overloading (and operator overloading): the compiler picks the method from the argument types. Runtime (dynamic) polymorphism is overriding virtual methods: the actual object's type decides which implementation runs.
L167.f: Can you overload by return type alone?

L169.a: Method hiding is when a derived class declares a member with the same signature as a non-virtual base member, using the `new` keyword. Which method runs depends on the variable's declared type, not the object's actual type, unlike overriding.
p: Usually a sign to rethink the design
L169.f: What warning do you get without the new keyword?

L170.a: `string` is immutable, so every change creates a new string, which is costly inside loops. `StringBuilder` keeps a mutable buffer and appends in place, which is much faster for many concatenations. For a few concatenations, plain strings or interpolation are fine and clearer.
L170.f: Is `a + b + c` in one expression slow?

L171.a: Explicit types state the type in code. `var` lets the compiler infer the type at compile time, so it is still strongly typed. `dynamic` skips compile-time checking and resolves members at runtime, so errors appear only when running; use it for COM interop or dynamic data, rarely otherwise.
p: var: compile-time inference, local variables only
dynamic: runtime binding, slower, no IntelliSense
Explicit: clearest when the type isn't obvious
L171.f: Can a var variable change type later?

L172.a: An array has a fixed size and a single element type. `ArrayList` is a legacy, resizable collection that stores `object`, so value types get boxed and you need casts. Use the generic `List<T>` instead of ArrayList in modern code.

L173.a: MVC splits an app into the Model (data and business rules), View (UI) and Controller (handles input). A request passes through middleware, routing selects a controller action, model binding and validation run, filters execute around the action, the action returns a result (usually a view with a model), and the view engine renders HTML for the response.
p: Filters wrap authorization, actions and results
Razor view engine renders the view
L173.f: Where would you put validation logic?

L174.a: ASP.NET MVC supports conventional routing, defined centrally with a pattern like `{controller=Home}/{action=Index}/{id?}`, and attribute routing, defined on controllers and actions with `[Route]` and `[HttpGet("...")]`. Areas add another level for large apps.
p: Conventional: one template for many controllers
Attribute: explicit routes per action, best for APIs
L174.f: Which routing would you use for a REST API and why?

L175.a: Common results: ViewResult (`View()`), PartialViewResult, JsonResult, ContentResult, FileResult, RedirectResult/RedirectToActionResult, StatusCodeResult (`Ok`, `NotFound`, `BadRequest`), EmptyResult and ObjectResult for APIs.
L175.f: What's the difference between Redirect and RedirectToAction?

L176.a: A partial view is a reusable piece of Razor markup rendered inside other views, like a product card or a form section. Use it to avoid duplication or to return HTML fragments for AJAX updates. Use View Components instead when the piece needs its own logic or data access.

L177.a: Get the actual execution plan and statistics (IO/TIME) to find the expensive operators, then fix the cause: add or adjust indexes, make predicates SARGable (no functions on indexed columns), avoid cursors and RBAR loops in favour of set-based logic, reduce row counts early, and handle parameter sniffing. Update statistics and check for blocking.
p: Actual plan + SET STATISTICS IO, TIME ON
Index scans → seeks with better indexes
OPTION(RECOMPILE) or plan guides for sniffing issues

L178.a: A primary key uniquely identifies each row and can't be NULL; a table has one. A unique key also enforces uniqueness but allows a NULL (one, in SQL Server) and there can be many. A clustered index defines the physical order of rows (one per table; the primary key by default). A non-clustered index is a separate structure pointing to rows; a table can have many.
p: PK = unique + not null + one per table
L178.f: Should the clustered index always be on the primary key?

L179.a: 200 OK, 201 Created, 204 No Content; 301/302 redirects and 304 Not Modified; 400 Bad Request, 401 Unauthorized (not authenticated), 403 Forbidden, 404 Not Found, 409 Conflict, 422 Unprocessable, 429 Too Many Requests; 500 Internal Server Error, 502 Bad Gateway, 503 Service Unavailable, 504 Gateway Timeout.
p: 2xx success, 3xx redirect, 4xx client error, 5xx server error
L179.f: Which status would you return for a validation error?

L180.a: Measure first: check APM traces and logs for slow endpoints and where time goes (database, external calls, CPU, GC, thread pool). Then fix the bottleneck: optimise queries and indexes, add caching, make I/O async, remove sync-over-async, cut payload sizes, enable response compression, and scale out if needed.
p: Profile DB queries; fix N+1 and missing indexes
Check thread pool and GC metrics
L180.f: How would you confirm the fix worked?

L181.a: Add resilience policies with Polly or Microsoft.Extensions.Http.Resilience: timeouts, retries with exponential backoff and jitter for transient errors, a circuit breaker to stop hammering a failing service, and a fallback (cached data or a friendly error). For non-urgent work, call the API asynchronously through a queue.
p: Queue and retry later for background work
L181.f: Why can unlimited retries make an outage worse?

L182.a: Make the operation idempotent: the client sends an idempotency key per payment attempt, the server stores it with the result under a unique constraint, and repeated requests with the same key return the stored result instead of charging again. Also disable the button client-side and use the payment provider's idempotency support.
p: Unique index on the key; check inside a transaction
Return the original response on replay
Payment gateways support idempotency keys too
L182.f: How long should you keep idempotency keys?

L183.a: Accept the request, store the job, return 202 Accepted with a job id, and process it in the background (a BackgroundService reading a queue, or Hangfire/Azure Functions/Service Bus). The client polls a status endpoint or receives a SignalR/webhook notification when it finishes.
p: Durable queue so jobs survive restarts
Notify via polling, SignalR or webhooks
L183.f: Why not just use Task.Run in the controller?

L184.a: Watch memory with dotnet-counters (GC heap size, gen 2 collections, LOH), take dumps at intervals with dotnet-dump or gcdump and compare which types grow and what roots hold them. Typical causes are unbounded caches, static collections, event handlers never removed, undisposed resources and large object allocations.
L184.f: What is the large object heap and why can it fragment?

L185.a: Register several implementations of an interface and choose at runtime: keyed services (.NET 8 `AddKeyedScoped` + `[FromKeyedServices]`), a factory that picks by customer or config, or the strategy pattern with `IEnumerable<IStrategy>` and a `CanHandle` method.
L185.f: How would you add a new customer type without touching existing code?

L186.a: Use optimistic concurrency: add a concurrency token (a `rowversion` column marked `[Timestamp]`). EF includes it in the UPDATE's WHERE clause; if another user changed the row, no rows match and EF throws `DbUpdateConcurrencyException`. Catch it, reload current values, and either merge, retry or show the user the conflict.
p: Resolve: client wins, store wins, or ask the user
Pessimistic locking only for short critical sections
L186.f: When is pessimistic locking a better choice?

L187.a: Gather evidence from production: structured logs with correlation ids, exception details, APM traces, and the exact inputs and environment (config, data, versions, load). Compare environments, reproduce with production-like data in staging, add targeted logging or feature flags if needed, and capture a memory dump for crashes or hangs.
p: Dumps and snapshot debugging for hard cases
L187.f: What information should every error log include?

L188.a: Make the API stateless so you can scale horizontally behind a load balancer, use async I/O everywhere, cache frequently read data, optimise and index database queries, use connection pooling, move slow work to queues, add rate limiting, and compress responses. Load test to find the next bottleneck.
p: Queues for heavy work; load testing
L188.f: How would you handle sessions when scaling out?

L189.a: Use the strangler fig pattern: identify bounded contexts, put a gateway in front, and extract one capability at a time into its own service with its own data, routing traffic gradually while the monolith keeps working. Start with low-risk, well-isolated domains, add observability and CI/CD first, and sync data with events during the transition.
p: Strangler fig behind an API gateway
L189.f: When should you not split a monolith?

L190.a: First restore service: declare an incident, assign an incident commander, assemble the right owners, and stabilise with rollbacks, failover, feature flags or traffic shedding guided by dashboards and traces. Communicate on a fixed cadence to executives and customers with impact, actions and ETA. After recovery, run a blameless post-mortem with timeline, root cause and tracked action items.
p: Clear roles: commander, comms, scribe, responders
Regular status updates in business terms
Blameless RCA with owners and deadlines
L190.f: How do you find which of 300 services is the origin of the failure?

L191.a: Inventory and prioritise apps by business value and migration effort, then create a paved road: templates for .NET 8, Dockerfiles, CI/CD pipelines, observability and security baselines. Migrate in waves, starting with simpler apps, use the .NET Upgrade Assistant, test thoroughly, run old and new side by side, and cut over gradually.
L191.f: How would you handle apps that depend on Windows-only APIs?

L192.a: Contain and investigate first (rotate secrets, revoke tokens, patch the hole), then harden: centralise identity on Entra ID with OAuth 2.0/OIDC, short-lived JWTs and MFA, least-privilege access, secrets in Key Vault, fix OWASP Top 10 risks, and add DevSecOps (SAST, dependency and container scanning, IaC checks) to every pipeline, with monitoring and incident drills.
p: Security scanning in CI/CD and continuous monitoring
L192.f: How would you secure service-to-service calls?

L193.a: Cache aggressively at every layer (CDN, Redis, in-memory), keep services stateless behind load balancers with autoscaling, process heavy or bursty work asynchronously through queues, tune the database (indexes, read replicas, partitioning, connection pooling), and trace everything with OpenTelemetry to find bottlenecks.
p: Distributed tracing, SLOs and load testing
L193.f: How do you keep caches consistent with the database?

L194.a: ASP.NET (classic) runs on .NET Framework, Windows/IIS only, with separate MVC and Web API stacks and System.Web. ASP.NET Core is a cross-platform, open-source rewrite that runs on Kestrel, has a unified MVC/Web API model, built-in DI, configuration and logging, a middleware pipeline, and much better performance.
L194.f: What replaced Global.asax in ASP.NET Core?

L195.a: Routing maps incoming URLs to endpoints (controller actions, Razor Pages, minimal API handlers). `UseRouting` matches the request to an endpoint and `UseEndpoints`/`Map...` executes it. Routes are defined conventionally or with attributes, with parameters, defaults and constraints such as `{id:int}`.
L195.f: How do you generate a URL to a named route?

L196.a: ASP.NET Core Web API is the framework for building HTTP APIs that return data (usually JSON) rather than HTML views. In ASP.NET Core, MVC and Web API share the same controller base; API controllers use `ControllerBase` with `[ApiController]`, while MVC controllers derive from `Controller` and return views. In classic ASP.NET they were separate frameworks.
p: Minimal APIs as a lighter alternative
L196.f: What does [ApiController] change about model binding?

L197.a: .NET 10 (LTS, November 2025) brings runtime and JIT performance improvements, better Native AOT, file-based apps (`dotnet run app.cs`), built-in validation for Minimal APIs, OpenAPI 3.1 support, and EF Core 10 features such as LeftJoin and vector search. C# 14 adds extension members (extension properties and static extensions), the `field` keyword for properties, null-conditional assignment, implicit span conversions and more. Check the official release notes for the latest details.
L197.f: Why choose an LTS release for production?

L198.a: Abstraction is about design: exposing only essential behaviour and hiding complexity (an interface `IPaymentGateway.Pay()`). Encapsulation is about implementation: bundling data with methods and restricting access with access modifiers so state can only change through controlled methods.
p: Encapsulation → how its data is protected
Encapsulation via private fields and properties
L198.f: Can you have encapsulation without abstraction?

L199.a: A `sealed` class can't be inherited. Use it to prevent unintended extension, protect invariants or security-sensitive logic, and it can let the JIT devirtualise calls. `sealed` on an override method stops further overriding.
p: Records and static classes relate to sealing too
L199.f: Why would you seal a class by default?
