p: Load polyfills only for browsers that need them

L570.a: `display: none` removes the element from layout entirely: it takes no space, isn't rendered and is hidden from screen readers. `visibility: hidden` hides it visually but it still occupies its space; it's also hidden from assistive tech and not clickable. `opacity: 0` keeps it in layout and still interactive.
p: Use a visually-hidden class to hide only visually
L570.f: How do you hide text visually but keep it for screen readers?

L571.a: Media queries respond to the viewport (or device) size. Container queries respond to the size of a containing element marked with `container-type`, so a component adapts to the space it's given, such as a card that looks different in a sidebar and in the main column.
L571.f: Can you still use media queries alongside container queries?

L572.a: `:has()` selects an element if it contains (or is followed by) something matching the selector list inside it, which acts as a long-awaited parent selector. Examples: `.card:has(img)` styles cards with images, `form:has(:invalid)` styles a form with invalid fields, `h2:has(+ p)` targets headings followed by a paragraph.
p: Specificity of its most specific argument
Can be expensive on huge DOMs
L572.f: How would you style a label whose checkbox is checked using :has()?

L573.a: CSS custom properties (`--brand: #2b54d6`) are declared on elements and inherited down the tree, then used with `var(--brand, fallback)`. Unlike Sass variables they exist at runtime, so you can change them with media queries, classes or JavaScript, which makes theming (dark mode) easy.
p: Inherited and cascade like other properties
Change at runtime via JS: el.style.setProperty
L573.f: What does @property add to custom properties?

L574.a: Transitions animate a property change between two states when something triggers it (hover, class change) and need a start and end value. Animations use `@keyframes` to define multiple steps, can run automatically, loop, alternate and be paused, without a state change.
L574.f: How do you pause an animation on hover?

L575.a: Sass adds variables, nesting, mixins, functions, partials and imports/modules, loops and conditionals, making large stylesheets more organised and DRY. Many features now exist natively (custom properties, nesting), so modern projects use Sass less, or use PostCSS instead.
p: Native CSS now covers variables and nesting
L575.f: Sass variables vs CSS custom properties?

L576.a: Ship less CSS (remove unused styles, split CSS per route), inline the critical CSS needed for above-the-fold content and load the rest asynchronously, minify and compress, avoid @import chains, keep selectors simple, and animate only transform and opacity.
p: Critical CSS inline in the head
Load non-critical CSS with media/preload tricks
PurgeCSS/Tailwind JIT to remove unused rules
L576.f: How do you generate critical CSS automatically?

L577.a: BEM (Block, Element, Modifier) is a naming convention: a block is a standalone component (`.card`), an element is a part of it (`.card__title`), and a modifier is a variation (`.card--featured`). Flat, predictable class names keep specificity low and make CSS easier to scale.
L577.f: How does BEM compare with CSS Modules?

L578.a: Controllers in Web API are classes deriving from `ControllerBase`, usually with `[ApiController]` and `[Route]`, that group related endpoints for a resource. Their action methods handle HTTP requests, bind and validate input, call services and return results like `Ok(dto)`, `CreatedAtAction` or `NotFound()`.
p: Attribute routes and HTTP verb attributes
L578.f: Why derive from ControllerBase rather than Controller?

L579.a: Conventional routing defines URL patterns centrally (`{controller}/{action}/{id?}`) and matches controllers by convention, which suits MVC sites. Attribute routing puts routes on controllers and actions (`[Route("api/orders")]`, `[HttpGet("{id:int}")]`), giving precise control, which is preferred for REST APIs.

L580.a: Model binding maps data from the HTTP request (route values, query string, form fields, headers and body) to action method parameters and model properties, converting types automatically. Attributes like `[FromBody]`, `[FromQuery]`, `[FromRoute]` and `[FromHeader]` control the source, and validation runs after binding.
p: Sources: route, query, form, body, headers
Custom model binders for special formats
ModelState holds binding and validation errors
L580.f: Why can only one parameter use [FromBody]?

L581.a: Content negotiation lets the client choose the response format via the `Accept` header (for example JSON or XML), and the server picks a matching output formatter. ASP.NET Core uses JSON by default; add XML formatters with `AddXmlSerializerFormatters()`, and return 406 if `ReturnHttpNotAcceptable` is enabled and nothing matches.
L581.f: How is the request body format detected?

L582.a: Swagger (OpenAPI) describes your API in a machine-readable document and Swagger UI lets you explore and test endpoints in the browser. In ASP.NET Core add Swashbuckle (`AddEndpointsApiExplorer`, `AddSwaggerGen`, `UseSwagger`, `UseSwaggerUI`); .NET 9+ also has built-in `AddOpenApi`/`MapOpenApi`, with UIs like Scalar or Swagger UI.
p: XML comments and attributes enrich docs
Generate client SDKs from the spec
L582.f: How would you add JWT auth to Swagger UI?

L583.a: Use data annotations (`[Required]`, `[StringLength]`, `[Range]`, `[EmailAddress]`) or FluentValidation for richer rules. Validation runs after model binding; with `[ApiController]` an invalid model returns 400 with problem details automatically; otherwise check `ModelState.IsValid`. Implement `IValidatableObject` or custom attributes for cross-field rules.
L583.f: How do you customise the validation error response?

L584.a: Write a class with a constructor taking `RequestDelegate next` and an `InvokeAsync(HttpContext context)` method that does work before and/or after `await _next(context)`, then register it with `app.UseMiddleware<T>()` (usually through an extension method). Inject scoped services as `InvokeAsync` parameters, not in the constructor, because middleware is a singleton.
L584.f: Why can't you inject a DbContext into the middleware constructor?

L585.a: Use HTTPS everywhere, authenticate with OAuth 2.0/OIDC (JWT bearer) and authorize with policies, validate all input, rate-limit, restrict CORS, keep secrets in a vault, log and monitor, and keep dependencies patched. An API gateway (Azure API Management, AWS API Gateway, YARP, Kong) is a single entry point in front of many services that centralises authentication, rate limiting, routing, caching, versioning and analytics; use it when you have several services or external consumers.
p: Gateway for cross-cutting concerns across services
L585.f: What belongs in the gateway vs in each service?

L586.a: Use response caching (`[ResponseCache]` headers so clients and proxies cache), output caching (.NET 7+ `AddOutputCache`/`CacheOutput()` stores responses on the server), in-memory caching with `IMemoryCache` for data, and distributed caching with Redis (`IDistributedCache`/HybridCache) for multi-instance apps. Choose expirations carefully and invalidate on writes; use ETags for conditional requests.
L586.f: How do you invalidate output cache entries when data changes?

L587.a: HATEOAS (Hypermedia as the Engine of Application State) is a REST constraint where responses include links to related actions and resources, so clients discover what they can do next from the response instead of hard-coding URLs, for example an order response containing links to cancel or pay.
p: Clients follow links instead of building URLs
L587.f: What benefit does HATEOAS give API evolution?

L588.a: Design APIs around business capabilities with clear contracts (OpenAPI), stateless services behind a gateway, pagination, filtering, idempotent writes, async messaging for long or cross-service work, and resilience (timeouts, retries, circuit breakers). Version only on breaking changes: prefer additive, backward-compatible changes; when you must break, use URL or header versions, run versions side by side, publish deprecation timelines and consumer-driven contract tests.
p: Explicit major versions with deprecation policy
L588.f: How do contract tests prevent breaking consumers?

L589.a: An idempotent operation gives the same result no matter how many times it's applied. GET, PUT and DELETE should be idempotent by design. For POST and payments, the client sends an `Idempotency-Key`; the server stores the key with the result (unique constraint) and returns the saved response on retries instead of executing again.
p: Design PUT/DELETE to be safe to repeat
Handle concurrent duplicates with a lock or unique index
L589.f: What should happen if the same key arrives with a different body?

L590.a: OpenTelemetry is an open, vendor-neutral standard and SDK for collecting traces, metrics and logs. Distributed tracing follows a single request across services: each service creates spans that share a trace id propagated through HTTP headers (W3C traceparent), so you can see the full call graph and where time is spent in tools like Jaeger, Zipkin, Application Insights or Grafana Tempo.
p: Traces, metrics, logs under one standard
Spans with trace/span ids propagated across calls
Auto-instrumentation for ASP.NET Core, HttpClient, EF Core
Export to any backend via OTLP
L590.f: How does sampling affect what you can see?

L591.a: Measure first, then: optimise database access (indexes, projections, AsNoTracking, no N+1), cache hot data, make I/O async, return paginated and smaller payloads, enable response compression and HTTP/2, use connection pooling and HttpClientFactory, offload heavy work to background jobs, and scale out. Re-measure after each change.
L591.f: Which metric tells you you've fixed the right thing?

L592.a: Useful patterns: virtual scrolling (render only visible rows), composition and compound components (flexible APIs), state machines (explicit UI states like idle/loading/error), feature flags (ship dark, roll out gradually), skeleton loading (perceived performance), design tokens (consistent theming), container/presentational split, optimistic updates, and error boundaries.
p: Consistency: design tokens and component libraries
L592.f: When does a state machine beat a few boolean flags?

L593.a: A hydration error means the HTML the server rendered doesn't match the first client render of the same tree: different text, attributes or element structure. Common causes: using `Date.now()`, `Math.random()` or locale formatting that differs between server and browser, reading `window`/localStorage during render, invalid HTML nesting the browser repairs (a div inside a p), browser extensions modifying the DOM, and data that changed between the two renders.
p: Same components must produce identical markup on both sides
suppressHydrationWarning only for known, harmless cases
L593.f: How would you render a timestamp without a mismatch?

L596.a: Server Components can be async and fetch data directly on the server (database, internal APIs) during rendering, close to the data, without client-side useEffect, loading waterfalls in the browser, or exposing secrets. The result streams as rendered UI; only interactive client components ship JS. Caching and revalidation are handled by the framework, and Suspense boundaries stream slower parts.
p: `async function Page() { const data = await db.query(...) }`
No API layer needed for internal reads
Less client JS and no client fetch waterfalls
L596.f: How do you avoid request waterfalls between nested server components?

L610.a: Arrow functions never get their own `this`; they use the surrounding scope's. Class methods get `this` from how they're called, so passing `this.method` as a callback loses it unless you bind it or define the method as an arrow class field. In DOM event handlers registered with a normal function, `this` is the element (`event.currentTarget`); with an arrow function it's the outer `this`.
p: Class method: call-site this; bind or arrow field
L610.f: Why do React class components often bind handlers in the constructor?

L611.a: A Provider holds a value; any component below that calls `useContext` reads the nearest provider's value and re-renders whenever that value changes (by `Object.is`). It hurts performance when the value is a new object every render or changes frequently, because every consumer re-renders, even if it uses only part of it. Fix by memoising the value, splitting contexts, separating state and dispatch, or using a store with selectors.
p: Provider → consumers re-render on value change
New object each render = re-render all consumers
L611.f: Why does memoising the consumer component not stop it re-rendering on context change?

L612.a: LCP: speed up the server response, preload and prioritise the hero image (fetchpriority="high", modern formats), remove render-blocking CSS/JS, use SSR/SSG and a CDN. CLS: give images and embeds explicit dimensions, reserve space for ads and dynamic content, avoid inserting content above existing content, and use font-display with size-adjusted fallbacks. INP: keep handlers fast, break long tasks, defer non-urgent work (transitions), reduce JS and third-party scripts.
p: Measure with field data (CrUX/RUM), not only Lighthouse
L612.f: How do you find which interaction causes a poor INP?

L613.a: Define colours as CSS custom properties with light and dark values (switched by a `data-theme` attribute or class on `<html>` and the `prefers-color-scheme` media query), keep the user's choice in context and localStorage, apply it before first paint with a tiny inline script to avoid a flash, and expose a toggle.
p: Inline script in <head> prevents flash of wrong theme
L613.f: How would you support a "system" option alongside light and dark?

L614.a: XSS: rely on framework escaping, sanitise any HTML, avoid eval and inline scripts, set a strict CSP. CSRF: SameSite cookies, CSRF tokens for cookie-based auth, check Origin. Token leakage: keep tokens in httpOnly Secure cookies or memory (not localStorage), never in URLs or logs, short lifetimes with refresh rotation. Secure flows: Authorization Code + PKCE with an IdP, HTTPS, MFA, logout that revokes tokens.
p: httpOnly cookies, no tokens in URLs
L614.f: Why is the implicit OAuth flow discouraged?

L615.a: Keep a deque of indices whose values are in decreasing order. For each new element, drop indices that left the window from the front and smaller values from the back, push the index, and once the first window is full the front is the maximum. O(n).
L615.f: Why is dq.shift() acceptable here, and how would you avoid it?

L616.a: Merge lists pairwise in a divide-and-conquer fashion (O(N log k)), or push each list's head into a min-heap and repeatedly pop the smallest. Divide and conquer is easiest in JavaScript since there's no built-in heap.
p: Pairwise merging halves the number of lists each round
L616.f: What's the complexity of merging them one by one into the result?

L617.a: Reverse by walking the list and pointing each node's next back to the previous node. Merge two sorted lists by repeatedly attaching the smaller head to a tail pointer, starting from a dummy node.
p: Return prev as the new head
L617.f: Write the recursive version of reverse.

L618.a: Separate people from the problem: make sure each option is understood, agree on criteria (performance, maintainability, cost, deadline), and use data, prototypes or small spikes to compare. If it's still split, the decision owner decides, the reasoning is written down (an ADR), and everyone commits; revisit if new evidence appears.
L618.f: Give an example where you disagreed and committed.

L619.a: Encapsulate fetch state in a hook that accepts a URL and options, aborts on change/unmount, exposes data, error, loading and a refetch function.
L619.f: Why isn't opts in the dependency array, and how would you handle it?

L620.a: Decode the user's role from the auth context (set after login from the JWT or a /me endpoint), and wrap routes in a guard that redirects unauthenticated users to login and unauthorised users to a forbidden page. Use nested routes with `<Outlet />` so whole sections share a guard.
p: Auth context provides user and role
L620.f: How do you send the user back to the page they wanted after login?

L621.a: Use a reducer: add increments quantity if the item exists, remove filters it out, update sets a quantity (removing at 0), and derive the total with reduce rather than storing it.
L621.f: How would you handle prices in floating point safely?

L622.a: On file selection, validate the type and size, create a preview URL with `URL.createObjectURL(file)` (revoke it on change/unmount), show it in an ``, and on submit send the file with FormData.
p: Show progress with XHR or axios onUploadProgress

L623.a: A store keeps state, a reducer, and a set of listeners: getState returns state, dispatch runs the reducer and notifies listeners, subscribe adds a listener and returns an unsubscribe. Connect it to React with useSyncExternalStore.
L623.f: How would you add middleware support?

L625.a: Because arrays are objects and `===` compares object references, not contents. Each `[1,2]` literal creates a new array in memory, so they're two different objects.
p: Compare with a loop, every() or a deep-equal helper
L625.f: Is JSON.stringify a good way to compare arrays?

L626.a: `+` is overloaded: if either operand is a string it concatenates, so `4 + '3'` is "43". `-` is only numeric, so `'3'` is converted to a number and `4 - '3'` is 1.
p: Leads to subtle bugs with form inputs

L627.a: `filter(Boolean)` removes falsy values: false, 0, -0, 0n, "", null, undefined and NaN. Objects used as keys in a plain object are converted to the string "[object Object]", so different objects map to the same key and overwrite each other silently; use a Map (or WeakMap) when keys are objects.
p: Boolean as a predicate keeps truthy values
Map keeps object identity as the key
L627.f: How would you keep 0 but remove null and undefined?

L629.a: Use fetch with async/await, check `response.ok`, parse JSON, and handle errors (optionally with a timeout via AbortSignal).
p: fetch doesn't reject on HTTP errors
L629.f: How would you add query parameters safely?

L630.a: Wrap the feature in a feature flag read at runtime from a flag service or remote config (LaunchDarkly, Unleash, Azure App Configuration, ConfigCat, or your own endpoint). Turning the flag off in the dashboard disables the feature for everyone or specific users instantly, without redeploying. Keep a safe default, cache flags, and remove old flags.
L630.f: What are the risks of having too many feature flags?

L631.a: Micro-frontends split a frontend into independently built and deployed parts owned by different teams. Types by composition: build-time (packages combined at build), server-side composition (SSI/edge or server assembling fragments), client-side runtime composition (Module Federation, import maps, single-spa), iframes (strong isolation, poor UX), and Web Components as framework-agnostic wrappers.
L631.f: Which type would you choose for a migration from Angular to React?

L632.a: `useEffect` runs side effects after render (fetching, subscriptions, DOM work) and returns nothing used in rendering. `useMemo` runs during render and returns a cached computed value that's recalculated only when dependencies change. Don't use useEffect + setState to compute derived values; use useMemo or plain calculation instead.
p: Deriving state with effects causes extra renders
useMemo must not have side effects
L632.f: Why is "useEffect to sync derived state" an anti-pattern?

L633.a: Sort descending and take index k-1 (O(n log n)), keep a min-heap of size k (O(n log k)), or use quickselect (average O(n)).
p: Heap of size k for streams
L633.f: Why does randomising the pivot matter?

L634.a: Start from the operations the system needs. For an elevator: pending requests per direction fit two priority queues or sorted sets (min-heap for floors above going up, max-heap for floors below going down, as in the SCAN/LOOK algorithm); elevator state is a small object or state machine; requests from many elevators use a queue with a dispatcher; hash maps give O(1) lookup of elevators or floors. Choose by access pattern and complexity, not habit.
p: List required operations and their frequency
L634.f: How would you assign requests across multiple elevators?

L635.a: `a || b` returns b when a is any falsy value (0, "", false, NaN, null, undefined). `a ?? b` returns b only when a is null or undefined, so legitimate values like 0 or "" are kept. Use ?? for defaults when 0/empty are valid.
p: Can't mix ?? with || or && without parentheses

L636.a: `ReactDOM.render(<App />, el)` is the legacy root API; in React 18 it runs in legacy mode without concurrent features and was removed in React 19. `createRoot(el).render(<App />)` creates a concurrent root that enables automatic batching everywhere, transitions, Suspense improvements and streaming; `hydrateRoot` replaces `hydrate` for SSR.
L636.f: What changed about batching inside setTimeout with createRoot?

L637.a: Circular dependencies happen when an effect updates a value that is also its dependency (directly or through another effect), causing loops. Break the cycle: derive the value during render instead of syncing it, use functional updates so the state isn't a dependency, add a guard comparing new and old values, merge related effects, move logic into the event handler that causes the change, or use a ref for values that shouldn't trigger the effect.
p: Event handlers instead of chained effects
L637.f: When are chained effects legitimately needed?

L638.a: Next.js automatically splits code per route (each page/layout gets its own chunks) and shares common dependencies, so users only download what the current route needs; `next/dynamic` adds component-level splitting, and the Link component prefetches routes in view. For SSR it renders pages on the server (per request or statically, depending on data and caching), streams HTML with Suspense, and hydrates client components in the browser.
p: Route-based chunks out of the box
L638.f: How does Next.js decide whether a route is static or dynamic?

L639.a: `.env.local` holds local overrides and secrets for your machine (not committed) and is loaded in all environments except test. `.env.production` holds defaults used when running `next build`/`next start` in production mode (and `.env.development` for `next dev`). Precedence: `.env.$(NODE_ENV).local` > `.env.local` > `.env.$(NODE_ENV)` > `.env`. Only variables prefixed `NEXT_PUBLIC_` are exposed to the browser.
p: NEXT_PUBLIC_ prefix → bundled into client code
L639.f: Are NEXT_PUBLIC_ values read at build time or runtime?

L640.a: Optimistic updates change the UI immediately and roll back if the server fails, giving instant feedback for actions that usually succeed (likes, toggles, reordering). Pessimistic updates wait for the server's confirmation before updating the UI, which is safer for critical or failure-prone actions (payments, deletions with side effects).
p: Optimistic: fast UX, needs rollback logic
Pessimistic: simple and accurate, slower feel
Choose by failure rate and cost of being wrong
L640.f: How do you handle two optimistic updates in flight at once?

L641.a: Use OAuth 2.0 / OpenID Connect with the Authorization Code flow + PKCE: the app redirects to the provider (Google, GitHub), the user consents, the provider redirects back with a code, your backend exchanges it for tokens, verifies the ID token, finds or creates the user (linking accounts by verified email), then issues its own session: a short-lived access JWT and a rotating refresh token in httpOnly cookies. Handle state/nonce for CSRF and replay, logout and token revocation.
p: Code flow + PKCE, state and nonce
Backend exchanges code; never expose client secret
Own session tokens, httpOnly cookies, refresh rotation
L641.f: Why shouldn't you use the provider's access token as your app's session?

L642.a: A client-side limiter controls how often the SPA calls the API: wrap the API client with a token bucket or sliding window (e.g. 10 requests/second), queue extra requests instead of dropping them, cap concurrency, dedupe identical in-flight requests, debounce noisy triggers, and back off when the server returns 429 with Retry-After. The server must still enforce its own limits.
L642.f: How would you prioritise user-initiated requests over background ones?

L643.a: Core: a single store with getState, dispatch and subscribe; slices that define initial state and reducers and auto-generate action creators; immutable updates made ergonomic with Immer; middleware for async logic and logging; memoised selectors; React bindings via useSyncExternalStore with selector-based subscriptions to limit re-renders; DevTools integration; and a data-fetching layer with caching and invalidation.
L643.f: How would you implement time-travel debugging?

L644.a: Use cursor-based pagination from the API (stable under inserts), fetch the next page when an IntersectionObserver sentinel nears the viewport, keep pages in a cache keyed by query (useInfiniteQuery), guard against duplicate and out-of-order requests, virtualise rendering, handle end-of-list, errors with retry, and restore scroll position on back navigation. Page size can adapt to viewport and network.
L644.f: Why is offset pagination problematic for feeds?

L645.a: Represent the document with a CRDT (Yjs, Automerge) or Operational Transformation so concurrent edits merge consistently. Clients apply edits locally for instant feedback, send operations over WebSockets to a collaboration server that broadcasts to others and persists snapshots plus operation logs. Add presence (cursors, selections), offline editing with sync on reconnect, permissions, version history, and scaling by sharding documents across servers.
p: CRDT or OT for conflict-free merging
L645.f: CRDT vs OT: what are the trade-offs?

L646.a: `Hashtable` is the older non-generic collection that stores keys and values as `object` (boxing, casts, no type safety) and is thread-safe for one writer. `Dictionary<TKey,TValue>` is generic, type-safe, faster, throws KeyNotFoundException for missing keys, and isn't thread-safe; use ConcurrentDictionary for concurrency.
p: Missing key: Hashtable returns null, Dictionary throws
L646.f: Why use TryGetValue instead of ContainsKey + indexer?

L647.a: Primary constructors (C# 12 for classes and structs, earlier for records) declare parameters right on the type, `class OrderService(IRepo repo, ILogger log)`, and those parameters are in scope throughout the class; ideal for DI. Secondary (regular) constructors are additional constructors in the body; when a type has a primary constructor, other constructors must chain to it with `: this(...)`.
p: Parameters aren't automatically properties in classes (they are in records)
L647.f: Why might you still assign primary constructor parameters to readonly fields?

L648.a: `obj.ToString()` throws a NullReferenceException if obj is null. `Convert.ToString(obj)` handles null and returns an empty string (or null for a null string argument). Both otherwise call the object's ToString implementation.
L648.f: What does string interpolation do with null values?

L649.a: `First()` returns the first matching element and throws if none. `FirstOrDefault()` returns default (null/0) if none. `Single()` returns the only matching element and throws if there are zero or more than one. `SingleOrDefault()` returns default for zero matches but still throws for more than one.
p: First*: stops at the first match
Single expresses "exactly one" intent, e.g. by primary key
L649.f: Which is faster on a database query and why?

L650.a: Neither is "better"; they have different purposes. GET retrieves data, is safe and idempotent, cacheable and bookmarkable, with parameters in the URL (visible, length-limited). POST sends data in the body to create or process something, isn't cached or idempotent by default, and is used for sensitive or large inputs.
p: GET: read, cacheable, params in URL
L650.f: Is sending a password in a GET query string unsafe even over HTTPS?

L651.a: Accept page and pageSize (or a cursor) as query parameters, validate and cap pageSize, apply `Skip((page-1)*size).Take(size)` on an ordered IQueryable so the database paginates, run a Count for the total, and return items plus metadata (total, page, hasNext). For large tables use keyset pagination (`WHERE Id > @lastId`).
L651.f: Why can OFFSET-based paging return duplicates when data changes?

L652.a: Call the AI provider's API from the backend through an SDK or HttpClient (Semantic Kernel, Microsoft.Extensions.AI, or the provider's .NET SDK), keep the API key in a vault, stream responses to the client, and add retries, timeouts and rate limits. A chatbot design: conversation history store, a system prompt, retrieval (RAG) over your documents for grounded answers, tools/functions for actions, moderation and logging. To handle wrong answers, ground responses in retrieved sources and show citations, constrain with clear instructions, validate outputs, let users report errors, evaluate regularly, and hand off to a human for high-stakes cases.
p: Evaluation and monitoring of answer quality
L652.f: How would you test a chatbot's answers before release?

L653.a: Don't bypass authorization silently inside the method. Model the condition as part of the policy instead: use a custom authorization requirement/handler or resource-based authorization with `IAuthorizationService.AuthorizeAsync(User, resource, "Policy")`, so the exception is explicit, tested and audited. If the endpoint must be reachable without auth in some cases, mark it `[AllowAnonymous]` and enforce the rules inside, carefully.
p: AllowAnonymous + explicit checks if truly needed
Log and test the bypass path
L653.f: How does resource-based authorization differ from policy attributes?

L654.a: Configure the JSON serializer to skip nulls: in System.Text.Json set `DefaultIgnoreCondition = JsonIgnoreCondition.WhenWritingNull` in `AddJsonOptions`, or use `[JsonIgnore(Condition = JsonIgnoreCondition.WhenWritingNull)]` on specific properties. With Newtonsoft.Json use `NullValueHandling.Ignore`.
p: Clients must treat missing and null the same

L655.a: `SELECT * INTO NewTable FROM OldTable WHERE 1 = 0` creates a new table with the same columns and data types but copies no rows (the condition is always false), a quick way to clone structure. `WHERE 1 = 1` is always true and copies all rows; it's also used as a placeholder in dynamically built queries so every extra condition can be appended with AND.
p: SELECT INTO doesn't copy indexes, constraints or keys
Postgres/MySQL use CREATE TABLE ... AS / LIKE
L655.f: How would you copy indexes and constraints too?

L656.a: Use OFFSET/FETCH (SQL Server, standard) or LIMIT/OFFSET (MySQL, PostgreSQL) with a deterministic ORDER BY. For deep pages, keyset pagination is faster.
p: Always ORDER BY a unique key
L656.f: How do you return the total count efficiently?

L657.a: Use a DEFAULT constraint for age and a CHECK constraint restricting gender to the allowed values.
p: DEFAULT applies when the column is omitted
Some databases use ENUM types instead
L657.f: What happens if you explicitly insert NULL into Age?

L658.a: Use DENSE_RANK to find the 3rd highest distinct value, and GROUP BY with HAVING to find names that appear more than once.
p: OFFSET 2 ROWS FETCH NEXT 1 with DISTINCT also works
Join back to get full duplicate rows
L658.f: How would you delete the duplicates but keep one row each?
L658.c:
SELECT DISTINCT Salary FROM (SELECT Salary, DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY Salary DESC) r FROM Employee) t WHERE r = 3;
SELECT Name, COUNT(*) AS Cnt FROM Employee GROUP BY Name HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;

L659.a: Create an object whose methods update an internal total and return the object itself; expose the result through a `value` getter.
p: Return this (or the object) from each method
L659.f: How would you make each call return a new immutable calculator?

L660.a: Put the count state and the increment, decrement and reset functions in a hook so any component can reuse the logic.
L660.f: How would you add a maximum value?

L661.a: The parent passes a callback to the child; whenever the child's count changes, the child reports it through the callback (in an effect or right in its handler), and the parent stores the latest value in a ref or state to show on its button click. Alternatively lift the state to the parent entirely.
p: Callback prop reports child state upward
Parent keeps the latest value in a ref (no re-render)
Lifting state up is often simpler
L661.f: How would you do it with useImperativeHandle instead?

L662.a: First-class functions can be treated like any value: stored in variables, passed as arguments, returned from functions and kept in data structures. A pure function always returns the same output for the same inputs and has no side effects; an impure function depends on or changes external state (globals, I/O, DOM, randomness, time).
p: Impure: needed for I/O, isolate it
L662.f: Is a function that logs to the console pure?

L663.a: A `WeakRef` holds a reference to an object without preventing it from being garbage collected; `deref()` returns the object or undefined if it was collected. `FinalizationRegistry` lets you run a cleanup callback after collection. They suit caches of large objects, but GC timing is unpredictable, so code must not depend on when (or whether) objects are collected. WeakMap/WeakSet are usually the better tool.
p: Avoid for program logic; GC is non-deterministic
L663.f: Why is WeakMap safer than WeakRef for associating data with objects?

L664.a: Streams process data in chunks as it arrives instead of loading it all into memory (Readable, Writable, Duplex, Transform). Backpressure is the mechanism that slows a fast producer when the consumer can't keep up: `write()` returns false when the internal buffer is full and you wait for the `drain` event. `pipe()`/`pipeline()` handle backpressure automatically.
p: Constant memory for large files and network data
Use stream.pipeline for errors and cleanup
L664.f: What happens if you ignore backpressure?
L664.c:
const { pipeline } = require("node:stream/promises");
await pipeline(fs.createReadStream("big.csv"), zlib.createGzip(), fs.createWriteStream("big.csv.gz"));

L665.a: V8 gives objects with the same shape a shared hidden class and optimises property access with inline caches. `delete` changes the shape in a way that often switches the object to slow "dictionary mode", making property access slower and de-optimising functions that use it. Prefer setting the property to undefined or building a new object without it (rest destructuring).
p: Hurts inline caching in hot code
Use undefined, rest destructuring or Map for dynamic keys
L665.f: When is a Map better than an object for frequently added and removed keys?

L666.a: Closures keep references to variables (bindings), not snapshots of values: if the variable changes later, the closure sees the new value. The engine keeps the captured environment alive as long as any closure referencing it is reachable; once no closure references it, the GC can collect it. Engines may keep the whole shared context alive even if a closure uses only part of it.
p: Loops with var share one binding; let gives one per iteration
Reachable closure → captured scope stays in memory
L666.f: Why does a closure in a for-var loop see the final value?

L667.a: JavaScript itself runs on one thread, but I/O is handed off to the host: browsers' network and timer machinery, or Node's libuv (OS async APIs and a thread pool for some operations). The JS thread continues running other code; when the I/O completes, its callback (or promise continuation) is queued, and the event loop runs it once the call stack is free.
p: libuv thread pool for fs, DNS, crypto
Callbacks queued back to the single JS thread
L667.f: Which Node operations use the thread pool?

L668.a: V8 assigns hidden classes (shapes) to objects based on their properties and the order they were added. Objects sharing a shape let V8 use inline caches and optimised machine code for property access. Adding properties in different orders, adding them later, deleting them or mixing types creates many shapes (polymorphic/megamorphic code) and slows things down. Initialise all properties in constructors, in the same order.
p: Inline caches depend on stable shapes
Avoid delete and late property additions
L668.f: What does "megamorphic" mean for a property access?

L669.a: Memoisation (React.memo, useMemo, useCallback, selectors) decides whether to recompute by comparing references. Mutating an object in place keeps the same reference, so the comparison says "unchanged" and the memoised value or component isn't updated, showing stale data. Always create new objects for changes.
p: Reference comparison can't see in-place mutations
L669.f: How would you detect accidental mutation in development?

L670.a: Lazy loading components defers downloading their code (React.lazy, dynamic import) until they're needed, reducing the initial bundle. Lazy loading data defers fetching data until it's needed (on scroll, tab open, or interaction), reducing initial requests and server load. They're complementary; with Suspense you can coordinate both.
p: Data on demand: fewer initial requests
Prefetch on hover or idle to hide latency
L670.f: How do you avoid a waterfall when both code and data load lazily?

L671.a: useState holds local state (form fields, toggles). useEffect runs side effects after render (fetching, subscriptions, syncing with external systems). useMemo caches expensive computed values. useCallback keeps function references stable for memoised children or effect dependencies. useRef stores DOM nodes or mutable values that persist without re-rendering (timers, previous values).
p: useRef: DOM access and instance variables
L671.f: Which of these do you overuse most often, and why?

L672.a: Analyse the bundle (webpack-bundle-analyzer, source-map-explorer, Rollup visualizer), split by route and by heavy features with dynamic imports, share vendor chunks sensibly, remove or replace heavy dependencies, ensure tree shaking (ES modules, sideEffects flag), lazy-load below-the-fold UI and third-party scripts, and enforce size budgets in CI.
L672.f: How do you split a large shared component library effectively?

L673.a: `1 + 2` logs 3, `1 + "2"` logs "12" (string concatenation), and `1 + A` throws `ReferenceError: A is not defined` because A was never declared, which stops the script at that line.
L673.f: What if A were declared with `let A;` and not assigned?

L674.a: Clarify requirements and scale first (users, features, teams, performance targets), then design: rendering strategy (SSR/SSG/CSR per area), module boundaries (feature folders, packages or micro-frontends), state strategy (server cache, local, global), API contracts, design system, performance budgets, accessibility, i18n, security, observability, testing pyramid and CI/CD. Discuss trade-offs and how it evolves.
L674.f: How would you let 10 teams ship independently in this design?

L675.a: An id must be unique in the page and has high specificity (1,0,0); a class can be reused on many elements and has lower specificity (0,1,0). Use classes for styling and ids for unique hooks (anchors, label `for`, ARIA references). Styling by id makes overrides hard.
p: ids for fragments and accessibility references
L675.f: How many classes does it take to beat one id selector?

L676.a: React has a simple mental model (UI as a function of state), a component model that scales, a huge ecosystem and community, flexibility to choose routing/state/styling tools, React Native for mobile, strong frameworks (Next.js, Remix), modern features like Server Components and concurrent rendering, backing from Meta, and a large hiring pool. Compared with Angular it's a library, lighter and less opinionated; compared with Vue/Svelte it has a bigger ecosystem.

L677.a: A pure component (`React.PureComponent`, or `React.memo` for functions) skips re-rendering when its props and state are shallowly equal, a performance optimisation. A higher-order component is a function that takes a component and returns a new one with extra behaviour (auth, data, logging), a code-reuse pattern. They're unrelated concepts and can be combined.
L677.f: How can an HOC break React.memo on the wrapped component?

L678.a: Use semantic HTML in JSX (buttons, not clickable divs), label form controls (`htmlFor`), manage focus on route changes and in modals, add alt text, announce dynamic updates with live regions, support keyboard interaction for custom widgets, use ARIA correctly, keep contrast high, and test with eslint-plugin-jsx-a11y, axe/jest-axe and screen readers. Fragments help avoid invalid markup.
L678.f: How do you announce route changes to screen reader users in a SPA?

L679.a: Render crawlable HTML for important pages (SSR/SSG with Next.js or prerendering), set unique titles, meta descriptions and canonical URLs per page (React 19 metadata or framework APIs), use semantic headings, structured data (JSON-LD), clean URLs with real links (<a href>), correct status codes, sitemaps and robots.txt, fast Core Web Vitals, and lazy-load without hiding important content.
p: Real links, semantic HTML, structured data
L679.f: Why does client-only rendering risk delayed indexing?

L680.a: Template literals use backticks and allow embedded expressions with `${...}`, multi-line strings without escapes, and tagged templates where a function processes the string parts and values (used for styled-components, GraphQL queries and safe HTML).
L680.f: How do tagged templates help prevent XSS?
L680.c:
const name = "Asha";
`Hello, ${name}! You have ${2 + 3} new messages.`;

L681.a: A Promise represents a single future value, is eager (starts immediately), and can't be cancelled. An Observable (RxJS) represents a stream of zero or more values over time, is lazy (runs only when subscribed), can be cancelled by unsubscribing, and offers operators (map, filter, debounceTime, switchMap) for composing streams.
L681.f: When would you choose RxJS over promises in a frontend?

L682.a: `slice(start, end)` returns a shallow copy of part of an array without changing the original. `splice(start, deleteCount, ...items)` changes the original array in place, removing and/or inserting elements, and returns the removed elements.
L682.f: How would you insert an element at index 2 without mutating?

L684.a: `Object.keys(obj)` returns an array of the object's own enumerable string keys, `Object.values(obj)` their values, and `Object.entries(obj)` [key, value] pairs. Entries pair well with `Object.fromEntries` for transforming objects.
p: Same order: integer keys ascending, then insertion order
L684.f: How do you include symbol keys?

L683.a: Measure with DevTools and real-user metrics, then: ship less JavaScript (code splitting, tree shaking), avoid long tasks (chunk work, Web Workers), minimise DOM work and layout thrashing (batch reads/writes), debounce or throttle frequent events, use efficient algorithms and data structures, cache and memoise, lazy-load resources, and clean up listeners and timers to avoid leaks.
p: Less JS and fewer long tasks
L683.f: What is layout thrashing and how do you avoid it?

L685.a: The DOM (Document Object Model) represents the page's content as a tree you can read and change (`document`, elements, events). The BOM (Browser Object Model) is the set of browser APIs around the page: `window`, `navigator`, `location`, `history`, `screen`, timers, alerts and storage. The DOM is standardised by WHATWG; the BOM is a collection of browser-provided APIs.
p: window is the global object containing both
Use them to build interactive pages
L685.f: Is localStorage part of the DOM or the BOM?

L686.a: Destructuring unpacks values from arrays or properties from objects into variables in one statement, with renaming, default values, rest elements and nesting. It makes function parameters, React props, API responses and swapping values concise and readable.
p: Arrays by position, objects by name
Rest to collect the remaining items
Common in function parameters and hooks
L686.f: What happens when you destructure null?

L687.a: `filter()` returns a new array with all elements that pass the test (possibly empty). `find()` returns the first element that passes and stops searching, or undefined if none does. Use find for a single item by id and filter for all matches.
p: find: first match, element or undefined
L687.f: Which is faster when you need just one element?

L688.a: Both use promises. `.then()` chaining passes results through callbacks and handles errors with `.catch()`; async/await writes the same flow as sequential code with try/catch, which is easier to read, debug and use with loops and conditionals. Use .then for simple one-liners or when combining with Promise combinators inline.
p: Avoid mixing styles in one function
L688.f: How do you run awaited calls in parallel?

L689.a: The critical rendering path is the sequence of steps the browser takes to show the first pixels: downloading and parsing HTML into the DOM, CSS into the CSSOM, running render-blocking scripts, building the render tree, layout and paint. Optimising it means fewer and smaller critical resources: inline critical CSS, defer non-critical JS and CSS, preload key assets and reduce round trips.
p: HTML → DOM, CSS → CSSOM → render tree → layout → paint
CSS and sync JS are render-blocking
L689.f: Why does a font sometimes delay text rendering?

L690.a: A REST API exposes resources (users, orders) at URLs and lets clients manipulate them with standard HTTP methods (GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE), using representations like JSON, stateless requests, standard status codes and cacheable responses.
L690.f: What makes an API "RESTful" versus just HTTP-based?

L691.a: `forEach()` runs a function for each element and returns undefined (side effects only); `map()` returns a new array of transformed values. `some()` returns true if at least one element passes the test (stops at the first match); `every()` returns true only if all elements pass (stops at the first failure).
L691.f: What do some and every return for an empty array?

L692.a: Memory leaks are memory that is no longer needed but still reachable, so the garbage collector can't free it. Common causes: forgotten timers and intervals, event listeners not removed, detached DOM nodes still referenced, closures holding large data, growing global caches and unclosed subscriptions or sockets. Detect them with DevTools Memory heap snapshots and allocation timelines; prevent them with cleanup functions, bounded caches and WeakMap.
L692.f: How would you confirm a leak in a long-running SPA?

L693.a: The call stack tracks function calls in progress (last in, first out): each call pushes a frame with its local variables, returning pops it. The heap is the large memory area where objects, arrays and closures live, managed by the garbage collector. The scope chain is how variables are resolved: the engine looks in the current scope, then each outer (lexical) scope up to global.
p: Closures keep outer scopes alive on the heap
L693.f: Why does deep recursion overflow the stack but not the heap?

L694.a: Immutability means not changing existing data but creating new copies with changes. In large apps it makes data flow predictable, prevents bugs from shared references, enables cheap change detection by reference (React, Redux, memoisation), supports undo/time-travel and makes concurrent code safer. Use spread, map/filter, toSorted, structuredClone or Immer.

L695.a: Module pattern (encapsulating private state, now ES modules), Singleton (one shared instance like an API client or store, usually just a module export), Observer/pub-sub (event emitters, store subscriptions), Factory (creating objects based on input, e.g. different notification types), plus Strategy, Decorator (wrapping functions with logging/caching) and Proxy. Give a concrete example for each you've used.
L695.f: Why are singletons considered risky for testing?

L696.a: `Object.create(proto)` creates an object whose prototype is `proto` directly, without running a constructor, which is handy for pure prototypal inheritance or prototype-less dictionaries (`Object.create(null)`). Constructor functions with `new` create an object linked to `Fn.prototype` and run initialisation code to set instance properties.
L696.f: How would you implement inheritance between two constructor functions with Object.create?

L697.a: Pure functions return the same output for the same input and cause no side effects. They're easy to unit test (no setup or mocks), safe to cache and memoise, easy to reason about and reuse, parallelisable, and they keep side effects at the edges of the system, which makes large codebases more predictable and scalable.
L697.f: How do you handle unavoidable side effects in a functional design?

L698.a: Debounce waits for a pause in events before running once; throttle runs at most once per fixed interval. Both are time-based. A requestAnimationFrame-based approach runs at most once per frame, synced with the browser's repaint (~16 ms at 60 fps), which is ideal for visual updates like scroll-linked animations or resize layout, because it never does more work than can be displayed.
L698.f: Why is rAF better than throttle(…, 16) for animations?

L699.a: `JSON.parse(JSON.stringify())` is fast for plain data but loses Dates, Maps, undefined and functions and fails on cycles. `structuredClone` handles most built-in types and cycles, with moderate cost. Library deep clones (lodash cloneDeep) are flexible but slower. A custom recursive clone can be fastest for known shapes. Often the best option is avoiding deep clones with structural sharing (immutable updates copying only changed paths).
L699.f: Why is structural sharing cheaper than deep cloning for Redux state?

L700.a: Define a small, focused API with pure, well-typed functions (TypeScript), ship ES modules with `sideEffects: false` so it's tree-shakeable, organise by domain with per-function imports, document with examples, test thoroughly (unit + property tests), version with semver and changelogs, avoid heavy dependencies, support both browser and Node where relevant, and measure bundle size in CI.
L700.f: How would you deprecate a function without breaking users?

L701.a: Pick real cases and structure them as problem, diagnosis, fix, result. Typical ones: a huge bundle slowing first load (fixed with route splitting and replacing heavy libraries), long tasks from processing large arrays on the main thread (moved to a Web Worker or chunked), excessive re-renders in a dashboard (memoisation and state colocation), layout thrashing in scroll handlers (batched reads/writes with requestAnimationFrame), and memory leaks from uncleaned listeners. Quantify the improvement.
p: Describe the symptom and how you measured it
Root cause with the tool you used
L701.f: How did you make sure the problem didn't come back?

L702.a: Normalise to lowercase, split into words (strip punctuation), and count in a Map or object.
L702.f: How would you return the top 3 words?

L703.a: Count each character in one pass, tracking the maximum as you go.
p: Decide whether to ignore spaces and case
Ties: keep the first or return all

L704.a: Track the largest and second largest distinct values in one pass.
p: Return undefined/null if no second value
Sorting works but is O(n log n)
L704.f: Generalise it to the kth largest.

L705.a: Walk the array with a Set of seen values; the first value already in the set is the first repeating element (in order of second occurrence). If you need the element whose first occurrence is earliest, count first, then scan for the first count > 1.
p: Clarify which definition of "first" is meant
L705.f: Return the element whose first appearance is earliest among repeats.

L706.a: The pivot index is where the sum of elements to the left equals the sum to the right. Compute the total, then walk the array keeping a running left sum: at index i, right sum = total - left - nums[i].
L706.f: How would you find all pivot indices?

L707.a: Insert an underscore before each uppercase letter and lowercase it.
L707.f: How would you convert snake_case back to camelCase?
L707.c:
const toSnake = s => s.replace(/[A-Z]/g, c => "_" + c.toLowerCase()).replace(/^_/, "");
toSnake("thisIsATest"); // "this_is_a_test"

L708.a: Layout thrashing happens when code alternates DOM writes (changing styles or content) with reads of layout properties (offsetHeight, getBoundingClientRect, scrollTop) in a loop; each read forces the browser to recalculate layout synchronously. Prevent it by batching all reads first, then all writes, using requestAnimationFrame for writes, caching measurements, and preferring transforms over layout-affecting properties.
p: Write → read → write forces sync layout
Look for "Forced reflow" warnings in DevTools
L708.f: Which properties trigger a forced layout when read?

L709.a: The browser won't paint until it has the CSSOM, because rendering without styles would show unstyled content and then reflow (FOUC), so stylesheets in the head block rendering. Synchronous `<script>` tags block HTML parsing (and must wait for preceding CSS since scripts may read styles), delaying rendering of everything after them. `defer`, `async` and `type="module"` avoid parser blocking; media attributes make non-matching CSS non-blocking.
p: defer/async/module scripts don't block the parser
Inline critical CSS; load the rest asynchronously
L709.f: Why does a script after a stylesheet wait for the CSS?

L710.a: After a task finishes and the microtask queue is emptied, the browser may run a rendering opportunity (typically about every 16 ms at 60 Hz, only if something changed and the page is visible): it runs requestAnimationFrame callbacks, recalculates style and layout, runs ResizeObserver/IntersectionObserver steps, paints and composites. So DOM changes made within one task are painted together afterwards, never in the middle of a task.
p: rAF callbacks run just before style/layout/paint
L710.f: Why does changing a style and reading it back in the same task not show an intermediate frame?

L711.a: In TLS 1.3 the client sends a ClientHello with supported ciphers and a key share; the server replies with ServerHello, its key share, its certificate and a signature proving it owns the certificate's private key. Both sides derive the same session keys from the key exchange (ECDHE), the client verifies the certificate chain against trusted CAs and the hostname, and encrypted application data flows, all in one round trip (0-RTT on resumption).
L711.f: What is certificate pinning and why is it rarely used on the web?

L712.a: Reproduce and measure: run Lighthouse/WebPageTest and look at the network waterfall. Check TTFB (slow server, no CDN or caching), large or render-blocking resources (big JS bundles, CSS, fonts, unoptimised images), too many requests or redirects, slow third-party scripts and slow API calls blocking rendering. Compare with field data, then fix the biggest item first and re-measure.
p: TTFB vs download vs main-thread time
L712.f: How would you tell a backend problem from a frontend one?

L713.a: Don't render 50,000 DOM rows: virtualise the list (react-window, TanStack Virtual) so only visible rows plus a buffer exist, memoise row components with stable keys and props, paginate or fetch on demand from the server, do sorting/filtering in a Web Worker or on the server, and debounce/defer filter input with useDeferredValue.
L713.f: How do you keep keyboard navigation and screen readers working with virtualization?

L714.a: Run many stateless WebSocket gateway servers behind a load balancer (sticky sessions or connection-aware routing), keep per-connection state minimal, and share messages across servers with a pub/sub backbone (Redis, Kafka, NATS). Tune OS limits (file descriptors), use heartbeats and reconnection with backoff, shard by room/user, and offload work to backend services; or use a managed service (Azure SignalR, Pusher, Ably).
p: OS and memory tuning per connection
L714.f: How do you deliver a message to a user connected to a different server?

L715.a: `id` must be unique on the page (used for anchors, labels, ARIA references and JavaScript lookups); `class` can be shared by many elements for styling and grouping. `<div>` is a block-level generic container; `<span>` is an inline generic container for parts of text. Neither div nor span has semantic meaning.
p: Prefer semantic elements when they fit
L715.f: Can an element have multiple classes and multiple ids?

L716.a: ARIA (Accessible Rich Internet Applications) is a set of attributes (roles, states and properties like role="dialog", aria-expanded, aria-label, aria-live) that tell assistive technologies what custom widgets are and how they behave when native HTML can't express it. It's important for complex UIs, but it doesn't add behaviour (keyboard handling is still on you), and wrong ARIA is worse than none.
p: Fills gaps native HTML can't cover
First rule: use native elements when possible

L717.a: Common issues: missing alt text, poor colour contrast, unlabeled form fields, clickable divs that aren't keyboard accessible, missing or invisible focus indicators, focus not managed in modals and route changes, incorrect heading structure, relying on colour alone, auto-playing media, missing captions, and inaccessible custom widgets.
L717.f: Which of these can automated tools catch, and which can't?

L718.a: A screen reader is assistive software (NVDA, JAWS, VoiceOver, TalkBack) that reads the interface aloud or to a braille display. It uses the browser's accessibility tree, built from the DOM's semantics, names, roles and states, and lets users navigate by headings, landmarks, links and form controls with keyboard shortcuts or gestures.
p: Reads the accessibility tree, not the visual layout
Test with at least one real screen reader
L718.f: How can you inspect the accessibility tree in DevTools?

L719.a: Use a `<nav>` landmark with an accessible name, a list of real links, indicate the current page with `aria-current="page"`, and for dropdown submenus use buttons with `aria-expanded` and `aria-controls` that toggle the submenu, support Tab, Enter/Space, Escape and arrow keys, keep visible focus styles, and make the mobile toggle a button with a label.
L719.f: Why is the "menu" role usually wrong for site navigation?

L720.a: A native `<button>` is focusable, activates with Enter and Space, submits forms, works with disabled, and is announced correctly, all for free. `role="button"` on a div only changes how it's announced; you must add `tabindex="0"`, key handlers for Enter and Space, disabled handling and focus styles yourself. Use the real element.
p: Must add tabindex and key handlers manually
L720.f: When might you legitimately use role="button"?

L721.a: Combine automated tools (axe DevTools, Lighthouse, WAVE, jest-axe/Playwright axe in CI) with manual checks: keyboard-only navigation, visible focus, screen reader testing (NVDA, VoiceOver), zoom to 200–400%, colour contrast checks, reduced motion, and reviewing against WCAG criteria, ideally with real users.
L721.f: How would you add accessibility checks to CI?

L722.a: Inline the critical above-the-fold CSS, load the rest asynchronously, remove unused CSS, minify and compress (Brotli), split CSS by route, avoid @import chains, serve from a CDN with long-cache hashed filenames, and use media attributes so non-matching stylesheets (print) don't block rendering.
L722.f: How do you measure how much CSS is unused?

L723.a: TTFB is the time until the first byte of the response arrives. Improve it with CDN/edge caching of HTML, static generation or ISR, server-side caching of data and rendered pages, faster backend code and database queries, reduced redirects, keeping connections warm (HTTP/2/3, keep-alive), deploying close to users, and streaming HTML so the head arrives early.
L723.f: Why can SSR increase TTFB compared with a static page?

L725.a: Depend on abstractions instead of concrete classes: extract interfaces for each dependency, inject them through constructors via the DI container, split classes that do too much (SRP), and make behaviour extensible through new implementations rather than edits (Open/Closed). Add unit tests with fakes as you go, and refactor incrementally behind the new interfaces.
p: Tests with mocks make changes safe
L725.f: How would you introduce DI into a legacy class that news up everything?

L726.a: Use the Strategy or Composite pattern with DI (or Decorator/Observer): define an `ILogSink` interface, implement FileSink, DbSink and ThirdPartySink, and have a composite logger iterate over all registered sinks. Adding a new destination means adding a class and registering it, without modifying existing code (Open/Closed). In practice ILogger providers or Serilog sinks already work this way.
L726.f: How would you make a slow sink not block requests?

L727.a: Issue JWTs from a trusted identity provider (or your auth service) with role/permission claims, short expiry and refresh token rotation; configure `AddAuthentication().AddJwtBearer()` to validate issuer, audience, lifetime and signing key; protect endpoints with `[Authorize(Roles = "Admin")]` or, better, policy-based authorization; store signing keys in a vault and use HTTPS.
L727.f: Why are permission-based policies more flexible than roles?

L728.a: Write middleware that reads or creates a correlation id, adds it to the response headers and the logging scope, starts a Stopwatch, awaits the next middleware, then logs method, path, status code and elapsed time (in a finally block so failures are logged too). Register it early in the pipeline.
p: Correlation id from header or new Guid
Logging scope so all logs include it
Log in finally; forward the id to downstream calls
L728.f: How would you pass the correlation id to outgoing HttpClient calls?

L729.a: A domain model represents business entities and rules; a ViewModel is shaped for one view: only the fields it needs, display formatting and validation attributes, which keeps the domain clean and prevents over-posting. Put data annotations on the ViewModel for server-side validation (check `ModelState.IsValid`) and enable client-side validation with jQuery Unobtrusive Validation (or matching JS rules), mapping ViewModel to domain model with a mapper.
p: ViewModel per screen; domain model for rules
L729.f: Why should you never bind directly to entity classes?

L730.a: SRP: an OrderService that also sends emails and writes PDFs gets split into OrderService, EmailNotifier and InvoiceGenerator, so each changes for one reason. Open/Closed: discount rules implemented as IDiscountRule classes; adding a festival discount means a new class, not editing a switch statement. Dependency Inversion: OrderService depends on IPaymentGateway, not StripeClient, so switching to Razorpay or mocking in tests needs no change to the service.
p: DIP: high-level code depends on abstractions
L730.f: How do you avoid over-engineering while applying SOLID?

L731.a: Group, order inside each group and take N. In EF Core, `GroupBy` + `Take` inside a projection now translates (using window functions) in recent versions; otherwise use raw SQL with ROW_NUMBER. LINQ hurts performance when queries are materialised too early (filtering in memory), when N+1 queries occur, when client evaluation pulls large data, when you select whole entities instead of projections, or when you enumerate deferred queries repeatedly.
p: Raw SQL with ROW_NUMBER as fallback
Avoid early ToList, N+1 and over-fetching
L731.f: How would you verify the query runs as a single SQL statement?
L731.c:
var top3 = await db.Employees
    .GroupBy(e => e.DepartmentId)
    .Select(g => new { Dept = g.Key, Top = g.OrderByDescending(e => e.Salary).Take(3).ToList() })
    .ToListAsync();

L732.a: Both rank rows by an ORDER BY within optional partitions and give ties the same rank. RANK() leaves gaps after ties; DENSE_RANK() doesn't. For salaries 100, 90, 90, 80: RANK gives 1, 2, 2, 4 and DENSE_RANK gives 1, 2, 2, 3. ROW_NUMBER gives 1, 2, 3, 4 regardless of ties.
p: Ties share a rank in both
L732.f: Which would you use for top-3 per department including ties?
L732.c:
SELECT name, salary,
  RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rnk,
  DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) AS dense_rnk
FROM Employee;

L733.a: Capture the deadlock graph (Extended Events system_health / trace flags) to see which statements and resources were involved, then fix the cause: access tables in a consistent order, keep transactions short, add indexes so fewer rows are locked, avoid user interaction inside transactions, use appropriate isolation (READ COMMITTED SNAPSHOT), and add retry logic for the victim (error 1205) in the application.
L733.f: Why does adding an index often reduce deadlocks?

L734.a: Order by a unique key, then OFFSET (page - 1) * size ROWS and FETCH NEXT size ROWS ONLY (SQL Server 2012+).
L734.f: Why does performance degrade on very high page numbers?

L735.a: Keep component state local, share feature state through injectable services with signals or BehaviorSubjects, and for large, complex apps use a store: NgRx (Redux-style with actions, reducers, effects, selectors, or the lighter SignalStore), NGXS or Akita/Elf. Keep server data cached (e.g. with TanStack Query for Angular), use OnPush change detection and selectors to limit updates.
p: Services + signals for simple shared state
Separate server state from UI state

L736.a: Create a guard (functional `CanActivateFn` in modern Angular) that reads the current user's role from an auth service and returns true or a UrlTree to redirect; attach it to routes with `canActivate` and pass required roles via route `data`. Use `canMatch` to prevent lazy modules from even loading for unauthorised users. The backend must still enforce authorization.
L736.f: What's the difference between canActivate and canMatch?

L737.a: Unsubscribe from long-lived observables: use the async pipe in templates, `takeUntilDestroyed()` (or takeUntil with a destroy subject), and avoid manual subscriptions where possible. Remove event listeners and clear timers in ngOnDestroy (or DestroyRef), detach third-party widgets, avoid holding component references in singleton services, and check with DevTools heap snapshots.

L738.a: React.memo wraps a component so it skips re-rendering when its props are shallowly equal to the previous ones. Don't use it when props change on almost every render anyway (new objects/functions, children elements), when the component is cheap to render, or when you haven't measured a problem; then it only adds comparison cost and complexity. It also doesn't stop re-renders caused by the component's own state or context.
L738.f: How does passing children break React.memo?

L739.a: Model each request with explicit states (idle, loading, success, error), show skeletons for loading and actionable messages for errors, retry transient failures automatically with backoff (only idempotent requests) and offer a manual retry button, cancel stale requests, and centralise error handling in the API client. React Query handles caching, retries and states out of the box.
L739.f: How many automatic retries would you allow and why?

L740.a: Common bottlenecks: unnecessary re-renders from state kept too high or context values recreated each render, unstable props breaking memoisation, expensive computations during render, rendering huge lists without virtualisation, large bundles, heavy third-party components, and effects that cause extra renders. Identify them with the React DevTools Profiler (why did this render), the browser Performance panel, Web Vitals (INP) and bundle analysis.
L740.f: What's the first thing you look at in a Profiler flame graph?

L741.a: Check that every element is less than or equal to the next one; stop at the first violation.
p: Empty and single-element arrays are sorted
L741.f: How would you check if it's sorted in either direction?
L741.c: const isSorted = arr => arr.every((x, i) => i === 0 || arr[i - 1] <= x);

L742.a: Linear search checks each element in order, O(n), works on any array. Binary search works on sorted arrays: compare with the middle element and discard half each step, O(log n).
p: Watch the mid calculation and bounds
L742.f: How would you find the first occurrence with binary search when duplicates exist?

L743.a: With a Set, return the first value already seen (O(n) time, O(n) space). For the classic constraint (n+1 numbers from 1..n, one duplicate, O(1) space) use Floyd's cycle detection on indices.
p: Floyd's tortoise and hare for O(1) space
L743.f: Why does the cycle start equal the duplicate?

L744.a: Walk the array once with a Map from value to index; for each number, check whether its complement (target - n) is already in the map.
p: Check before inserting to avoid using the same element twice
L744.f: How would you find all unique pairs?

L745.a: The majority element appears more than n/2 times. Boyer-Moore voting finds it in O(n) time and O(1) space: keep a candidate and a counter, increment for matches and decrement otherwise, switching candidates at zero; verify afterwards if a majority isn't guaranteed.
p: Verify with a second pass if needed
HashMap counting is the simple alternative
L745.f: How would you find all elements appearing more than n/3 times?

L746.a: Fibonacci: iterate keeping the last two numbers. Factorial: multiply from 1 to n (BigInt for large n). Prime check: test divisors up to √n.
L746.f: How would you list all primes up to 1,000,000?

L747.a: Count consecutive 1s, resetting at each 0, and track the maximum.
p: Variant with k flips uses a sliding window
L747.f: How would you allow flipping one zero?

L748.a: Lowercase the string and test each letter: vowels against a set, other letters a–z as consonants, ignoring digits, spaces and punctuation.
L748.f: How would you support accented characters?

L749.a: Split on whitespace, reverse the array of words and join with single spaces.
p: In-place variant reverses the whole string then each word
L749.f: Reverse the letters of each word but keep word order.
L749.c:
const reverseWords = s => s.trim().split(/\s+/).reverse().join(" ");
reverseWords("  hello   world from js "); // "js from world hello"

L750.a: Extract the digit characters and sum them as numbers.
L750.f: How would you sum the numbers "12" and "34" as whole numbers?
L750.c:
const sumDigits = s => (s.match(/\d/g) || []).reduce((t, d) => t + Number(d), 0);
sumDigits("a1b2c34"); // 10

L751.a: Use two nested loops over start and end positions; there are n(n+1)/2 substrings.
p: Use a Set for unique substrings
L751.f: How do subsequences differ, and how many are there?

L752.a: Split into words (stripping punctuation) and keep the shortest with reduce.
p: Same approach for the longest word
L752.f: How would you return all words of the minimum length?
L752.c:
const smallestWord = s => (s.match(/[A-Za-z']+/g) || []).reduce((a, w) => (w.length < a.length ? w : a));
smallestWord("I love JavaScript a lot"); // "I"

L753.a: Wrap each callback API in a function returning a Promise (or use util.promisify), chain with .then, then rewrite with async/await and a single try/catch.
p: Promisify: resolve on success, reject on error
One error handler instead of one per level
L753.f: When would you still run two of these in parallel?

L754.a: Concatenate both arrays and dedupe with a Set of a composite string key (key + value), so objects are only removed if both key and value match an earlier one.
L754.f: How would you instead dedupe by key only, keeping the latest value?

L755.a: Take the first word and shrink it until every word starts with it. For ["flow","float","flute","flower","abc"] the result is "" because "abc" shares no prefix.
p: Shrink the prefix while any word doesn't start with it
Sorting and comparing first/last also works
L755.f: How would a trie solve this for many queries?

L756.a: An enum names a set of related constants, giving readable, type-checked values. Example: order status `enum OrderStatus { Pending = "PENDING", Shipped = "SHIPPED", Delivered = "DELIVERED" }` used in API types and switch statements. Many teams prefer string-literal unions (`type Status = "PENDING" | "SHIPPED"`) or `as const` objects, which add no runtime code.
p: Numeric enums auto-increment; string enums are clearer
const enums are inlined (with tooling caveats)
Union types are a lighter alternative
L756.f: Why might a team ban enums in favour of union types?

L757.a: HTTP interceptors sit between HttpClient and the server, letting you modify every request or response: add auth tokens, set headers, log, show loaders, cache, retry and handle errors centrally. In modern Angular write a functional interceptor and register it with `provideHttpClient(withInterceptors([...]))`.
p: Registered at the root via provideHttpClient
L757.f: How would you skip the interceptor for a specific request?

L758.a: Angular calls lifecycle hooks in order: ngOnChanges (when input properties change, before ngOnInit and on each change), ngOnInit (once, after first inputs; init logic and data loading), ngDoCheck (every change detection run; custom change detection), ngAfterContentInit/ngAfterContentChecked (projected content), ngAfterViewInit/ngAfterViewChecked (component's view and children), and ngOnDestroy (cleanup). Newer APIs add afterNextRender/afterRender and DestroyRef.
p: Avoid heavy work in *Checked and DoCheck
L758.f: Why can't you access @ViewChild elements in ngOnInit?

L759.a: A pure pipe (default) runs only when its input value changes by reference, so it's efficient and cached. An impure pipe (`pure: false`) runs on every change detection cycle, needed when it depends on mutable data or external state (e.g. filtering an array that's mutated in place, or the async pipe), but it can hurt performance.
p: Prefer pure pipes with immutable data
L759.f: Why doesn't a pure filter pipe update when you push into the array?

L760.a: Zoneless Angular runs change detection without zone.js: instead of patching every async API to know when to check, Angular schedules change detection from signals, template events, the async pipe and explicit `markForCheck`. Enable it with `provideZonelessChangeDetection()`. Benefits: smaller bundles, better performance, clearer stack traces and easier interop.
p: Code relying on implicit zone triggers needs updating
L760.f: What breaks when you remove zone.js from an older app?

L761.a: Common operators: map/filter for transforming, switchMap for cancelling previous requests (search), mergeMap for parallel work, concatMap for ordered work, exhaustMap to ignore clicks while busy, debounceTime/distinctUntilChanged for input, combineLatest/forkJoin to combine streams, catchError/retry for errors, takeUntil/take for completion, shareReplay for caching. An Observable is unicast and lazy (each subscriber gets its own execution); a Subject is both observable and observer and multicasts the same values to all subscribers.
p: switchMap vs mergeMap vs concatMap vs exhaustMap
L761.f: Which flattening operator would you use for a "save" button and why?

L762.a: An Observable produces values for each subscriber independently and lazily. A Subject is a multicast observable you can push values into with next(); late subscribers only get future values. A BehaviorSubject requires an initial value, stores the latest value, and immediately emits it to new subscribers, which makes it ideal for state (current user, settings). ReplaySubject replays a buffer of past values.
p: BehaviorSubject: current value, emits on subscribe
L762.f: Why expose a BehaviorSubject as asObservable() from a service?

L763.a: A form submits when a submit button is clicked or Enter is pressed in a field: the browser fires a `submit` event, validates constraints, serialises named fields (application/x-www-form-urlencoded by default, or multipart/form-data for files) and navigates with a GET or POST to the `action` URL. A `<button>` inside a form defaults to `type="submit"`, so use `type="button"` for other buttons.
p: method GET → query string, POST → body
L763.f: How does implicit submission with the Enter key work?

L764.a: Nesting interactive elements (a button inside a link, a link inside a button, an input inside a label's other control) is invalid HTML. Browsers may restructure the DOM, clicks become ambiguous (which one fires?), keyboard focus and screen reader announcements break. Keep interactive elements as siblings and use CSS for layout, or make a whole card clickable with a single link and pseudo-element overlay.
p: Invalid per the HTML content model
Use siblings or the stretched-link pattern
L764.f: How would you make a whole card clickable but keep a separate button inside?

L765.a: The browser decodes bytes into characters, a tokenizer turns them into tokens (start tags, end tags, text), and the tree builder constructs the DOM according to the HTML spec, including error recovery for malformed markup. Synchronous scripts pause parsing while they download and run; a preload scanner fetches upcoming resources in parallel; parsing is incremental, so rendering can start before the whole document arrives.

L766.a: The main axis follows `flex-direction` (row = horizontal, column = vertical) and the cross axis is perpendicular. `justify-content` aligns items along the main axis; `align-items` aligns them on the cross axis (per line), `align-self` overrides it per item, and `align-content` distributes multiple lines when wrapping. Switching to column swaps which visual direction each property controls.
L766.f: How do you push one item to the far right in a row?

L767.a: After computing styles, the browser walks the render tree and calculates each box's size and position according to the formatting context: block and inline flow, flex, grid, tables, positioned elements. Widths usually flow from parent to child and heights from children up. Layout is cached and incremental; changes to geometry invalidate parts of it, and reading layout properties after changes forces synchronous recalculation.
L767.f: What does `contain: layout` do to this process?

L768.a: A union type `A | B` means a value is one of the types; you can only use members common to all until you narrow it. An intersection `A & B` means a value has all members of both types at once, useful for combining object types.

L769.a: `any` turns off type checking: anything can be assigned to it and it can be assigned to anything, so errors aren't caught, autocompletion disappears and `any` spreads silently through the codebase. Prefer `unknown` (forces narrowing before use), proper types, generics, or targeted type assertions; enable `noImplicitAny` and lint against explicit any.

L770.a: Overloading means several methods with the same name but different parameter lists in the same class, chosen at compile time. Overriding means a derived class provides a new implementation of a virtual/abstract base method with the same signature using `override`, chosen at runtime based on the object's type.
p: Overloading: compile-time, same class, different parameters
L770.f: Can you override a static method?

L771.a: A static class can't be instantiated, implement interfaces, be passed as a parameter or be mocked; it's just a holder of static members.
