A singleton is a normal class with one instance, so it can implement interfaces, be injected via DI, hold state with lazy initialisation and be replaced in tests. In ASP.NET Core prefer DI singletons (`AddSingleton`) over hand-written singletons.
p: Testing: singletons via DI are mockable
Static is fine for pure helpers
L771.f: How do you make a hand-written singleton thread-safe?

L772.a: `partial` lets a class, struct, interface or method be split across multiple files that the compiler merges. It's used mainly with generated code (WinForms/WPF designers, EF scaffolding, source generators) so your hand-written code lives in a separate file that isn't overwritten, and for organising very large classes. Partial methods let generated code declare hooks you can optionally implement.
p: Compiler combines parts into one type
All parts must use the same accessibility and namespace
L772.f: What are partial properties in newer C# versions?

L773.a: Managed code runs under the CLR, which handles memory (garbage collection), type safety, exception handling and security; C# compiles to managed IL. Unmanaged code runs directly on the OS (C/C++ native libraries, COM, Win32 APIs) and manages its own memory. .NET calls unmanaged code through P/Invoke or COM interop, and unmanaged resources must be released with IDisposable.

L774.a: Use explicit interface implementation: implement each method with the interface name as a prefix (`void IPrinter.Print()`, `void IScanner.Print()`). Each implementation is only accessible when the object is used through that interface. If one shared implementation is fine, a single public method satisfies both.
p: Single public method if behaviour is the same
L774.f: How do default interface methods interact with this?

L775.a: In the Startup class pattern, `ConfigureServices(IServiceCollection services)` registers dependencies in the DI container (MVC, DbContext, authentication, your services) and runs first. `Configure(IApplicationBuilder app, IWebHostEnvironment env)` builds the middleware pipeline (exception handling, routing, auth, endpoints) that handles each request. Since .NET 6 both live in Program.cs (`builder.Services` and `app.Use...`).
p: Minimal hosting merges them in Program.cs
L775.f: Can you resolve services inside Configure?

L776.a: `Use()` adds middleware that can run code before and after calling the next component (or short-circuit). `Run()` adds a terminal middleware that never calls next, ending the pipeline. `Map()` branches the pipeline based on the request path (MapWhen on a condition), so a separate sub-pipeline handles matching requests.
L776.f: What happens to middleware registered after app.Run?

L777.a: Register a named policy with `AddCors` specifying allowed origins, methods and headers, then call `app.UseCors("Policy")` after UseRouting and before UseAuthorization (or apply per endpoint with RequireCors / [EnableCors]). Allow only the specific frontend origins, and use AllowCredentials only with explicit origins.
p: Specific origins, not AllowAnyOrigin with credentials
L777.f: Why doesn't CORS protect your API from non-browser clients?

L778.a: Pros: productive LINQ queries, change tracking and unit of work, migrations, cross-database support, type safety. Cons: generated SQL can be inefficient, risk of N+1 and over-fetching, overhead compared with raw ADO.NET or Dapper, complex queries are harder to express. Compiled queries (`EF.CompileAsyncQuery`) pre-translate a LINQ query once and reuse it, saving translation cost on hot paths.
p: Mitigate with projections, AsNoTracking, raw SQL where needed
Compiled queries for frequently executed queries
L778.f: When would you choose Dapper over EF Core?

L779.a: Clustered index: defines the physical order of rows (one per table). Non-clustered index: separate structure with keys and row pointers (many allowed). Unique index: enforces uniqueness. Composite index: on multiple columns (leftmost prefix matters). Covering/included-column index: contains all columns a query needs. Filtered index: indexes a subset of rows. Full-text index: word-based searching in text. Also columnstore (analytics), spatial and XML indexes.
p: Full-text and columnstore for special workloads
L779.f: Why does column order matter in a composite index?

L780.a: Aggregate functions compute one value from many rows: COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX (plus STRING_AGG and others). WHERE filters individual rows before grouping and can't use aggregates; HAVING filters groups after GROUP BY and can use aggregates.
p: Use WHERE when possible for performance
L780.f: What is the difference between COUNT(*) and COUNT(column)?
L780.c:
SELECT dept_id, AVG(salary) AS avg_sal
FROM Employee
WHERE active = 1
GROUP BY dept_id
HAVING AVG(salary) > 50000;

L781.a: A primary key uniquely identifies each row, can't be NULL, and there is one per table. A unique key also enforces uniqueness but allows NULL (one NULL in SQL Server) and a table can have several. A foreign key is a column referencing another table's primary/unique key, enforcing referential integrity between tables.
p: PK: unique + not null, one per table
L781.f: Should every foreign key be indexed?

L782.a: A composite key is a key made of two or more columns that together identify a row, such as (OrderId, ProductId) in an order-lines table; it can be the primary key or a unique key. A primary key (single or composite) is the main row identifier, not null and one per table. A unique key enforces uniqueness on other columns or combinations and allows nulls.
p: Can serve as PK or unique constraint
L782.f: When would you prefer a surrogate key over a composite key?

L783.a: INNER JOIN returns only rows with matches in both tables. LEFT JOIN returns all rows from the left table and matched rows from the right (NULLs where no match). RIGHT JOIN is the mirror image. FULL OUTER JOIN returns all rows from both, matching where possible. CROSS JOIN returns every combination; a SELF JOIN joins a table to itself.
p: Filter on the right table in ON, not WHERE, to keep LEFT semantics
L783.f: How do you find customers with no orders?

L784.a: Triggers are procedures that run automatically on INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE (or DDL/logon events). Uses: audit logging, enforcing complex business rules, maintaining derived or denormalised data, and preventing certain changes. Use sparingly: they hide logic, can hurt performance, and must handle multi-row operations (inserted/deleted tables).
p: Hidden side effects; prefer constraints or app logic when possible
L784.f: Why is a trigger that assumes a single row dangerous?

L785.a: A deadlock occurs when two (or more) transactions each hold a lock the other needs, so neither can proceed; the database detects the cycle and kills one as the victim (SQL Server error 1205). Example: transaction A updates Accounts row 1 then row 2, while transaction B updates row 2 then row 1; each waits forever for the other's lock.
p: Database chooses a victim and rolls it back
L785.f: How is a deadlock different from blocking?

L787.a: The browser parses HTML into the DOM and CSS into the CSSOM, then combines them into a render tree (style calculation). Layout computes each element's geometry. Paint records drawing commands for text, colours, borders and images into layers. Compositing combines layers (often on the GPU) into the final frame. Changing geometry repeats layout, paint and composite; changing colours repeats paint; changing transform or opacity can be composite-only.
p: Cost depends on which stage you invalidate
L787.f: What promotes an element to its own compositing layer?

L788.a: Every component that consumes a context re-renders whenever the provider's value changes. Frequent re-renders happen when the value object is recreated on every provider render, when fast-changing and slow-changing data share one context, or when many components consume it. Fix by memoising the value with useMemo, splitting contexts (state vs dispatch, or by domain), keeping fast-changing state local, or switching to a store with selectors (Zustand, Redux, use-context-selector).
p: Consumers re-render on any value change
L788.f: Why doesn't wrapping a consumer in React.memo help?

L789.a: `React.lazy(() => import("./Page"))` returns a special component. When React first renders it, it calls the loader, which starts the dynamic import and returns a promise; React throws that promise to the nearest Suspense boundary, which shows the fallback. When the module resolves, React caches the result and re-renders with the module's default export. Bundlers split the dynamically imported module into its own chunk.
p: Dynamic import() creates a separate chunk
Needs a default export (or a wrapper)
L789.f: How would you preload a lazy component before the user clicks?

L790.a: Move public pages to SSR or SSG (Next.js) so crawlers get full HTML and users see content fast, add per-page metadata and structured data, shrink and split JavaScript to improve TTI (route splitting, lazy-loading non-critical components, removing heavy dependencies and third-party scripts), use streaming and selective hydration or Server Components to reduce hydration cost, and optimise images and fonts.
p: Optimised images/fonts; measure with Lighthouse and CWV
L790.f: How would you migrate an existing CRA app incrementally?

L791.a: Extract words and keep the longest with reduce.
p: Sorting by length also works but is slower
L791.f: How would you return all longest words?
L791.c:
const longestWord = s => (s.match(/[A-Za-z']+/g) || []).reduce((a, w) => (w.length > a.length ? w : a), "");
longestWord("The quick brown fox jumped"); // "jumped"

L792.a: Count frequencies of arr1 values squared and of arr2 values, then compare the two frequency maps. O(n).
L792.f: Why is the indexOf/splice approach O(n²)?

L793.a: Dedupe by name using a Map (keeps the last) or a Set of seen names (keeps the first).
p: Map keyed by the identifying field
L793.f: How would you dedupe by several properties?
L793.c:
const people = [{ name: "A" }, { name: "B" }, { name: "A" }];
const uniqueByName = [...new Map(people.map(p => [p.name, p])).values()]; // [{name:"A"},{name:"B"}]

L794.a: Flatten the nested array (flat(Infinity)) and take the maximum, or recurse without flattening.
p: Spread into Math.max can overflow for huge arrays
L794.f: Find the depth of the most nested element too.
L794.c:
const maxNested = arr => arr.reduce((m, x) => Math.max(m, Array.isArray(x) ? maxNested(x) : x), -Infinity);
maxNested([1, [5, [9, 2]], 3]); // 9

L795.a: Pass a numeric comparator to sort; without it, numbers are compared as strings.

L796.a: Split the path on dots and build objects from the inside out with reduceRight (or walk down creating objects as needed when setting into an existing object).
L796.f: How would you guard against prototype pollution ("__proto__" keys)?

L797.a: Count frequencies, get the distinct frequencies sorted ascending, and return a number with the 3rd smallest frequency.
p: Return null if fewer than 3 distinct frequencies
L797.f: How would you return all numbers with that frequency?

L798.a: For many apps, yes: useState/useReducer plus Context handle shared client state, and React Query handles server state, which was most of what Redux held. Not fully for large apps with complex, frequently updated shared state: Context lacks selector-based subscriptions (causing broad re-renders), middleware, DevTools time-travel and established conventions that Redux Toolkit provides.
p: Hooks + Context cover simple global state
Server state belongs in React Query
Redux adds selectors, middleware, DevTools, structure
L798.f: What signals tell you it's time to introduce a store?

L799.a: Keep field definitions in data (a schema array), render inputs from it, store values in one object keyed by name, support add/remove for repeating groups (React Hook Form's useFieldArray), and validate with a schema library (Zod/Yup) that can express conditional rules. Show errors per field and validate on blur and submit.
p: Zod/Yup for validation, including conditional rules
L799.f: How would you validate that at least one phone number is provided?

L800.a: Lift the shared state to their nearest common parent and pass it down as props (with callbacks to update it). For distant siblings use Context, the URL (query params), or a small store (Zustand); events/pub-sub work but are harder to trace.
p: Lift state up to the common parent
L800.f: When is URL state a better fit than React state?

L801.a: In shouldComponentUpdate you return false to skip rendering. A shallow comparison checks each top-level prop/state value with ===, which is fast and is what PureComponent does, but misses changes inside mutated nested objects and treats new-but-equal objects as changed. A deep comparison checks nested contents, catching more cases but costing time on every update, possibly more than re-rendering. Prefer immutable data plus shallow checks.
L801.f: Why can a deep comparison be slower than just re-rendering?

L802.a: Serve static assets and cacheable HTML from a CDN with edge locations near users, deploy servers or edge functions in multiple regions, use HTTP/2 or HTTP/3, compress (Brotli), cache aggressively with long-lived hashed assets, optimise and resize images per device, reduce JavaScript, preconnect to required origins, and monitor real-user performance by region.
L802.f: How would you handle personalised pages that can't be fully cached?

L803.a: Reproduce in a branch, read the library's changelog and migration guide, and check `npm ls` for duplicate or conflicting versions. Fix by adapting code to the new API, pinning or using `overrides`/`resolutions` to align versions, or rolling back. Prevent it with a lockfile, upgrading one dependency at a time, automated update PRs (Renovate/Dependabot) gated by tests and visual regression checks.
p: npm ls / why to find conflicts
Small upgrades behind tests and CI
L803.f: How do peer dependency conflicts arise?

L804.a: Use the strangler pattern: keep the old app running and replace it piece by piece. Mount new framework components inside the legacy app (or route new pages to the new app behind a shared shell), share auth and design tokens, migrate the highest-value or most-changed areas first, cover behaviour with end-to-end tests, release behind feature flags and remove legacy code as each area finishes.
p: E2E tests as a safety net
L804.f: How do you share state between old and new parts during the migration?

L805.a: Minimise what reaches the client, never store secrets or sensitive data in localStorage or code, keep session tokens in httpOnly Secure cookies, use HTTPS, mask sensitive fields in the UI, clear data from memory/state on logout, disable autocomplete where appropriate, avoid logging personal data to analytics or error tools, protect against XSS with escaping and CSP, and rely on the server for authorization and encryption at rest.
p: httpOnly cookies, no sensitive data in storage
L805.f: Is encrypting data in localStorage with a key in your JS useful?

L806.a: Collect details (browser, version, OS, device, steps) from error monitoring and session replay, reproduce on real browsers (BrowserStack/Playwright across engines), check console errors, unsupported APIs or CSS features (caniuse), timing/race conditions and network failures, extensions and caching of old bundles. Fix with feature detection, polyfills or fallbacks, and add cross-browser tests for the case.
p: Check feature support and race conditions
L806.f: How do you tell a race condition from a browser incompatibility?

L807.a: Mitigate first: turn the feature off or switch to a degraded mode with a feature flag, roll back the last deploy if it's the cause, serve cached or static fallbacks, and scale or rate-limit the backend. Communicate status, watch dashboards, then find the root cause (load test, traces), fix it and write a post-mortem with preventive actions.
L807.f: What would you build in advance so this is easy next time?

L808.a: Capture JS errors (window error, unhandledrejection, error boundaries) with stack traces mapped via source maps, Web Vitals and custom performance marks, failed API calls with status and latency, and user context (route, release, browser) without personal data. Batch and send with `navigator.sendBeacon`, sample high-volume events, aggregate on the backend into dashboards and alerts per release, and add session replay for hard bugs, or use Sentry/Datadog.
p: Batched beacon sending, sampling, PII scrubbing
L808.f: How do you avoid the monitoring script slowing the page?

L809.a: Do heavy processing (parsing, sorting, filtering) in a Web Worker or in chunks that yield to the browser (requestIdleCallback, scheduler.yield, setTimeout), render only what's visible with virtualization, paginate or stream data, use transferable objects to move large buffers cheaply, and use canvas/WebGL for very large visualisations.
L809.f: How do you share large data with a worker without copying it?

L810.a: Record it in the DevTools Performance panel (with CPU throttling or remote debugging on the device) and look for long frames, layout and paint costs. Usual causes: animating layout properties (top, width, height) instead of transform/opacity, large paint areas, heavy box-shadows/filters, too many layers, and main-thread JavaScript during the animation. Fix by animating transform/opacity, using will-change sparingly, reducing painted area and moving work off the main thread.
p: Profile on a real or throttled device
Reduce paint cost and layer count
L810.f: How does the Rendering tab's "Paint flashing" help?

L811.a: Production builds differ: minification, real data volumes, third-party scripts, CDN/network conditions and real devices. Profile the production build (with a profiling build of React or source maps), use real-user monitoring to see which pages and devices are slow, check bundle size and network waterfalls, compare data sizes with dev, and look for features enabled only in production (analytics, A/B tools, logging).
p: Third-party scripts and real data sizes
L811.f: How do you profile React in production?

L812.a: Create an AbortController in the effect, pass its signal to fetch (or axios), and call `abort()` in the cleanup function; ignore AbortError in the catch. Data libraries like React Query cancel automatically.
p: Abort in cleanup on unmount or dependency change
Prevents state updates after unmount and wasted bandwidth
L812.f: How do you cancel an axios request?

L813.a: Ship less JavaScript (code splitting, removing heavy libraries, Server Components), avoid long tasks during interaction (transitions, workers), virtualise lists, memoise expensive renders, optimise images (responsive sizes, modern formats, lazy loading), reduce animations to transform/opacity, test with CPU and network throttling on real low-end devices, and track INP and LCP for mobile users.
L813.f: What's a reasonable JS budget for mobile?

L814.a: Load flags at startup from a flag service or config endpoint (LaunchDarkly, Unleash, ConfigCat, your own), expose them through context or a `useFlag` hook, render features conditionally, and lazy-load flagged code so disabled features cost nothing. Support user targeting and percentage rollouts, provide defaults when flags fail to load, and remove flags once rolled out.
L814.f: How do you test both branches of a flag?

L815.a: Components dispatch actions; middleware intercepts them; reducers compute new state; subscribed components re-render via selectors. Async actions are handled in middleware: a thunk is a function action that receives dispatch and getState, dispatches "pending", awaits the API, then dispatches "fulfilled" or "rejected" (createAsyncThunk automates this). RTK Query goes further with cached endpoints.
p: RTK Query for data fetching and caching
L815.f: Why can't reducers make API calls?

L816.a: Every render creates new functions that close over that render's props and state. An event handler or effect therefore "remembers" the values from the render in which it was created; for example a setTimeout in a click handler logs the count from when it was clicked, not the latest. That's why effects need correct dependencies and why functional updates or refs are used to read the latest value.
p: Each render has its own closures
Stale closures in timers and effects
Fix with deps, functional updates or refs
L816.f: How would you alert the latest count instead?

L817.a: TypeScript catches wrong props, missing fields and null handling at compile time, documents component APIs, improves autocompletion and makes refactoring safe across a large codebase. Generics let a component work with any item type while keeping type safety, for example a `List<T>` that takes `items: T[]` and `renderItem: (item: T) => ReactNode`, so callers get correct types without casting.
p: Typed props, state, events and hooks
Generic components for reusable lists, tables, selects
L817.f: How do you type a component that accepts an `as` prop?

L824.a: Observe a sentinel element at the bottom with IntersectionObserver (no scroll listeners to throttle), fetch the next page when it appears and nothing is loading, append results to state, track page/cursor, loading, error and hasMore, show a spinner or skeleton row, and stop when there's no more data. useInfiniteQuery handles caching and deduplication.
L824.f: Why is IntersectionObserver better than a throttled scroll handler?

L825.a: Keep the query in state and debounce it (300 ms); for client-side data, filter with useMemo and render through virtualization, using useDeferredValue to keep typing smooth. For server-side search, send the debounced query to the API, cancel previous requests with AbortController, cache results by query and show loading and empty states.
L825.f: How would you highlight matches without hurting performance?

L826.a: Store fields as an array of objects with stable ids, render them with map, add and remove items immutably, and validate with a schema (Zod/Yup) per item. React Hook Form's useFieldArray gives this with uncontrolled inputs (fewer re-renders); controlled inputs are simpler for small forms where every keystroke must drive UI.
p: Stable ids as keys, not indexes
Controlled for small, uncontrolled for large forms
L826.f: Why do index keys break dynamic forms?

L827.a: Keep all steps' data in one form state at the wizard level (useReducer, context or a form library), render one step at a time, validate only the current step's fields before moving forward, allow going back without losing data, persist progress (sessionStorage) for long forms, and submit everything at the end.
p: Single source of truth for all steps
L827.f: How would you put the current step in the URL?

L828.a: Use a library like dnd-kit (accessible, keyboard support) or the HTML Drag and Drop API: on drag start remember the item, on drag over compute the target index, and on drop reorder the array immutably (remove from the old index, insert at the new one). Provide keyboard alternatives and persist the new order.
L828.f: How do you make reordering work on touch devices?
L828.c: const move = (arr, from, to) => { const a = [...arr]; const [x] = a.splice(from, 1); a.splice(to, 0, x); return a; };

L829.a: Login via an auth server; keep tokens in httpOnly cookies (or the access token in memory), store user and roles in an AuthContext, protect routes with a guard that redirects unauthenticated users and checks roles for authorization, refresh tokens automatically on 401 in an API interceptor, log out on refresh failure, and sync logout across tabs. The backend always enforces permissions.
L829.f: How do you decode token expiry without trusting the token?

L830.a: Redux gives a single predictable store for shared client state, with explicit actions, pure reducers, DevTools time-travel and middleware, which helps in large apps with many components reading and updating the same data. Reducers must be pure and synchronous, so Redux Thunk adds a middleware that lets action creators return functions which perform async work (API calls) and dispatch actions when results arrive.
L830.f: Thunk vs saga: when would you choose saga?

L831.a: Yes. `structuredClone(obj)` deep copies nested objects, arrays, Dates, Maps, Sets and circular references (not functions or DOM nodes). `JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(obj))` works for plain JSON data only. Libraries like lodash `cloneDeep` handle more cases, and a custom recursive function gives control over special types.
L831.f: Why doesn't structuredClone copy class methods?

L832.a: The standard way is a callback prop: the parent passes a function and the child calls it with data. Alternatives: the parent passes a ref and the child exposes methods or values with useImperativeHandle, shared state through Context or a store, or lifting the state into the parent entirely.

L833.a: Fetch the endpoint (fetch or axios) in an effect or, better, with React Query, check the response status, parse the JSON, store it in state, and render loading, error and data states; send JSON with the right headers for POST/PUT and update or refetch afterwards.
p: Mutations with JSON body and invalidation
L833.f: How do you refresh the list after creating a user?
L833.c: const { data, isLoading, error } = useQuery({ queryKey: ["users"], queryFn: () => fetch("/api/users").then(r => r.json()) });

L834.a: Common React patterns: container/presentational components, composition with children, compound components, higher-order components, render props, custom hooks, controlled vs uncontrolled components, provider pattern (Context) and state reducers. Render props pass a function as a prop that returns UI, letting a component share logic while the caller decides rendering. Mixins were the old `createClass` way to share behaviour; they were deprecated because of name clashes and implicit dependencies, replaced by HOCs, render props and now hooks.
L834.f: Why did hooks largely replace HOCs and render props?

L835.a: `<!DOCTYPE html>` tells the browser to render the page in standards mode with the HTML5 parser rules; without it browsers use quirks mode, which emulates old, inconsistent layout behaviour. With invalid or unclosed tags, the HTML parser's error recovery fixes the DOM (auto-closing elements, moving misplaced nodes), so the page usually renders, but the resulting DOM may differ from your intent and break styling, scripts and accessibility.
L835.f: Name a layout difference between quirks and standards mode.

L836.a: `<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">` tells mobile browsers to set the layout width to the device's width instead of a desktop-sized virtual viewport (~980 px) that gets zoomed out. Without it responsive CSS and media queries don't work properly on phones and text appears tiny.

L837.a: `colspan` makes a table cell span multiple columns horizontally; `rowspan` makes it span multiple rows vertically. Both are set on `<td>` or `<th>`.
p: Remove the cells the span covers
Keep header associations clear for screen readers
L837.f: How do you keep complex tables accessible?

L838.a: HTML5 added semantic elements (header, nav, main, article, section, aside, footer, figure, time, mark), media elements (audio, video, canvas, svg inline), new input types (email, url, tel, number, range, date, time, color, search) and attributes (placeholder, required, pattern, autofocus, autocomplete, min/max, multiple, data-*), plus APIs like localStorage, geolocation, drag and drop, history and Web Workers.
p: Form input types and validation attributes
L838.f: Which new input types improve mobile keyboards?

L839.a: HTML5 APIs are browser JavaScript APIs introduced with HTML5: Web Storage (localStorage/sessionStorage), Geolocation, Canvas, Drag and Drop, History API, File API, Web Workers, WebSockets, IndexedDB, Notifications and media APIs. A Web Worker runs a script in a background thread, communicating with the page via postMessage, so heavy computation doesn't block the UI; workers can't touch the DOM.
p: Storage, Geolocation, Canvas, History, File APIs

L841.a: Updating state in an effect schedules another render after the current commit; the effect runs again only if its dependencies changed. If the updated state is in the dependency array (or there's no array), it can loop forever. It's legitimate for syncing with external data (fetch results), but if you're computing a value from props/state, derive it during render instead.
p: Loops if the state is also a dependency
Derive values instead of syncing state
L841.f: How does useLayoutEffect change when that second render becomes visible?

L842.a: Memoise with useMemo keyed on the inputs, move the calculation out of render if it's not needed for UI, compute on the server or in a Web Worker for very heavy work, keep urgent input responsive with useTransition/useDeferredValue, and reduce the work itself (better algorithm, precomputed indexes, pagination).
L842.f: How do you verify useMemo is actually helping?

L843.a: Core Web Vitals (LCP, INP, CLS), plus TTFB, FCP and TBT; JavaScript error rate; API latency and failure rate from the client's perspective; bundle size and long tasks; memory usage in long sessions; and business metrics like conversion by performance bucket. Track percentiles (p75, p95) per page, device and region, from real users.
L843.f: Why use p75 instead of averages?

L844.a: Keep the current page (ideally in the URL) and page size, fetch or slice that page, and render Prev/Next and page buttons with disabled states; for server data request `?page=&size=` and use the total from the response.
L844.f: Why keep the page in the URL?

L845.a: Pick one real component (a data grid, rich editor, dashboard, autocomplete) and explain: requirements and constraints, the architecture (state shape, composition API, accessibility), the performance problem you measured (slow renders, big lists, layout thrashing), the fixes (virtualization, memoisation, workers, debouncing, splitting state) and the measured result, plus what you'd improve.
L845.f: What would you do differently if you rebuilt it?

L853.a: There's no meaningful runtime performance difference between class and function components in modern React; function components are slightly lighter and work with hooks, the compiler and concurrent features, so they're preferred. Stateful components own state (useState); stateless ones render only from props, which makes them simpler, easier to test and to memoise.
p: Functions + hooks are the modern default
Stateless components are pure and reusable
L853.f: What can class components do that functions still can't?

L854.a: Virtualise rows and, for wide tables, columns too; keep the raw data compact (arrays instead of objects, only needed fields), fetch pages on demand from the server rather than holding everything, avoid per-cell closures and heavy components, memoise rows, and use a dedicated grid library (AG Grid, TanStack Table + Virtual) or canvas rendering for very large tables.
p: Lightweight, memoised cells or canvas grids
L854.f: How do you keep sticky headers working with virtualization?

L855.a: Function declarations and arrow functions perform the same. What matters is where they're created: an inline function (either kind) inside a component is recreated every render, which only matters when it's passed to a memoised child or used as an effect dependency; then wrap it with useCallback or define it outside the component if it doesn't use props/state. In class components, arrow class fields avoid per-render bind calls.
p: Recreation per render matters with memo or deps
L855.f: Will the React Compiler make useCallback unnecessary?

L856.a: A thunk is a function dispatched instead of a plain action; the thunk middleware calls it with dispatch and getState, so it can dispatch "pending", await the API call and dispatch "fulfilled" or "rejected"; reducers store the result. Thunks don't cache by themselves: each dispatch refetches unless you add a condition (check if data is fresh in getState, or createAsyncThunk's `condition` option). RTK Query provides real caching, deduplication and invalidation.
p: RTK Query for caching and dedupe
L856.f: How do you cancel a createAsyncThunk request?

L857.a: Browsers cap memory per tab/process. As it nears the limit, garbage collection runs more often and the page slows; if memory keeps growing, the browser kills the renderer process and shows an "Aw, Snap!"/"Out of memory" error page, losing unsaved state. Mobile browsers may also discard background tabs, reloading them when revisited. Avoid it by fixing leaks, bounding caches and handling large data in chunks.
p: Tab crash when the limit is hit
L857.f: How can you persist user work so a crash doesn't lose it?

L858.a: When the user logs out, broadcast an event to other tabs with BroadcastChannel (or by writing a key to localStorage so other tabs get a `storage` event). Each tab listens, clears its in-memory auth state and caches, and redirects to the login page. The server also invalidates the session so any API call returns 401, which the global handler treats as logout.
p: Clear state and redirect in every tab
L858.f: How would you handle a login in one tab updating the others?

L860.a: Dynamically typed: types belong to values, not variables, and are checked at runtime, so a variable can hold a number and later a string. Weakly typed: the language implicitly converts between types in operations (`"5" * 2` is 10, `"5" + 2` is "52", `[] == false` is true) instead of throwing errors.
p: TypeScript adds static checking; === avoids coercion in comparisons
L860.f: Is Python dynamically and weakly typed too?

L861.a: Declaring creates a variable (`let x;`), assigning gives it a value (`x = 5;`), and they can be combined (`let x = 5`). `var` is discouraged because it's function-scoped (leaks out of blocks like loops and ifs), hoisted with undefined (silent bugs instead of errors), can be redeclared, and creates properties on the global object at top level. `let` and `const` are block-scoped and safer.
L861.f: Why does a var loop variable leak outside the loop?

L862.a: Use `Array.from(arguments)` or the spread `[...arguments]` (works for iterables); older code used `Array.prototype.slice.call(arguments)`. In modern code, use rest parameters (`...args`) instead of `arguments`.
p: Array.from works for array-likes and iterables
L862.f: Do arrow functions have an arguments object?
L862.c:
function f() { return Array.from(arguments).map(x => x * 2); }
const g = (...args) => args.map(x => x * 2);

L863.a: Code splitting (routes and heavy features), tree shaking with ES modules and `sideEffects: false`, minification (Terser/esbuild/SWC), modern-only builds without unnecessary polyfills, replacing heavy dependencies, dynamic imports for rarely used code, Brotli compression, long-term caching with hashed filenames, and bundle analysis with size budgets in CI.
L863.f: Why might tree shaking fail for a library?

L865.a: It doesn't. Browsers only run JavaScript, so TypeScript is compiled (transpiled) to JavaScript first by `tsc`, esbuild, SWC or Babel as part of the build, and type annotations are erased. Type checking happens at build time, not at runtime. (Node and Deno can strip types on the fly, but browsers still receive JavaScript.)
p: Source maps map JS back to TS for debugging
Runtime validation needs libraries like Zod
L865.f: Why do you still need runtime validation for API data?

L866.a: The microtask runs first, as long as the current script (task) has finished: after each task the event loop empties the whole microtask queue before taking the next macrotask. So the order is: current task completes → the 1 microtask → then the 100 macrotasks one by one (with microtasks drained after each).
p: Macrotasks run one per loop iteration
L866.f: What if a macrotask queues a new microtask?

L867.a: Reserve space for everything that loads later: set width/height or aspect-ratio on images and videos, skeletons with the final dimensions for async content, fixed slots for ads/embeds, avoid inserting banners above existing content, use font-display with matched fallback metrics, and animate with transform. For perceived performance use skeletons, optimistic updates, streaming with Suspense and transitions to keep old UI visible.
p: No content injected above the fold
L867.f: How do you find which element caused a layout shift?

L868.a: Use what's already available: error tracking with source maps and breadcrumbs, session replay, browser DevTools on production (with source maps) and network logs, server/APM traces with correlation ids, feature flags to toggle suspected code, reproducing with the same data and environment, and comparing releases (git bisect on deploys). Snapshot debugging or log points can capture state without code changes.

L869.a: Webpack is a module bundler: starting from entry points it builds a dependency graph of JS, CSS, images and more, transforms them with loaders (Babel, TypeScript, CSS), applies plugins (HTML generation, minification, environment variables) and outputs optimised bundles. Benefits: code splitting, tree shaking, asset hashing for caching, dev server with HMR and a huge plugin ecosystem.
p: Loaders transform files; plugins extend the build
L869.f: Why have many projects moved to Vite?

L870.a: Lab tools (Lighthouse, WebPageTest, DevTools Performance panel) for controlled, repeatable tests and debugging; field data (Chrome UX Report, web-vitals library, RUM tools) for what real users experience; measure Core Web Vitals, TTFB, bundle size and custom marks with the Performance API, and track them over releases with budgets.
L870.f: Why can lab and field results disagree?

L871.a: Make the parent a positioned container and place three equal boxes along the diagonal, using a grid with three rows and columns (each box in cell n, n) or flexbox with align-self.
L871.f: How would you do it with flexbox?

L872.a: Wrap storage writes in try/catch to handle QuotaExceededError, check usage with `navigator.storage.estimate()`, store less (only what's needed, compressed), evict old entries (LRU with timestamps), version and clean old service worker caches on activate, request persistent storage if appropriate, and fall back to memory when storage fails.
L872.f: How do service worker caches get cleaned up?

L873.a: Use React DevTools Profiler with "record why each component rendered" and highlight updates to see which prop, state or context change triggers it. Typical causes: parent re-renders passing new objects/functions, a shared context whose value changes, state kept too high. Fix by colocating state, splitting context, memoising props with useMemo/useCallback, and wrapping the component in React.memo.

L874.a: It loops forever. An effect with no dependency array runs after every render; it logs "hello" and calls `setC(c + 1)` three times, but all three use the same `c` from that render, so c increases by only 1 per render. That update triggers another render, which runs the effect again, so "hello" logs endlessly and c keeps climbing by 1 each time (React may warn about too many updates).
p: No deps → runs after every render
Fix: add deps or move logic to an event
L874.f: What changes with setC(prev => prev + 1) three times?

L875.a: JavaScript has no true method overloading: defining a function twice with the same name just replaces it, so you emulate overloading by checking argument count or types inside one function (or using default/rest parameters). Overriding works through prototypes and classes: a subclass method with the same name shadows the parent's, and `super.method()` calls the original.
p: super to call the parent method
L875.f: How does TypeScript provide overload signatures?

L876.a: JSX `<Comp a={1} />` compiles to `React.createElement(Comp, { a: 1 })` (or `jsx()` with the new transform), so they're equivalent; JSX is more readable. Calling a component as a plain function `Comp(props)` is different: it isn't a separate element, so it has no own hooks state, breaks rules of hooks and isn't tracked by React. `createElement` is useful without a build step or for dynamic types.
p: Calling Comp() directly is not the same
L876.f: Why does calling a component as a function break hooks?

L878.a: Use HTTP caching headers: `Cache-Control` sets rules (max-age, no-cache, no-store, public/private, immutable, stale-while-revalidate); `ETag` is a fingerprint of the resource that the browser sends back as `If-None-Match`, letting the server answer 304 Not Modified without the body. Give hashed static assets a one-year immutable cache, HTML no-cache with an ETag, and add a CDN and service worker for further caching.
p: Hashed assets: long cache; HTML: revalidate
L878.f: What's the difference between no-cache and no-store?

L879.a: A DocumentFragment is a lightweight, in-memory container for DOM nodes that isn't part of the page. You build many nodes inside it and append the fragment once; its children move into the DOM in a single operation, reducing reflows. `<template>.content` is a DocumentFragment too.
p: Not in the live DOM until appended
L879.f: Is a DocumentFragment still faster than setting innerHTML?

L880.a: Compress and resize images to their display sizes, serve modern formats with fallbacks, use responsive `srcset`, lazy-load offscreen images, inline small SVG icons, subset and self-host fonts with font-display, minify and compress text assets, and cache with hashed names on a CDN. WebP (and AVIF) gives smaller files than PNG/JPEG at similar quality and supports transparency; PNG is lossless (good for sharp graphics with transparency); JPEG is lossy and suited to photos.
p: PNG for lossless graphics, JPEG for photos (fallback)
SVG for icons; lazy load and CDN
L880.f: When is SVG better than any raster format?

L881.a: Cancel the previous request when a new one starts (AbortController stored in a ref), and also ignore responses that aren't from the latest request (a request id), so only the last click's result updates state. Optionally disable the button or debounce clicks.
p: React Query handles this with query keys
L881.f: Why keep the id check if you already abort?

L882.a: The spec doesn't mandate an algorithm, only (since ES2019) that sort is stable; V8 uses TimSort. `[1, null, 5, 2, undefined].sort()` gives `[1, 2, 5, null, undefined]`: without a comparator, elements are converted to strings and compared ("1" < "2" < "5" < "null"), and undefined values are always moved to the end.
p: undefined always sorts last; holes after that

L883.a: In order: `readystatechange` (loading → interactive), `DOMContentLoaded` when the HTML is parsed and deferred scripts have run, `readystatechange` (complete) and `load` when all resources (images, styles, iframes) have loaded, `pageshow`. On leaving: `visibilitychange`, `pagehide`, `beforeunload`, `unload` (deprecated). Individual resources fire their own load/error events.
L883.f: Why is the unload event discouraged?

L884.a: `srcset` on `` (or ``) lists image candidates with their widths (`400w`) or pixel densities (`2x`); combined with `sizes`, which tells the browser how wide the image will display, the browser picks the most appropriate file for the screen size and resolution, saving bandwidth on small screens.
L884.f: When do you need <picture> instead of srcset?

L885.a: Webpack reads the config, starts at the entry points and resolves every import into a module graph; each file passes through the matching loaders (Babel/TS, CSS, assets); plugins hook into compilation stages; the optimiser tree-shakes unused exports, splits code into chunks, minifies and hashes filenames; finally it emits bundles and assets (plus source maps and a manifest) to the output directory.
p: Optimisation: tree shaking, splitting, minification, hashing
L885.f: What's the difference between a loader and a plugin?

L886.a: Use responsive, mobile-first design (fluid layouts, media and container queries), shared design tokens and components, adaptive loading for slower devices, touch and keyboard support, an API-first backend (REST/GraphQL, BFF per client type if needs differ), PWA features for offline use, and possibly React Native or Flutter sharing business logic for native apps. Test across devices and screen sizes.
L886.f: When would separate BFFs per device type make sense?

L887.a: HTTP headers carry metadata about the request or response: content type and length, authentication (Authorization), caching (Cache-Control, ETag), cookies (Cookie/Set-Cookie), CORS (Origin, Access-Control-*), compression (Accept-Encoding, Content-Encoding), content negotiation (Accept), security (CSP, HSTS, X-Frame-Options) and custom data like correlation ids.
L887.f: Which security headers should every site set?

L888.a: Render-blocking resources delay the first paint because the browser must load and process them before rendering: stylesheets in the head (and @imports), and synchronous scripts in the head. Fix by inlining critical CSS and loading the rest asynchronously, using `defer`/`async` or `type="module"` for scripts, media attributes for non-critical CSS, and removing unused code.
p: CSS in the head blocks rendering

L889.a: No. Arrow functions take `this` lexically from their surrounding scope, and `bind`, `call` and `apply` can't change it (bind still works for presetting arguments). Calling `new` on an arrow function throws `TypeError: ... is not a constructor`, because arrow functions have no `[[Construct]]` behaviour and no `prototype`.
L889.f: What does `this` refer to inside an arrow function defined in a class field?

L890.a: Web Components are reusable custom elements built with Custom Elements, Shadow DOM and templates, usable in any framework. Web workers run scripts on background threads for heavy computation. Service workers are background scripts that intercept network requests, enabling offline caching, push notifications and background sync. A PWA is a web app that uses a service worker, a web app manifest and HTTPS to be installable, fast and work offline.
p: Service workers: network proxy and offline
L890.f: Can a service worker access the DOM?

L891.a: ES6 classes are syntax over prototypes: methods defined in a class go on `ClassName.prototype`, and `extends` links prototypes. Differences: classes must be called with `new`, aren't hoisted like function declarations (TDZ), run in strict mode, have non-enumerable methods, support `super`, static members, private `#fields` and getters/setters more cleanly.
L891.f: How would you write a class's method on the prototype manually?

L892.a: `requestAnimationFrame(callback)` asks the browser to run the callback right before the next repaint (typically 60 times a second), passing a high-resolution timestamp. It's the right tool for animations and visual updates because it syncs with the display, batches with rendering and pauses in background tabs, unlike setTimeout.
L892.f: Why is setTimeout(fn, 16) worse for animations?

L893.a: Create an AbortController, pass `controller.signal` to `fetch(url, { signal })`, and call `controller.abort()` to cancel; the fetch promise rejects with an AbortError (and the network request is cancelled). `AbortSignal.timeout(ms)` creates a timeout signal and `AbortSignal.any([...])` combines several.
p: One controller can cancel multiple requests
Use in effect cleanup to cancel on unmount
L893.f: Does aborting guarantee the server stops processing?

L894.a: They reduce unnecessary work. Debouncing collapses bursts of events (typing) into one call after a pause, throttling caps how often a handler runs (scroll, resize), and memoisation caches results of expensive pure computations so repeated calls are instant. Together they cut API calls, re-renders and CPU usage, keeping the main thread free and the UI responsive.
p: Debounce: fewer calls for bursty input
Throttle: steady rate for continuous events
L894.f: What's the memory cost of memoisation?

L896.a: `setTimeout(fn, ms)` runs fn once after at least ms milliseconds; `setInterval(fn, ms)` runs it repeatedly every ms until cleared. Intervals can drift and pile up if fn takes longer than the interval; recursive setTimeout schedules the next run after the previous one finishes, which is often safer. Clear them with clearTimeout/clearInterval.
L896.f: Why can setInterval callbacks overlap with slow work?

L897.a: Rest parameters (`...args`) give a real array of the remaining arguments, work in arrow functions, and are explicit in the signature. The `arguments` object is array-like (no map/filter without conversion), contains all arguments, isn't available in arrow functions, and in sloppy mode is linked to named parameters.
L897.f: Can rest parameters appear anywhere but last?
L897.c: function sum(...nums) { return nums.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0); }

L898.a: Arrays are ordered, integer-indexed collections with a length and array methods; objects are collections of named properties (string/symbol keys) without guaranteed semantic order for non-integer keys. Clone shallowly with spread (`[...arr]`, `{ ...obj }`) or `Object.assign`, deeply with `structuredClone`, and avoid JSON round-trips for data with Dates, Maps or undefined.

L899.a: Custom events are events you create with `new CustomEvent("name", { detail, bubbles: true })` and fire with `dispatchEvent`, letting components communicate through the DOM. They work like native events (listeners, bubbling, capture), but native events are fired by the browser in response to user or system actions and are trusted (`isTrusted: true`), while custom ones are untrusted and carry your own `detail` data.
p: dispatchEvent on any element or EventTarget
L899.f: Can you create your own event bus with EventTarget?
L899.c:
el.addEventListener("cart:add", e => console.log(e.detail.id));
el.dispatchEvent(new CustomEvent("cart:add", { detail: { id: 7 }, bubbles: true }));

L900.a: The CLR (Common Language Runtime) executes .NET code: JIT compilation, memory management, type safety and exceptions. The CTS (Common Type System) defines how types are declared and used across .NET languages so they can interoperate. The CLS (Common Language Specification) is a subset of CTS rules that libraries should follow to be usable from any .NET language (e.g. no public unsigned types).

L901.a: `Task<T>` represents one asynchronous result and always allocates. `ValueTask<T>` is a struct that avoids allocation when the result is often available synchronously (cache hits); await it once only. `IAsyncEnumerable<T>` represents an asynchronous stream of many values consumed with `await foreach`, ideal for streaming database rows or paged API results.
p: Task: single async value, simple default
IAsyncEnumerable: async stream with yield return
Use Task unless profiling shows a need
L901.f: How does cancellation work with IAsyncEnumerable?

L902.a: A delegate is a type-safe function pointer. `Func<T..., TResult>` is a built-in delegate that returns a value, `Action<T...>` returns void, and `Predicate<T>` takes one argument and returns bool (used by List.FindAll etc.). They're used for callbacks, LINQ and events, usually with lambdas.
p: Custom delegates vs built-in generic ones
Lambdas and method groups convert to delegates
L902.f: Why are events based on delegates?

L903.a: Generics let you write classes, methods and interfaces with type parameters (`List<T>`, `Repository<T>`), so code is reused across types while staying type-safe. Benefits: compile-time type checking, no casting, no boxing for value types (better performance), and clearer APIs; constraints (`where T : class, new()`) restrict allowed types.
L903.f: What do covariance and contravariance mean for generics?

L904.a: `ControllerBase` provides everything for API controllers: model binding, validation, and helpers like Ok, BadRequest, NotFound, CreatedAtAction. `Controller` derives from ControllerBase and adds view support (View, PartialView, ViewBag, TempData, Json helpers) for MVC apps that return HTML. Use ControllerBase for Web APIs.

L905.a: In-memory caching (`IMemoryCache`) stores objects in the app's own memory: fastest, but per instance and lost on restart. Distributed caching (`IDistributedCache`) stores data in an external store shared by all instances (Redis, SQL Server); values are serialized and there's a network hop. Redis is the most common distributed cache: fast, supports expiration, eviction and pub/sub. .NET 9's HybridCache combines a local L1 and distributed L2 with stampede protection.
L905.f: How do you prevent cache stampedes?

L906.a: `DbContext` is EF Core's main class representing a session with the database: it exposes `DbSet<T>` properties for querying and saving entities, tracks changes to loaded entities, manages the connection and transactions, and translates LINQ into SQL. `SaveChanges` writes tracked changes as a unit of work. Configure it with OnModelCreating and register it as scoped.
L906.f: When would you use DbContext pooling?

L907.a: Normalization organises data into related tables to remove redundancy and update anomalies (1NF, 2NF, 3NF, BCNF): each fact stored once. Denormalization deliberately duplicates data (pre-joined tables, summary columns) to speed up reads at the cost of extra storage and keeping copies in sync. OLTP systems lean normalized; reporting/analytics and read-heavy views often denormalize.
p: Use materialized views/caches as controlled denormalization
L907.f: Give an example of a denormalized column you'd add.

L908.a: A transaction groups statements into an all-or-nothing unit (ACID). Isolation levels control what concurrent transactions see: READ UNCOMMITTED (dirty reads possible), READ COMMITTED (default in SQL Server; no dirty reads), REPEATABLE READ (no non-repeatable reads), SERIALIZABLE (no phantoms, strictest), and SNAPSHOT/RCSI (row versioning: readers don't block writers). Higher isolation means fewer anomalies but more blocking.
L908.f: What problem does SNAPSHOT isolation introduce?

L909.a: AngularJS (1.x) is the original JavaScript framework using controllers, $scope, two-way binding with digest cycles and directives; it reached end of life in 2021. Angular (2+) is a complete TypeScript rewrite with components, dependency injection, RxJS, ahead-of-time compilation, a CLI, better performance and mobile support, and now signals and standalone components.
L909.f: How would you migrate an AngularJS app to Angular?

L910.a: Components are UI building blocks: a TypeScript class with a template and styles. Directives add behaviour to elements: structural (`*ngIf`, `*ngFor`, or the new `@if`/`@for` control flow) change the DOM layout; attribute directives (`ngClass`, custom ones) change appearance or behaviour. Modules (NgModules) grouped declarations and providers, though standalone components now make them optional. Services are injectable classes holding shared logic and data (API calls, state).
L910.f: When would you create a custom attribute directive?

L911.a: Interpolation `{{ value }}` displays data as text. Property binding `[src]="url"` sets an element or component property. Event binding `(click)="save()"` listens to events. Two-way binding `[(ngModel)]="name"` (banana-in-a-box) combines property and event binding to keep a value and an input in sync; signals offer `model()` for two-way component inputs.
L911.f: How does [(value)] work for custom components?

L912.a: `*ngIf` (or `@if`) adds or removes the element from the DOM entirely, destroying and recreating the component and its state. `[hidden]` keeps the element in the DOM and hides it with CSS (`display: none`), so it stays initialised and keeps its state. Use ngIf for heavy or rarely shown content, hidden for frequent toggles of cheap content.
p: ngIf: removes from DOM, destroys state
hidden can be overridden by CSS display rules
L912.f: Why might [hidden] not work if the element has display: flex in CSS?

L913.a: Angular's DI system creates and supplies dependencies: classes declare what they need (via constructor parameters or `inject()`), and injectors provide instances based on providers registered at the root (`providedIn: 'root'`, singletons), in route or component providers (scoped instances), or via injection tokens. It makes code modular, testable and configurable.
L913.f: How do you provide a different implementation in tests?

L914.a: The Router maps URL paths to components, supports parameters, child routes, lazy loading (`loadComponent`/`loadChildren`) and navigation APIs. Guards control navigation: `canActivate` decides if a route can be entered (auth/roles), `canDeactivate` asks before leaving (unsaved changes), `canMatch` controls whether a route even matches/loads, and `resolve` prefetches data. Modern guards are simple functions using inject().
p: Routes with params and lazy loading
L914.f: How do you pass data from a resolver to a component?
L914.c: export const unsavedGuard: CanDeactivateFn<{ dirty: boolean }> = c => !c.dirty || confirm('Discard changes?');

L915.a: Change detection checks component templates for changed values and updates the DOM. Traditionally zone.js patches async APIs (events, timers, HTTP) and triggers a check of the whole component tree from the top after each one. `OnPush` components are checked only when inputs change by reference, events fire inside them, async pipes emit or they're marked for check. Signals enable fine-grained, zoneless change detection where only affected views update.
p: Signals and zoneless for fine-grained updates
L915.f: Why does mutating an input object not update an OnPush component?

L916.a: Template-driven forms define the form in the template with `ngModel` and directives; they're simple for small forms but harder to test and to build dynamically. Reactive forms define the form model in the component class with FormGroup/FormControl/FormArray (typed in recent versions), giving explicit, synchronous access, easy dynamic fields, custom validators and unit testing; preferred for complex forms.
L916.f: How do you write a cross-field validator (password confirmation)?

L917.a: Make it a compound component (Accordion, Accordion.Item, Header, Panel) with an `allowMultiple` prop: store open item ids in a Set (multiple) or a single id (single mode). Headers are buttons with `aria-expanded` and `aria-controls`, panels have `role="region"`, and it supports controlled and uncontrolled usage plus keyboard navigation.
L917.f: How would you animate panel height smoothly?

L918.a: Render N stars as buttons or radio inputs with labels for accessibility, show hover previews, and support half stars by detecting which half of a star the pointer is over (or using two clipped halves/overlays). Store the value as a number (e.g. 3.5), display partial stars with a width-clipped overlay, and support keyboard arrows in steps of 0.5.
p: Half stars via pointer position or 0.5 steps
L918.f: How would keyboard users choose a half star?

L919.a: Drive it from a steps config (label, component, validate function). Keep the current index and completed steps, block "Next" until the current step validates, allow clicking back to completed steps, and render a progress bar whose width is (current / total). Use `aria-current="step"` and an accessible progressbar.
L919.f: How would you persist progress if the user reloads?

L920.a: Support both: if a `checked` prop is passed, it's controlled (parent owns state and gets `onChange`); otherwise it keeps internal state initialised from `defaultChecked`. Render a real `<button role="switch" aria-checked>` (or a checkbox input) so it's keyboard and screen-reader accessible, with a visible label.
p: Don't switch modes during the component's life
L920.f: Why warn when a component switches from uncontrolled to controlled?

L921.a: Store comments normalised (a flat map by id with parentId, or the API's tree) and render recursively: a Comment component renders itself and maps over its replies with Comment again. Add collapse/expand for deep threads, load replies lazily, cap visual indentation, and update a reply immutably by id in the normalised map rather than walking the whole tree.
L921.f: How would you add a reply optimistically?

L922.a: Keep all filters in one state object synced to URL query params (shareable, back-button friendly), derive results with useMemo for client data or send the filters to the API for large catalogues, debounce sliders, show result counts and active-filter chips with clear buttons, and combine criteria with AND across categories and OR within a category.
p: Single filter state ↔ URL search params
L922.f: How do you show how many products each filter option would return?

L923.a: Describe fields in JSON (name, type, label, validation, options, conditions), map each type to an input component through a registry, keep values in one state object, validate from the schema (or convert it to Zod/Yup), and support conditional visibility and field arrays. The same schema can come from the server so forms change without redeploying.
L923.f: How would you allow custom field types from outside the library?

L924.a: Expose a `toast()` function via context (or a small external store) that pushes { id, message, type, duration } into a queue; a portal-rendered container shows up to N toasts at once, auto-dismisses each after its duration (pausing on hover), lets users close them, and promotes queued ones as space frees. Announce with an aria-live region.
L924.f: Why should the dismiss timer start only when a toast becomes visible?

L925.a: Never mount 1000 images: render only the current slide plus a few neighbours (windowing), load images lazily with priority for the active one and prefetch the next/previous, use responsive srcset and thumbnails, transform-based animations, placeholders (blurred previews or dominant colour) to avoid layout shift, keyboard/swipe navigation and ARIA carousel semantics.
L925.f: How would you handle thumbnails for 1000 images?

L926.a: Render a responsive grid with fixed aspect-ratio boxes, use `loading="lazy"` (or IntersectionObserver) for images, show a low-quality placeholder or blurred thumbnail until the full image's onLoad fires, serve srcset sizes, handle errors with a fallback, and virtualise if the gallery is huge.
L926.f: How would you open a full-screen lightbox accessibly?

L927.a: Keep sort, filters and page in state (or the URL), derive the visible rows with useMemo for client data, or send them to the server for large datasets. Memoise rows, virtualise when showing many rows, debounce filter input, use stable keys, and make headers buttons with aria-sort. TanStack Table provides the logic headlessly.
L927.f: Where would you keep the table state to make it shareable?

L928.a: Split the file into chunks (e.g. 5 MB) with `file.slice()`, upload them sequentially or with limited concurrency to an endpoint that accepts chunk index and upload id, track progress as uploaded bytes / total, retry failed chunks, support pause/resume by remembering completed chunks, and finalise with a "complete" call. XHR or axios gives per-request progress; the S3 multipart API works this way.
L928.f: How would you resume an upload after the browser reloads?

L929.a: Keep a small, stable core (document model, commands, selection, rendering) and expose a plugin API: plugins register commands, keybindings, toolbar items, schema extensions (node/mark types) and event hooks through a registry, with lifecycle methods (init, destroy). Communicate through an event bus and transactions so plugins don't touch internals, sandbox or validate third-party plugins, and version the API. ProseMirror and Tiptap are good references.
p: Registry for commands, keymaps, UI, schema
L929.f: How would you prevent one plugin from slowing down typing?

L930.a: Split by business domain: a monorepo (Nx/Turborepo) with feature packages owned by teams, a shared design system and utilities package, and an app shell that composes features through routes (or micro-frontends if teams need independent deployments). Enforce boundaries with lint rules, use code owners, shared conventions (TypeScript, testing, API clients) and CI that only builds and tests affected packages.
p: Shared design system and core libs
Affected-only CI; micro-frontends only if needed
L930.f: When would you choose micro-frontends over a monorepo?

L931.a: Separate state types: server data (widget queries) in React Query with per-widget keys, caching and refetch intervals; global dashboard filters (date range, region) in the URL or a small store that widgets subscribe to by selector; layout and user preferences in a persisted store; and local widget UI state inside the widget. Real-time updates write into the query cache, batched to limit renders.
p: Global filters in URL/store with selectors
Local state stays local; batch live updates
L931.f: How do you avoid every widget re-rendering when one filter changes?

L932.a: Use a typed event bus (EventTarget or a tiny pub/sub) where components publish domain events (cart:item-added) and others subscribe without knowing each other. Keep payloads small and typed, unsubscribe on unmount, document events as a contract, and avoid using it for state that should be shared directly. It's useful across micro-frontends or loosely related widgets.
L932.f: How do you debug which component emitted an event?

L933.a: Use semantic versioning: patch for fixes, minor for backward-compatible features, major for breaking changes. Automate with Changesets or semantic-release from commit messages, publish changelogs, deprecate before removing (console warnings, codemods), support peer dependency ranges, run visual regression tests, and publish canary/beta versions for early adopters.
L933.f: Is changing a default prop value a breaking change?

L934.a: Define routes as a nested config tree (path, element, children, guard, loader); the router matches the URL against the tree, renders layouts with an outlet for child routes, runs guards top-down before rendering (redirecting if they fail), loads data per route in parallel, and lazy-loads route code. React Router's data APIs (loaders, `<Outlet />`, `redirect`) implement exactly this.
p: Route-level data loaders and code splitting
Redirects, 404 and error boundaries per route
L934.f: Where would you handle "unsaved changes" warnings?

L935.a: A WeakMap holds its keys weakly so entries disappear when the key object is garbage collected. That only makes sense for values with identity and a lifetime the GC tracks, which means objects (and, since ES2023, non-registered symbols). Primitives like strings or numbers have no identity to collect, so they can't be weak keys. Because entries can vanish at any time, WeakMaps also aren't iterable.
p: Great for metadata/private data per object
L935.f: Give a use case for WeakMap in a UI library.

L936.a: `requestAnimationFrame` runs a callback right before the next paint, for visual updates and animations. `requestIdleCallback` runs a callback when the browser has idle time after rendering a frame (with a deadline telling how much time is left), for low-priority background work like analytics or prefetching; it may not run for a long time on busy pages, so pass a timeout.
p: rIC isn't supported in all browsers (Safari)
L936.f: Why shouldn't you modify the DOM in requestIdleCallback?

L937.a: A tagged template calls a function with the template's literal string parts and the interpolated values separately: tag`Hello ${name}`. The function can transform, escape or build anything from them. Uses: escaping HTML or SQL safely, styled-components and css-in-js, GraphQL (gql``), i18n, and String.raw.
L937.c:
const safe = (strs, ...vals) => strs.reduce((out, s, i) => out + s + (i < vals.length ? String(vals[i]).replace(/[<>&"]/g, c => `&#${c.charCodeAt(0)};`) : ""), ""); safe`

${userInput}

`;

L938.a: Reflect provides methods matching the internal object operations (get, set, has, deleteProperty, defineProperty, ownKeys, apply, construct). Unlike some Object methods, they return booleans instead of throwing (Reflect.defineProperty), work as functions instead of operators (Reflect.has vs in), and mirror Proxy traps one to one, which makes them the natural way to forward default behaviour inside a Proxy.
L938.f: Why pass the receiver argument to Reflect.get?
L938.c: const logged = new Proxy(obj, { get(t, k, r) { console.log("get", k); return Reflect.get(t, k, r); } });

L939.a: Number can only represent integers exactly up to 2^53 - 1 (Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER); beyond that precision is lost. BigInt represents arbitrarily large integers exactly (`123n`, `BigInt("9007199254740993")`). Use it for large IDs (e.g. 64-bit database or Twitter IDs), cryptography and precise big-number math; it can't be mixed with Number in arithmetic without explicit conversion and isn't supported by JSON directly.
p: No mixing with Number; no Math methods
L939.f: Why shouldn't you use BigInt for money with decimals?

L940.a: The Intl API formats and compares locale-sensitive data without libraries: `Intl.NumberFormat` for numbers, currencies, percentages and compact notation; `Intl.DateTimeFormat` for dates and times in any locale and time zone; `RelativeTimeFormat` ("3 days ago"), `PluralRules`, `ListFormat` and `Collator` for locale-aware sorting.
L940.c:
new Intl.NumberFormat("en-IN", { style: "currency", currency: "INR" }).format(1234567.5); // ₹12,34,567.50
new Intl.DateTimeFormat("en-GB", { dateStyle: "long", timeZone: "Asia/Kolkata" }).format(new Date());

L941.a: Inside a function or constructor, `new.target` refers to the constructor that was invoked with `new`, or is undefined if the function was called normally. Uses: enforcing that a function is called with `new`, creating abstract base classes (throw if `new.target === Base`), and knowing which subclass is being constructed.
p: Points to the actual subclass in class hierarchies
Not available in arrow functions (inherits outer)
L941.f: How else could you prevent calling a function without new?

L942.a: Normally `postMessage` copies data to a worker with the structured clone algorithm, which is slow for large data. Transferable objects (ArrayBuffer, MessagePort, ImageBitmap, OffscreenCanvas, streams) can instead be transferred: ownership moves to the other thread with zero copy, and the sender's reference becomes unusable (detached).
p: Pass in the transfer list: postMessage(msg, [buffer])
L942.f: When would SharedArrayBuffer be better than transferring?
L942.c:
const buf = new Float32Array(10_000_000).buffer;
worker.postMessage({ buf }, [buf]); // buf.byteLength is now 0 here

L943.a: Both run callbacks from queues on a single JS thread with microtasks drained between tasks, but Node's loop (libuv) has explicit phases: timers, pending callbacks, poll (I/O), check (setImmediate), close callbacks, and `process.nextTick` runs before promise microtasks. Browsers have task queues for events, timers and messages plus a rendering step (rAF, layout, paint) that Node doesn't have.
p: Node phases: timers → poll → check → close
Browser has rendering steps and rAF
Microtasks drain after each callback in both (Node ≥ 11)
L943.f: In what order do setTimeout(0) and setImmediate run in Node?

L944.a: `import("./module.js")` loads a module at runtime and returns a promise resolving to its namespace object. It works anywhere (inside functions, conditionally), and bundlers split the imported module into a separate chunk loaded on demand, which enables code splitting, lazy routes (React.lazy) and loading heavy libraries only when needed.
p: Returns a promise of the module namespace
L944.f: How do magic comments like webpackChunkName help?

L945.a: For cross-origin requests that aren't "simple" (methods other than GET/HEAD/POST, custom headers like Authorization, or JSON content type), the browser first sends an OPTIONS preflight asking whether the real request is allowed; the server must answer with Access-Control-Allow-Origin/Methods/Headers (and Allow-Credentials) before the browser sends it; Access-Control-Max-Age caches the answer. SameSite controls whether cookies are sent on cross-site requests: Strict (never), Lax (only top-level navigations with safe methods, the default), None (always, requires Secure), which mitigates CSRF.
p: Preflight = OPTIONS check for non-simple requests
Server must return matching Allow-* headers
L945.f: Why does a JSON POST trigger a preflight but a form POST doesn't?

L946.a: Security headers tell browsers to enforce protections. Content-Security-Policy restricts where scripts, styles, images and frames can load from (mitigating XSS). X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff stops browsers from guessing MIME types, preventing scripts disguised as other files. Others: Strict-Transport-Security (force HTTPS), X-Frame-Options or CSP frame-ancestors (clickjacking), Referrer-Policy and Permissions-Policy.
L946.f: How do nonces make inline scripts safe under CSP?

L947.a: Source maps map minified, bundled or transpiled code back to the original source files and lines. They let DevTools show your real code when debugging and let error tracking tools (Sentry) turn production stack traces into readable ones. Generate them in builds, but consider uploading them privately to the error tracker rather than serving them publicly.
p: Hidden or private source maps for security

L948.a: Retry automatically only when it's safe: idempotent requests (GET, PUT, DELETE) and transient failures (network errors, 502/503/504, 429). For POSTs, send an idempotency key so the server can deduplicate a retried request. Use exponential backoff with jitter, a retry limit and timeouts, and surface a manual retry when automatic retries fail.
L948.f: What happens if a retry succeeds but the original also went through?

L949.a: Backpressure is when a consumer can't keep up with a producer, so data piles up in buffers (growing memory) unless the producer is slowed down. Async systems handle it by pulling instead of pushing (async iterators, Streams API `pull` with highWaterMark), awaiting writes (`await writer.ready`), dropping or sampling events (throttle), or bounded queues that block or reject.
L949.f: How does the Streams API signal backpressure to a producer?

L950.a: Fetch the full list once (or request pages from the server), keep page and page size in state, slice the visible rows, reset to page 1 when the size changes, and disable Previous/Next at the bounds.
L950.f: How would you fetch only the current page from the API?

L951.a: Read window size into state, update it on resize (optionally throttled with rAF), and clean up the listener.
L951.f: How would you make it SSR-safe?

L952.a: Make a `useCountdown(start)` hook that decrements every second with setInterval, stops at 0, and exposes reset; use it in a component.
p: Use timestamps for drift-free timing if needed
L952.f: Why use setTimeout per tick here instead of setInterval?

L953.a: Fetch albums, take the first 10, keep selected ids in a Set, enable Submit when at least 5 are selected, and transform each title by uppercasing the second character of every word.
L953.f: How would you test the title transformation?

L954.a: Fetch posts and comments, compute counts per postId with useMemo (a single pass into a Map), and render a bar chart (SVG or a chart library like Recharts) next to a table; use CSS grid that switches from two columns to one on small screens. Type the data with interfaces.
p: Chart + table share the same derived data
L954.f: How would you make the chart accessible to screen readers?

L955.a: Recursively visit each node: return it if its id matches (stop early), and collect all nodes whose classList includes the class name. An iterative stack avoids deep recursion.
p: Iterative version for very deep trees
L955.f: How would you implement querySelector-like matching for "div.card"?

L956.a: Keep tasks with a `done` flag; the Complete button sets done for that task immutably and is disabled once done, with a strikethrough style.
L956.f: How would you add an "undo complete" option?

L957.a: Track loaded pages and a cursor; "Load more" fetches the next page and appends. Cache pages in a Map keyed by query + page (or use React Query's useInfiniteQuery) so going back or remounting reuses them instead of refetching; disable the button while loading and hide it when there's no more data.
p: Cache by key; reuse on remount
L957.f: How would you invalidate the cache after a new item is added?

L958.a: Create a factory or hook that takes a base URL and returns a request helper (and/or a data hook) that prefixes paths, sets JSON headers, handles errors and aborts on unmount.
L958.f: How would you add an auth token to every request?

L959.a: Keep the active tab in state (or the URL), render accessible tabs (role="tablist", "tab", "tabpanel", arrow-key navigation), and inside the data tab keep its own page state and slice or fetch the current page; preserve each tab's page when switching by lifting page state per tab or keeping panels mounted but hidden.
p: Lazy-load tab content on first open
L959.f: How would you implement arrow-key navigation between tabs?

L960.a: Create a class component with `getDerivedStateFromError` to store the error and `componentDidCatch` to log it; render the error message (and a retry button) instead of the children when an error occurs, and wrap the risky component with it.
p: Wrap only the parts that may fail
L960.f: Why can't function components be error boundaries yet?

L963.a: Because negatives make squares unsorted, use two pointers from both ends and fill the result from the back with the larger square. O(n).
p: Largest squares are at the ends
Sorting squares is O(n log n)
L963.f: Why does sorting work but cost more?

L964.a: Use the Dutch national flag algorithm with three pointers: low (next 0 position), mid (current) and high (next 2 position). Swap 0s to low, 2s to high, and move past 1s, in one pass with O(1) space.
p: Don't advance mid after swapping with high
Counting sort is a two-pass alternative
L964.f: Why don't you increment mid after swapping with hi?

L965.a: Sort the array, fix one element (two for 4Sum), and find the remaining pair with two pointers moving inward; skip duplicates at each level. 3Sum is O(n²), 4Sum O(n³).
p: Fix i (and j), two pointers for the rest
L965.f: How would you write 4Sum reusing this?

L966.a: Start with pointers at both ends; the area is width × the shorter height. Move the pointer at the shorter line inward, because moving the taller one can't increase the area. Track the maximum. O(n).
p: Area limited by the shorter side
L966.f: Why is moving the taller pointer never better?

L967.a: Find the shortest contiguous subarray whose sum is at least the target (positive numbers). Use a sliding window: expand right adding to the sum, and while the sum meets the target, record the length and shrink from the left.
L967.f: What changes if the array can contain negatives?

L968.a: Sliding window with a Map of character counts: expand right, and when more than K distinct characters are in the window, shrink from the left until it's valid again; track the maximum window length.
p: Same pattern as "at most two distinct" (fruit baskets)
L968.f: How would you return the substring itself?

L969.a: Sliding window counting zeros in the window: expand right, and when zeros exceed K, move left forward (decrementing when a zero leaves); the longest window is the answer.
p: Window may contain at most K zeros
Shrink when the zero count exceeds K
Same pattern as longest substring problems
L969.f: How does this relate to "max consecutive ones" with no flips?
