L1181.a: Use a CRDT (Yjs/Automerge) or OT document model so clients apply edits locally at 60fps and merge concurrently; sync deltas over WebSockets to horizontally scaled collaboration servers sharded by document, with Redis/NATS pub-sub between nodes; send ephemeral presence (cursors) at throttled rates over a separate lightweight channel; persist snapshots + update logs; render with canvas/WebGL or virtualised DOM and batch remote updates per animation frame.
L1181.f: How do you keep 10,000 cursors from overwhelming every client?

L1182.a: Build components as Web Components (Custom Elements + Shadow DOM, e.g. with Lit or Stencil) so they work natively in React, Angular, Vue and plain HTML, share design tokens as CSS custom properties, and generate thin framework wrappers for idiomatic props/events (Stencil output targets). Alternatively keep framework-agnostic logic in headless packages and implement thin per-framework view layers.
p: Web Components as the common runtime
L1182.f: What friction do Web Components have with React?

L1183.a: Animate only transform and opacity (compositor-friendly), avoid animating layout or paint-heavy properties (width, top, box-shadow, filters), keep the main thread free during animations, use CSS animations or the Web Animations API rather than JS-driven frame updates, limit simultaneous animations and layer count, use will-change sparingly, and respect prefers-reduced-motion; test with CPU throttling.
L1183.f: Why can will-change make performance worse?

L1190.a: No. forEach (like map, filter, some, every and reduce) skips holes in sparse arrays: missing indices aren't visited. Elements explicitly set to undefined are visited. for...of, Array.from and spread treat holes as undefined.
L1190.c:
[1, , 3].forEach(x => console.log(x)); // 1, 3
for (const x of [1, , 3]) console.log(x); // 1, undefined, 3

L1191.a: Define routes the same way on server and client (a shared route config). On the server, render the matched route for the request URL (React Router's static handler/StaticRouter or a framework like Next.js/Remix), run loaders to fetch data, and embed that data in the HTML. On the client, create the browser router with the same routes and call `hydrateRoot`, passing the serialised data so the first client render matches the server HTML exactly.
p: Server: match URL, load data, render

L1192.a: Authenticate users through an identity provider (OIDC, MFA, SSO); issue short-lived tokens with roles/permissions claims; model authorization as permissions grouped into roles (RBAC), with attribute-based rules for ownership/tenancy (ABAC) where needed; enforce checks centrally in the backend (policies/middleware) for every request including object-level checks; mirror permissions in the UI for route guards and hidden actions; audit log sensitive actions and support role changes without re-login (token refresh).
p: RBAC with permissions, ABAC for ownership
L1192.f: How do you handle a user whose role changes mid-session?

L1193.a: Sort with a comparator that splits each string into its letter prefix and numeric part and compares letters alphabetically, then numbers numerically; or use `localeCompare` with `{ numeric: true }` (or Intl.Collator), which does natural sorting.
p: Intl.Collator for performance in large sorts
Stable sort keeps ties in order
L1193.f: How would you implement it without localeCompare?

L1194.a: `process.nextTick(cb)` queues cb to run immediately after the current operation, before promise microtasks and before the event loop continues to the next phase. `setImmediate(cb)` queues cb for the check phase of the event loop, after I/O polling. So nextTick runs first; recursive nextTick calls can starve I/O, while setImmediate yields to the event loop.
p: nextTick: before promises and the next phase

L1195.a: Separate route files (Express routers per resource) enable route-level middleware and auth per module, lazy or conditional mounting, versioning (/v1, /v2 routers), independent testing of each router, clearer ownership and fewer merge conflicts, smaller files for code review, and easier splitting into separate services later.
L1195.f: How would you structure controllers and services behind routers?

L1196.a: SQL (relational: PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQL Server) suits structured data with relationships, strong consistency, ACID transactions, complex joins and reporting: orders, payments, inventory. NoSQL (document, key-value, wide-column, graph: MongoDB, Redis, Cassandra, Neo4j) suits flexible or evolving schemas, massive scale-out, high write throughput, caching or specific access patterns like graphs. Many systems use both.
p: Choose by data model and query patterns

L1197.a: A serverless application runs code in managed functions (AWS Lambda, Azure Functions, Vercel/Cloudflare functions) and managed services, where the provider handles servers, scaling and availability, and you pay per execution. Use it for event-driven or spiky workloads, APIs with variable traffic, background jobs, webhooks and prototypes; avoid it for long-running, latency-critical (cold starts) or steady high-throughput workloads where containers are cheaper.
p: Great for events, webhooks, spiky traffic
Watch cold starts, time limits, vendor lock-in
L1197.f: How do you reduce cold-start latency?

L1198.a: React is a JavaScript library for building user interfaces from components. You describe UI as a function of state using JSX; when state or props change, React re-renders the affected components, builds a new element tree, diffs it against the previous one (reconciliation) and applies only the needed DOM changes in a commit phase, scheduling work with its Fiber architecture.
L1198.f: What triggers a component to re-render?

L1199.a: React Fiber is the reimplementation of React's reconciler (React 16) that represents work as a linked tree of "fiber" units, so rendering can be split into chunks, paused, prioritised, aborted and resumed. Concurrent Mode (now "concurrent features" in React 18+ via createRoot) uses Fiber to render interruptibly, prioritising urgent updates and enabling transitions, Suspense for data and streaming SSR.
L1199.f: What are lanes in React's scheduler?

L1200.a: Test behaviour, not implementation: render the component, interact like a user and assert what users see. Common libraries: Jest or Vitest (runner, assertions, mocks), React Testing Library + user-event (rendering and interaction), MSW (API mocking), jest-axe (accessibility), Playwright or Cypress (end-to-end), and Storybook with interaction/visual tests (Chromatic).
L1200.f: How do you test a custom hook in isolation?

L1208.a: Use `Promise.allSettled` so the two successful results are kept and the failure is reported individually; handle each result by status, retry the failed one if it's transient, and show partial data with an error for the missing part. If all three are required, use Promise.all with try/catch and fail the whole operation; wrap each task with its own catch if you want to continue with defaults.
L1208.f: How would you cancel the other tasks if one critical task fails?

L1213.a: Atomicity: a transaction's statements all succeed or all fail. Consistency: a transaction moves the database between valid states, respecting constraints. Isolation: concurrent transactions don't interfere (controlled by isolation levels). Durability: committed changes survive crashes (via logs).
L1213.f: Which ACID property do isolation levels trade off?

L1214.a: Normalization organises tables to reduce redundancy and anomalies by storing each fact once and splitting data into related tables (1NF, 2NF, 3NF…). A primary key uniquely identifies each row (unique, not null); a foreign key is a column that references another table's primary key, enforcing that related rows exist (referential integrity).

L1215.a: Window functions compute values across a set of rows related to the current row without collapsing them (unlike GROUP BY): ranking (ROW_NUMBER, RANK, DENSE_RANK), running totals (SUM() OVER (ORDER BY …)), moving averages, LAG/LEAD, using OVER (PARTITION BY … ORDER BY …). CTEs (WITH name AS (…)) are named temporary result sets for one statement that make complex queries readable and allow recursion (hierarchies).
p: CTEs for readability and reuse within a query
L1215.f: Write a recursive CTE for an employee-manager hierarchy.
L1215.c:
WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT name, dept, salary, RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY salary DESC) AS r,
         SUM(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY dept) AS dept_total
  FROM Employee)
SELECT * FROM ranked WHERE r <= 2;

L1216.a: The third argument can be a boolean (useCapture) or an options object: `capture` (listen in the capture phase), `once` (remove after first call), `passive` (promise not to call preventDefault, enabling smooth scrolling for touch/wheel), and `signal` (an AbortSignal; aborting removes the listener).
L1216.f: Why are touchstart listeners passive by default on the document in Chrome?

L1219.a: `<div>` is a generic block-level container that starts on a new line and takes full width, used to group sections. `<span>` is a generic inline container that flows within text, used to style or target parts of a line. Neither has meaning; use semantic elements where possible.
p: Display can be changed with CSS
L1219.f: Can a span contain a div?

L1220.a: Override specificity by writing a more specific selector (add a class or parent), placing the rule later at equal specificity, using cascade layers (later layers win regardless of specificity), inline styles, or `!important` as a last resort (then only another !important with higher specificity, or a later layer rule in reverse order, wins). Better: keep specificity low with single-class selectors and :where() so overrides are easy.
p: More specific selector or later source order
Inline styles and !important as last resorts
:where() keeps base styles easy to override
L1220.f: How does !important interact with cascade layers?

L1221.a: SSG renders pages to HTML at build time and serves them as static files (fastest, but data is as old as the last build). ISR is SSG plus regeneration: pages are rebuilt in the background after a revalidate interval or on demand, so they stay fast and reasonably fresh. SSR renders HTML on every request on the server (always fresh and personalised, but slower and more server load).
p: Choose by freshness vs speed vs cost
L1221.f: Which would you use for a product page with prices that change hourly?

L1222.a: Fonts: self-host and subset them, use WOFF2, preload the critical font files, set `font-display: swap` (or optional), use size-adjust/fallback metrics to avoid layout shift, and limit weights and families. CSS: inline critical CSS, load the rest asynchronously, remove unused CSS, minify and compress, avoid @import chains, and split CSS by route.
L1222.f: Why does a font preload need the crossorigin attribute?
L1222.c:
<link rel="preload" href="/fonts/inter-latin.woff2" as="font" type="font/woff2" crossorigin>
@font-face { font-family: Inter; src: url(/fonts/inter-latin.woff2) format("woff2"); font-display: swap; }

L1223.a: Technical: crawlable server-rendered HTML, fast Core Web Vitals, mobile-friendly responsive design, HTTPS, clean URLs, sitemaps and robots.txt, canonical tags, correct status codes and structured data. On-page: unique titles and meta descriptions, semantic headings, descriptive alt text, internal linking and quality content matching search intent. Off-page: reputable backlinks.
L1223.f: How do canonical tags prevent duplicate content issues?

L1224.a: Single Responsibility: a module/class should have one reason to change. Open/Closed: open for extension, closed for modification (add behaviour with new code, e.g. strategy objects). Liskov Substitution: subtypes must work wherever their base type is expected. Interface Segregation: prefer small, focused interfaces over large ones. Dependency Inversion: depend on abstractions, injecting dependencies rather than hard-coding them. In JavaScript they apply to modules, functions, components and hooks too.
p: ISP + DIP: small interfaces, injected dependencies
L1224.f: Give a React example of the Open/Closed principle.

L1225.a: Abstraction hides complexity by exposing only what's essential: users call `payment.charge(amount)` without knowing the gateway details (an interface or simple API). Encapsulation hides internal state and implementation details by bundling data with the methods that operate on it and restricting direct access (private fields, closures), so state only changes in controlled ways.
L1225.f: How do JavaScript modules provide encapsulation?

L1226.a: `line-clamp` truncates text to a given number of lines with an ellipsis. Use `display: -webkit-box; -webkit-box-orient: vertical; -webkit-line-clamp: 3; overflow: hidden;` (widely supported); the standard `line-clamp` property is coming.
p: Keep full text accessible (title or expand)
L1226.f: How would you show a "Read more" toggle only when text is actually clamped?

L1227.a: A service worker is a background script that intercepts network requests for its scope, enabling caching strategies, offline pages, push notifications and background sync. IndexedDB is the browser's asynchronous, transactional database for storing large amounts of structured data (objects, blobs) with indexes. Together they power offline-first apps: the service worker serves cached assets and the app reads and writes data in IndexedDB, syncing when online.
p: Service worker: network proxy and cache
Use wrappers like Workbox and idb
L1227.f: Why is localStorage a poor choice for offline data?

L1228.a: Network interception means catching outgoing requests to inspect, modify, cache, mock or block them. In browsers it's done with service workers (`fetch` event and `event.respondWith`), HTTP client interceptors (Axios, Angular HttpInterceptor), wrapping `window.fetch`, or test tools like MSW and Playwright's `page.route`.
L1228.f: Why can't a service worker intercept requests on the very first page load?

L1229.a: CSS custom properties are declared with `--name: value` (usually on :root) and used with `var(--name, fallback)`; they cascade, inherit and can change at runtime (themes, media queries, JS). Sass variables use `$name: value`, are resolved at compile time, don't exist in the output CSS and can't change at runtime, but work in Sass functions and loops.
L1229.f: Can you use a CSS variable inside a media query condition?

L1230.a: Mutating methods: push, pop, shift, unshift, splice, sort, reverse, fill and copyWithin (and assigning to length or indices). Non-mutating alternatives return new arrays: concat, slice, map, filter, flat, and the ES2023 methods toSorted, toReversed, toSpliced and with. `const x = [1,2,3,4]` can still be mutated by these; const only prevents reassignment.
L1230.f: Why does mutation matter for React state?

L1231.a: Named slots let a child component define multiple insertion points (`<slot name="header">`), filled by the parent with `<template #header>`. Scoped slots let the child pass data back to the slot content (`<slot name="item" :item="item">`), so the parent's template can render using the child's data (`<template #item="{ item }">`), useful for lists and tables with custom rendering.
p: Scoped slots expose child data to parent templates
Similar to render props in React
L1231.f: How would you check whether a slot was provided?
L1231.c: • {{ i.name }}

L1232.a: `v-model` creates two-way binding between form inputs (or components) and state: on inputs it binds the value and listens to input/change events. On components it uses the `modelValue` prop and `update:modelValue` event (Vue 3), supports multiple named v-models (`v-model:title`) and modifiers (.trim, .number, .lazy); `defineModel()` simplifies it in script setup.
L1232.f: How do you implement a custom modifier?
L1232.c:
<input v-model.trim="name" />
<!-- Child with defineModel -->
<script setup>const model = defineModel()</script>
<template><input v-model="model" /></template>

L1233.a: `provide(key, value)` in an ancestor makes a value available to all its descendants, which read it with `inject(key, default)`, avoiding prop drilling through intermediate components. Provide refs or reactive objects to keep injected values reactive, and use Symbols as keys to avoid collisions; app-level `app.provide` works for global values.
L1233.f: How is provide/inject different from Pinia?

L1234.a: Lifecycle hooks run at stages of a component's life: setup (Composition API entry), onBeforeMount/onMounted (DOM available), onBeforeUpdate/onUpdated (after reactive changes re-render), onBeforeUnmount/onUnmounted (cleanup), plus onErrorCaptured and onActivated/onDeactivated for keep-alive. Options API equivalents: created, mounted, updated, unmounted (beforeDestroy/destroyed in Vue 2).
L1234.f: Where would you fetch initial data in Vue 3?

L1235.a: `watch` explicitly watches specific sources (refs, getters, arrays), is lazy by default (runs on change, not immediately), and gives old and new values. `watchEffect` runs immediately and automatically tracks every reactive dependency used inside it, re-running when any changes, without access to old values. Use watch for targeted reactions, watchEffect for side effects that depend on several values.
p: watch: explicit sources, lazy, old/new values
L1235.f: How do you make watch run immediately?

L1236.a: The Options API organises a component by option type (data, methods, computed, watch, lifecycle hooks), which is approachable for small components. The Composition API (setup / script setup with ref, reactive, computed, watch) organises code by feature, enables reusable composables, better TypeScript inference and less `this`. Vue 3 supports both; Composition API is preferred for larger apps.
p: Better TS support with Composition API
L1236.f: How did mixins in the Options API cause problems?

L1237.a: Composables are functions using Vue's Composition API (ref, computed, watch, lifecycle hooks) to encapsulate reusable stateful logic, named useX (useMouse, useFetch). In Nuxt, composables in the `composables/` directory are auto-imported, and Nuxt ships built-ins like useFetch, useAsyncData, useState, useRoute and useHead.
L1237.f: Why must composables be called inside setup?

L1238.a: `computed` derives a cached value from reactive state, recalculated only when its dependencies change, used in templates like a property (pure, no side effects). `watch` runs side effects in response to changes (API calls, logging, syncing to storage) and doesn't return a value. Use computed for derived data, watch for effects.
L1238.f: When would a computed property not update?

L1239.a: Pinia is the officially recommended Vue store (successor to Vuex): simpler API without mutations (state, getters, actions only), first-class TypeScript inference, modular stores by default instead of nested modules, Composition API style stores, devtools and SSR support, and smaller size. Vuex uses state, getters, mutations (synchronous) and actions with a single store and namespaced modules.
L1239.f: How do you persist a Pinia store?

L1240.a: Nuxt uses file-based routing; files or folders with square brackets in `pages/` create dynamic routes: `pages/users/[id].vue` matches /users/42 and exposes `route.params.id`; `[[slug]]` is optional and `[...slug].vue` catches all segments. Fetch data per param with useFetch/useAsyncData, and validate params with `definePageMeta({ validate })`.
p: Validation and data fetching per route
L1240.f: How do you generate static pages for dynamic routes?

L1241.a: In Vue 3, `ref()` creates a reactive reference for any value (accessed with .value in script, unwrapped in templates), the basic unit of reactivity. Template refs (`ref="input"` with `const input = ref(null)` or `useTemplateRef`) give direct access to DOM elements or child component instances after mounting, for focusing, measuring or calling exposed methods.
L1241.f: ref vs reactive: when would you use each?
L1241.c:
<script setup>
const input = ref(null)
onMounted(() => input.value.focus())
</script>
<template><input ref="input" /></template>

L1242.a: Nuxt route middleware runs before navigating to a route: use it for auth checks, redirects and permissions. Define named middleware in `middleware/auth.ts` with `defineNuxtRouteMiddleware((to, from) => { ... return navigateTo('/login') })` and apply it with `definePageMeta({ middleware: 'auth' })`; `.global` files run on every route; server middleware in `server/middleware` runs on server requests.
L1242.f: Where does route middleware run during SSR?

L1243.a: `v-if` conditionally renders: the element and its components are created or destroyed when the condition changes (higher toggle cost, lower initial cost when false). `v-show` always renders the element and toggles CSS `display: none` (cheap toggling, always rendered). Use v-show for frequent toggles, v-if for rarely changing conditions or expensive subtrees.
L1243.f: Why shouldn't v-if and v-for be on the same element?

L1244.a: React is a UI library focused on components and rendering, so you choose your own router, state management and data tools, whereas Angular is a full framework with everything built in. React uses JSX and one-way data flow with explicit state updates, while Vue and Angular offer template syntax and two-way binding options. React's virtual DOM/reconciler, hooks, huge ecosystem, React Native and frameworks like Next.js distinguish it.
L1244.f: What does React leave for you to decide?

L1245.a: An incoming request goes through routing, which picks a controller and action based on the URL; the controller handles the request, works with models (data and business logic) and services, and returns an ActionResult; for views, the Razor view engine renders the view with the model into HTML, and the response is sent back. Filters can run around the action and result.
L1245.f: How does model binding fit into this flow?

L1246.a: Filters run custom code at specific stages of action execution: authorization filters (run first, can block), action filters (before/after the action method), result filters (before/after the result executes), and exception filters (handle unhandled exceptions). They're applied as attributes on actions/controllers or globally, removing cross-cutting code like logging, caching and validation from actions.
L1246.f: How would you write a custom action filter for logging?

L1247.a: The controller receives the request routed to it, binds and validates input, calls models/services for business logic and data, chooses the response (view with a model, JSON, redirect, status code) and returns it. It coordinates between the model and view without containing business logic itself.

L1248.a: Routing maps URLs to controller actions. Conventional routing is configured centrally, e.g. `routes.MapRoute("Default", "{controller}/{action}/{id}", defaults)` in RouteConfig (or `app.MapControllerRoute` in ASP.NET Core); attribute routing is defined with `[Route]`/`[HttpGet("...")]` on controllers and actions, enabled with `MapMvcAttributeRoutes()` in classic MVC.
p: Route order matters in conventional routing
L1248.f: How do you generate URLs from route names?

L1249.a: Authentication: ASP.NET Identity (or Forms/OWIN cookie authentication, external providers via OAuth/OpenID Connect) signs users in and sets an auth cookie. Authorization: the `[Authorize]` attribute (with Roles or policies in ASP.NET Core) on controllers/actions, `[AllowAnonymous]` for public actions, global filters, and checks in code with `User.IsInRole` or claims.
L1249.f: How do you protect against CSRF in MVC forms?

L1250.a: `_Layout.cshtml` is the master page template shared by views: it defines the common HTML structure (head, navigation, footer, scripts) and calls `@RenderBody()` where each view's content goes, plus `@RenderSection()` for optional sections like page-specific scripts. Views set it via `_ViewStart.cshtml` or the Layout property.
L1250.f: How do you use a different layout for admin pages?

L1251.a: Use exception filters or the global HandleErrorAttribute (classic MVC) / exception handling middleware (`UseExceptionHandler`, ProblemDetails) in ASP.NET Core, custom error pages for 404/500 (`UseStatusCodePagesWithReExecute`), try/catch for expected errors in actions, logging of all exceptions, and showing friendly messages without leaking stack traces in production.
p: Developer exception page only in development

L1252.a: RESTful services expose resources over HTTP using standard methods (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE), URLs and status codes, usually with JSON. They relate to MVC through shared concepts: ASP.NET Web API (and ASP.NET Core API controllers) uses the same controller/routing model as MVC but returns data instead of views, so the same app can serve HTML pages and REST endpoints.
L1252.f: How do you version a REST API in ASP.NET Core?

L1253.a: Day to day: type annotations for function parameters and returns; interfaces/type aliases for object shapes (props, API responses); union types and discriminated unions for variants and states; generics for reusable functions and components; type inference to avoid redundant annotations; optional properties/parameters (?); enums or literal unions for fixed sets; access modifiers (private, readonly) in classes; and strict null checks with non-null handling (optional chaining, narrowing).
L1253.f: When would you prefer an interface over a type alias?

L1255.a: Use destructuring to swap, spread + reverse to reverse, Fisher–Yates for an unbiased shuffle, string indexing for capitalisation and Math.random scaling for a range.
L1255.f: Why is sort(() => Math.random() - 0.5) a biased shuffle?

L1256.a: A tail-recursive function makes its recursive call as the very last action, passing accumulated results as arguments (e.g. factorial with an accumulator). With tail-call optimisation the engine can reuse the stack frame, so deep recursion doesn't overflow. In JavaScript only Safari implements TCO, so in practice use loops or trampolines for deep recursion; tail recursion still clarifies converting recursion to iteration.
p: TCO reuses stack frames (only Safari in JS)
L1256.f: Write a trampoline that runs a tail-recursive function safely.
L1256.c: const fact = (n, acc = 1) => (n <= 1 ? acc : fact(n - 1, acc * n));

L1266.a: Bootstrap provides prebuilt components (navbars, modals, grids) and JS, so you ship standard UIs fast with less design work, but sites look similar and customisation means overriding styles. Tailwind is utility-first: you compose designs from small classes, getting full design freedom, consistent tokens, tiny production CSS (unused classes removed), but verbose markup and no ready-made components (pair it with headless libraries or shadcn/ui). Choose Bootstrap for quick, conventional admin UIs; Tailwind for custom designs and design systems.
p: Bootstrap: components out of the box
Team familiarity and design needs decide
L1266.f: How do you avoid class-list bloat in Tailwind components?

L1268.a: It logs false, "object", "53", 2 and 1. 0.1 + 0.2 is 0.30000000000000004 due to binary floating point. typeof null is "object" (a historic bug). "5" + 3 concatenates. "5" - 3 converts to numbers. true + false is 1 + 0.
L1268.f: How would you compare 0.1 + 0.2 with 0.3 safely?

L1270.a: An API is any interface for programs to communicate (library APIs, browser APIs, web APIs). A web service is an API accessed over a network via web protocols; all web services are APIs but not all APIs are web services. SOAP is a strict XML-based protocol with WSDL contracts and built-in standards (WS-Security), common in enterprise systems. REST is an architectural style using HTTP verbs, URLs and usually JSON, simpler, cacheable and dominant on the web.
L1270.f: When is SOAP still used today?

L1271.a: PUT replaces the entire resource with the request body (send the full representation; omitted fields may be reset) and is idempotent. PATCH applies a partial update with only the changed fields (or a JSON Patch document); it isn't guaranteed idempotent, depending on the patch semantics.
p: JSON Merge Patch vs JSON Patch

L1272.a: 2xx success (200 OK, 201 Created, 204 No Content); 3xx redirection (301 permanent, 302/307 temporary, 304 Not Modified for caching); 4xx client errors (400 Bad Request, 401 Unauthorized, 403 Forbidden, 404 Not Found, 409 Conflict, 422 validation, 429 Too Many Requests); 5xx server errors (500 Internal Server Error, 502 Bad Gateway, 503 Service Unavailable, 504 Gateway Timeout).
L1272.f: Which status should a successful DELETE return?

L1273.a: OAuth 1.0 required cryptographically signing every request with consumer and token secrets, which was complex but worked without HTTPS. OAuth 2.0 relies on HTTPS and bearer tokens, is much simpler to implement, defines multiple grant types (authorization code with PKCE, client credentials, device code, refresh tokens) for web, mobile and server apps, and is the basis of OpenID Connect; OAuth 1.0 is obsolete.
L1273.f: Why is PKCE required for public clients?

L1274.a: `@keyframes` defines the stages of a CSS animation with percentages (or from/to) and the styles at each stage; you apply it with the `animation` shorthand (name, duration, timing function, delay, iteration count, direction, fill mode, play state).

L1275.a: Use alias, string and distinct functions on the Worker table (SQL Server syntax shown; MySQL uses SUBSTRING/LOCATE/CONCAT/CHAR_LENGTH).
L1275.f: How does CHARINDEX differ between SQL Server and MySQL's INSTR?

L1276.a: Use ORDER BY for sorting, IN / NOT IN for lists of values and LIKE with % wildcards for pattern matching.
p: ORDER BY with ASC/DESC and multiple columns
NOT IN with NULLs can return no rows
L1276.f: Why can NOT IN behave unexpectedly with NULL values?

L1277.a: A JOIN combines rows from two or more tables based on a related column. Types: INNER JOIN (only matching rows), LEFT JOIN (all left rows, matching right or NULL), RIGHT JOIN (mirror of left), FULL OUTER JOIN (all rows from both), CROSS JOIN (every combination) and SELF JOIN (a table joined to itself, e.g. employees and managers).
L1277.f: What's the difference between filtering in ON vs WHERE for a LEFT JOIN?
L1277.c: SELECT e.name, m.name AS manager FROM Employee e LEFT JOIN Employee m ON e.manager_id = m.id;

L1278.a: GROUP BY groups rows that share values in the specified columns so aggregate functions (COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX) compute one result per group; every selected non-aggregated column must be in GROUP BY. HAVING filters those groups by aggregate conditions after grouping.
L1278.f: Can you use a column alias from SELECT in HAVING?
L1278.c:
SELECT department, COUNT(*) AS staff, AVG(salary) AS avg_salary
FROM Employee
GROUP BY department
HAVING COUNT(*) > 5;

L1279.a: DELETE removes rows one at a time (optionally with WHERE), logs each row, fires triggers, keeps identity values and can be rolled back. TRUNCATE removes all rows by deallocating pages: much faster, minimal logging, resets identity, can't have WHERE, doesn't fire DELETE triggers and fails if foreign keys reference the table (it can be rolled back inside an explicit transaction in SQL Server).
p: TRUNCATE: all rows, fast, resets identity
Both keep the table structure (unlike DROP)
L1279.f: Which one needs ALTER permission in SQL Server?

L1280.a: An index is a data structure (typically a B-tree) storing column values in sorted order with pointers to rows, so the database can seek directly to matching rows instead of scanning the whole table. It speeds up WHERE filters, JOINs, ORDER BY and GROUP BY; covering indexes avoid table lookups entirely. The cost is extra storage and slower writes.
L1280.f: Why might an index not be used for WHERE YEAR(created_at) = 2024?

L1283.a: WHERE filters individual rows before grouping and can't use aggregate functions. HAVING filters groups after GROUP BY and can use aggregates like COUNT or SUM. A query can use both: WHERE to limit rows, HAVING to limit groups.
p: Use WHERE when possible for performance
L1283.f: Can HAVING be used without GROUP BY?
L1283.c: SELECT customer_id, SUM(total) FROM Orders WHERE status = 'paid' GROUP BY customer_id HAVING SUM(total) > 1000;

L1284.a: A subquery is a query nested inside another query (in SELECT, FROM, WHERE or HAVING). A non-correlated subquery runs independently once and its result is used by the outer query. A correlated subquery references columns from the outer query, so it's logically evaluated for each outer row, which can be slower (optimisers often rewrite it as a join).
L1284.f: When is EXISTS better than IN?

L1285.a: Read the actual execution plan, then: add or adjust indexes (including covering indexes) for the filter, join and sort columns; make predicates SARGable (no functions on indexed columns, avoid leading-wildcard LIKE); select only needed columns; replace correlated subqueries or cursors with set-based joins; reduce rows early; update statistics; paginate; and check for blocking and parameter sniffing.
L1285.f: How would you find the most expensive queries on a server?

L1286.a: Constraints are rules enforced by the database to keep data valid: NOT NULL, UNIQUE, PRIMARY KEY, FOREIGN KEY (referential integrity), CHECK (value conditions) and DEFAULT (value when none given). Define them in CREATE TABLE or add them later with ALTER TABLE ... ADD CONSTRAINT.
p: Declared at table creation or via ALTER TABLE
Named constraints are easier to manage
L1286.f: Should business rules live in constraints or code?
L1286.c:
CREATE TABLE Orders (
  Id INT PRIMARY KEY,
  CustomerId INT NOT NULL REFERENCES Customers(Id),
  Total DECIMAL(10,2) CHECK (Total >= 0),
  Status VARCHAR(20) DEFAULT 'new',
  Code VARCHAR(20) UNIQUE
);

L1287.a: A transaction is a group of statements executed as one unit (ACID). COMMIT makes all changes permanent; ROLLBACK undoes all changes since the transaction began; SAVEPOINT (SAVE TRANSACTION in SQL Server) marks a point you can roll back to without undoing the whole transaction.
L1287.f: What happens to locks after a rollback to a savepoint?

L1288.a: 1NF: atomic column values, no repeating groups, each row unique. 2NF: 1NF and every non-key column depends on the whole primary key (no partial dependency on part of a composite key). 3NF: 2NF and no transitive dependencies (non-key columns depend only on the key, not on other non-key columns). BCNF: every determinant is a candidate key, a stricter form of 3NF.
p: BCNF: every determinant is a key
L1288.f: Give an example table that violates 3NF.

L1289.a: All three assign numbers within ordered (optionally partitioned) rows. ROW_NUMBER gives unique sequential numbers (1, 2, 3, 4) even for ties. RANK gives ties the same rank and skips the next numbers (1, 2, 2, 4). DENSE_RANK gives ties the same rank without gaps (1, 2, 2, 3).
L1289.f: Which would you use to delete duplicates?
L1289.c:
SELECT name, salary,
  ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) rn,
  RANK()       OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) rk,
  DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) drk
FROM Employee;

L1290.a: DDL: CREATE TABLE defines a table, ALTER TABLE adds/modifies/drops columns or constraints, DROP TABLE removes it. DML: INSERT adds rows, UPDATE changes rows (always with a WHERE), DELETE removes rows.
L1290.f: How would you rename a column safely in production?

L1291.a: Mapped types create new types by transforming each property of an existing type with `[K in keyof T]`, optionally changing modifiers (readonly, ?) and remapping keys with `as`. Built-in utilities like Partial, Required, Readonly, Pick and Record are mapped types.
p: [K in keyof T]: transform each property
L1291.f: How would you make every property nullable with a mapped type?

L1292.a: Session-based auth stores session state on the server and gives the browser a session id cookie; each request looks up the session (stateful, easy to revoke, needs shared storage when scaling, CSRF protection). JWT auth issues a signed self-contained token with claims, sent on each request and verified without a lookup (stateless, scales easily, works across services/mobile, but hard to revoke before expiry and must be stored safely). Many systems combine them (short JWTs + server-side refresh sessions).
L1292.f: How would you implement logout with JWTs?

C1.a: It logs 456. Object keys are strings, so both `b` and `c` are converted to the same key "[object Object]". The second assignment overwrites the first, and `a[b]` reads that same key.
p: Objects used as keys are stringified
Use a Map for object keys
C1.f: How would a Map behave here?

C2.a: It logs `new value another value new value`. obj1, obj2 and obj3 all start pointing at the same object, so changing obj1.key changes it for all of them. Then obj2 is reassigned to a brand-new object, which doesn't affect obj1 or obj3.
p: obj3 still points to the original object
C2.f: What if obj2.key were changed instead of reassigning obj2?

C3.a: `obj.b()` logs "foo" because it is called as a method of obj. `c()` is a plain function call, so `this` is undefined in strict mode (TypeError) or the global object in sloppy mode, where `this.a` is undefined, so it logs undefined.
p: this depends on the call site
Extracting a method loses its object
C3.f: How would you make c() log "foo"?

C4.a: After one second it logs 5 five times. `var i` is a single function-scoped variable shared by all callbacks; by the time the timeouts run, the loop has finished and i is 5.
p: var has one binding for the whole loop
Callbacks run after the loop ends
Use let for a new binding per iteration (0–4)
Or capture i with an IIFE
C4.f: What does it print with let?

C5.a: It logs "1undefined". A function expression used as the `if` condition is truthy, but its name `f` is only in scope inside that function, so `typeof f` is "undefined" and 1 + "undefined" concatenates.
p: Named function expressions don't create an outer binding
typeof an undeclared name returns "undefined" without throwing
The if branch runs because functions are truthy
C5.f: What if it were a function declaration before the if?

C6.a: It logs false, false, true, false. x and y are different arrays even with the same contents; z holds the same reference as y; z and x are different arrays.
p: == and === behave the same for two objects
Compare contents with every or JSON
C6.f: How would you compare x and y by content?

C7.a: After about one second it logs 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. Each callback increments the shared variable x and logs it; they run in order, so the values climb from 1 to 5.
p: All five timeouts fire after ~1 s
They share the outer var x
let i doesn't matter here since i isn't logged
C7.f: What would logging i instead print?

C8.a: It logs 2 4 6. forEach receives each object by reference, and `obj.x = obj.x * 2` mutates the original objects, so a, b and c all change.
p: Array holds references to the same objects
Mutation inside forEach affects the originals
Use map with spreads for immutable updates
C8.f: How would you double the values without mutating a, b and c?

C9.a: It logs 1, then 0. Inside test, `var num = 1` declares a new local variable that shadows the outer let, so the function returns 1 and the outer num stays 0.
p: Function scope creates a new variable
Shadowing doesn't modify the outer one
Without var, it would assign to the outer num
Mixing let and var names is legal across scopes
C9.f: What if the inner line were `num = 1;`?

C10.a: It logs 25, then 30. Spreading copies obj's properties into a new object, and the later `age: 30` overrides the copied age, leaving obj unchanged.
p: Nested objects would still be shared

C11.a: It logs 3, 7, 12. add() uses both defaults (1 + 2); add(5) uses b's default (5 + 2); passing undefined triggers a's default, so add(undefined, 10) is 1 + 10.
p: Defaults apply when an argument is missing or undefined
Defaults are evaluated at call time

C12.a: It logs "object", "undefined", false, true. `typeof null` is "object" (a historic bug). null and undefined are different types, so strict equality is false, but loose equality treats them as equal.
C12.f: How would you check for "null or undefined" in one comparison?

C13.a: It logs 10, then 5. The inner `let x` is a separate block-scoped variable that exists only inside the braces; outside, the original x is still 5.
p: Inner declaration shadows the outer one
With var it would be a redeclaration of the same variable
C13.f: What would happen if both were declared with var?

C14.a: It logs [1, 2, 3] and [1, 2, 3, 4]. The spread creates a new array, so pushing to arr2 doesn't change arr1.
p: Copies are independent at the top level
Nested objects would still be shared
C14.f: What if arr1 contained objects you then mutated through arr2?

C15.a: It throws `ReferenceError: Cannot access 'x' before initialization`. The inner `const x` is hoisted to the top of foo's scope but stays in the temporal dead zone until its declaration, so it shadows the outer x and can't be read yet.
p: The inner x shadows the outer one for the whole function
Accessing it in the TDZ throws
C15.f: What would it log with var instead?

C16.a: It logs ["Google", "Facebook", "Apple"]. The comparator returns -1 when a.name is greater, which puts larger names first, so the companies are sorted in descending alphabetical order.
p: sort mutates the array in place
Prefer localeCompare and return 0 for equal values
C16.f: How would you sort ascending with localeCompare?

C17.a: It logs: number, string, boolean, object, object, object, undefined, function. Arrays and null are both "object"; functions get their own "function" result.
C17.f: How would you reliably detect an array?

C18.a: It logs undefined (option B). `var result` is hoisted to the top of the function and initialised to undefined, so logging it before the assignment prints undefined rather than throwing.
p: var declarations are hoisted with undefined
let/const would throw in the TDZ
Code after the log never affects that output
C18.f: What if result were declared with let?

C19.a: It logs 20 then 10 (option A). The `let x = 20` inside the if block is a new block-scoped variable; after the block, the function sees the outer x, which is still 10.
p: With var inside the block, the second log would be 20
C19.f: What changes if the inner declaration uses var?

C20.a: It logs 30 (option A). Object.freeze makes the object's properties read-only; in non-strict code the assignment fails silently, so age stays 30. In strict mode the assignment throws a TypeError.
p: freeze prevents changes, additions and deletions
TypeError in strict mode (and in modules/classes)
C20.f: How would you freeze nested objects too?

C21.a: It logs undefined (option C). The `var x` inside the if block is hoisted to the top of `outer`, even though the block never runs, so the local x shadows the global one and is undefined when logged.
p: Local x shadows the outer x
let inside the block would log 10
C21.f: Why does the declaration count even though the branch never runs?

C22.a: It logs 1 2 3 (option A). a and b come from the top level, and `c: { a: nestedA }` destructures the nested object's a into a new variable named nestedA.
p: Nested destructuring follows the object shape
c itself is not declared as a variable
No conflict because the nested a is renamed
C22.f: What happens if obj.c is undefined?

C23.a: It logs `{ value: 1, done: false }`, `{ value: 2, done: false }`, then `{ value: 3, done: true }`. Each next() resumes the generator to the next yield; the return value appears with done: true.
p: yield produces values with done: false
return gives the final value with done: true
Further next() calls return { value: undefined, done: true }

C24.a: It logs 30. map doubles each number to [2, 4, 6, 8, 10] and reassigns numbers (allowed because it's let), then reduce sums them to 30. There is no error.
p: reduce without an initial value starts from the first element
Would fail on an empty array without an initial value
C24.f: Why is it safer to pass 0 as the initial value?

C25.a: Filter out non-positive numbers and sum the rest, in one reduce.
p: Ignore non-numbers if input may be mixed
C25.f: How would you also return the count of positives?
C25.c:
const sumPositive = arr => arr.reduce((s, n) => (n > 0 ? s + n : s), 0);
sumPositive([1, -4, 7, 12]); // 20

C26.a: Replace vowels with a case-insensitive regular expression, or filter characters against a set of vowels.
p: Decide on y and accented vowels
C26.f: How would you count vowels instead?

C27.a: Copy the array and sort with localeCompare so case and accents are handled sensibly, without mutating the input.
p: Default sort compares UTF-16 code units

C28.a: Use bitwise operations: XOR adds bits without carry, AND shifted left gives the carry; repeat until there's no carry. (Shortcuts like `a - -b` also avoid +.)
C28.f: Does this work for negative numbers?

C29.a: Split on dots: there must be exactly four parts, each made of 1–3 digits, between 0 and 255, and without leading zeros (unless the part is "0").

C30.a: Generate a random number between 0 and 0xFFFFFF, convert it to hex and pad it to six characters.

r4.s: useState is a component's memory for data that changes (form inputs, API data, search text, modal open state, loading). A normal variable can change but React doesn't track it, so the UI won't update; calling the state setter stores the new value and re-renders the component. Use the updater form (prev => prev + 1) when updates depend on the previous value because updates are batched, keep state immutable (spread objects instead of mutating) since React compares references, keep state minimal and avoid duplicated or derived state.

n1105.s: The call stack tracks running functions (push on call, pop on return). The callback queue holds async callbacks such as setTimeout and DOM events. The microtask queue holds promise callbacks and MutationObserver callbacks. The event loop waits for the stack to empty, drains all microtasks, then takes the next task from the callback queue — which is why Promise.then runs before setTimeout, and timers run only after synchronous code and microtasks.

The call stack is LIFO and single. Web APIs (timers, fetch, DOM events) run outside the engine. Queues: the macrotask queue (timers, DOM events, I/O), the microtask queue (promise then/catch/finally, queueMicrotask, MutationObserver) and the animation-frame queue (requestAnimationFrame). Loop: when the stack is empty, run all microtasks, render if needed, then run one macrotask and repeat. Priority: sync code → microtasks → animation frames → macrotasks. setTimeout(fn, 0) isn't instant, async/await is sugar over promises, and long tasks block everything — use Web Workers or chunk work.

L553.s: Debounce waits until activity stops and runs once — for search inputs, API calls and validation; a useDebounce hook sets a timeout in useEffect that updates the debounced value and clears it in cleanup. Throttle runs at most once per interval — for scroll, resize and mouse moves; track the last call time. Don't debounce critical actions like payments, don't throttle when the final value matters, wrap handlers in useCallback and always clean up timers.

L554.s: A compact, signed token carrying user claims. It enables stateless auth that scales across distributed systems and services: the user logs in, the server issues a JWT, the client sends it with each request and the server validates it. L624.s: Global scope: the global object (window). Regular function: window in sloppy mode, undefined in strict mode. Method call: the object. DOM listener with a regular function: the element (not with arrows). Callbacks: this is often lost when a method is passed detached from its object.

L628.s: Async work is handed to Web APIs; completed callbacks go to the callback queue, while promise reactions (including fetch's) go to the higher-priority microtask queue. The order is always call stack → microtasks → callbacks, so setTimeout(…, 0) still runs after synchronous code and promises; an endless stream of microtasks can starve the callback queue.

L852.s: setState schedules an update without touching the DOM. In the render phase React re-runs component functions to build a new virtual DOM (plain JS objects — cheap). Reconciliation diffs old and new trees using element type and keys; no changes means no work. The commit phase applies the minimal DOM changes (the expensive part). Then the browser does layout and paint. useLayoutEffect runs before paint (blocking, for layout-critical work); useEffect runs after paint. React is fast because re-renders are cheap, not because it avoids them — so optimize by cutting unnecessary re-renders, not by memoizing everything.

r106.s: Install @reduxjs/toolkit and react-redux, create the store with configureStore, define state logic with createSlice, wrap the app in <Provider store>, then use useSelector and dispatch in components. RTK removes boilerplate, centralizes predictable state and supports async logic; Zustand, Jotai and Recoil are growing alternatives.

L859.s: Promise.then runs first. The microtask queue (Promise.then, async/await continuations, queueMicrotask) has priority over the macrotask queue (setTimeout, setInterval, DOM events, network callbacks), so logging 1, a timeout 2, a promise 3 and 4 prints 1, 4, 3, 2.

L864.s: Add/remove: push/pop (end), unshift/shift (start), splice (any position). Search: indexOf, lastIndexOf, includes, find, findIndex. Transform: map, filter, reduce, reduceRight. Reorder: sort, reverse, flat, flatMap. Iterate/test: forEach, every, some. Combine: slice (copy part), concat, join. Utility: toString, Array.from, Array.isArray, fill.

L877.s: header.payload.signature — the header names the algorithm and type, the payload carries claims, and the signature (from the encoded header and payload plus a secret key) detects tampering. The user logs in, the server issues a signed JWT, the client stores it and sends it in the Authorization header on later requests. Stateless, signed and compact.

L895.s: Use the resize property (both, horizontal or vertical) together with any overflow value other than visible (scroll or auto) — no JavaScript needed; handy for textareas and adjustable containers.

L961.s: setTimeout accepts any number of arguments after the delay and passes them to the callback, which avoids closure/scope pitfalls (e.g. passing the loop variable into the callback).

L962.s: Use two indices to traverse a structure — from opposite ends moving inward, fast and slow pointers (cycle detection, middle element), or a sliding window — turning many O(n²) nested-loop solutions into O(n) for arrays, strings and linked lists.

L970.s: You can't override a non-virtual/abstract method (only hide it with new); constructors can't be virtual or abstract; sealed classes can't have virtual methods; a class inherits one class but many interfaces.

L971.s: A static class can have a static constructor that runs once automatically but can't be instantiated; sealing a method stops further overriding; a private constructor is typical for the Singleton pattern; only one static constructor is allowed and static members can't be overridden.

L972.s: const is compile-time only and implicitly static; readonly can be assigned at runtime in the constructor. A ref argument must be initialized before the call; out need not be, but must be assigned inside the method; you can't use ref and out on the same parameter. MemberwiseClone makes a shallow copy and static fields aren't serialized.

L991.s: In reverse order of declaration, so anything built on top of an earlier effect is torn down first — e.g. a listener added in effect 2 is removed before the connection from effect 1 is closed.

L992.s: Not in the component (components are just functions with no memory between renders) but in the component's Fiber node, which holds state, memoized values, effects and scheduling info. That's why the rules of hooks exist: React maps each hook call to its slot by call order, so hooks can't be conditional.

L1186.s: Reference vs primitive types: mutating an object/array keeps the same reference so React sees no change. Reference equality: objects/functions created during render are new each time ({} !== {}), causing infinite useEffect loops, breaking React.memo, making useCallback useless when its deps change, and re-rendering all context consumers when the provider value is a fresh object. Closures: handlers capture state from when they were created (stale state), and multiple setState calls in one event see the same initial value; old closures can also hold references and leak memory. Event loop/batching: setState is async, so console.log right after shows the old value.

L1201.s: (1) Always return something predictable — e.g. return await fetchUser() inside try, return null in catch. (2) await only works inside async functions (or modules); at top level wrap in an async IIFE. (3) An async function always returns a Promise; await pauses that function until it settles without blocking the thread. (4) Handle errors with try...catch — log and rethrow rather than failing silently. (5) Don't await independent calls one after another; run them in parallel with const [user, posts] = await Promise.all([fetchUser(), fetchPosts()]). (6) Don't mark functions async when they do nothing asynchronous.

L1202.s: Empty: Object.keys(obj).length === 0. Merge: { ...obj1, ...obj2 }. Shallow copy: { ...original }. Deep copy: JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(obj)). Count: Object.keys(obj).length. Keys/values: Object.keys(obj) / Object.values(obj). Has property: obj.hasOwnProperty("name"). Pairs: Object.entries(obj). Methods: Object.keys(obj).filter(k => typeof obj[k] === "function").

r326.s: RSCs render on the server and send ready HTML, so less JavaScript ships to the browser. You can't use browser features (window, document, localStorage) or hooks like useState/useEffect, and you can't import client components directly unless lazy-loaded; mark interactive components with 'use client'. They need framework support (Next.js 13+ App Router; not CRA or plain Vite). Benefits: smaller bundles, data fetched before render, sensitive work stays on the server, SEO-friendly HTML.

L1203.s: Vite serves native ES modules in development instead of bundling everything up front, so the dev server starts almost instantly and HMR is fast; production builds use Rollup. It has simple vite.config.js config (plugins, ports, aliases) and built-in TS/JSX. CRA is zero-config and fine for learning but slow to start/rebuild, rigid, and scales poorly. Start: npm create vite@latest my-app -- --template react. Migration: install vite + React plugin, add vite.config.js, move index.html to the root with a module script, update package.json scripts, run npm run dev.

L1204.s: CSR renders in the browser: JS loads, then fetches and renders content — rich interactivity but slower first load and weaker SEO (you see a spinner first). SSR renders HTML on the server: faster first paint and better SEO, at the cost of server load and complexity. Use CSR for dashboards and internal tools, SSR for public pages like blogs, e-commerce and marketing; Next.js supports hybrid CSR/SSR/SSG per route.

L1205.s: Loop with a Set of seen characters and return false on the first repeat, else true (O(n) time, O(1) lookups — the hashing pattern). One-liner: const isUnique = str => new Set(str).size === str.length.

n1033.s: The DOM is the browser's tree representation of the page's HTML. JavaScript uses it to find elements (querySelector), change content and styles, add/remove elements, and listen for events (addEventListener('click', ...)) — the foundation of all web interactivity, including React.

L1206.s: useFormState (renamed useActionState) manages form state from an action; useFormStatus exposes a form's pending submission state so you can disable buttons/show spinners; useActionState handles async actions with built-in status instead of hand-rolled isLoading/error flags; useOptimistic shows UI changes instantly (likes, toggles) and reverts if the server rejects; use() reads a promise or context directly in render, replacing useEffect+useState fetching patterns.

L1207.s: A Promise represents the eventual success or failure of an async operation, with states pending, fulfilled, rejected. Create with new Promise((resolve, reject) => ...); consume with .then/.catch/.finally; chain .then calls (fetch → res.json() → data); run in parallel with Promise.all([...]); promisify callbacks, e.g. const wait = ms => new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, ms)). async/await is cleaner syntax over the same promises.

L1209.s: SELECT name, COUNT(*) FROM employees GROUP BY name HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;

L1210.s: SELECT customer_id, MAX(order_date) AS latest_order FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id;

L1211.s: SELECT MAX(salary) AS second_highest FROM employees WHERE salary < (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM employees);

L1212.s: SELECT c.customer_id FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id WHERE o.order_id IS NULL;

L1217.s: Arrays/strings: sorted → binary search, two pointers or prefix sums; max/min/subarray optimisation → sliding window, DP or greedy; duplicates/frequencies → HashMap/HashSet/counting array; substrings or fixed-size subarrays → sliding window with two pointers; frequent min/max in a window → monotonic deque or heap; subsets/permutations/combinations → backtracking; matching/parsing characters → stack. Graphs: unweighted shortest path → BFS; weighted → Dijkstra/Bellman-Ford/A*; components or cycles → DFS or Union-Find; ordering → topological sort (Kahn's or DFS); MST → Kruskal/Prim. Trees: traversals (in/pre/post/level order); balance or diameter → postorder with heights; LCA → recursive DFS or parent map. Linked lists: cycles → slow/fast pointers (Floyd); reversal → prev/curr/next juggling; middle or intersection → two pointers. DP: overlapping subproblems → memoisation or tabulation; subset/knapsack → 1D/2D arrays; string edits → DP matrix (edit distance, LCS).

L1218.s: An execution context is the environment in which code is evaluated: it holds variables, functions, the value of this and the scope chain. A global context is created when a script loads and a new function context each time a function runs. They organise what runs when, manage local vs global scope, let nested functions resolve the right variables, and isolate each call so code doesn't overwrite other state (e.g. an "Add to Cart" handler runs in its own context without touching the global cart variable). Understanding them explains closures, hoisting and this, and helps debug scope bugs.

L1254.s: click/dblclick fire on clicks; mouseenter/mouseleave when the pointer enters/leaves an element; keydown/keyup on key press/release (keypress is deprecated); submit when a form is submitted; focus/blur when an element gains/loses focus; change fires when an input/select/textarea value is committed, input fires on every value change; resize on window resize; scroll when an element scrolls; touchstart when a touch begins. All are attached with element.addEventListener(type, handler).

L1257.s: Node.js is a runtime for executing JavaScript outside the browser, used for scalable back-ends; JavaScript is the language, Node is its server-side runtime. It runs your JS on a single thread but achieves concurrency through event-driven, non-blocking I/O and the event loop.

L1258.s: Buffers are temporary storage for binary data; streams process continuous data flows piece by piece instead of loading everything into memory. Stream types: readable, writable, duplex and transform.

L1259.s: spawn() launches a new process for any command; fork() is a special case that creates a Node child process with an IPC channel to the parent for message passing.

L1260.s: setTimeout schedules a callback after a minimum delay (timers phase); setImmediate runs after the current poll/I/O phase (check phase), so inside an I/O callback setImmediate always runs first.

L1261.s: The cluster module forks worker processes (one per CPU core) that share the server port, so a single-threaded Node app can use all cores.

L1262.s: Middleware are functions in the request-response cycle (logging, auth, parsing). body-parser parses request bodies, cors enables cross-origin requests, express-session manages sessions, Passport (with JWT) handles authentication, and Multer handles file uploads.

L1263.s: Deeply nested callbacks that are hard to read and maintain; avoid with promises, async/await, or by splitting into small named modules.

L1264.s: npm is Node's package manager for dependencies and versions; package.json is the metadata file listing dependencies, scripts and versions; REPL is the interactive shell for running Node code.

L1265.s: Command-line arguments are in process.argv; the crypto module provides hashing, encryption and decryption; the tls module implements TLS/SSL for secure connections.

r249.s: Mounting: constructor() initialises state and binds methods; static getDerivedStateFromProps() syncs state from props before render; render() is the only required method; componentDidMount() is for API calls and subscriptions. Updating: getDerivedStateFromProps(); shouldComponentUpdate() to skip unnecessary renders; render(); getSnapshotBeforeUpdate() captures DOM info (e.g. scroll position) just before changes are applied; componentDidUpdate() for post-update work like DOM changes or analytics. Unmounting: componentWillUnmount() cleans up timers and subscriptions.

L1267.s: The Virtual DOM is a lightweight in-memory copy of the real DOM used by libraries like React to compute and apply only the parts that changed (a rendering optimisation). The Shadow DOM is a browser feature for Web Components that gives a component its own encapsulated DOM subtree so its styles and scripts don't leak into or get affected by the main document (encapsulation).

r275.s: The React Compiler can memoise automatically, reducing the need for manual useMemo/useCallback/React.memo; Server Components are integrated natively for faster, SEO-friendly pages; Actions plus new hooks — useActionState for form/action state, useOptimistic for optimistic updates, useFormStatus for submission state; use() reads promises/context during render instead of useEffect+useState fetching; better support for loading assets and improved error reporting.

L1269.s: Git is a version control system tracking changes in a repository. git init creates a repo; git clone <URL> copies one; git add stages changes; git commit -m saves them; git branch creates branches and git checkout/git switch moves between them; git merge combines branches (resolve conflicts when changes overlap); git status shows state; git log shows history; git pull fetches and integrates remote changes; git push uploads commits; .gitignore excludes files; git restore / git reset undo changes; git tag marks releases; git diff compares changes; git rebase / squash cleans history.

n1018.s: JavaScript runs your code on a single main thread with the event loop handling async work, but Web Workers run scripts in separate threads in parallel without blocking the UI. They communicate with the main thread via postMessage/onmessage and suit heavy work like image processing, data analysis, in-browser ML inference and encoding.

r147.s: An HOC is a function that takes a component and returns an enhanced component, reusing logic across components. It keeps components focused, handles cross-cutting needs like authentication, logging or state handling, and reduces duplication. To create one: write a function taking a component, add the shared logic inside, and return the wrapped component.

L1281.s: GET retrieves data from the server; POST creates new data; PUT updates (replaces) existing data; PATCH partially updates existing data; DELETE removes data.

L1282.s: Code splitting to cut initial load time, lazy loading components and images, and memoization to prevent unnecessary re-renders.

L1293.s: map() returns a new array with each element transformed; filter() returns a new array of elements that pass a test; push() adds to the end and returns the new length; unshift() adds to the start and returns the new length; pop() removes and returns the last element; shift() removes and returns the first element; join() builds a string from the elements with a separator; concat() returns a new array combining arrays.

L1294.s: find()/findIndex() return the first matching element or its index; some() checks whether at least one element passes and every() whether all do; splice() adds/removes elements in place at a position, while slice() extracts a portion without modifying the original; includes() checks whether a value is present; Array.isArray() tells whether a value is an array. forEach iterates, map transforms, filter selects, reduce combines into one value, sort reorders with custom logic, concat merges.
